- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 504): **To falsify an interpretation, corrupt everything at once while preserving the one property you claim matters, and compare against corrupting only that property — a single ablation cannot distinguish "this feature is used" from "this information is used in some form".** The IOI result is the clean template: three simultaneous perturbations (all names replaced, filler prepended, filler inserted between the two names) leave only the before/after-`and` fact intact and recover 93% of the logit difference, while changing only `and` to `alongside` — one corruption, strictly less damage except at the hypothesised site — recovers 43%, and the other single-token replacements fall between 0.29 and 0.68. That ordering is the claim: the property preserved is worth more than the tokens destroyed. Two consequences. First, **the preservation test must be paired with a same-shape control that destroys the property and nothing else**, otherwise the 93% is uninterpretable. Second, **a heterogeneous control set beats one control** — the single `alongside` example would look like an anecdote, the six-way replacement table makes it a distribution. The cross-language patch (about 0.40 against a 0.48 base) and the function-vector complement (about 0.80, flipping language and not meaning) are what turn "concept" from a label into a claim about content.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 503): **A single-mechanism account of a capability should be doubted until you name the variant the mechanism cannot produce and check it — because a mechanism that explains the examples it was fitted to will look complete, and the second route is only found by asking for the behaviour the first one structurally cannot do.** Token induction explains copying right up to the moment the copied unit's token count changes, and that is exactly where translation, synonyms and antonyms sit; the concept route is found by fixing the target on the next-next token, which a token-level copier has no motive to raise. The procedure transfers cheaply: for any mechanism in our own accounts, write down one behaviour that shares the surface description and needs something the mechanism does not have, then check whether the mechanism's score is silent there. Two guards come with it. First, the control must aim the *same intervention at the wrong target* — here the identical patch scored against a future random token, at least three times weaker — because a causal score with no wrong-target baseline only says the head matters for something. Second, a two-route claim is falsifiable in a way a one-route claim is not, and the falsifier is a 2x2 grid in which each route is ablated against each task family and the off-diagonal cells must stay intact. Coreference `arxiv-2304.05969` (parroting: one head carrying two behaviours, the single-component version of the same discovery) and `arxiv-2610.02098` (a score preferring the wrong circuit is a defect of the measurement, not of the candidate).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 503): **A training-free weight-side read-out is available for any head set — sum the OV matrices, apply the final norm and decoder, and read vocabulary space — and its credibility rests entirely on the baseline lens built the same way from all heads.** The concept lens decodes the token "inals" of "cardinals" into sports vocabulary, Vatican vocabulary or birds according to context, a strong claim about what a head-set contributes that needs no training and no probes; but the same figure set shows the all-heads sum already reveals some of that signal, so the lens is being read as a *contrast* against redundancy rather than as an absolute. Two consequences for our accounts. First, every weight-side or lens-style read-out we publish should ship with the all-components baseline beside it, for the same reason the delegation experiment beats two independent scores: without it, a lens that works because the residual stream is generally decodable is indistinguishable from one that works because it selected the right heads. Second, **the read-out is only as selective as the ranking that chose the heads**, and here that ranking is a causal score with its own wrong-target control — so the lens inherits every defect of its selection step and none of its evidence is independent of it. Coreference `arxiv-2410.16443` (the delegation gain: fit the standard post-hoc method and report the signed delta) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a read-out trusted because it is computable, with no baseline of the same shape).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 499): **When a method's headline is an edit, the deliverable is not the edit but a declared equivalence class around it — the set of behaviours the edit promises not to touch, derived before training from the model's own representation and scored separately from the target.** Here the neighbourhood was named first (top-K classes by embedding cosine to the target's mean generated-image embedding), made a term in the objective, and then reported as its own column, and the payoff is diagnostic as much as methodological: because erasure and retention were both printed, the baselines separated into two families that a single "success" number would have merged — the ones that erase cleanly and wreck the neighbours, and the ones that keep the neighbours by barely erasing. For our batteries the rule is to fix the equivalence class at the same time as the intervention and publish the inside/outside pair, never the target score alone, because a lone score tells the reader which side of the trade the author bought but not that a trade exists. Coreference `arxiv-2605.31317` (the same similarity-ordered collateral curve measured as a diagnostic; the two entries are the measurement-side and objective-side halves of one idea) and `arxiv-2603.18353` (corrected-and-disrupted columns in LLM intervention, the same anti-correlation between the two halves of an outcome).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 499): **The instrument can flatter the method by the size of its own design freedom, and the honest place to look is the gap between two evaluators of the same object — here the automated classifier says 99.60% erasure and forty humans say 51.94%, and nothing in the paper reconciles them.** The classifier was fine-tuned on the generating model's own images, so it inherits the distribution the unlearnt model still produces; the humans were shown real examples beforehand but judged the images themselves. The transferable discipline: whenever the evaluation model and the evaluated model were fitted on each other's outputs, the number is a statement about a closed loop, and a second evaluator with a different provenance must be reported beside it — and when the two disagree by a factor of two, the disagreement is the result, not a nuisance. - Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 498): **Every intervention result in this folder needs two columns and a control, and the cheap way to produce the second column is to count what broke.** The concept arm corrected 20% of missed hazards and would have read as a modest success — except it broke 53% of correct detections, and the random-concept control broke 61.7%, so the "correction" is general perturbation rather than targeted intervention. The rule for our batteries: **report corrected and disrupted together, in the same table, with a random perturbation of matched magnitude at the same site as an explicit row**, and quote the net in points. This is the measurement-side twin of `arxiv-2605.11161`'s actionability argument (the entry already in the folder that says explanations must change behaviour) and it is the cleanest available demonstration that a single success rate is not a result. - Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 498): **Near-perfect probe accuracy is evidence of *information*, never of *causal sufficiency*, and the gap between the two is measurable in one number: the net correction achieved by the direction built from the probe's own class means.** Here the probe sits at 0.982 AUROC and the direction derived from its true-positive and false-negative means corrects at most 24% of errors — the read-out almost perfectly separates the classes and the handle almost does not control the output. For our predictive white-box model this forbids AUC as a headline metric for any read-out we intend to intervene on: the headline has to be net correction under intervention against a random control, with the probe AUC demoted to a statement about available information. The mechanism the authors give for the failure — residual-stream compensation at single layers, and hazard computation living in high-dimensional geometry rather than in token-probability space — is the empirical counterpart of `arxiv-2609.13529`'s architectural argument (native and causally intervenable by construction) and `arxiv-2410.16443`'s layer-statistics argument for reading in patches. Coreference `arxiv-2605.31317` (the retain-set result: exact agreement on what you kept, unconstrained subspace everywhere else — the same "fits on one side, no control on the other" shape).

- Done 2026-11-20 (run 497, written entries 498): `arxiv-2609.13529` — Generative Interpretability via Scalable Neuro-Symbolic Models. Read from: **full text** — v2 HTML, **38,452 clean chars** (121,067 raw) via `lit-tools/fetch.py` on the first call, and the paper is short enough that the whole thing was read in three slices: abstract and banner; §1-§2 (introduction, then post-hoc interpretability split into anatomical and physiological branches, then their shared limitation); §3 (Definition 3.1 of generative interpretability with its footnote defining inference pass vs inference path, the human-understandability and causal-intervention requirements and the two things they exclude, §3.2 the temporal and spatial axes, §3.3 the minimality argument and the partial order); §4 (§4.1 neuro-symbolic checkpoints and NLProlog, §4.2 the three challenges), §5 conclusion and acknowledgements; then the reference list, which was scanned rather than read. **Verified there are no appendices and no experiments** — a heading grep of the whole file returns exactly eleven numbered headings (§1-§5 with §2.1-2.3, §3.1-3.3, §4.1-4.2) and the references begin immediately after the acknowledgements. **Substance**: the contribution is a definition and a taxonomy, not a result. The definition requires checkpoints that are (i) *natively* meaningful — a pre-declared concept schema whose values are filled by an opaque sub-computation — and (ii) *causally intervenable by construction*, so do-interventions have counterfactuals that follow from the architecture rather than from a fitted tool. The axes place white-box models before-inference and throughout, concept bottlenecks during and single-checkpoint, post-hoc work after-inference and external, and the proposed point during with multiple checkpoints, and the axes are read as partial orders of commitment. The minimality argument rules out the weaker positions (after-inference cannot audit before generation; chain-of-thought audits already-generated tokens and is cited as unfaithful; a single checkpoint audits one cross-section, cited as empirically insufficient) and the stronger one (monosemantic throughout-readability would collapse the near-orthogonal packing superposition depends on, since a *d*-dimensional space admits exponentially many such directions). The three named obstacles are the absence of a universal symbolic system (Cyc as the cautionary case), neural-symbolic integration degenerating into task-specific templates, and the unprincipled boundary between graded-similarity knowledge and exact-rule knowledge.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 497): **Two properties separate a read-out that can support a causal claim from one that can only describe, and they are checkable before any experiment: whether the meaning is *native* (fixed by a vocabulary declared in advance) or *assigned afterwards by a search*, and whether the computation *functionally depends* on the site, so that altering it propagates with a counterfactual you can write down.** This paper states the pair as the definition of its target and then uses it as the blade for everything else, and it cuts the whole stack this folder has accumulated: a dictionary label, a probe direction and an attribution-graph edge all score zero on the first property, because the concept is found by a fitted tool after the fact, and every one of their intervention results therefore has a *contingent* effect size rather than a structural one. For our batteries the transferable deliverable is a **two-column table for every read-out site we name** — native vs assigned, and dependence verified vs assumed — because the honest state of almost all of our instruments is "assigned meaning, dependence partly verified", and printing that in a column is much stronger than leaving the reader to infer it. The corollary that matters most for our own goal is about prediction under intervention: if the meaning was assigned post-hoc, then a successful patch is evidence that *that* patch worked, never that the named concept was the mechanism, and the correct claim is always conditional on the assignment procedure. Coreference `arxiv-2505.00808` (Information / Use / Misrepresentation — the empirical triple this pair is the architectural version of, with *native* standing in for the missing half of Information) and `arxiv-2610.02098` (whose restoration experiment is exactly the demonstration that a post-hoc score's failure is contingent rather than structural).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 497): **The cheapest defensible position for a new method is "the weakest commitment that still buys the capability you need, and no stronger", and the way to argue it is a partial order over the alternatives with an explicit cost paid by each stronger rung — which is an argument, not an evaluation, and must be labelled as one.** This paper does it in two moves that are worth copying in form: it orders the paradigms by which *auditable content* each one exposes (boundary, single checkpoint, multiple checkpoints, throughout; before, during, after inference), and then refuses the top of its own order on cost grounds — full throughout-readability would spend the representational capacity that makes the model work, so interpretable-in-patches is claimed as the optimum rather than a compromise. Two rules for our write-up follow. First, **state the cost column explicitly**, because a minimality claim without one is just a preference: every added structural commitment buys auditability and spends capacity, expressiveness or fidelity, and the reader needs both numbers or the trade is invisible. Second, **do not let a partial order stand in for a benchmark** — this paper benchmarks against nothing and the shape of its argument makes that look principled, which is precisely the failure mode to avoid; if we position our contribution on an axis rather than against a baseline, we should say in the same sentence that the axis is a claim about what matters, not a measurement of who won. - Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 496): **An aggregate score is not a summary, it is a lossy projection, and the cheapest cure is to bin the pointwise error by the structural variable the mechanism names and print the whole curve — because the curve is where the finding lives and the mean is where it hides.** This paper's result would be invisible in a table: every method's aggregate gap is a two-digit number, and the same methods differ by tens of points on the similarity bin closest to the removed data (dropped-class retained accuracy 66.6 against 99.7, where the aggregate moves by five). Three rules for our batteries follow. First, **every explanation score we report should come with its per-bin curve against at least one structural variable** — distance along a feature direction, similarity to a probe's anchor set, layer index — because the constant is a property of the pool and the curve is a property of the object. Second, **the reference must be the expensive-correct model, and the number must be a difference from it**, exactly as every column here is a deviation from retraining; an absolute accuracy on our own candidates is uninterpretable without the same-shaped number for the honest baseline. Third, **a mechanism built to explain the curve gives you a mitigation for free, and the mitigation is the test**: LTD follows from "the target on the forget set is inconsistent with retraining" and would be pointless if the curve had been flat. Coreference `arxiv-2610.02098` (the same discipline on circuit scoring: the deficit distribution, not the rate) and `arxiv-1911.03681` (a benchmark partitioned by a shortcut, scored on each side — the discrete ancestor of this paper's similarity bins).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 496): **Passing the retained set is not the same as surviving the neighbourhood, and there is a clean formal statement of why: a fit can be made exact on every example you kept while an entire subspace of query directions remains wrong, because what you removed had nonzero components along those directions and nothing in the retained data constrains them.** Retain fine-tuning's proposition here says agreement on retained training points can be reached while the residual on general queries is exactly the part lying in the forget span — and empirically the high-similarity test bins are where every baseline is worst. For our instruments the translation is direct and worth a standing column: **for any read-out, report the score separately on items near the anchor of the read-out and on items far from it**, because a probe fitted on the near items can be perfect there while the far ones are unconstrained or worse than a null. The corollary that matters for editing and steering: after an intervention, verifying on the same data that motivated the intervention proves nothing about nearby inputs — and "nearby" is measurable in representation space, which is what makes this a column and not a caveat. Coreference `arxiv-2605.11161` (whose whole point is whether an explanation changes the behaviour you care about on new inputs) and `arxiv-2610.02098` (the repair experiment, where restoring a few specific pathways flips the verdict — the same "which part of the input space was actually constrained" question).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 495): **The mean of an interpretability score is close to worthless on its own — the number that decides whether a read-out works is its dispersion across layers, because a mean can be manufactured by two excellent layers and says nothing about whether a randomly chosen layer can be read.** This paper's cleanest column is the variance one: at six layers the random-only score averages 6.36 against GPT-2's 3.14, which is already a win, but the variances are 1.87 against 18.39, and that is the claim that survives scrutiny — one architecture is readable everywhere and the other is readable in patches, which is exactly the difference between a representation and a lucky layer. Two rules for our batteries follow. First, **report mean and variance of every per-layer interpretability statistic side by side and never the mean alone**, and treat a high variance as a failure of the *instrument's portability* even when the mean is good, since the practical question is whether reading an unseen layer works. Second, **the same column applies to probe and steering batteries**: a direction whose separation score is high on average but concentrated in one layer, one head or one prompt family has the same defect and is invisible in the mean. Coreference `arxiv-2010.07693` (per-layer coefficient-of-variation as the statistic that decides which perturbation family a network loses to) and `arxiv-2505.00808` (explanatory faithfulness as agreement *at each named layer*, the definitional form of the same demand).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 495): **The cheapest way to show a representation is already in the form your post-hoc method was going to search for is to fit that method anyway and measure what it adds — and the delegation experiment is the template: the gain from a dictionary fitted on architecture A over A versus the gain over architecture B, under identical training and interpreter.** Here the built-in-sparsity model gains *less* from an added SAE than the ordinary transformer does (+6.5 versus -10.2 on one metric, +38.1 versus +34.8 on another), and the authors read the gap as evidence that the built-in code is already close to what the dictionary is looking for. Two things make this a reusable instrument rather than a rhetorical device. First, **the sign of the delegation gain can be negative** — fitting an SAE to an already-sparse code can *hurt* its interpretability score — so the statistic must be reported as a signed difference with both raw scores printed, not as an improvement. Second, **the same construction tests our own read-outs**: for any direction, feature or probe we build, fit the standard post-hoc alternative on the same activations and report the delta; a small delta is direct evidence that the representation, not the method, is doing the work, and it is much harder to dismiss than a comparison of two scores computed by different pipelines. Coreference `arxiv-2310.17611` (a read-out trusted because it is computable, with no statement of what it was supposed to add) and `arxiv-2610.02098` (the pairwise-gap form of the same discipline, where what matters is the gap between two instruments rather than either score).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 494): **Behavioural faithfulness and explanatory faithfulness are different claims, and every patching or ablation score the folder has recorded measures only the first — so the field's standard instrument does not test the thing MI says it wants.** The distinction is one sentence: behavioural faithfulness asks that the explanation and the model produce the same **outputs**; explanatory faithfulness asks that the expert's **stated intermediate stages** match the model's actual intermediate activations, layer by layer, for inputs in the distribution. Two consequences for our batteries. First, the cheapest upgrade is to record, for every candidate explanation, **the activation agreement at each site the explanation names**, not only end-task agreement — which is measurable with the interventions we already run, requires no new method, and is exactly the axis `arxiv-2610.02098` found can diverge from output agreement by tens of points. Second, **the two can come apart in both directions and the report must say which was measured**: an explanation can reproduce outputs while prescribing a wrong intermediate route (routinely, when the replacement input hands the unit a usable signal it would not have computed) and can prescribe the right route while losing some output fidelity (the "non-trivial change to performance if patched" case the paper raises). Naming the claim is the whole deliverable here; a number labelled "faithfulness" without the label behavioural or explanatory is ambiguous in a way that has been silently tolerated across this folder's circuit entries. Coreference `arxiv-2610.02098` (the gap measured: scores preferring the worse-behaving candidate) and `arxiv-2407.08734` in `core/` (faithfulness numbers not robust across corruption), plus `arxiv-2505.14685` (a case where the *intermediate* pointer/payload separation, not the answer, carried the finding).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 494): **Three criteria turn "this activation contains information about X" into "this is a representation of X", and only the third is the one probes almost never test — so a probe screen alone can never establish a representation, however high its accuracy.** Information is a trainable probe; **Use** is an intervention that removes the information and must degrade the relevant downstream task; **Misrepresentation** is the sharper one — patching in information about a property the input lacks must predictably make the model treat the input as having that property. The third is what forbids the "it correlates, therefore it represents" inference, because it requires the code to be *causally readable by the model* rather than merely decodable by us, and it is where our batteries should spend their effort: a misrepresentation test is a counterfactual patch with a known expected error, not a score. Two practical notes. First, **Use and Misrepresentation need not agree** — a direction can be causally load-bearing without being patchable into a false belief, and a direction patchable into a false belief may be downstream decoration for the task we chose to measure; report them as separate columns with the task named. Second, **the whole triple is task-relative**, so "representation" is always short for "representation of X, for task T, on distribution D", and any claim omitting the three is unfalsifiable. Coreference `arxiv-1803.06959` (discriminability and necessity as separate measured properties — the empirical version of Information versus Use) and `arxiv-2610.02098` (whose restoration intervention is effectively a Use test run at the component level).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 494): **A method's "unsupervised" label hides a theory, and the way to surface it is to ask which structural claims the architecture would be false under — because those claims are priors, not findings, and they restrict what the read-out can ever report.** The worked case is decisive and cheap: an SAE commits to features being sparse and linearly accessible, and choosing TopK or JumpReLU adds the further claim that features are not typically both small and important — so a feature dictionary is evidence *conditional on* two or three conjectures, none of which the dictionary itself tests. For our reports the operational form is a **declared-prior line**: name the structural assumptions under which the read-out was produced (sparsity, linearity, gate shape, dictionary width, layer set), because a later reader cannot recover them from the dictionary. The second half of the rule is the one that bites: **an assumption we do not know we hold cannot be audited**, which is why the honest framing is "we chose this prior for these reasons" rather than "we made no assumptions". Same lesson at the measurement end as the precision point above. Coreference `arxiv-2310.17611` (a read-out trusted because it was computable, with no stated prior) and `goodfire-com-blog-a-practical-guide-to-saes` (the engineering side of the same choice, where the gate shape is a hyper-parameter with consequences).

Read from: **full text** — v2 HTML, **133,854 clean chars** (877,628 raw) via `lit-tools/fetch.py` on the first call, read end to end in six slices: abstract and byline; §1 introduction; §2.1-2.2 the two suites, edge-mask representation, the intervention family, the three faithfulness metrics and the `Q` behavioural criterion, and the misranking definition with the size-matching control; §3 controlled edits with **Table 2** (per-task misranking rates and deficits), **Table 3** (deficit distributions), the edit-size and metric sweeps; §4 discovery with **Tables 4-6**; §5 context restoration with **Algorithm 1**, **Table 7** and Figures 3a-b; §6 related work; §7 discussion and the limitations paragraph; Appendices A-E — A.1 models and hardware (Trillium H100), A.2 score definitions, A.3 ties/tolerance/paired bootstrap, B.1 the InterpBench **edge-closure** conversion with its numerical agreement check, B.2 candidate generation, B.3 reference behaviour, B.4 **Tables 12-16**, C discovery budgets and **Tables 17-20**, D cohort selection and **Tables 21-26**, E the eight-way metric-overlap partition with **Tables 27-29**. **Substance**: misranking is a property of the *evaluation*, demonstrated with no discovery algorithm at all — one component swap is enough; 13.2-24.4% of Human discovery candidate pairs under ordinary resampling; ~25 pp and 61.29 pp mean deficits in the worst cells; all three metrics agree on the wrong circuit 1,354 + 3,019 times; restoring selected intact-model signals reverses 96/100.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 493): **The measure that decides whether an explanation is trustworthy is not its own score but the gap between the candidate the score prefers and the candidate that behaves best — and that gap is measurable on a single split without any new method.** Take two candidates of identical size, score both under the intervention on a validation split, measure both on a disjoint split under one fixed protocol, and count pairs where the two orderings disagree, reporting the reversal rate *and* the distribution of how much behaviour the score's choice costs. Three things make this the strongest version of the discipline the folder keeps arriving at. First, **ties belong in the denominator** — a score that cannot separate two candidates has not distinguished them, and reporting only strict reversals over strict pairs flatters it. Second, **the deficit distribution is the result, not the rate**: a score that often switches near-ties is a nuisance while one that occasionally prefers an explanation losing a quarter of the model's behaviour is a hazard, and median-IQR plus a count above a five-point threshold separates the two. Third, **size matching is what makes the comparison an evaluation rather than a search result** — with unequal sizes the score can be accused of preferring bigger, and here every pair is at equal executable edge count, so the reversal can only be the score's doing. Coreference `arxiv-2606.06267` (evaluation granularity moving circuit rankings) and `openinterp-2026-cosine-causal-gap-crosscoder` (the gap between what a read-out measures and what is claimed for it).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 493): **Ablation-based evidence is biased, not merely noisy, and the bias has a signature that is easy to predict and easy to detect: the retained computation is being rewarded for co-operating with whatever stands in for the signal you removed.** Context distortion says a circuit evaluated under donor, mean or zero replacement is a different computation from the intact one, so a circuit that happens to use the replacement signal well will look faithful while reproducing less behaviour. The detection protocol is one extra experiment and it is decisive: put a *subset* of the genuine intact signals back, leave the masks and all other replacements untouched, and check whether the ranking flips. Here that repairs 96 of 100 persistent reversals, and at the 5 per cent level a median of one receiving-node group with seventeen excluded connections is sufficient in 60 cases — which is the interesting part, because it means the distortions are concentrated in a few specific incoming pathways rather than spread evenly. For our batteries the rule is to **never report a faithfulness number without naming what was substituted outside the unit, and to run a one-pathway restoration check whenever the number is load-bearing.** Corollary the authors state and we should copy: a suppression or restoration diagnostic is not a score — restored signals may hand the unit information it would not compute — so it earns a causal claim about the score's failure, not a new ranking metric. Coreference `arxiv-2005.01641` (the read-out's objective as the thing under test) and `arxiv-1802.08760` (off-manifold sensitivity measured along paths, the geometric form of the same concern).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 493): **When three scoring formulas that share an execution pipeline fail on the same items, the failure is in the pipeline and not in the formula — and the way to establish that cheaply is to hold the executions fixed and change only the score.** KL, logit difference and probability difference are computed here from identical intervened forward passes, so their overlap is not confounded by different candidates, prompts or donors, and all three prefer the worse circuit on 1,354 Human and 3,019 InterpBench discovery comparisons. That is a two-line experimental design with a large payoff: it converts "our metric is bad" into "the quantity being measured is not the quantity we want", which is why the paper can then trace it to the *context* instead of proposing yet another metric. The accompanying discipline is the honest negative half: an absence of reversals can mean the metric works *or* that the pool is full of ties — 17,130 of the 30,134 "no misranking" InterpBench discovery comparisons have tied behaviour — so every table of agreement has to be read alongside its tie count. Coreference `arxiv-1805.01070` (two ranking metrics with opposite signs on the same models) and `arxiv-1807.01697` (two normalisations of one table inverting a verdict).

- Done 2026-11-20 (run 492, written entries 492): `arxiv-1608.04207` — Fine-grained Analysis of Sentence Embeddings Using Auxiliary Prediction Tasks (Adi & Goldberg — Bar-Ilan University; Kermany & Lavi — IBM Haifa Research Lab; Belinkov — MIT CSAIL). arXiv:1608.04207v3 [cs.CL], **2017-02-09, three versions**, ICLR 2017. Read from: **full text** — v3 HTML, **45,155 clean chars** (137,684 raw) via `lit-tools/fetch.py`, read end to end in four slices: abstract and byline; §1 introduction including the authors' own **Limitations** paragraph and their **Summary of Findings**; §2 related work; §3-3.1 the three prediction tasks with their exact class bins (5-8 through 34-70), the 20.1% majority baseline and the two 50% balanced floors, and the word-content negative-sampling rule (a word that appears positively elsewhere but not in this sentence, to stop the probe treating words as fixed positives/negatives); §4 the three encoder families; §5 setup (1M Wikipedia sentences, 50k vocab, lengths 5-70, k in {100,300,500,750,1000}); §6.1-6.3 the result curves; §7 the "natural languageness" controls — random-word substitution, the CBOW norm argument, the sentence-vector-removal order test, and the permuted dataset; §8 skip-thought with **Table 1**; §9 conclusion; references; **Appendix I** encoder and classifier setup, **Appendix II** technical details (Tesla K40, AdaGrad, dropout 0.1 for the encoder and 0.8 for the probes), **Appendix 10** content-vs-length, **Appendix III Tables 2-4** the paired-t-test p-values. **Substance:** LSTM-ED length 82-87% and order up to 91% at 1000 dims; **content peaks at 750 dims and falls at 1000 while decoder BLEU keeps rising**; CBOW length 45-65% (floor 20.1%) and order 70% (floor 50%). The two controls do the paper's interpretive work: random-word substitution barely moves CBOW's length score, and CBOW's **vector norm falls as sentence length rises** (central-limit argument, strongest for short sentences); removing the sentence vector from the CBOW order probe costs almost nothing (~3 points) while the LSTM-ED collapses, so CBOW's order score is English word-pair statistics. Permutation leaves the LSTM-ED three-task profile intact while its decoder BLEU falls 32.5 to 8.2, and **degrades skip-thought** (length 82.1 to 68.2, content 79.7 to 76.4) — skip-thought is natural-text-specialized, the LSTM-ED is a general sequence encoder. Closing warning: **BLEU over the decoder is sub-optimal for selecting an encoder.** Limits named by the authors: surface properties only, no syntax or semantics, conclusions may not generalize past these datasets, complementary tasks explicitly left for future work. Limits visible but unstated: **the probe corpus is a subset of the encoders' own training data**, no seeds or variance (only probe-run t-tests), probe capacity never varied, skip-thought compared across corpora and dimensions.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 492): **The cheapest way to convert an impressive probe score into a null result is to edit the dataset instead of the model, and the two edits worth standardising are "destroy the lexical content but keep the structure" and "destroy the structure but keep the lexical content" — because between them they exhaust the two ways a read-out can be riding on something other than what the task names.** Here random-word substitution keeps length and kills identity, and permutation keeps identity and kills order, and the pair resolves a result that would otherwise have been published as a finding: CBOW scores 70% on word order from a representation that cannot represent order, and the pair of controls shows the score is a property of English word-pair statistics with about three points contributed by the sentence. Two discipline points come with it. First, **the control must be passed through the identical trained encoder**, not through a retrained one — this paper reuses the same weights on permuted input, which is why the LSTM-ED's *flat* profile under permutation is interpretable at all. Second, **run the control at evaluation time and report the delta, never the raw score**, because the raw score here is identical in form to a score that would have been reported as evidence of order encoding. Coreference `arxiv-1909.03368` (the same logic moved from the data to the output: control tasks randomise the *labels* by word type, so the probe must memorise rather than read) and `arxiv-1805.01070` (the construction-side version, where the bias is removed at dataset-building time rather than measured afterwards).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 492): **A magnitude confound is the most common unnoticed shortcut in any read-out whose value is a function of how many things were combined, and the diagnostic is embarrassingly cheap: plot the statistic against the nuisance variable and see if it moves.** Averaging more roughly zero-centred vectors pulls the mean toward the origin, so a sentence vector's norm is a monotone function of sentence length without the encoder doing anything at all — which is why an order-blind average can score 45-65% on length prediction. The general form for our instruments: **whenever a pooled or aggregated representation is the unit (mean-pooled activations, summed attention, averaged gradients), the aggregate's norm is confounded with the number of pooled items**, so any probe or cosine screen that keys on magnitude will partially succeed by counting. The fix is one extra column, not a new experiment: report the correlation between the statistic and the pooling count, and for length-sensitive tasks re-fit on norm-normalised vectors. Coreference `arxiv-1802.08760` (whose per-unit aggregate carries a size term that must be regressed out before it can rank models) and `arxiv-1805.01070` (pooling choice as the thing being varied, with a mean-pooling failure recorded in the medical-monitor work).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 492): **When the downstream proxy and the probe disagree in sign, the proxy is usually measuring the part of the pipeline you are about to throw away — and this paper has the cleanest available demonstration because the encoder and decoder are separable by construction.** Word-content accuracy peaks at 750 dimensions and drops at 1000 while reconstruction BLEU rises monotonically over the same range, and the authors' reading is that a stronger decoder carries more of the sentence itself, letting the encoder be less informative. The transferable rule is for any pipeline in which we keep one component and score the pair: **score the kept component on the property it is kept for, not the loss of the end-to-end system**, and where the two are reported together, expect them to come apart at large capacity. This is the same instrument-gap the probe-versus-parser entry found from the training-objective side (a read-out adequate for its purpose scoring badly on a yardstick it was not built for), arriving here from the capacity side; the shared prescription is to name the loss the number was computed under and to check it against the consumer. Coreference `arxiv-2005.01641` (two ranking metrics with opposite signs on the same models) and `arxiv-1807.01697` (raw versus baseline-subtracted aggregates inverting a ranking).

NAACL-HLT 2019, pp. 4129-4138. Read from: **full text** — Anthology PDF, **10 pages, 33,127 chars** via `pypdf`, read end to end in four slices: abstract and §1 introduction; §2.1 the distance probe with its PSD-form equation and the |s|²-normalised L1 loss, §2.2 the properties it buys, §2.3 the depth probe; §3 experiments with the three representation models, PTB/Stanford Dependencies data, the four baselines and both metric definitions, then **Table 1** and §4 results with the model and layer orderings; §4.1 the rank sweep; §5 discussion with the reviewers' headedness objection; acknowledgements; references; **Appendices A-B** (Adam at 0.001, batch 20, 40 epochs, dev-loss learning-rate reset, DyNet and PyTorch implementations; Figures 6-9 with the worked trees). **Substance:** the whole point is that tree reconstruction is a *global metric* claim, so the same matrix B is fitted across every sentence and a per-sentence parser-like probe cannot hide in it. Table 1: LINEAR 48.9 UUAS / 0.58 DSpr / 2.9 root% / 0.27 NSpr, ELMO0 26.8/0.44/54.3/0.56, DECAY0 51.7/0.61/54.3/0.56, PROJ0 (random BiLSTM) 59.8/0.73/64.4/0.75, ELMO1 77.0/0.83/86.5/0.87, BERT-base7 79.8/0.85/88.0/0.87, BERT-large15 82.5/0.86/89.4/0.88, BERT-large16 81.7/0.87/90.1/0.89. Ordering BERT-large > BERT-base > ELMo > PROJ0 > the rest; syntax peaks in the upper-middle layers, not monotonically. **Rank sweep: no accuracy gain past k of 64-128**, so the recovered tree lives in a small subspace of a 768/1024-dim layer, and all three models need roughly the same rank, which the authors leave unexplained. Limits: strict single hypothesis, probe supervised on the trees it is scored on, a deep parser would beat it, squared-distance choice unexplained, no seeds or variance, hypothesis built on LSTMs and applied unchanged to self-attention.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 491): **The strongest control for a supervised read-out is the same architecture with the same capacity and no training, and this paper is the clearest statement of why: the probe is a linear map fitted on the trees it is later scored against, so the number that licenses the claim is not the probe's accuracy but the gap between it and a random map of identical shape — and here even a randomly initialised BiLSTM with all of ELMo's contextualising capability, fed context-free embeddings, reaches 59.8 UUAS against ELMo1's 77.0.** Two rules follow for our batteries. First, **always report the untrained-capacity baseline on the same axis**, because a context-free and a distance-decayed baseline sitting at or near the left-to-right-chain oracle (26.8 and 51.7 against 48.9) tells the reader that the metric's floor is high and that only the model's margin over 59.8 is learned. Second, **the corpus's own trivial structure is a baseline too** — the linear chain is not a strawman, it is what a position-encoding-only model achieves, and it means any probe score under roughly 50 on this task carries no syntactic information at all. Coreference `arxiv-1805.01070` (the untrained same-architecture control at source, the identical device in the sentence-embedding register) and `arxiv-2005.01641` (the paper that attacks this probe, whose own point is that the probe's architecture smuggles in the answer).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 491): **A directional claim about a representation should come with the smallest dimension in which it holds, and the cheap way to get that number is to sweep the rank of the read-out and find where it saturates — here 64 to 128 dimensions out of 768 or 1024, with no gain beyond.** This is the constructive form of "the information is in a low-rank subspace", and it is measurable with no extra data, just a second axis on an experiment already being run. Two consequences for our instruments. First, **a full-rank fitted direction is not evidence of a full-rank property**: a k-dimensional explanation that ties a full-rank one is the better explanation, and the swept curve is what makes the tie visible. Second, **the saturation point is itself a comparable statistic across models** — the paper notices that ELMo, BERT-base and BERT-large all need roughly the same rank and flags it as unexplained, which is exactly the kind of cross-model invariant worth reporting even when it has no story yet, because it constrains later mechanistic accounts. Coreference `arxiv-2010.07693` (dimensionality measured on representations and on differences, the same low-rank question asked of an intervention) and `arxiv-1802.08760` (a per-unit aggregate whose value depends on how many units are summed — the dual warning that a dimension count must be named precisely). **Warning to pair with both: report the dimension of the read-out's *footprint*, and never let it be read as the dimension of the computation.**

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 491): **Stating an interpretability result as a hypothesis about a structural property of the whole space — an existence claim about a metric — rather than as a classifier accuracy changes what counts as a refutation, because a baseline that cannot possibly possess the property falsifies it outright while a weak baseline only makes an accuracy claim look impressive.** This is the framing transfer, and it is the folder's most reusable idea for our white-box goal: "there exists a linear map under which squared distance equals tree distance, for every pair in every sentence" is the kind of statement a white-box model can be asked to satisfy and then checked against, whereas "our probe reaches 80% on the task" is the kind of statement that only ever measures the probe. The companion discipline is to pick the *strongest* baseline you can bear: the authors knowingly include a randomly initialised network of full width because it is "surprisingly strong", and the resulting margin is the claim. Coreference `arxiv-2005.01641` (which argues the same metric claim is unattested in the parsing literature — the two papers are the two halves of one argument and should be read as a pair) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a score read as a presence claim, the failure this framing is designed to prevent).

- Done 2026-11-20 (run 490, written entries 490): `arxiv-1911.03681` — E-BERT: Efficient-Yet-Effective Entity Embeddings for BERT (Poerner — LMU Munich CIS; Waltinger — Siemens AG Munich; Schütze — LMU Munich CIS). arXiv:1911.03681v2 [cs.CL], **2020-05-01, two versions** (v1 2019-11-09 under the title *BERT is not a Knowledge Base (yet)*), licence arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive, **no Comments line, no journal reference, no venue, no funding line, no data statement; the code link printed in v1 is an anonymised placeholder (github.com/anonymized) and the promise to release LAMA-UHN and both E-BERT sizes is unverified in this record**. Read from: **full text** — v2 HTML, **64,232 clean chars** (431,397 raw) via `lit-tools/fetch.py`, read end to end in five slices: abstract and byline; §1 introduction with the five-item contribution list; §2.1-2.5 related work (BERT, ERNIE/KnowBert and the KEPLER/K-Adapter contrast, Wikipedia2Vec's three loss terms, cross-lingual vector alignment, unsupervised QA); §3.1-3.3 the least-squares map fitted on the shared wordpiece-and-word vocabulary, the concat and replace input forms, the 2.7M-entity vocabulary and the computational-cost paragraph; §4.1-4.5 LAMA data, baselines, the Hits@k measure, LAMA-UHN's two heuristics with **Table 2**, and **Table 3** plus the per-relation discussion with **Table 1**; §5.1 relation classification (**Table 4**) and §5.2 entity linking with the [E-MASK] formulation, the log-prior bias, iterative refinement and **Tables 5-6**; §6 conclusion; references; **appendix** — the Wikidata SPARQL queries used instead of LAMA's oracle ids, the FewRel/ERNIE preprocessing with its # and $ span markers, the AIDA chunking rule, and **Tables 7-11** (dataset statistics and mean Hits@1 with question counts for every relation). **Substance:** the LAMA gain is 36.2 vs 29.2 Hits@1 for E-BERT-concat-base against BERT (30.4 ERNIE, 31.7 KnowBert) and 34.2 vs 30.6 at large size; the decomposition is the contribution — BERT loses about nine points between original LAMA and LAMA-UHN (29.2 to 20.2) while entity-only E-BERT loses about one (29.1 to 28.2), so roughly a third of the surface-form model's score was the name shortcut, and the per-relation table shows it concretely (named-after 61.6 to 5.0 after the string filter, native language 72.2 to 45.8 after both, country of citizenship 25.4 to 69.9 with entity vectors). Relation classification 88.38 vs 85.45 macro F1 test; entity linking 85.0 micro F1 on AIDA-B, 90.8 on dev, with unsupervised AIDA F1 of 31.5 for the aligned MLM against 2.3 unaligned and 2.2 with a random head.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 490): **A benchmark can be partitioned by a surface shortcut, and the score difference across the partition is a direct, cheap estimate of how much of the measured performance is the shortcut — no retraining, no adversary, no second model, and it needs only a heuristic you can run on the benchmark itself.** The two heuristics here are the reusable part and they escalate in sophistication: a literal substring test (the answer appears in the question's subject name) catches the blunt cases at 12% of triples but up to 81% of one relation, and a *model-generated* association test catches the subtle ones — ask the model whether either half of a person's name is a common name in the answer's language and delete items where its own top-3 agrees with the gold. The second is the general construction: **use the model's own cheap-to-query behaviour to find the items it can answer without the ability you are trying to measure, then delete those items and score again.** For our batteries this is a standing report column, not an optional appendix: for any probe or benchmark we build, run the model's shallow/associative baseline, report the score on items that baseline gets right and the score on items it misses, and print both with the subset sizes. Coreference `2020.acl-main.698` (the negation and misprime probes, which change the item instead of deleting it — the same logic applied to the question rather than the item selection) and `arxiv-2005.01641` (metric choice changing the ranking, the same lesson in the scoring register). Carried forward from the previous run's note: **the honest form of this claim is "score minus shallow-baseline score on the same items", never "score" alone**, and where the subset is built by deletion the subset's size is part of the result.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 490): **When an external representation is spliced into a model, the alignment step is the object under test and the unaligned control is what proves it — the papers that omit that control cannot separate "we added information" from "we added information in a readable form".** E-BERT's ablation is unusually clean because it holds everything constant and only skips the least-squares map between the two vector spaces: concat macro F1 falls 88.38 to 85.84 and replace falls 87.22 to 77.45, and unsupervised entity-linking F1 collapses from 31.5 to 2.3, which is the strongest single number for the claim since a random prediction head over aligned vectors still scores only 2.2. The interpretive point generalises to any dictionary, probe or direction we insert into the model's space: **the correct null is the same vectors, unmapped or randomly rotated, run through the identical downstream pipeline**, because a coordinate-system match is a property of the whole pipeline and cannot be inferred from the vectors' content alone. Design consequence: treat the map itself as a fitted object with its own fit set (here the shared vocabulary), report what it was fitted on, and never fit it on the evaluation items. Coreference `arxiv-1805.01070` (the untrained-architecture control, the same "hold the instrument, vary the one thing" discipline) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a read-out trusted because it is computable, without a null).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 490): **A gain that grows with k is a different kind of gain from a gain at top-1, and reporting the curve rather than the scalar is what makes the distinction visible: here the advantage over every baseline widens at larger k, meaning the model is better at ranking the right answer near the top than at naming it first.** This is a reporting rule for our probe evaluations with an operational payload — if a method improves recall@k but not precision@1, then it has improved the *ordering* of the candidate set, and downstream finetuning that consumes distributions rather than argmaxes should benefit more than the top-1 number suggests, which is exactly the paper's own argument for why entity vectors help a downstream task even where single-answer accuracy saturates. Two consequences. First, **always report Hits@k or recall@k across at least three values of k with a log axis**, because that is the cheapest way to see a ranking improvement that a single-number comparison would show as a small win. Second, **when two methods tie on top-1 and diverge at k=5, treat that as evidence they differ in what they encode, not as noise** — and check it against the lexical-overlap frequency of the relations, which is what this paper does by plotting per-relation delta against substring rate. Coreference `2020.acl-main.698` (rank-1 overlap versus rank correlation, the same statistic reported at two resolutions) and `arxiv-1807.01697` (raw versus baseline-subtracted aggregates, the summarisation-rule version).

- Done 2026-11-20 (run 489, written entries 489): `2020.acl-main.698` — Negated and Misprimed Probes for Pretrained Language Models: Birds Can Talk, But Cannot Fly (Kassner & Schütze — LMU Munich, CIS). ACL 2020, pp. 7811-7818, DOI 10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.698, long paper in the main proceedings. Read from: **full text** — Anthology PDF, **8 pages, 34,867 chars** via `pypdf` 7.1.0, read end to end in three slices: abstract and byline; §1 introduction; §2 data and models (LAMA's four sources, the five backends, the negated and misprimed variants); §3 results with **Table 2** (Spearman and rank-1 overlap for all five models), **Table 3** (precision drop under four misprime modes), **Table 4** (sixteen worked original/negated/misprimed prediction examples), **Table 5** (synthetic-corpus accuracy); §4 discussion; §5 related work; §6 conclusion with its three stated implications; acknowledgements; references; **Appendix A.1-A.2** — the ConceptNet negation subset rule (2,996 of 11,458), the mode A-D definitions, the exact list of twenty neutral sentences, the 349-token vocabulary and **Tables 6-7** for pretraining and finetuning hyper-parameters. **Substance:** negated and original predictions agree at mean Spearman above 85% in most cells of Table 2 — ConceptNet 89.9-96.8 across models, SQuAD 86.5-97.1, T-REx N-1 84.8-96.3 — with rank-1 overlap reaching 89.4 (ELMo 5.5B on T-REx N-1); BERT is least affected, and T-REx 1-1 and Google-RE birth-date are the interpretable exceptions where the models change to a different plausible sentence rather than to a truth judgement. Mispriming with the model's own near-miss filler costs more than 60% precision in most relations of Table 3 (Google-RE birth-place 99.5, death-place 98.9, birth-date 100.0) and survives twenty intervening sentences, while random misprimes are far weaker (the prose states the drop is on average more than 35 points lower for mode A than mode D). On the synthetic balanced corpus, BERT-base pretrained from scratch scores 0.9 on both polarities for seen sentences and 0.2 on both for unseen ones — chance for the construction — with test accuracy stagnating as training loss falls, and reaches 1.0 on all four cells after finetuning on true/false labels.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 489): **The cheapest possible test of whether a read-out carries a proposition rather than a string is a minimal pair with the truth value flipped, and the statistic to report is *agreement*, not accuracy — because on a flip task the correct outcome is disagreement, and a high score on either item alone licenses nothing.** This inverts the usual battery framing, where the intervention is expected to damage the measurement; here a representation that ignores the flip is exactly the one whose original score cannot be trusted, and the two numbers (rank correlation between the two output distributions, rank-1 overlap) are reported side by side because they answer the same question at different resolutions. For our probes the transfer is direct: for any sentence-level pair we can construct — negated, subject swapped, relation inverted — compute the correlation of the two output distributions, and treat agreement above the positive-positive control as evidence the read-out is keyed to lexical co-occurrence. The control is the reusable part: unrelated prompts sharing a template give the null level, and it must be printed, because "the two distributions correlate" is uninterpretable without knowing what two unrelated prompts correlate at. Coreference `arxiv-1805.01070` (the untrained-architecture baseline, the same logic one level down: a level has to sit on the same axis to be interpretable) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a cosine screen read as a content claim, the mechanised version of this failure).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 489): **A distractor ladder ordered by plausibility is a better stress test than any single perturbation, and its result is a rule about what random controls can and cannot show: the model here resists implausible prefixes and is wrecked by the one wrong word it was about to say.** Modes A through D are not four conditions but four rungs — random word, same-type wrong entity, the model's own near-miss filler, and that same filler pushed twenty sentences away — and the dose-response across them (mode A weakest, mode C strongest, mode D barely attenuated) is what makes the claim causal rather than demonstrative. Two consequences for our batteries. First, **a random-direction or random-token ablation is a floor, not a test**: any intervention suite that only perturbs randomly will systematically understate sensitivity to the perturbations the model is actually near. Second, **distance is a separate axis from strength and must be swept independently** — twenty intervening sentences changing almost nothing establishes that the effect is neither recency nor adjacency, which no amount of amplitude sweeping could have shown. The transferable construction for a feature or direction is therefore a three-way grid: perturbation magnitude times perturbation *plausibility* times intervening length, with the null printed on the same axis. Coreference `arxiv-1802.08760` (sensitivity measured along trajectories known to approach and depart from the data, the geometric form of the plausibility axis) and `arxiv-1903.12261` (cumulative-perturbation flip rate, the amplitude axis alone).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 489): **A finetuned-versus-pretrained gap on the identical sentences is the cleanest statement of decodable-but-unused available, and the synthetic control is what makes it a mechanism rather than an anecdote: the pretrained model memorises both polarities of seen sentences and sits at chance on unseen ones while its training loss falls, then reaches perfection once a label names the distinction.** The information is present and usable — a supervised head extracts it instantly — and yet the model's own predictions do not deploy it, and the plateau-versus-loss divergence rules out the obvious rival explanation that the pattern was never learned. Three reporting rules come out of the design. First, **when a probe succeeds and a behavioural test fails on the same data, that pair is the finding**, and both numbers belong in one table rather than different sections. Second, **build the balanced synthetic control rather than arguing about frequency**: it costs a few hundred tokens of vocabulary and one pretraining run, and it converts "negated sentences are probably rare" from a suspicion into a measured difference between the real and balanced settings. Third, **check the memorisation confound by holding entire items out** — seen-versus-unseen splits are the discrete version of an on-manifold/off-manifold split, and the gap between them is what a lookup table with no abstraction looks like. Coreference `arxiv-1805.01070` (the untrained-architecture control, the same "what stays constant when nothing is learned" question) and `arxiv-1802.08760` (on-manifold versus off-manifold sensitivity, the continuous analogue).

Read from: **full text** — v2 HTML, **90,655 clean chars** (278,908 raw) via `lit-tools/fetch.py`, read end to end in six slices: abstract and byline; §1 introduction (the unit-hunting framing, the average-versus-worst-case distinction credited to Hendrycks and Dietterich, four stated contributions); §2.1-2.2 related work (weight and activation sparsity, low-rank regularisation, the frequency-domain route to average-case robustness, the equivocal single-unit-ablation literature); §3 Approach (the SI index equation, the loss with its signed scale and within-then-across-layer mean, FGSM and PGD at 16/255, the per-unit and per-layer coefficient-of-variation definitions); §4.1-4.4 (the corruption sweep under a pre-declared three-outcome framing, the adversarial reversal, the Jacobian, the CV results, the dimensionality results at 95% variance); §5 Discussion; acknowledgements; references; **Appendix A.1-A.9** — A.1.1 training details (SGD, momentum 0.9, weight decay 1e-4, maxpool removed for 64x64 inputs, 90 epochs at batch 4096/1400, 200 epochs at batch 256 for ResNet20), A.1.2 datasets including the honest note that Tiny ImageNetC is built from *different* ImageNet images than Tiny ImageNet's test set, A.1.4 both dimensionality definitions (PCA at 90/95/99%, and the Facco et al. nearest-neighbour ID estimator), A.2-A.3 clean-accuracy normalisation with its floor-effect caveat, A.4 AugMix parameters and result, A.5 the gradient-masking control, A.6 ImageNet-A (74 shared classes, 2,957 downsampled images, chance 1.35%), A.7 PGD training and dead units, A.8 the CV components, A.9 the 90/99% and intrinsic-dimension replication figures. **Substance:** the same signed knob as the workshop version, swept across 20 seeds; corruption accuracy peaks at 17% versus 13.5% unregularised for ResNet18 on Tiny ImageNetC at a scale of −2.0, helps 15/15, 14/15 and 14/19 corruption types across the three model/dataset pairs, and the ordering reverses under both attacks, with the Jacobian norm inversely proportional to selectivity in all three models. What is new here is the mechanism: early-layer representation dimensionality inversely proportional to selectivity (to about layer 9 in ResNet18, all of ResNet20); perturbation-induced change more high-dimensional in low-selectivity networks and more so for adversarial than corrupted inputs; and the input-unit gradient's coefficient of variation **proportional** to selectivity, both across samples per unit and across units per layer — high-selectivity units are erratically perturbable, low-selectivity units consistently so, which is the paper's explanation for why the larger, more distributed code is the more exploitable one. Bidirectionality is checked with AugMix (lowers selectivity, to roughly a −0.1/−0.2 scale equivalent) and PGD training (raises it, monotonically only after dead units are excluded). ImageNet-A accuracy is flat across the whole sweep.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 488): **"Which robustness" was never one question, and this paper's real contribution to us is a third axis rather than a third result: the quantity that decides which perturbation family a network loses to is not how much a unit responds but how *reliably* it responds, and reliability is a dispersion statistic — the coefficient of variation of a per-unit gradient — computed with forward and backward passes only.** Per-unit perturbability dispersion tracks selectivity in the same direction as worst-case vulnerability, so the two named axes (how many dimensions, how stable in input–output terms) turn out to be read-outs of one structural property: a distributed code has many units participating consistently, which is good under naturalistic noise and fatal against an adversary that can exploit the consistency. For our batteries the transfer is concrete: for any probe direction, attention head or SAE feature we care about, compute the dispersion of its per-example gradient norm over a held-out set and report it beside its separation score, per layer, because a read-out that fires with wildly varying strength across examples and one that fires uniformly are different objects even when their mean magnitude is identical — and the uniform one is the more fragile to any intervention that pushes on it. Coreference `arxiv-1802.08760` (the input–output Jacobian instrument this paper uses as its network-level analogue, and the source of the off-manifold warning) and `arxiv-1903.12261` (the flip-rate statistic, the same "conservation under a small push" question asked discretely).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 488): **Dimensionality is the routing variable that makes one property trade one robustness for another, and the reusable form of the claim is a *matched pair* of measurements: the dimensionality of the clean representation and the dimensionality of the clean-minus-intervened difference, both per layer, against the same baseline.** Three transferable rules come out of how the paper does it. First, the direction of the difference-matrix statistic is counter-intuitive and worth internalising — state changes are *more* high-dimensional than the states themselves, so "the representation barely moved" is not the same as "few units moved". Second, because the two read-outs are separate numbers, an intervention that changes the *dimensionality* of the representation and one that changes which *dimensions* a perturbation uses can be disentangled, which single-read-out batteries cannot do. Third, the caveat the authors carry along is the one the folder has now recorded three times and should treat as standing: a difference matrix's dimensionality describes how the perturbation acted, not what the network computes, so every effective-dimension number we quote must name whether it is of a representation or of a difference. Coreference `arxiv-2007.04440` (the same measurements taken on one representative perturbation per family) and `arxiv-2003.01262` (the PWCCA distance, which answers the same "did the geometry change" question with an affine-invariant distance rather than a count).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 488): **A causal claim is much harder to dismiss when it can be driven in both directions by methods designed for something else, and that is the cheapest available replication: instead of only sweeping your own knob and reading the outcome, take two published training recipes that target the same downstream quantity and check whether each moves your property along the same axis.** AugMix (a corruption-robustness method) lowers selectivity to roughly a small negative scale's level, and PGD training (an adversarial-robustness method) raises it in proportion to attack strength, so the relation survives being approached from both ends, which a one-directional sweep cannot show. Two disciplines travel with it. First, **check whether the back-direction signal is contaminated by a label artefact** — PGD training kills units, and dead units score zero on this statistic, so the effect is monotone only after they are excluded — meaning any statistic averaged over units needs an explicit dead-unit policy. Second, **report the benchmark where the knob does nothing**: ImageNet-A accuracy is flat across the entire sweep, which tells the reader the mechanism is specific to perturbations that exploit coding geometry rather than to distribution shift in general; a table of only responsive benchmarks would have overstated the finding. Coreference `arxiv-1611.03530` (the relabelling ladder, the same "drive it from the other side" logic applied to data instead of to the training procedure) and `arxiv-1807.01697` (whose failed enhancement attempts are the negative half of the same reporting discipline).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 487): **A probe score is a property of the pair (representation, probe objective), not of the representation, and the way to make that concrete is to hold capacity fixed and vary only the loss: here two models with an identical rank-r bilinear parameterisation rank in opposite orders under the two metrics each was trained for.** The consequence for our batteries is a reporting rule with two halves: state the probe's objective beside every score, and always score the object the downstream consumer actually receives rather than the raw regression output — because the parser's near/far matrix looks terrible on distance correlation and is worth nothing less once the tree is decoded from it, which is exactly the kind of lossless compression that a naive read-out penalises. This is the same instrument-gap the folder keeps meeting from the ablation side, arriving from the loss side: a read-out can be adequate for its purpose and still score badly on a yardstick it was not built for, so a low score licenses no inference about the representation until the objective has been declared. Coreference `arxiv-1803.06959` (discriminability and necessity as separate properties, two instruments) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a screen whose score was read as a presence claim).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 487): **A metric introduced by the same paper that introduces the method is a hypothesis, not a yardstick, and the audit that catches it is one line of work: recompute the score after undoing whatever encoding choice the read-out made, and see whether the advantage survives.** The Prim-then-Floyd-Warshall recomputation is the template — it cost one post-processing step and it turned a nine-for-nine win into a 0.0006 draw. Two transferable rules follow. First, for any invented metric in a battery, include a *field-standard* metric on the same axis, because familiarity is the cheapest available validation and the standard metric here is the one with the clear trend. Second, when a new metric is proposed, the burden of proof is on the proposal to show what it is sensitive to, and that exploration should be reported separately from any claim about the probed model — the authors insist on keeping "what this tells us about BERT" apart from "what this tells us about how to measure BERT", and that separation is the reason the paper can conclude something at all. - Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 486): **The most useful baseline in a probing battery is an untrained network of the same architecture, and leaving it out converts an architectural prior into a spurious training effect.** Every text-classification probe here is a classifier fit on frozen vectors, so the vectors' readability is the measurement — and a randomly initialised max-pooling LSTM over frozen word vectors already reaches 88.8 on word content and 73.3 on the substitution task, i.e. most of the reported "the encoder learned X" is architecture plus a lookup table. The generalisable rule for our batteries is a four-level ladder reported on the same axis for every readout: chance, trivial-feature baseline, untrained same-architecture control, achievable ceiling. The paper also shows why the second level cannot be skipped — the bag-of-averaged-vectors baseline sits at 89.1 on tense while the best trained encoder reaches only 90.9, so the *apparent* effect of a million-dollar training pipeline is one point over averaging word embeddings, and the honest reading of that table is "redundancy in language, not structure". Coreference `arxiv-1611.03530` (the same lesson in the capacity register: damage the labels and see how much of the effect survives) and `arxiv-2007.04440` (whose selectivity effects are only interpretable because the unregularised run at the same scale is printed beside them).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 486): **When a ceiling is estimated rather than known, a model that beats it is the signal that the ceiling is a label artefact — and here the tell is exact: sequence-to-tree training exceeds the human bound on precisely the probes derived from the parser it was trained to imitate, and nowhere else.** That is a cheap, general self-audit for any benchmark whose labels are machine-generated: compare the ceiling against models trained on the generating annotation, and if they cross, the excess is copying the annotator's errors rather than solving the task. The complementary finding is that the hard probes here are hard for a real reason — tree depth, acceptability and clause inversion all sit 10-20 points under their ceilings for every model and every objective, while length saturates at 99.1 and then *declines* with training as the objective gets better. Two design consequences for us: report a per-task ceiling and floor so a score's position is computable rather than comparative, and treat a saturating-and-then-decaying probe as evidence that capacity is being reallocated, not as noise. Coreference `arxiv-2003.01262` (a statistic whose measured value must be read against a fitted upper bound, the same ceiling logic in the direction-sense) and `arxiv-1807.01697` (the per-corruption AlexNet normaliser, i.e. a ceiling-by-reference-model rather than ceiling-by-annotator).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 486): **A published diagnostic battery stops being a diagnostic the moment it becomes a target, and the countermeasure is either to keep the split private or to build the leakage controls into the task construction — three devices here cost nothing and each closes a distinct cheat: disjoint target items across train and test, de-correlation of a probe from the nuisance variable it naturally rides on, and frequency-matching of the manipulation to its control.** The paper states the intent explicitly (the tasks exist to explore encoders, not to be optimised) and then violates its own hope in the way the honest version of this always looks: its strongest models are strong partly because they were trained on the parser that generated the labels. For us the transfer is twofold. First, a probe battery we use to make claims should have a practice split separate from a scored split, with the same family structure on both sides. Second, the *construction* controls above are worth more than statistical correction, because no post-hoc adjustment recovers a probe whose answer is memorisable from a lexical cue. Coreference `arxiv-1807.01697` (the publish-the-generator, never-train-on-test-and-ship-extra-validation-families triad, the benchmark-side version of the same argument) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a read-out interpreted as content when its cue may be lexical, the failure this construction is designed to prevent).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 485): **The perturbation axis is the cheapest in the folder, and it reframes what an intervention has to prove: instead of asking whether a read-out is correct, ask whether it is stable under a change too small to matter — and the construction costs no labels, no adversary and no second model.** ImageNet-P's recipe is one paragraph: take a real input, apply a small *cumulative* perturbation across many frames so no single step leaves the data manifold, and count label flips between adjacent frames. The result is a number that is interpretable without any ground truth beyond the first frame, which is exactly the property our probe batteries need, and the paper's own numbers show why it is not a formality — a ResNet-18 changes its top-1 answer on more than one in seven frames of a pure scale sequence, with no attacker present. The transfer is direct: for any read-out we already compute (a probe's argmax, a SAE feature's top index, a steering direction's sign) we can walk a short path between two real activations and report a flip rate, which is a stability statistic in the same family as the Jacobian norm of `arxiv-1802.08760` but requires only forward passes and needs no output dimension. Coreference `arxiv-2007.04440` (which measures robustness of accuracy, the correctness question, on a nearby construction) and `arxiv-1611.03530` (whose corrupted-label sweep is the discrete version of the same idea: move the intervention, watch what breaks).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 485): **Corruption and perturbation robustness are separable, and the two readings disagree about the same models in a way that is informative rather than contradictory: batch norm helped VGG-19 under corruption and hurt it under perturbation, and VGG nets that are worse than ResNets on corrupted accuracy are as good or better on prediction stability.** The generalisable rule is that "stress test" is not one axis, and any claim that property X makes a model robust is incomplete without naming which perturbation class — the same lesson `arxiv-1807.01697` drew from style versus subtype, arriving from the temporal side. Two design consequences for us. First, when scoring an intervention on a battery of perturbations, report the *per-family* table, because an aggregate mean across fifteen corruptions and a mean across ten perturbations are two different summaries of two different objects. Second, the striking dissociation here is a free validation of construct: if the two metrics had always agreed, one of them would be redundant, and the paper's own defence of having both is that they do not. Coreference `arxiv-1807.01697` (the same dissociation across style and subtype) and `arxiv-2007.04440` (where a single knob moves the average-case and worst-case axes in opposite directions).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 485): **A broken method can be the most informative instrument in the paper, and the reason is selection: ALP was tuned against worst-case gradients and failed there, yet it cut average-case perturbation instability by about 40% — a transfer nobody designed for and nobody would have found without a battery that admitted failures next to successes.** The engineering point is that our evaluation tables should have a column for methods that were designed for something else, because transfer across perturbation classes is the mechanism by which we learn what the classes share. The reporting discipline attached is the folder's recurring one, and this paper states it explicitly: **score models with a perturbation class they were not tuned on**, and forbid training on the scored conditions while shipping separate validation families so that tuning is possible without contamination. Concretely, a probe battery with a published practice split and a scored split, plus one foreign intervention deliberately included, is the copyable form. Coreference `arxiv-1807.01697` (the same four-families-for-validation device at source) and `doi-10.1016_j.jmva.2013.02.012` (calibration constructions kept separate from the claim).
