Read from: **full text** — v3 HTML, **68,379 clean chars** (278,705 raw) via `lit-tools/fetch.py`, read in four slices end to end: abstract and byline; §1 introduction (the narrow-input-domain argument with the cubic-sine illustration, the explicit scoping to image classification and the warning about weather forecasting); §1.1-1.2 outline and contributions; §2.1-2.4 related work (complexity metrics and the Raghu/Pascanu/Montufar linear-region line, regularisation, SGD's inductive bias, adversarial examples with the average-case distinction); §3 both metrics in full, including the Gaussian-perturbation derivation that makes the Frobenius norm the expected output change per unit input perturbation and the transition-count formula with its curvature analogue; §4.1 the three trajectory types and the on/off-manifold result; §4.2-4.2.1 the matched-pair study, its four binary factors and the diagonal-plot reading convention; §4.3 the large sweep and why transitions fail; §4.4 per-point prediction; §5 conclusion; references; **Appendix A in full** — A.1.1-A.1.2 encoding and counting edge cases, **A.2 the Occam's-razor discussion** (the evidence-spreading argument for why parameter count misleads, and the conjectures about robust-solution volume), **A.3 the Jacobian-loss bounds equations 2-7**, A.4 the five activation definitions, and **A.5.1-A.5.7 every experimental setup** (seeds, 2^18/2^19 step budgets, the 335,671-network hyperparameter space, the 2160/2097 smaller sweeps, the per-point and cross-entropy analyses). **Substance:** both metrics are properties of the whole trained function measured on unlabelled inputs — Jacobian norm of the softmax-composed map (the logit Jacobian was less predictive, stated in a footnote) and a count of linear-region code changes along a closed trajectory built from horizontal translations of a test image. On-manifold sensitivity is far lower than off-manifold along all three trajectory types, and post-training region boundaries are strongly anisotropic with data points in low-transition-density cells. All four matched-pair factors move the Jacobian norm with the generalization gap (random labels up, augmentation down, ReLU down versus HardSigmoid, mini-batch down versus full-batch); transitions match on three and fail on the optimiser comparison. The 335,671-network sweep gives Jacobian norm against generalization gap on all four datasets, and transition count loses correlation once network size varies. Per-point, the target-class Jacobian norm is bounded in terms of e^-l(1-e^-l) by equations 5-7 under a uniform-logit-derivative assumption, so the relation is real but non-monotone-injective; high-norm points are mostly misclassified but some misclassified points are orders of magnitude less sensitive than correct ones.
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 484): **Two read-outs of the same underlying geometry can rank models identically in a matched-pair design and disagree completely once scale varies, and the second regime is the one the paper actually needs — so instrument validation has to be done on the population you intend to compare, not on the cleanest experiment available.** The mechanism is mechanical and generalises: the transition count grows with the *number of units and layers* by construction, so a statistic built by summing over units or directions picks up a size term, and a correlation computed on pairs that share architecture is blind to it. For our batteries the rule is concrete: any per-direction or per-unit aggregate must be validated on a model population that varies width and depth, and compared against a size-only baseline, before it is allowed to rank models; the cheap diagnostic is to regress the statistic on parameter count alone and keep only the residual. Coreference `arxiv-1807.01697` (the same lesson in the normalisation register: raw versus baseline-subtracted aggregates can invert a ranking) and `arxiv-1803.06959` (a pooled correlation that reversed sign inside its own clusters, the population-heterogeneity version).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 484): **A property of the function is only meaningful relative to a region of input space, and the cheap way to make that concrete is to measure the same statistic along trajectories that are known to approach and depart from the data — here the function is markedly more stable near the data than in a random ellipse, which is why a global average of sensitivity is a mixture of two regimes.** The engineering transfer for us: when reporting any sensitivity, stability or curvature read-out on activations, report it separately on-manifold (interpolations between real examples, small perturbations of real inputs) and off-manifold (random directions, scaled-up perturbations), because averaging the two produces a number that depends mostly on the ratio of the two regimes in the sample and so is not comparable across models. The paper's construction also gives a free control: the same-class three-anchor ellipse is closer to the manifold than the different-class one, so a *dose-response* in the metric across the three trajectory types is available without any extra labelling. Coreference `arxiv-2007.04440` (the Jacobian magnitude read-out this paper originates, used there as a per-layer stability measure) and `arxiv-2411.13117` (reporting a statistic with its null so magnitude is interpretable).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 484): **A matched-pair experiment — two networks identical in architecture, optimiser and seed, differing in exactly one factor — is the cheapest causal design in this folder, and the reason it is convincing is that the confound-free comparison costs nothing extra beyond the training run you were already doing for each setting.** In this paper it converts four separate intuitions into four one-directional measurements, and one of them (ReLU networks being more robust than saturating ones despite unbounded activations) comes out against intuition, which is the point: the design produces results you would not have predicted. The reusable discipline for our interventions is to pair every steering, ablation or regularised training run with an otherwise identical unmodified run at the same seed, and to plot the *pair* rather than the two marginal distributions — the scatter-against-the-diagonal form makes the per-pair direction visible even when the pooled distributions overlap heavily, which is what happened here for the smaller effects. Coreference `arxiv-1611.03530` (the randomised-label ladder built on the same idea of holding everything but the data fixed) and `arxiv-2003.01262` (a signed training-time scale swept, the continuous version of the same design).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 484): **A read-out that needs neither labels nor a fitted model is the closest thing in this folder to a usable instrument, and this paper shows why: the Jacobian norm is a derivative of the output map at a point, computable with one backward pass, with no probe to train, no capacity to select and no class-balance or null-hypothesis machinery — and yet it correlates with held-out performance across a hyperparameter space of hundreds of thousands of models.** For our batteries this is a direct addition: per-layer Jacobian norms on held-out inputs give a stability profile of the network that costs roughly one backward pass per example, and the appendix's derivation supplies an interpretation for the number rather than leaving it uncalibrated. The warning attached is equally usable and is stated by the authors themselves — the quantity is a *derivative*, so it measures how fast the output moves, not where it moves to or what the network computes; a low Jacobian norm next to a working probe says the representation is smooth, and says nothing about whether the direction the probe found is used. Coreference `arxiv-2007.04440` (the same instrument used per layer with the selectivity interaction) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a cosine screen reported as a presence score, the same category error about read-outs that are not function).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 483): **Two normalisations of the same table can produce opposite conclusions, and the discipline is to publish both rather than to argue for one — here raw mCE says architectures improved steadily for six years while the degradation-relative-to-AlexNet version says not one of them improved at all.** The mechanism is worth keeping because it generalises to every aggregate we compute: subtracting the unperturbed baseline from numerator *and* denominator converts "how good is this model under stress" into "how much does this model break when stressed", and those are different questions that a single ratio conflates. The paper's own framing makes the sharper point — Relative mCE is *above* 100 for every post-AlexNet model, so the accuracy gains bought no resilience whatever. For our batteries the concrete rule is that any score computed under intervention should be reported twice, once raw and once baseline-subtracted, with the baseline named; and if the two disagree about the ranking, that disagreement is the result, not a formatting problem to be resolved by picking the friendlier number. Coreference `arxiv-2007.04440` (its corruption-vs-adversarial pair is the qualitative version of the same two-sidedness) and `arxiv-1611.03530` (whose corrupted-label continuum is the same baseline-subtraction question asked about randomisation instead of corruption).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 483): **A benchmark's value is set by what it makes hard to fake, and the three anti-gaming devices here are cheap enough to copy verbatim: publish the generation code so the test set can be recreated rather than only downloaded; forbid training on the scored conditions; and ship an explicitly separate set of *extra* conditions for training and validation.** The third is the clever one, because it lets a research programme obtain robustness without fitting the test, and it forecloses the honest-but-useless objection that the benchmark punishes anyone who trains on similar distortions. The transferable rule for us is that a probe battery should have a published "practice" split distinct from its "scored" split, with the same family structure on both sides, so that hyperparameter choice can be made without contaminating the number we report. The corollary the paper states and then demonstrates is the inverse risk: it warns that directly fitting the test corruptions would overestimate robustness, and four of the eight interventions it tries nonetheless fail to generalise across conditions, which is the empirical proof that the warning was needed. Coreference `arxiv-2411.13117` (size and power on the same table) and `doi-10.1016_j.jmva.2013.02.012` (whose applied example similarly separates the construction used for calibration from the one used for the claim).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 483): **Reporting the failures with the same numbers as the successes is what makes a benchmark paper citable as evidence rather than as advocacy, and the most instructive failure here is the one that fixed its own target and broke everything else: denoising removed the noise it was designed to remove and raised aggregate mCE by 5.4 points because the residual smoothing leaked into the non-noise conditions.** That is the single-target-versus-full-battery lesson in its purest form, and it is the same trap as an intervention that improves one probe's read-out while degrading the battery — the fix is structural: score every intervention on all conditions, not on the condition it was designed for. The second half of the pattern is that the *ordering* of capabilities is not stable across perturbation families: DenseNet and ResNeXt beat ResNet on corruption robustness, lose to it on held-out style, and beat it again on held-out subtype, so a claim of the form "architecture A is more robust" is incomplete without naming which perturbation class. For us that means a single robustness or faithfulness score over a bundle of interventions can average away exactly the structure we would want to publish. Coreference `arxiv-2003.01262` (a training-time knob whose global effect reversed on the robustness half) and `arxiv-1803.06959` (a pooled correlation that reversed sign inside its own clusters).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 482): **A capacity result and a behavioural result answer different questions, and conflating them is the single most common mis-citation of this paper: the corrupted-label experiment shows that no architecture- or algorithm-level complexity measure can explain generalization, while the 2n+d theorem shows the weights can represent any assignment — neither says anything about whether two networks that fit the same data have different internal structure.** For us that gap is the opening, not a footnote: nobody in this ladder (this paper, the 2018 selectivity paper, the 2020 pair) compares activations, probes or circuits between a true-label network and a random-label network at matched accuracy. A predictive white-box model is exactly the thing that would differ across that pair, so the experiment is available and has not been run. The concrete proposal for our battery: train the same architecture to zero training error on true labels and on shuffled labels, then run the identical probe and intervention suite on both — any read-out that behaves the same in both is measuring representational capacity, and the interesting instruments are the ones that separate the conditions. Coreference `arxiv-2003.01262` and `arxiv-2007.04440` (which borrow this paper's construction as a robustness ladder rather than as a capacity statement, a different use of the same instrument) and `arxiv-1803.06959` (whose reliance-on-single-directions statistic is the natural template for closing the gap).

A randomization test that holds architecture, size, hyperparameters and optimizer fixed and destroys only the data-label relation: networks fit RANDOM LABELS perfectly (CIFAR10 Inception/AlexNet/MLPs at 100% train, 9.78-10.61% test), fit shuffled pixels and Gaussian noise (converging faster than random labels do), and on ImageNet reach 95.20% top-1 train on a million random labels at 0.11% test; the corruption ratio sweeps smoothly from signal to chance. Regularization is neither necessary nor sufficient — all explicit regularizers off costs 85.75% vs 89.05% on CIFAR10 and 59.80% vs 77.84% top-1 on ImageNet, batch norm is worth only 3-4% on CIFAR10, and one exception (AlexNet with weight decay) fails to converge on random labels. Theory: a 2n+d-weight depth-2 ReLU net represents any labelling of n points in d dimensions, equivalently depth k at width O(n/k); exact kernel interpolation generalizes well (1.2% MNIST, 0.6% with Gabor filters, 46% CIFAR10 raw pixels) while minimum-norm does not predict it (norm 220 -> 390 as error halves). Limits: no explanation offered, no seeds or error bars, scalar generalization only, and no activation- or feature-level comparison between true-label and random-label networks..
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 482): **Sweep the intervention level, do not toggle it: the randomized-label curve from p = 0 to p = 1 is one panel of training loss, one of convergence slowdown and one of test error, and that three-panel form is cheaper evidence than any before/after comparison because the intermediate levels test monotonicity and the endpoints alone cannot.** The same design shows a result worth carrying for its own sake — convergence time rises by only a small constant factor while generalization error grows smoothly to the chance level, so the difficulty of optimization and the presence of signal are nearly decoupled, which is why the paper can conclude that whatever makes optimization easy must be different from whatever causes generalization. For our intervention reports the transferable rule is to render any label corruption, ablation fraction, steering coefficient or noise scale as a swept curve with the null level labelled on the same axis, and to report the cost axis (here wall-clock/epochs) beside the performance axis. Coreference `doi-10.1016_j.jmva.2013.02.012` (a power curve swept rather than quoted at one point) and `arxiv-2411.13117` (size and power in the same table, the discrete version of the same discipline).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 482): **A negative result should come with the list of things it rules out and the label on each — here VC dimension, Rademacher complexity and uniform stability are each dismissed by a named mechanism rather than collectively by the experiment, and the distinctions are reusable: a hypothesis-class complexity measure is dismissed because the randomization test forces it to its trivial value (~1 on random ±1 labels), while an algorithm-level stability measure is dismissed on a structural ground, that it is independent of the data labels and therefore cannot distinguish two runs whose generalization differs hugely.** That second argument is the sharper one for us, because it applies to any property computed from the training procedure alone — weight norms, step counts, implicit-bias descriptions — none of which can respond to a relabelling that leaves the procedure unchanged. So: before claiming a property explains behaviour, check it varies with the thing being explained while the rest is held fixed, and if it is a procedure property, the relabelling test is the cheapest way to find out. The paper is also honest in the third state — it marks its early-stopping remark as merely potential because a proper test needs a second held-out split — which is the same three-state labelling (proved / observed / potential) recorded from `arxiv-1902.03291`. Coreference `arxiv-1803.06959` (uniform stability's failure restated as the premise for a data-dependent AUC statistic).

20 seeds per setting, bootstrapped 95% CIs, best-validation epoch used, final layer excluded everywhere. Results: suppressing selectivity **raises** mean corrupted accuracy by as much as **4%** on Tiny ImageNetC (normalised corrupted/clean accuracy qualitatively the same), improving normalised accuracy in **12 of 15** Tiny ImageNetC types and **15 of 19** CIFAR10C types and in **all** types under absolute accuracy; the same intervention **lowers** accuracy under both FGSM and PGD in both models, i.e. a genuine sign reversal; the input–output Jacobian is **inversely proportional** to selectivity in both models, supplying the stability explanation for the adversarial half; clean representation dimensionality is inversely proportional to selectivity in early ResNet18 layers (**≤ layer 9**) and across **all** of ResNet20; perturbation-induced change is **higher-dimensional** in low-selectivity networks for both families and higher-dimensional than the clean representation itself under corruption; and the early-layer dimensionality increase is **much larger for adversarial** than for naturalistic perturbations. **Limits as stated:** dimensionality is offered as intuition not demonstrated mechanism, with the explicit caveat that changes need not project onto coding-relevant dimensions; **one representative perturbation per family** for all dimensionality numbers (PGD-25; brightness severity 3 for Tiny ImageNetC, motion blur severity 3 for CIFAR10C); two small models on two classic datasets; and (mine, marked) the regulariser is a single global scale, so the experiment cannot localise which layers or units carry the effect — the very question `arxiv-2003.01262`'s layer-restriction sweep was built to answer, and which this paper does not repeat.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 481): **A property can be worth exactly its trade-off, and the trade-off only becomes visible when you measure both tails of the perturbation distribution — here selectivity makes networks worse under average-case corruption and better under worst-case adversarial attack, the same knob, both models, opposite signs.** Two lessons. First, **any "does property X help?" question with a one-sided robustness metric has a 50% chance of being reported backwards**, and the fix is structural, not statistical: report the property's effect on at least one average-case and one worst-case measure, and if only one is available, say in the entry which half of the trade-off is unmeasured. Second, the pairing also disciplines the *claim*: this paper can say "class selectivity mediates a trade-off" precisely because both halves are causal sweeps of the same knob with the same seeds. For us the concrete rule is that a steering or regularisation intervention that improves a probe battery's score must be accompanied by the metric it is expected to lose on, named in advance — otherwise we are reporting a zero-sum result as a gain, which is the same failure `arxiv-2003.01262` (the paper that built the knob used here) diagnosed on the accuracy side. Coreference `arxiv-1803.06959` (the selectivity index and its ablation instrument) and `arxiv-2611.11035` (where only one outcome of the pushback intervention was reported initially, and the verdict reversed once both were scored).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 481): **A cheap, label-free second instrument can be built from the input–output Jacobian, and it earns its place because it answers a question a probe cannot: how far the output moves per unit input move — the paper finds Jacobian magnitude inversely related to selectivity, which is the whole "why" behind the adversarial half.** For our batteries this is a directly usable addition: a Jacobian-norm read-out per layer is computable from forward-mode or finite-difference passes on held-out inputs, needs no fit, no labels and no probe capacity choice, and is a legitimate stability measurement to report beside a separation measurement. The warning attached is equally usable: **dimensionality of a *difference* matrix is not a mechanism.** The paper measures that adversarial changes are higher-dimensional than corruptions, and its own honest caveat is that neither change need project onto coding-relevant dimensions — so a "the representation moved along N directions" statement describes how the perturbation acted, not what the network computes. Whenever we report a dimensionality, rank, or effective-dimension statistic, name whether it is of the representation or of a difference, because the two answer different questions and only the first is about the model's own geometry.
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 481): **Write the competing predictions down before the sweep — "property helps / property hurts / property is orthogonal, with this observation distinguishing each" — and the paper's three-outcome preamble for corruption robustness is the cleanest example of that discipline in this folder.** It costs three sentences, it converts a post-hoc story into a test, and here it did real work: the *opposite* outcome to the intuitive one came out for corruption, and the authors could state it without hedging because they had already committed to it as one of the live hypotheses. The reusable variant for us: our probe and intervention reports should open with the two or three mutually exclusive readings of the measurement and the number that would separate them, because the folder's recurring failure mode is an instrument (ablation, probe accuracy, cosine screen) reported as though only one reading exists. Coreference `arxiv-2611.14483` (which supplies the claim-vocabulary this design operationalises: measurement-dependence, decodable-vs-used, causal relevance vs causal role) and `arxiv-2003.01262` (the same two-prediction structure applied to necessity and sufficiency).

§2 (the three models and their fixed hyperparameters, the ablation-to-zero convention, **§2.3's selectivity index (μ_max − μ_rest)/(μ_max + μ_rest)** with its stated limitation that it is a discriminability not an information measure, the mutual-information replication); §3 (3.1 corrupted-label ablation and noise curves, the 200-identical-network experiment, the description-length intuition, 3.2 the AUC predictor over training and across 96 hyperparameter settings, 3.3 the dropout-fraction argument and the batch-norm result, 3.4 the selectivity-versus-importance negative result and the per-layer breakdown); memorizing networks are more sensitive to cumulative ablation and to Gaussian noise along random bases; the effect survives with corrupted labels held out of the picture — among **200 identically-specified CIFAR-10 networks** differing only in init, data order and learning rate, the five best-generalizing are more robust than the five worst — but the AUC-versus-error scatter shows discrete clusters and a **negative correlation within a cluster**, so the relation is between-regime rather than monotone; over training the AUC turns at the same epoch train and test loss diverge (**Spearman −0.728** with test loss) and across 192 hyperparameter runs it tracks test accuracy (**Spearman 0.914**), with random 48-of-96 subsampling selecting a top-5 setting **83%** and a top-10 **98%** of the time and landing **1 ± 1.1 points** from the optimum; **dropout** regularizes reliance only up to the dropout fraction used in training while **batch normalization** measurably reduces it, lowers feature-map class selectivity and raises mutual information; and **class selectivity is a poor predictor of importance** — **Spearman 0.095** in the MNIST MLP, **−0.428** in the CIFAR-10 conv net with almost all of it driven by early layers, no relationship in ImageNet, mutual information equally weak, and the filter-weight L1 norm uncorrelated (ImageNet) or negatively correlated (CIFAR-10) with selectivity; early-layer ablations are more impactful than late-layer ones throughout, and selectivity rises with depth. - Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 480): **Discriminability and necessity are separate properties of a direction, and this paper is the measurement that says so — a direction's class tuning correlates with its ablation impact at essentially zero pooled in an MLP (Spearman 0.095) and *negatively* in a conv net (−0.428), so "this direction cleanly separates the classes" licenses no inference whatsoever about "the network uses this direction".** The engineering point is that the two properties need two different instruments and the failure is not a tuning problem: ablation-to-zero is a *removal* instrument, selectivity is a *separation* instrument, and redundancy makes the first systematically under-read, so the honest pairing is a removal measurement and a training-time or fine-tuning-time intervention — which is exactly what the 2020 successor does. For our probe batteries the rule is concrete: a probe's accuracy on held-out examples is a separation number and belongs in the report as such, never as evidence of use; any claim that a direction is the concept the model relies on needs an intervention outside the fit. Coreference `arxiv-2003.01262` (this index put in the loss with a signed scale — the intervention that resolves the gap, and the paper that inherits this failure as its premise) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a residual-cosine screen reported as a presence score, the separation side of the same confusion).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 480): **A shape statistic over an ablation sweep buys robustness against the redundancy objection at a fixed cost, and the cost is ordering variance — so the design that makes single-unit ablation trustworthy is (count many directions, ablate to the *gentlest* fixed value, average over several random orderings) and the read-out is the curve's area, not any single unit's delta.** Two sub-lessons worth copying verbatim. First, **the ablation value is a free parameter that changes the answer**: clamping to zero is less damaging than clamping to the empirical mean activation, so the conventional choice understates contribution and the conservative direction should be stated. Second, **the aggregate relation can be non-monotone where the individual relation is fine**: over 200 identically-specified networks the AUC-versus-error scatter splits into discrete clusters and the correlation *reverses sign inside a cluster*, so one Spearman coefficient over the pooled population would report a relationship that does not hold within either regime. For us: when we aggregate a probe score or an ablation delta across a heterogeneous population of models, dirs or layers, plot the scatter with clusters named before quoting a correlation, because the pooled number can be the wrong sign for every subgroup. Coreference `arxiv-1705.05598` (a method whose whole contribution is a corrected aggregation statistic) and `arxiv-1610.01644` (a linear-probe read-out reported without an intervention companion, the same instrument gap in the other tradition).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 480): **A cheap no-labels predictor is worth building and needs a discipline attached: area under the cumulative ablation curve tracks test accuracy across a 192-run hyperparameter sweep at Spearman 0.914 and turns at the epoch where train and test loss diverge (−0.728 across training), using only training data and forward passes — but the paper reports it as a proof of principle on MNIST and CIFAR-10 and says outright that viability on harder data is untested.** The reusable part is the *shape*: a measurement taken during training, with no held-out split, that predicts a held-out quantity. That is the closest thing in this folder to a white-box predictor of behaviour, and it is worth noting that it predicts *generalization*, not the network's function on any particular input — a distinction that matters for us, since our goal is the second kind of prediction. The discipline: report the correlation *and* the decision-theoretic consequence (here, top-1/top-5/top-10 selection rates and the 1 ± 1.1 point gap to the optimum), because a Spearman number does not tell a practitioner whether to act on it, and report the population over which it was computed. Coreference `arxiv-2003.01262` (which replaces this trained-network read-out with a training-time knob) and `arxiv-1711.06642` (a global test statistic whose usefulness is likewise reported as a profile over settings rather than a single number).

Read from: **full text** — v3 HTML, **100,780 clean chars** (355,562 raw) via `lit-tools/fetch.py`, read as main text (abstract, §1, §2.1-2.2, §3.1-3.3, §4.1-4.3, §5) plus the load-bearing appendices **A.1** (models, training, hyperparameters), **A.2** (training cost), **A.3** (PWCCA intuition, application and formal definition, including the 190-versus-400 pair construction), **A.7** (the fitted-orthonormal-basis upper bound on selectivity), **A.10** (dead units, "single unit necromancy", the leaky-ReLU rescue), **A.11** (activation minimization), **A.12** (VGG16), **A.13** (the precision metric), **A.14** (first-three/last-three-layer restriction) and **A.15** (the remaining comparison figures). **Substance:** class selectivity is the normalized gap between a unit's largest class-conditional mean activation and the mean over the remaining classes; because it is differentiable it can be subtracted from the cross-entropy loss with a signed scale, giving a single knob that raises or lowers selectivity across the whole network during training; averaging within layers before across layers prevents the deep layers, which have more channels, from dominating. Suppressing selectivity **raises** ResNet18/Tiny ImageNet test accuracy to 53.60 ± 0.13 at a scale of −1.0 versus 51.57 ± 0.18 unregularized (mean selectivity 0.22 versus 0.35, a 1.6-fold cut), returns to baseline by a scale of −3.0 (selectivity 0.12), and degrades only past −3.5; ResNet20/CIFAR10 shows no gain but tolerates a cut from 0.22 to 0.07 (>3-fold) before significance; VGG16 tolerates 5-fold for 0.5 point and 10-fold (to 0.03) for ~1 point. Promoting selectivity costs accuracy at the smallest tested scale and collapses it to ~25 percent by a scale of 5.0 in ResNet18 (worse in ResNet20), with the two curves diverging from a magnitude of 0.1 and reaching a ~6-point gap by 2.0. Controls: PWCCA (via the google/svcca implementation) is rotation- and affine-invariant, so the penalty-induced distance to the unregularized network exceeding the seed-only baseline (p < 1.3e-5 in ResNet18 for every scale but −0.1; p < 5e-6 in ResNet20 for all) rules out a re-basing, and the fitted orthonormal-basis upper bound on selectivity also falls with penalty magnitude, ruling out hidden selectivity in another basis — while that bound stays flat across penalties in the last two conv layers of both models, suggesting late layers are insulated. Promotion-side alternatives are closed: at scale 0.7 most ResNet20 units still fire on >80 percent of samples while accuracy is already down 5 points, dead units are ruled out by leaky-ReLUs restoring them without restoring accuracy, and precision moves with the index except where sparsity is a legal route to the index alone. Layer restriction localizes the effect to early layers (first-three restriction reproduces most of it; last-three gives at most a half-point gain in a narrow band in ResNet18 and a **decrease** in ResNet20). Training cost inside the useful range is modest — median epochs to 95 percent of max accuracy goes from 35 ± 1 to at most 51 ± 1.5 in ResNet18, ResNet20 stays at 45 ± 15 with overlapping IQRs.
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 479): **A necessity claim and a sufficiency claim are two different experiments with pre-registered predictions, and running both is what turns "this unit matters" into a falsifiable statement — suppress the property and accuracy must fall if it is necessary; amplify it and accuracy must rise if it is sufficient or merely beneficial.** Here the first prediction inverted (suppression *raised* accuracy by two points) and the second failed catastrophically (amplification collapsed it to a quarter), so the property is neither, and the paper can say so without a single correlational number. The generalisable engineering is what makes this cheap: **choose a unit-level statistic that is differentiable, put it in the loss with a signed scale, and sweep the scale** — because a differentiable statistic can be optimized against during training, which sidesteps the redundancy objection that poisons single-unit ablation (a replicated property survives removal of any one copy, so ablation reads harmless regardless of importance). For our batteries the rule is direct: every "direction D is the concept" claim should be accompanied by a training-time or fine-tuning-time sweep that pushes D up and down, because a read-out that predicts a label under one direction proves nothing about whether the network uses that direction. Coreference `arxiv-2211.04367` (the same dissociation from the ablation side, where probe-selected units and ablation-selected units barely overlap) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a residual-cosine screen whose claim is likewise about a read-out rather than about function).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 479): **Every claim that a property disappeared has a free escape hatch — the representation may have been re-coded off the axis you measured — and closing it needs two instruments, not one: an affine-invariant distance calibrated against a same-recipe seed baseline, and a re-optimized basis giving an upper bound on the property you claim to have removed.** The calibration is the part that is almost always skipped: the honest comparison is not "are the two representations different" but "are they more different than two runs of the identical recipe disagree by", and here that baseline is built from the 190 within-condition replicate pairs while the claim is tested on 400 cross-condition ones — a construction anyone can copy. The upper-bound instrument is sharper still, because it is exactly what a probe already is: fitting an unconstrained linear probe is a search over directions for the one that maximizes the very quantity in question, so **a fixed-direction probe and a best-of-all-directions probe answer two different questions, and reporting only the first cannot distinguish "the feature is gone" from "the feature moved"**. Concretely for us: whenever we report that a feature, direction or neuron set was suppressed by training, ablation or a steering intervention, report both the fixed-direction read-out and the best-direction upper bound on held-out data, and report a seed-matched null for both. Coreference `arxiv-2003.01262`'s own seed (Morcos et al.'s class selectivity index, unread here) and `arxiv-2412.06410` (a dictionary-based read-out whose completeness claims have the same off-basis problem in the other direction).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 479): **The layer-restriction ablation is the cheapest localiser in the box, and its result here runs against the intuition that abstract, output-adjacent units are the important ones: constraining only the first three layers reproduces most of the accuracy effect (both the gain from suppression and the loss from promotion), while constraining only the last three gives at most a half-point gain in a narrow band in one model and a genuine accuracy *decrease* in the other — so class selectivity is least necessary, and most harmful, early.** Two things to carry. (1) When a constraint has a large global effect, re-run it on a prefix and a suffix of the stack before attributing the mechanism to the property in general, because the global average hides whether the model is responding to the property or to its distribution across depth — and the cost is one extra sweep. (2) The counter-intuitive direction is itself a reportable finding: a statistic whose functional weight is greatest early is a statistic measured late by most pipelines, which read out near the output, and that mismatch is the same one the mechanistic-interpretability literature keeps finding when it probes final layers and then claims a concept is "used". Coreference `arxiv-2310.17611` (single-layer screens with no depth sweep) and `arxiv-1902.03291` (the same lesson about aggregation choices silently changing what a statistic measures).

Multivariate Anal.* **117 (2013) 193-213**, DOI 10.1016/j.jmva.2013.02.012, received 2010-08-12, online 2013-02-27, **code: R package `energy` (v1.1-1 at the time, GPL)**. Read from: **full text** — the published PDF from a course mirror, 12 pages, ~52,500 characters as extracted, read in four slices: abstract and §1 (the motivation, the prior-work ladder through Kosorok, Lyons, Schott, Ledoit-Wolf, Heer); §2 (dCov/dCor definitions, the explicit double-centred computing formula, §2.3's motivation — the diagonal-versus-off-diagonal expectation gap and the (n-1)/n^2 limit — §2.4's corrected entries A*, B*); §3 (Lemma 1, Lemma 2's identity linking the two corrected sums, Proposition 1's three-moment expansion, Proposition 2's unbiasedness, Lemma 3's Gaussian limit, **Theorem 1**'s Student-t limit with **nu = n(n-3)/2** degrees of freedom, Corollaries 1-2, Example 1 with the R console output); §4-5 (Proposition 3's random-window exchangeability, the AR(1) power study, the DJIA example) and Appendix A.1's bias derivation. **Substance:** for fixed n the off-diagonal entries of the double-centred matrix have expectation alpha/n and the diagonal alpha/n - alpha, and alpha = E|X - X'| diverges with dimension, so the plug-in coefficient converges to 1 under independence; the correction rescales off-diagonal entries by n/(n-1) after subtracting a_ij/n and diagonal entries to n/(n-1)(row mean - grand mean), which makes every entry mean-zero, and summing their elementwise products with a doubled diagonal term divided by n(n-3) is unbiased for the squared population dCov. In the limit the corrected coefficient is a cosine between independent Gaussian vectors in n(n-3)/2 dimensions, so its t-transform is Student t. **Numbers, as printed:** Table 1 at n = 30, uncorrected R from 0.4303 (p=q=1) to 0.99990 (p=q=16,384) while the corrected R* stays between -0.111 and 0.118 and T between -2.246 and 2.392; 1,000 replications give type-1 error 0.100 at the 10 per cent level and 0.046 at 5 per cent; the linear example rejects in 1,000 of 1,000 at 5 per cent; at n = 30 the degrees of freedom are 404; the DJIA table's largest T is 16.16 (C vs JPM) and its smallest -1.45 (INTC vs JNJ).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 478): **In the high-dimension regime the estimator's bias is not a small-sample nuisance but the entire signal, and it is diagnosable by a single ratio anyone can compute before trusting an aggregate number: compare the expectation of a matrix entry on the diagonal against the expectation off it, and if the two differ by a term that grows with the count of coordinates while the sample size is fixed, the normalisation is already broken.** The mechanism here is concrete and transfers: the diagonal entry of a double-centred distance matrix carries the mean distance, the off-diagonal carries a fraction 1/n of it, and the mean distance grows like the square root of the dimension — so the diagonal dominates exactly in the regime people actually use, and the statistic converges to its trivial maximum under a true null. The repair is equally transferable: **make every entry mean-zero by an explicit rescaling with a known constant**, then average. For our probe batteries the practical rule is to run the same test on the entries of whatever per-direction table we aggregate — an m-by-m matrix of pairwise neighbour scores, a direction-by-example matrix of probe read-outs — and check the diagonal and marginals sit on the same scale; if they do not, either drop the diagonal or rescale it, never average through it. This is the finite-n twin of `arxiv-1902.03291`, which proves the asymptotic version of the same collapse from the other end; read together they say the aggregate over many coordinates is trustworthy only after a correction whose constant is derived, and that a raw average over a large bundle of directions is close to uninformative.
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 478): **A statistic that is a ratio of a covariance-like quantity to the geometric mean of two variances inherits a free null whenever the same random scaling appears in numerator and denominator — here the corrected coefficient is a cosine of two independent Gaussian vectors, so the unknown variance cancels and the null becomes an exact Student t with a degrees-of-freedom count fixed by the sample size alone.** That is the reusable design idea: normalise so the nuisance does, then look up the law instead of resampling it. It buys two things the folder's other dependence tests paid ten to a hundred resamples for: a per-direction scan with no permutation cost, and a *readable strength number* — because the corrected coefficient no longer drifts to one, its magnitude means something in the same units across dimensions. The caveats travel with it and both are stated in the paper: the law is a limit in dimension, not in n, so the honest question is whether p is large relative to n (the paper offers no crossover guidance and its companion literature treats small p as outside the regime); and the corrected coefficient can be negative. For us the concrete use is a cheap screening pass over hundreds of candidate probe directions where the null is arithmetic, with any direction that survives followed up by the costlier exact tests the folder already holds. Coreference `arxiv-1602.04387` (a null derived by spectral factorisation — the same "make the null arithmetic" ambition reached by a different route) and `arxiv-1902.03291` (the negative result that no correction of the joint statistic recovers the omnibus property in high dimension — the limit on how far this pattern reaches).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 478): **Correlated observations can be made independent by construction rather than by modelling, and the construction is one line: take random contiguous windows of the fixed observed series, and the window vectors are exchangeable, hence conditionally iid given the permutation-invariant sigma algebra, which is enough for any test whose null law survives conditioning (and here the variance cancels, so the t law does).** Two generalisations for us. (1) Activation batteries have exactly the correlated-structure problem the time-series section names: adjacent token positions, overlapping prompts drawn from one session, multiple read-outs from one forward pass. The right fix is not to pretend they are independent but to *sample* exchangeable units — random windows of length p with p chosen so that the windows overlap into the regime that interests you — and to report the achieved level against a white-noise control, which is what the paper's Example 3 does and what a bootstrapped p-value over correlated activations silently skips. (2) The same section is an honest instance of the folder's recurring warning: strong stationarity alone guarantees nothing, the conditional CLT is an extra hypothesis the authors invoke rather than prove, and they say the test's validity on real financial series rests on assuming log-returns satisfy it. Coreference `arxiv-2411.13117` (size-and-power reported together — the discipline the paper's Example 3 restates) and `arxiv-1605.08732` (a statistic whose evaluation cost was the *only* thing established, licensing no claim about the data structure it ran on — the mirror image of this paper's applied section).

the leading term is a sum of squared *linear* cross-covariances, so the joint omnibus statistic degenerates to a linear-dependence functional as the dimension grows; the marginal aggregates are the unified quantity at absolute-distance and at kernelised distance, which is why they inherit the same t limit while keeping each coordinate's nonlinearity. **Numbers, as printed:** the Gaussian non-centrality sandwich 0.89^2 * phi_2 <= phi_1 <= phi_2; Table 3 (Y = X squared), n = 10, p = 30, alpha = 0.05: dCov 0.101 vs mdCov 0.526, hCov 0.098 vs mhCov 0.769 (Gaussian), hCov 0.124 vs mhCov 0.945 (Laplacian); n = 10, p = 5, alpha = 0.05: dCov 0.231 vs mdCov 0.495; n = 60, p = 30, alpha = 0.05: dCov 0.346 vs mdCov 1.000; Table 4 (sine/cosine), n = 10, p = 30, alpha = 0.05: dCov 0.066 vs mdCov 0.434; Table 2 (Gaussian alternative), n = 10, p = 30, alpha = 0.05: dCov 0.936 vs mdCov 0.849, hCov 0.935 vs mhCov 0.648, Laplacian hCov 0.921 vs mhCov 0.468; Table 1 (size), all six statistics near nominal at all three levels. 200 permutations, 5000 Monte Carlo repetitions throughout.
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 477): **An omnibus guarantee can be asymptotic in the sample and empty in the dimension, and the mechanism is a Taylor expansion that leaks the statistic's whole nonlinear content into a remainder: expand the pairwise distance around its expectation and the quartic kernel factors into a product of coordinate differences, so the sum over all p*q coordinate pairs becomes a sum of squared covariances.** The generalisable diagnostic for us is the *direction of aggregation*: aggregating **coordinates** averages their individual covariances and therefore keeps only the linear part, while aggregating **componentwise scores** averages nothing away and keeps each coordinate's nonlinearity. That rule can be applied without any theory — whenever a battery reports one dependence number over a large bundle of directions, ask whether the number was formed by summing the vectors or by summing per-direction statistics, because with p in the thousands the two are not merely different in power, they measure different things. A corollary worth keeping as a shortcut: in high dimension the squared distance correlation equals the much cheaper RV coefficient asymptotically, so the expensive instrument is buyable at a trace's price. Coreference `arxiv-1605.08732` and `arxiv-1504.00964` (the t\* family, whose entire appeal was the omnibus property this paper shows does not survive high dimension — the folder now holds both sides of that trade) and `arxiv-1708.05653` (where the same lesson appears as the partial-versus-joint multivariate extension).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 477): **The control that catches a blind screen is a designed alternative class, and here it is stated in one set-theoretic line any battery can copy: the sparse alternative is the set of pairs that are dependent coordinate-wise with *zero* cross-covariance.** Every statistic in the family reads exactly nominal size on it, so a practitioner who only benchmarks on Gaussian-copula dependence never discovers that their joint statistic has no power there — and the blindness is not a deficit more data fixes, because the joint tests' power does not climb with n while the marginal ones do. For our batteries the transferable object is the *class*, not the test: name the dependence structures a screen is provably blind to (here, any nonlinearity sitting inside a single coordinate pair), include one such row in every table, and report the joint and marginal statistics side by side on it so the blindness is visible in the same units as the successes. That is the same discipline as `arxiv-2411.13117`'s two-column reporting and `arxiv-1201.3522`'s null row printed beside its power cells, applied to the *alternative* side rather than the null side. Coreference this paper's own Table 3 and `arxiv-1711.06642` (the same swamping effect reached from the max-versus-sum norm choice).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 477): **Absence of an omnibus test is a claim about information rather than about estimators, and this paper states it in the only form that can be checked: it conjectures that at fixed sample size no omnibus test exists, and that even with n growing faster than the dimension it sees no asymptotic route to one.** The consequence for us is a scoping rule for our own prediction claims: a probe battery evaluated on one alternative family is not evidence of omnibus detection power, and the honest report says which family it was evaluated on. The second half of the pattern is a sentence-level habit worth copying — the authors keep apart what they **proved** (the decomposition and the trivial power), what they **observed** (the simulation ordering across kernels), and what they **conjectured** (no omnibus test), each in a different grammatical form. That three-state labelling is the folder's cleanest reporting template for a negative result. Coreference `arxiv-1804.07203` (a hardness theorem, the proved version of the same kind of statement) and `arxiv-1910.12327` (a strength estimate adopted precisely because a verdict's error direction is unreportable).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 476): **A quartic order statistic becomes quadratic when a symmetry of the kernel collapses the inner sum, and the collapse is worth more than any clever data structure: the expensive part of t\* is not that there are n^4 tuples, it is that nobody had noticed that the sum over all 24 orderings of a fixed four-element subset is a constant that depends only on the pattern class — 16, -8 or 0 — so the entire quadruple enumeration reduces to counting one class of quadruples.** The generalisable recipe, and it is the same one this folder recorded for range queries and for complement mass: **before optimising the enumeration, look for the group action that makes the summand constant on orbits**, because an orbit with a closed-form total turns a counting problem into a range-counting problem, and range counts are what trees answer in log time. The second, more uncomfortable half is that the constant is derived by a five-page case analysis and proved in an appendix — the "some thought" step is where the whole paper lives, and it is exactly the step a reimplementation will get wrong silently, since the algorithm is correct only if 16/-8/0 is right. For our own screens: when we score a bundle of tuples (four examples, four heads, four token positions), check whether the score is invariant to relabelling first, because if it is, the aggregate is a count and the count is cheap. Coreference `arxiv-1605.08732` (the same statistic in linear space, and it *quotes* this paper's 16/-8 decomposition rather than rederiving it) and `arxiv-1708.05653` (the generalised class whose rank-indicator-and-subgroup framing is the abstract reason the orbits have closed-form totals).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 476): **Ties are not a nuisance to be handled by jittering — they are a third pattern class, and the correct handling of a third class is over-count-then-subtract, with the correction computed by a second pass in the opposite direction.** The mechanical reason is worth carrying: the first pass can only see aggregate counts in the tree, and the condition that generates the over-count involves a relationship *between two earlier points* (they share a tied y value inside the straddled interval), which an aggregate query cannot express — so the algorithm deliberately lets the wrong answer in, then re-expresses the correction as a sum over the *later* point, where the same condition becomes two range queries, and sweeps in reverse. Two things follow for us. (1) When an exact counting algorithm is built on aggregate summaries, any condition internal to the summarised set has to be priced as a separate term and recovered by a complementary ordering — that is a reusable engineering pattern, not a quirk of this paper. (2) The paper's richer claim is that **the cost order is unchanged**: the general algorithm is still n^2 log n, only with more per-pair queries, and the appendix shows the biased V-statistic form is likewise free once correction coefficients of one half and one quarter are applied — so exactness under ties is an implementation detail and never an argument for approximation. Contrast with `arxiv-1605.08732`, where the tied case was where the elegant structure degraded; here the ties cost a second sweep and nothing more. Coreference `arxiv-1602.04387` (the same 'inseparable' class as a degeneracy condition in the null law) and `arxiv-1501.01732` (rank transforms, where the tie convention silently defines the statistic).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 476): **The most useful number in this paper is in the table that argues *against* the cheaper method, and the direction of the correction is counter-intuitive: subsampling quadruples (subset size four, the size the original authors suggested) leaves a relative variance of *fifty-seven times* the exact statistic's after twelve and a half thousand resamples, while raising the subset to thirty at *two hundred* resamples gives 8.24 and at 12,800 gives 1.04.** So the resample count is the wrong knob by orders of magnitude; the subset size is the knob, because variance scales with the size of the tuple the statistic is averaged over and only mildly with the count. This generalises directly to any bootstrap or subsample shortcut in our batteries — estimate on small subsets of examples and average — and the correction is to grow the subset, not the repeat count. The same paper also supplies the reporting convention the folder keeps paying for: the benchmark reports exact versus approximate on one axis and elapsed time on the other, so the reader sees what the speed cost in variance on the same page, which is the only place a reader will ever look for it. Coreference `arxiv-1401.5031` (precision/recall/seconds in one table) and `arxiv-1605.08732` (a complexity claim with no variance companion — this paper is the companion).

Read from: **full text** — v2 HTML, 58,516 clean chars, five slices, main text plus the whole supplement. **Substance:** the statistic T is a sum over all ordered pairs (i,j) of the Pearson chi-square statistic S(i,j) of the 2x2 table formed by "within d(x_i,x_j) of x_i" crossed with "within d(y_i,y_j) of y_i" over the remaining N-2 points; the oracle version (fixed centre and radii around a point of dependence) is trivially consistent, and using every point as a centre and every other point as a radius removes the oracle; distances need only be norm-induced, and inference is by permutation of the Y indices; consistency (Theorem 2.1, four continuous/discrete/mixed cases) is proved by choosing a positive-probability near region A1 and a middle annulus A2 around the point of dependence and using the triangle inequality to show A1 points are always ranked nearer to i than A2 points in *both* spaces, so T exceeds delta*N^3 with probability 1 while under independence S(i,j) is asymptotically chi-square-1 and T concentrates near N(N-1); O(N^2 log N) via merge-sort inversion counting. **Numbers, as printed:** at N=50, alpha=0.05, circle 0.993 vs dCov 0.000, two parabolas 1.000 vs 0.303, diamond 0.662 vs 0.037, W 1.000 vs 0.853, one parabola 0.998 vs 0.975, four-clouds null 0.050 vs 0.050; Y=log(X^2) in 5-D 0.945 vs 0.629 at N=50; Y_j=X_j*eps_j 0.968 vs 0.443; 1000-D mixtures of 10 components under multivariate t(3) 1.000 vs 0.345 at N=200 and 0.570 vs 0.100 at N=50, under multivariate Cauchy 0.580 vs 0.020 at N=300 (dCov has essentially none at any N up to 300); 100-D correlated-block null power 0.046/0.043/0.051 at N=30/40/50; HapMap chromosomes 21 vs 22, 43 subjects, 31,858 and 36,264 SNPs, p<1e-4 vs dCov 6e-4; aircraft data 230 designs both tests p<=0.00001 against Pearson 0.8001, and on 100 resamples of 30 points the new test is below 0.05 in 58 runs against 18 for dCov; a likelihood-ratio variant of the same aggregation has very similar power.
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 475): **A test statistic built as a sum of local 2x2 contingency tables over a sweep of scales is the cheapest way to get consistency without moment assumptions or a null limit law, and the price is exactly what we cannot pay — it certifies dependence but cannot say where or how.** The mechanism is worth keeping separately from the statistic: pick a local functional that is zero under independence *at a specific location and scale* (here chi-square on one 2x2 table), let the data sweep centre and scale rather than choosing them, sum the evidence, and calibrate by permutation. Consistency then follows from a single positive-probability pocket of dependence, which is why the arguments only need density continuity at one point and never a moment. The limitation is structural, not fixable by a better summand: the aggregate is a scalar, and reconstructing the local structure means going back to the individual terms with a multiple-comparison correction the paper does not supply. For us the transferable object is the *swept local functional*, not T — a per-pair score that we could read out as a map, with the permutation discipline as the calibration. Coreference `arxiv-1804.07203` (the theorem that a third route to the same certification — test soundness in a nonlinear conditional setting — is impossible) and `arxiv-1708.05653` (the consistency-only measure whose localisation was equally deferred).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 475): **Rank-based statistics survive the loss of moments that destroys the kernel-metric ones, and the paper's own numbers make that the dominant effect rather than a footnote: dCov is consistent only for laws with finite first moments, so under multivariate Cauchy it has essentially no power at any sample size tested while the rank-summed test reaches 0.58 at N=300 in 1000 dimensions.** The pattern to file is that any statistic whose null and alternative behaviour routes through a mean of distances inherits an integrability requirement that a statistic routing through *order* does not — and in our setting (activations, token-level scores, heavy-tailed read-outs) the tail assumption is precisely the one we have least warrant for. Practically: prefer order statistics over moment statistics when the read-out may be heavy-tailed, and quote the power comparison at the tails rather than only on Gaussian fixtures, because the Gaussian case is where the moment-based method looks fine. Coreference `arxiv-1909.10140` (a rank coefficient whose null is distribution-free for the same reason) and `arxiv-2411.13117` (size-and-power reporting in both regimes).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 475): **The same experiment doubled as the null check and the sanity check, and that habit is the one to copy: every simulation table carries the independence setting (four clouds, m1 = 0, I1 empty) as one of its own rows, so the reader sees the empirical level next to the empirical power in the same units.** That is cheaper and more convincing than a separate calibration section, and it caught the thing a power table alone hides — the new test's null row sits at 0.050 exactly, so the large power gaps are not bought by an inflated size. The third pattern, so it is the third pattern: it is a reporting convention rather than a mechanism, and it is the one we most often skip. Coreference `doi-10.3150_13-BEJ514` (its null cells reported the same way) and `arxiv-2411.13117`.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 474): **A dependence measure's null law is computable exactly when its kernel's second-order projection factorises, and the factorisation is what makes the spectrum a product of two one-dimensional spectra rather than the spectrum of an intractable operator: under independence the projected kernel splits into a pure-X part times a pure-Y part, so the eigenvalues are pairwise products, and in the continuous case the one-dimensional part is provably the Cramér-von Mises kernel whose spectrum is already known.** That is the mechanism behind the whole entry and it generalises into a practical test: **before reaching for a permutation loop, check whether the statistic's projection factorises under the null**, because if it does the null is arithmetic. For our batteries the payoff is direct — the order-n^4 sign covariance gets a null in closed form, so a rank screen over many read-out directions no longer pays a resample cost per direction, which is the objection every earlier entry in this arc had to concede. Extending our own probes rather than the statistic, we need the two-dimensional form of the same idea: any design whose two arguments are *drawn independently by construction* (a probe scored against a shuffled label, two heads evaluated on independent inputs) has this factorisation for free. Coreference `arxiv-1501.01732` (which reproves this null from the sums-of-rank-correlations side, with 36/pi^4 versus 1/pi^4 being the same random variable twice) and `arxiv-1605.08732` (the cheap evaluator — the other half of making the four-point screen affordable).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 474): **Degeneracy of the first-order projection is not a defect of the estimator but a fingerprint of exactly-independence, and the paper proves it in both directions: the projection vanishes identically under independence for any law, and for any continuous law with rectangular support it is strictly variable under any dependence whatsoever.** Two consequences. (1) A screen that reports the point estimate and its standard error is reporting the wrong object when the estimate is near zero — the diagnostic that carries the evidence is whether the projection is degenerate, because that is the quantity the theorem is about, and a small t* with a live projection is a finite-sample accident rather than a verdict. (2) The direction of the implication is a *continuity* hypothesis, so the guarantee is a property of the declared law class, matching the recurring lesson of this arc that positivity and consistency claims die outside the setting they were proved in: here the paper says outright that whether tau-star still vanishes only under independence for laws that are neither continuous, discrete-finite nor mixed is unknown, which means the test's consistency is inherited from `doi-10.3150_13-BEJ514` and not re-established. Coreference `arxiv-1708.05653` (the slowest-case theorem whose positivity hypothesis is likewise dimensional) and `arxiv-1909.10140` (a coefficient whose ceiling is an n-dependent finite-sample property rather than an asymptotic one).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 474): **Asymptotic accuracy and asymptotic validity are reported separately here and the split is instructive: the null approximation is shown to be close by n of 80 across three marginal types, while the power comparisons are one curve per alternative family against that family's own classical test, and the family that loses is the one where the dependence is deliberately non-ordinal — the sign covariance is beaten decisively by a contingency-table test there and wins just as decisively on the ordinal mixture.** That is the third confirmation in this arc that a rank measure's competence is a profile over alternative families and not a scalar, and it adds a reportable distinction for us: when a probe read-out is ordinal in the label (a graded sentiment, a Likert scale, a score), the four-point rank screen is the better instrument than a contingency test, and when the label is a nominal class, it is the worse one — a decision rule rather than a preference. The companion reporting habit is the sample-size section's: give a distribution-free variance bound *and* a distribution-specific one, plot both against simulation, and say which one you used, because the universal bound is drastically conservative and quietly drives sample-size decisions here. Coreference `arxiv-1711.06642` (a power profile with an explicit multiscale average instead of a chosen scale) and `arxiv-2411.13117` (the two-column size-and-power reporting rule).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 473): **"Zero exactly under independence" is bought by looking at four points instead of two, and the price is that the object stops being decomposable: replace squared distances in tau-squared with absolute differences and you get a kernel whose expectation is zero iff independent — but the resulting coefficient is provably not a Hilbert-Schmidt criterion and provably not the norm of a random element, which is why its positivity proof runs to five pages of conditional-CDF algebra where distance covariance's takes three lines.** That trade is the sharpest statement in the folder of what kernelisation buys and costs: a kernel representation is what licenses a closed-form null (eigenvalues of a Gram matrix), eigenvalues of a matrix, and a cheap estimator, and the four-point sign kernel gives up all three in exchange for a definition a reader can hold in their head. Practically, for us: use tau-star when the question is "is there *any* dependence" and the honest answer needed is a p-value from a permutation null, and use the distance/kernel family when the question is "how much, and through what", because the eigen-decomposition is what lets you say *which direction*. Coreference `arxiv-1708.05653` (which places tau* in a subgroup family and shows what the invariance costs) and `arxiv-1202.3775` (the kernel test whose entire advantage was a computable null — the exact thing tau* declines to have).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 473): **A coefficient's *definitional* complexity has a countable form — the number of independent replications it needs — and ranking measures by that number is a legitimate, checkable argument that the paper uses to justify its whole existence: tau needs two, rho needs three, tau-star needs four, Hoeffding needs five.** The companion finding is that the ranking does not transfer to power, and the paper's own numbers are the proof: on nine settings tau-star beats D in seven and H in four, but H wins decisively exactly where five-point concordance is geometrically easy (points on a single line or in a sharp zig-zag) and D wins on plain bivariate normal at correlation 0.5. **The explanatory mechanism is worth carrying as a general principle for choosing a battery: each statistic's power is high where its own combinatorial pattern is likely under the alternative, so a battery of measures with different pattern-arity is a coverage argument rather than a redundancy.** For our probe batteries this is the justification for carrying both a pairwise rank statistic and a four-point one: a relation that is monotone lights up the first, a relation that is a parity or zig-zag structure lights up the second, and neither is a mild variant of the other. Coreference `arxiv-1501.01732` (the same lesson at the block level: the norm over the signal vector chooses which alternative family you can see) and `arxiv-1605.08732` (the cheap evaluator for the four-point case, since n^4 is what makes the arity expensive).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 473): **A positivity proof that needs the real line is a genuine hypothesis and not a technicality: the authors exhibit an eight-point configuration in R^8 — two well-separated orthogonal blocks, each a simplex-like set of four vectors — where the very same coefficient is NEGATIVE, so the sign property is a property of the metric's dimension and geometry rather than of the construction.** That is the third distinct "the guarantee dies outside its declared setting" instance this arc has produced, alongside the singular-law failure of distance covariance on the unit circle and the parity blindness of the joint multivariate sign covariance, and it makes a general reporting rule: **state the ambient geometry a rank measure was proved in, because extrapolating a positivity/consistency theorem from R to a 4096-dimensional activation space is exactly the move a probing paper makes without noticing.** The safe move for us is to keep every such measure applied to a *scalar* read-out (one direction projected to a score), where the R-line hypothesis holds by construction, and to treat any multivariate version as a separate, weaker claim. Also worth copying as a convention: the theorem's hypothesis is explicitly flagged as conjecturally unnecessary, so the paper distinguishes what it proved, what it believes, and what it disproved — three states, each labelled. Coreference `arxiv-1708.05653` (the same three-state labelling, and the counterexample that kills its joint extension) and `arxiv-1910.12327` (a strength estimate with no positivity claim to protect, hence no geometric hypothesis to state).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 472): **A rank statistic that decomposes into a sum over pairs of range counts in the rank plane is quadratic, full stop — build one cumulative-count array with an inclusion–exclusion sweep and both quadrant terms of each pair become constant-time array lookups, no balanced tree and no hash — and the variant that needs a *weighted* range count (sums of within-value pairs rather than point counts) costs exactly one more sweep.** This closes the computational arc that `arxiv-1708.05653` opened and `arxiv-1501.01732` rescales, and the transferable form for our batteries is a recipe: sort each read-out direction against the label once (n log n), allocate one (n+1)² accumulator, sweep it once, then a plain double loop over pairs scores the whole sign covariance. Two caveats travel with it, both visible in the paper rather than stated by the authors. First, **the space term is quadratic too**, so what caps n here is the array and not the arithmetic — at the sample sizes our activation batteries run at, the accumulator is the allocation that decides feasibility, and the honest engineering note names it. Second, **ties multiply the work rather than the cost order**: the tie-free case needs one count, the tie case needs two counts plus five auxiliary quadrant/equality counts plus a second weighted array, and each term rests on a product formula the note *quotes* from Weihs et al. rather than rederives — which is the recurring shape of "the clean version is published, the version our data actually needs is a footnote". Coreference `arxiv-1708.05653` (the range-tree generalisation, whose own reported crossover at about 3,000 points is the timing evidence this note does not provide) and `arxiv-1501.01732` (where the per-pair matrix, not the null, is the expensive object — the same accounting turned round).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 472): **"Same estimator, cheaper evaluator" is a legitimate contribution and licenses nothing about usefulness, and this note is the folder's cleanest specimen of the distinction: it establishes a complexity class and then its last paragraph concedes that the *power* of the measure relative to finer-partition methods is an open question it did not touch.** That is the right shape for a methods section and the wrong shape for a results section, and the gap has a concrete version for us: a probe sweep that runs in seconds instead of hours is not evidence that the statistic it computes detects what we believe it detects, so the two claims need separate support and should be written in separate sentences. There is a second, subtler item worth copying — the abs page's title drops the hyphen in "Bergsma-Dassios" and drops the colon the in-paper reference uses, and this entry quotes the abs page verbatim rather than silently repairing it — the same literal-preservation rule that governs how we cite keys and identifiers. Also, as a corpus fact: this is the first entry in the recent run of **471** whose entire content is a short note with zero experiments and five references, and it is still worth the entry, because the method it describes is the one every later rank screen in this folder silently assumes is affordable. Coreference `arxiv-2611.09945` (a matched null for every headline number — the discipline that keeps a cheap statistic honest) and `arxiv-1804.07203` (a paper whose entire content is a bound and whose choices are likewise licensed separately from its computation).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 471): **"Here is one p-value for whether this whole block is independent" is a different test at every choice of norm over the signal vector, and the two choices in the literature are not ranked — they are optimal against different alternatives: the max-of-pairwise statistic is rate-optimal for the sup norm (one strong pair, threshold of order sqrt(log m / n)) and is proved here to have *no* power at all against constant-size equicorrelated signal, while the sum-of-squares statistics are rate-optimal for the Euclidean norm and read 0.020-0.058 in exactly the cells where a single strong pair would be caught.** For our batteries this settles a reporting question the folder has circled for many entries: when we test whether a bundle of directions or heads carries any relation to a label, the honest null is a sentence of the form "no pair out of m-choose-2 exceeds what the sup norm predicts" *or* "the total squared signal is below what the Euclidean norm predicts", and the two can disagree completely on the same data, so the choice belongs in the report rather than in the code. Rule: pick the norm that matches the hypothesis you actually care about — redundancy spread across many directions is a Euclidean claim, a single culprit direction is a sup claim — and if you want both, run both and say so, because neither test substitutes for the other. Coreference `arxiv-1711.06642` (a global MI test whose power is likewise a profile over alternative families) and `arxiv-2206.05829` (a relation stated over a region of conditioning sets rather than at a point — the same "which object is the claim about" discipline).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 471): **The cost of a global statistic is almost entirely in its per-pair kernel and nothing else, so the whole family is affordable if — and only if — each measure's recentring constant is known in closed form; here every constant is an elementary expression in n (decaying like n^-d for degeneracy order d) and tabulated for four measures, which is what lets a batteried test skip the permutation loop entirely.** Two consequences we can reuse. (1) The matrix of pairwise numbers is the expensive object, so compute it once and score all three statistics off it; the recentring term is separable across pairs and can be subtracted afterwards. (2) The unbiased variant costs a factor in the kernel degree (k to 2k) but can still be computed in O(n^k) by precomputing the kernel on every k-tuple and then answering each "how much kernel mass sits on the complement" query by inclusion-exclusion over subsets of the tuple — the same prefix-sum trick this folder recorded for range queries in `arxiv-1708.05653`, applied to combinatorial complement rather than geometric containment. For our probe batteries the practical lesson is that a rank screen over many candidate read-out directions is cheap *because* the per-direction statistic is O(n log n) and the null constant is analytic; the bottleneck is never the null. Coreference `arxiv-1708.05653` (range-tree box queries versus tuple enumeration, with the crossover reported) and `arxiv-1202.3775` (a Gamma moment-matched null replacing permutations, the same trade one level down).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 471): **Degeneracy order is the single number that decides the rate, and it is a property of the *estimator*'s kernel rather than of the dependence it measures — so two measures of the same ideal quantity can need scalings of different orders, and this is where a careful practitioner silently breaks a test.** The concrete case: Kendall's tau is non-degenerate (d = 1) while Hoeffding's D and the Bergsma–Dassios t* are degenerate of order two (d = 2) *under independence only*, so the sum statistics built on them need n-squared/m rather than n/m, and the tabulated zeta and eta constants differ by orders of magnitude (1/9 for tau and the Spearman term, 1/225 for t*, 1/810000 for D). The transferable rules: (a) whenever we assemble a battery of measures into one score, the rescaling must be *per measure*, never shared, and the paper's own Table 1 is the template; (b) an estimator that is degenerate under the null is precisely a measure that detects more kinds of dependence — t* sees what D sees and more — so the extra rescaling cost is the price of the wider alternative class, not an inefficiency to be tuned away; and (c) the bias of the plug-in statistic is likewise set by d (order n^-d), so recentring is arithmetic rather than bootstrap, which is what makes an exact-ish null affordable across thousands of pairs. Coreference `arxiv-1708.05653` (d = 2 degeneracy producing a chi-square-mixture limit and the 36/pi^4 versus 1/pi^4 constants — the same object seen from the bivariate side) and `arxiv-1606.00304` (an estimator family whose bias order, not variance, set every reported decimal).
