- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 470): **A dependence measure is a triple, not a formula, and naming the triple is what makes the invariances checkable: a rank indicator (which ordering pattern counts as concordant), a permutation subgroup with as many even as odd members (which arrangements cancel), and an integration measure over cutpoints (joint law or product of marginals).** Fix the triple and the two properties a probe screen actually needs come free — invariance to any strictly increasing per-coordinate change, and exact zero under independence — because both follow from parity bookkeeping in the group and from the indicator depending on the data only through ranks. What does *not* come free is detection, and the paper again and again separates the two: R is the same construction as D with the integration measure swapped and only R is proved to detect every dependence; Spearman's ρ is a *sum* of members but not a member, because its signs do not follow parity. For us the operational rule is that every "correlation between probe and label" number should be reported as a named triple, and that swapping the integration measure is a free, one-line change that can turn a measure with a counterexample into one without. Coreference `arxiv-1910.12327` (the later measure that gets detection for free by averaging conditional variances instead of fixing an ordering pattern) and `arxiv-1909.10140` (a coefficient whose ceiling depends on n, i.e. a property that likewise came from the construction rather than from tuning).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 470): **Maximal invariance and blindness are the same coin, and this is the folder's cleanest demonstration: the "joint" multivariate extension of the sign covariance is zero on any even-arity parity construction — the four-tuple order it looks for can only be satisfied by all-zeros then all-ones, which forces the response to be constant across the tuple, so the signed sum over the subgroup is identically zero — while the "partial" extension detects the same construction at both parities.** Parity over coordinate subsets is the canonical nonlinear thing a network computes, and every rank/ordering screen in this folder is a claim about which orderings can co-occur; a screen that has been made robust to a very wide class of transforms has necessarily stopped being able to see orderings that those transforms can manufacture, so the robustness has a measurable price. Two reporting consequences: report the measure's invariance group explicitly (the paper computes it — the sign covariance's is the two pairwise swaps, which is exactly why it is degenerate), because invariance beyond what the data actually needs is pure lost power; and treat a screen returning exactly zero on synthetic *parity* data as a failed screen until proven otherwise. Coreference `arxiv-1910.12327` (not monotone-invariant, and its threshold-averaging construction does read parity data) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (a residual-cosine screen whose blind spot is the same species of nonlinearity, arriving at the opposite error direction).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 470): **The same statistic can be estimated by counting boxes instead of by enumerating tuples, and the trick generalises to any statistic that depends on the sample only through joint ranks: precompute a prefix sum so "how many points fall in this box" costs O(1), then reduce each tuple's contribution to a fixed number of box queries by inclusion-exclusion — and the paper's own timings are the warning that asymptotics can lose to constants, since at three dimensions the naive enumeration wins below about 3,000 points, and for the partial extension the range-tree version is slower at every sample size tested.** Two things follow for our batteries. (1) The reason a rank screen over many directions is affordable is engineering, so the compute budget narrative should name the data structure and the crossover, not just the big-O. (2) The degeneracy result is a null-shape correction we owe our own screens: because the estimator is degenerate of order two under independence, the limit is a chi-square mixture rather than normal, so standardising by a root-n variance gives the wrong tail — the paper prints the correct constants (the same random variable up to 36/π⁴ versus 1/π⁴), and the practical substitute is a resample null whose resolution is one over the draw count, which is what the simulations end up doing anyway. Coreference `arxiv-1401.5031` (seconds versus hours on the same search, reported as elapsed time) and `arxiv-1202.3775` (a closed-form Gamma null instead of permutations — the opposite trade).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 469): **Consistency and efficiency are different claims and this paper is the crispest case in the folder of the gap between them: the nearest-neighbour entropy estimator converges at every dimension and is *efficient*, meaning it reaches the parametric variance, only up to d = 3, because above that a bias of order (k/n)^{2/d} — an integral of the density's Laplacian weighted by a power of the density — cannot be shrunk below the error budget.** The mechanism is worth carrying as a general diagnosis: the estimator is a plug-in through a functional that is non-smooth where the density vanishes, so the usual "the plug-in inherits the rate of the density estimate" argument fails and the residual is a curvature functional rather than a variance. For us the operational rule is to name the rate, not the convergence, whenever a probing paper reports an information-theoretic quantity on an embedding cloud: entropy, KL to a reference, and mutual information all inherit this bias, and in the dimensions our layer activations live in the estimator that produced the number is in the regime where the bias, not the sample size, sets the second decimal. Coreference `arxiv-1711.06642` (whose MI test is built on exactly this unweighted estimator, so its size guarantees transfer but its efficiency does not) and `arxiv-1202.3775` (a test whose whole contribution was a computable null, i.e. the other axis on which an estimator can be improved without changing the statistic).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 469): **The repair is linear algebra on the estimator family, not a better estimator: take one estimator per k, note that each carries the same functional of the density multiplied by a known constant — a ratio of Gamma functions in k and n — and choose weights, supported only on multiples of about k/d, that satisfy moment conditions making the sum of those constants vanish for the first floor(d/4) orders.** Two things follow that generalise well beyond entropy. First, a family of estimators indexed by a tuning parameter is a *basis*, and the right question is which linear functionals of the family are free of the nuisance term, not which single member is best — the same reasoning that makes a weighted combination of probes better than any one probe when they share a nuisance direction. Second, the price of the cancellation is paid in the variance: the fixed-k analysis shows the variance is inflated by a distribution-free factor that the paper tabulates (it starts above two at k = 1 in one dimension and drops below one by k = 2, then keeps falling), so a bias-cancel is never free and the trade-off can be read off a table rather than argued. Coreference `arxiv-1401.5031` (a test that trades exactness for cost by choosing which statistics to compute) and `arxiv-1910.12327` (the rank-based dependence measure that sidesteps the whole bias question by not estimating a density at all).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 469): **The conditions that make the proof go are stated with unusual honesty and they are the useful part: efficiency in arbitrary dimension needs smoothness above d/2 and a moment above d, both of which grow with the dimension, which is exactly the statement that "nonparametric in high dimension" is not a free lunch — and the authors concede their own β > d/2 exceeds what a compact-support estimator needs, attributing the gap to the entropy functional's non-differentiability where the density vanishes.** The contrast with the confidence-interval construction is the other transferable piece: intervals are built from a variance estimate that is *truncated at zero*, so the interval degenerates precisely when the variance is underestimated, which is the failure direction nobody checks. For a probing account the parallel is direct — any error bar we attach to a probe's information measure should name which direction of miscalibration collapses it, and a truncation at zero is a reliable tell that under-estimation was expected. Also worth noting as a structural fact about this folder: the paper has 69 pages, zero figures, no code and no experiments, and its entire claim rests on a lower bound; that is the shape of an entry that disciplines measures rather than one that supplies a method. Coreference `arxiv-1202.3775` (a test with a closed-form null and a conceded power deficit in the easy case) and `arxiv-1804.07203` (a hardness result that is likewise all bound and no experiment).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 468): **The cheapest route to a p-value for a conditional relation is to make the conditioning disappear arithmetically rather than to estimate it — the residual operator here is a single closed-form matrix applied as a sandwich on both sides, regularisation times the inverse of the regularised conditioning kernel, so "partial out Z" costs one matrix inverse of the kernel matrix we already built, and the statistic is afterwards just a trace of a product; the null then arrives in closed form as a weighted sum of one-degree-of-freedom chi-squares whose weights are the eigenvalues of the sandwich, and a two-parameter Gamma moment match removes even the simulation.** Two habits follow for our probe batteries. (1) Whenever a claim is "redundant given these other directions/neurons/layers", express the conditioning as an operator applied to the candidate's features and invert once, rather than fitting a separate regressor per feature — this is the same move as `arxiv-1401.5031`'s residual columns, but batched through the kernel matrix instead of per column, and it is what makes a battery of hundreds of conditional queries affordable. (2) **Match the null to a Gamma from two trace quantities and print the trace formula**, because a resample-count null has a resolution floor of one over the count while an analytic null has none — the folder's earlier entries all paid for exactness with permutations, and this is the first that shows the exactness was not needed to get the shape right. Coreference `arxiv-1401.5031` (residual columns and an exact permutation null, the same arithmetic at the cost of seconds) and `arxiv-1711.06642` (a permutation null whose resolution is bounded by its resample count).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 468): **The failure mode this test buys with its generality is quiet agreement, and the paper says so in the only place a reader can miss it: a footnote concedes that in the linear-Gaussian case the classical partial-correlation test has comparable size and much smaller Type II error, and the main figures show Type II error rising monotonically with the size of the conditioning set and hitting essentially one for the bootstrap-based baseline past three conditioning variables.** For us this is the sharpest statement in the folder of the asymmetry that governs every non-rejection: false rejection is visible in the size panel and false acceptance is invisible in a graph search, so an instrument tuned for generality fails in the direction nobody checks. The reporting rule that follows is the two-column one the folder adopted in `arxiv-2411.13117` applied to tests — report size *and* power against the case you actually have, and report them for the cheap assumption-laden test as well, because "our test is valid without assumptions" and "our test is the more useful one here" are different claims and this paper is honest enough to print both. It also reframes what a conditional-independence result can be used for: it licenses dropping a variable from a model, so an anti-conservative test does not just give a wrong p-value, it gives a wrong and simpler model. Coreference `arxiv-1804.07203` (the theory that says no uniformly valid test exists at all — this is what an invalid-by-design-nowhere, valid-in-practice approximation looks like) and `arxiv-1910.12327` (the strength estimate that replaces the binary verdict precisely because the verdict's error direction is unreportable).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 468): **A test statistic can be the same number as a famous one and still be worth publishing, provided the distribution you derive is of a *different* object: the unconditional statistic here is literally HSIC's biased estimator, and the contribution is that its null depends on the eigenvalues of the two regular kernel matrices instead of on the eigenvalues of an order-four tensor, which is the difference between two spectral decompositions you can compute and one you cannot.** The generalisable point is an accounting rule for instruments: when comparing against a known method, name the *estimator* and the *null* separately, because improvements in the second are invisible to anyone comparing formulas for the first, and a test whose estimator is unchanged but whose null became computable is a strictly better test with an identical-looking equation. It also fixes what to copy when a method's own null is unavailable: derive the limit under the *weaker* condition the characterisation actually gives you (here, uncorrelatedness of functions rather than independence) and let the independence case fall out as a special case with diagonal weights — a trick that costs no extra theory and yields a test for the weak condition for free, which is exactly what a probing account wants when its surrogate only promises uncorrelatedness. Coreference `arxiv-1401.5031` (a test whose null is enumerated by permutation because no analytic form exists for its statistic) and `arxiv-2206.05829` (a recovery guarantee stated for one thresholded second-order statistic and not for the class).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 467): **An independence claim about activations should be priced as a decision, not as a statistic, and the price is per query multiplied by the search: this test's entire contribution is trading 1,478 seconds for 17.5 seconds on 1,000 queries that a constraint-based search will issue tens of thousands of times, and its accuracy at scale is what makes the trade legitimate (0.96/0.75 in 54 seconds against 0.84/0.48 in 14.5 hours on the same 200-node graph).** Two habits follow. (1) Whenever we report a probe battery, print precision, recall and elapsed time for the *identical* search procedure rather than an accuracy number for the instrument alone, because an instrument that is 5% more accurate and 1,000× slower is not the better instrument for a search. (2) Note which one of the two cheap-and-precise correlation tests failed *how*: the rank test reached 0.90 precision with 0.10 recall and the linear one 0.21 with 0.18, so precision without recall is the wrong direction of failure and both numbers belong on the page. Coreference `arxiv-1804.07203` (the generalised covariance measure — the same residual-correlation family, arrived at six years later with asymptotic theory instead of a benchmark) and `arxiv-1711.06642` (cost also reported, but as permutation counts rather than seconds).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 467): **A complete basis for the space of square-summable transforms is the correct framing for "these two streams are unrelated", and the practical truncation can be as crude as the first seven powers — which is the cheapest nonlinear-dependence screen the folder has recorded: compute correlations between `r_X` and `r_Y`, `r_X` and `r_Y²`, `r_X²` and `r_Y`, and so on over a handful of powers, and control the family with a false-discovery-rate step rather than picking the maximum.** The argument for why powers suffice is worth keeping in words: any nonzero covariance of some transform pair implies a nonzero covariance of some pair of Hermite polynomials, which implies one of some pair of powers up to exact cancellation, and the paper's running example is the sharp one — a symmetric predictor with a quadratic response has exactly zero linear and rank correlation, and the second power recovers it immediately. For us this replaces the kernel Gram matrix in any first-pass check: the dependence a linear projection of a network state induces is usually either a trend (odd power) or a spread change (even power), so three or four powers catch the common cases in a matmul. The caveat that travels with it is the paper's own: the truncation makes the test approximate where a kernel test is asymptotically exact, so a null result from a three-power screen means "no dependence visible to these transforms", not independence. Coreference `arxiv-2610.21261` (an artefact labelled rather than clipped — the same distinction between a null and a blind instrument) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (the residual-cosine screen whose blind spot is exactly the even-power case).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 467): **The multiplicative-noise model is the recurring failure mode of every residual-based screen in this folder, and this is its earliest appearance: the author finds it the one connection type where precision is poor for *all* four tests, notes that the rank-based test's precision is not even defined there, and reports it without a remedy.** That is now three papers meeting the same construction from three directions — here as a benchmark row, in `arxiv-1804.07203` as the worked counterexample showing residuals can be uncorrelated while dependent, and in `arxiv-1711.06642` as one of three power settings for the mutual-information test. The operational rule is therefore settled: before trusting a conditional-independence verdict on a pair of activation streams, run the one-line check the multiplicative form defeats — the correlation of the *squared* residuals rather than the residuals — because the first screen and the second-order version that follows it are both blind to a variance that depends on the covariate while the mean does not. Second, and worth copying as a reporting convention: the paper says plainly that precision for this case is undefined rather than 0, and writes the undefined value on the page instead of silently plotting a zero. Coreference `arxiv-1804.07203` (the theorem behind the counterexample) and `arxiv-1910.12327` (a strength measure that *does* detect it, at the cost of a nearest-neighbour search).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 466): **Exact finite-sample size control is a property of exchangeability and not of the estimator, so it survives every tuning choice — and the cheap way to get it is to compare statistics in which the expensive unknown term is shared and therefore cancels.** Both practical tests compare the observed statistic against resampled ones by counting how often a resample is at least as large, and the marginal entropy of the untouched block appears on both sides of every such comparison, so it is never computed and never needs to be correct; the same cancellation removes the covariate-entropy term in the regression version. For us the rule is concrete: when we certify a read-out by substitution, build the comparison so that the component we cannot estimate well is common to numerator and denominator, and then the certificate is exact for whatever tuning we chose, rather than exact only in the limit of a well-chosen one. Coreference `arxiv-1807.05405` (its reweighted permutation null, where the analogous cancellation is invariance to the base measure) and `arxiv-1804.07203` (the conditional case where no such comparison exists at all).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 466): **A test's skill is a profile over alternative families, and the paper's own numbers show the profile crossing: the same statistic dominates where dependence is localised and merely competes where it is global and multiplicative, while a multiscale average over the tuning parameter beats both the data-driven choice and, in one setting, the per-setting oracle.** Two habits follow. (1) Never report one power curve as the competence of a dependence instrument — report the families it was powered against, because a detection claim is always relative to a hazard. (2) When a tuning parameter selects the scale of structure being looked for, averaging over that scale is not a hedge but a strictly better statistic than selecting one, which is the same lesson this folder keeps meeting in the SAE-featurewidth and dictionary-size entries; it is also the honest frame for our own probe batteries, where the analogue of k is the neighbourhood or token-window size and the multiscale average is the default rather than the fallback. Coreference `arxiv-2408.15510` (a verdict that is a function of the strength dial) and `arxiv-2610.21261` (an artefact labelled rather than clipped).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 466): **The best worked example in the paper is not a simulation but a repair sequence: reject the surrogate, isolate the structure the surrogate missed by a partial-regression residual plot, add that structure, and report a non-rejection of the repaired model — and the discipline that makes it legitimate is that the second test is run on the enlarged model rather than on a held-out slice of the same fit.** It is also a marker of how far these instruments are from our problem: the covariates here are two spatial coordinates and the response is a temperature, and the entire difficulty is that 56 points with a two-parameter trend leave almost no residual information, which is why the authors use a bootstrap-style resample count of order 1,785 to reach a p-value resolution of about 5.6e-4. For us the transferable part is the reporting template — reject, diagnose, repair, retest — and the warning that any test whose resolution is set by a resample count must state that count, since the smallest attainable p-value is one over it. Coreference `arxiv-2611.09945` (a matched null for every headline number) and `arxiv-1807.05405` (a real-data arm where the two tests agree to three decimal places).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 465): **A resampling null inherits its validity from what it holds fixed, and holding the multiset of observed values fixed is strictly cheaper than resampling them: the permutation version keeps every observed value and only reweights which value lands on which row, so the excess false-positive rate is bounded by the total variation distance to the true conditional law, and under the worst statistic it is provably never worse than the full resample, whose bound is tight.** Two habits for our shuffle nulls follow. (1) **Resample by reordering before resampling by generating** — a reorder needs only the *relative* conditional fit, and because per-value factors cancel across a permutation the test is invariant to any change of base measure, i.e. correct up to a factor in the value and a normalising term, which is a far weaker requirement on our surrogate than a full generative model of activations. (2) **Price every read-out built by substitution in the same currency**: state the distance between the estimated and reference conditional law and the resulting excess error, rather than reporting a p-value with an unstated dependence on how good the surrogate is — this is the natural-language version of the retention-filter habit the folder recorded earlier, with a theorem behind it instead of a heuristic. Coreference `arxiv-1804.07203` (the impossibility this is a restricted escape from) and `arxiv-2611.03518` (a substitution's fidelity reported as a retained fraction).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 465): **When M copies must be mutually exchangeable with the original, sample them from a shared hub and never in sequence, because sequential MCMC sampling makes adjacent copies correlated and the validity guarantee silently dies even though each copy individually looks like a draw from the target.** The paper's mechanism is worth copying exactly: run the chain S steps to produce one hub permutation, then initialise the original and every copy at that hub and run each S steps independently, so all M+1 objects sit the same distance from the centre and conditional on the hub are i.i.d. The byproduct is that initialising at the true state means the chain starts *in* the stationary distribution, so any S is valid — small S costs power, not validity, and the trace plots show 50 steps is enough here. For us this is the standing rule for matched-pair or matched-null batteries: one shared randomisation centre, arms drawn independently from it, and report S; a battery whose arms were drawn in a run is reporting a null with an unstated correlation between its own controls. Coreference `arxiv-2611.09945` (a matched null for every headline number) and `arxiv-1807.05405`'s own Table 1, where ten independent trials give near-identical CPT and CRT p-values on real data even where the theory says they may diverge.
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 465): **A comparison proved for the worst-case statistic and observed to be milder for the statistic people actually use is two claims, and the paper keeps them apart on the page: the tightness result is explicitly worst-case over an adversarially chosen T, and the authors say in the Discussion that intuitive statistics will likely suffer far less inflation, and that they cannot characterise the CPT's worst case the way they can the CRT's.** The transferable discipline is to label each robustness statement with the regime it holds in — *worst-case* over statistics, or *at this statistic* — and to refuse to promote the empirical ordering into a guarantee. Two smaller items travel with it: the screening rule that prunes on conditioning variables only is free (the conditioned law is unchanged, so no correction is owed), which licenses support-based pruning of evaluation sets; and the unexplained conservative behaviour when the surrogate is fitted on the test data is printed as unexplained rather than rationalised, the reporting convention the folder has rewarded repeatedly. Coreference `arxiv-2408.15510` (a method's verdict as a function of the strength dial, where a single point misleads) and `arxiv-2610.21261` (a sampling artefact labelled rather than clipped).

Substance: the theorem is a genuine impossibility over absolutely continuous laws (any bounded rejection region survives the splice construction because the new null law is ℓ∞-close to the alternative and the region is approximated by a finite union of boxes), it is *stronger* than the usual dense-null story (null and alternative are separated at the level of both TV and KL), and it does **not** apply to discrete Z; the constructive answer is the GCM whose validity condition is stated purely in terms of the two regressions' prediction errors, with the honest concession that choosing a regression "is mathematically an equally impossible problem"; and the paper supplies the folder's first law-based negative control — multiplicative noise, where a residual-independence test (HSIC on residuals, the Fan et al. recipe) fails level while the GCM holds it, which is precisely the shape a shuffled-label null would pass.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 463): **The dependence instrument a probing account should carry is a rank-difference sum, because it is the only strength measure in this family that costs nothing: one sorted array, one pass over consecutive rank differences, O(n log n), no bandwidth, no kernel, no tuning constant, and a null variance known in closed form so a p-value needs no permutation loop — at n = 10000 the permutation-based competitors take between 89 seconds and more than 30 minutes while this takes about 0.011 seconds.** The reason it works is worth holding onto as a template for inventing our own statistics: it never estimates a conditional distribution; instead it thresholds the target at every level, asks how much of that binary indicator's variance survives conditioning on the predictor, averages the ratio over levels, and then replaces the conditional expectation with the nearest neighbour in predictor order — so any quantity we care about that can be written as an averaged conditional variance of a threshold becomes computable from ranks alone. Coreference `arxiv-1910.12327` (the conditional version on the same identity, which pays a nearest-neighbour search in two sets instead of one) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (the residual-cosine threshold this replaces as a first-pass screen).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 463): **"this feature is represented with strength one" is a claim about a coefficient, not about a network, and the coefficient can be lying: on a mixture of two well-separated normal clusters, where the only thing recoverable about the target is which cluster it came from, MIC reads 1.00 and maximal correlation reads 0.99 while this coefficient reads 0.48 — and the paper proves the saturation is not a small-sample artifact but a theorem about any law supported on two disjoint rectangles of equal mass.** That is exactly the shape a discrete feature's activation geometry has — a couple of tight blobs — so the measures most likely to be reached for when someone wants a single number for "how strongly is concept X encoded" are the ones that will report a perfect score for mere cluster membership. The honest reporting rule this implies: pair every strength number with a *determination* check in the correct direction, since the reverse-direction value is what distinguishes "the predictor pins the target down" from "the predictor just sorts the target into buckets", the two directions differing by nearly an order of magnitude on Galton's peas (0.11 against 0.92). Coreference `arxiv-2406.01506` (a direction-as-concept claim that also needs to say whether the concept is a point or a region) and `arxiv-2206.05829` (a relation that holds over a lattice of conditioning sets rather than at a single score).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 464): **A conditional-independence star is not a weak claim, it is an unlicensed one — there is no test over continuous conditioning variables that keeps its size uniformly and still has power, so the sentence "X is independent of the label given this activation set" cannot be licensed by a p-value at all, only by a strength estimate with a declared sample size and conditioning dimension.** The theorem here is not the familiar "the null is dense" story: the authors exhibit an alternative at total-variation distance at least 1/24 from every null law, and a Gaussian alternative at KL divergence ½·log((1+σ²)/σ²), so the two hypotheses are genuinely far apart — the failure comes from the *convex hull* of the null swallowing the alternative, which is why the practical recipe is not "use a better test" but "declare the subclass". Two habits follow for our probing accounts. (1) Replace "independence not rejected given the conditioning set" with "residual dependence estimated at 0.03 on a scale where 1 means determination, at n examples and a conditioning set of dimension k", and pair it with the two-coefficient instruments we already hold. (2) When a conditional claim must be made, state the conditioning set *and* the size of the subclass the test was validated on, because the validity we can buy is only inside a declared family. Coreference `arxiv-1910.12327` and `arxiv-1909.10140` (the strength instruments, both of which are honest at any conditioning dimension because they estimate rather than test) and `arxiv-2206.05829` (the lattice that says which conditioning sets even need asking).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 464): **The negative control this folder keeps reaching for — shuffle the labels, permute the directions, regress out the confound and check the residual — is a *distributional* control and it is strictly weaker than a *law-level* control, and the gap has a name: residuals can be uncorrelated and still dependent.** The multiplicative-noise construction here (X = Z·N_X, Y = Z·N_Y with independent normal factors) is conditionally independent given Z, has exactly zero conditional mean for both variables, and therefore passes any residual-correlation or partial-correlation screen while cov(R₁², R₂²) is non-zero; the authors' simulation shows the residual-then-HSIC test failing level on it while their covariance measure holds it. Every "we controlled for the layer / the prompt / the topic and nothing remained" claim in this folder has the same shape, and the cheap upgrade is available without new theory: a covariance-of-residual-products statistic is sensitive to variance-modulation dependence that a cosine of residuals is blind to, and it costs one pass. Corollary for the folder's nulls: a permutation test is available for *unconditional* independence at no cost, so the missing control is never "shuffle harder" but always "construct a law that keeps the marginal story identical and changes the conditional one". Coreference `arxiv-2206.05829` (whose thresholded generalised partial correlation is exactly the second-order screen this defeats) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (the residual-cosine threshold that opens the same gap).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 464): **The licensing of a statistic is a *product* of two error terms, not a sum, and this is the cheapest general template the folder has for validating any number whose null distribution we cannot compute from the data.** Because the GCM's numerator decomposes into a central-limit term from the true residuals plus leakage terms from imperfect regressions, each individual regression only has to beat n^(-1/4) and their squared errors only have to multiply to o(1/n); the same structure underlies double/debiased machine learning and the semiparametric functional literature the paper positions itself against. The generalisable measurement rule: whenever we normalise a residual covariance — a probe score against a label after removing a projection, a direction's effect after partialling out a confound, an attribution after removing the mean state — the honest sentence is "valid provided *both* removals beat 1/√n at this sample size", and the falsification is a demonstration that one of them does not. The paper is also admirably explicit about where the guarantee *breaks*: the no-free-lunch sweep is produced by a family whose RKHS norm grows like exp(a²), so the uniformity assumption in their own theorem fails at a known rate — which is the model for how we should present the limits of our own predictors, as a parameterised family plus the value of the parameter at which the guarantee lapses. Coreference `arxiv-2607.02964` (recovery and inverse arms as a paired licensing requirement) and `arxiv-2606.06267` (a faithfulness score that inflates precisely as its edge set destabilises).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 463): **A statistic's finite-sample ceiling is part of its meaning: with distinct values the largest attainable value here is (n-2)/(n+1), about 0.86 at n = 20, so a reported 0.86 on twenty examples is a perfect score and a reported 0.86 on ten thousand is not — and the floor near -1/2 is not a weakness in the relation but evidence that the sample is not i.i.d., which makes the statistic double as a data-hygiene check.** For a probing loop this is a concrete reporting discipline: print the sample size beside every correlation-like number and normalise against the attainable ceiling, because a sweep over layers or prompts that compares raw values across different sample counts is comparing a ceiling against a value. It also vindicates the folder's insistence on naming the evidence unit — the power comparison here is 500 simulations per point at a fixed n = 100, and the paper states plainly that it loses on smooth alternatives, which is precisely the regime in which marginal activation statistics live. Coreference `arxiv-1810.04882` (within-set dispersion deciding whether a per-set claim holds, with the noise floor set by corpus frequency) and `arxiv-2406.01506` (an effect measured against the noise band from a shuffled control rather than against zero).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 462): **"These two relations are the same direction" is never a fact about a space; it is the claim that one named statistic is constant across the pairs you gathered, and here that statistic is directed — csPMI(x,y) = PMI + log p(x,y), which reads as log p(y|x) and is not symmetric in the two words — so an account that certifies a direction by clustering its pairs under cosine has certified something weaker than the theorem's condition.** The empirical shadow of this is the run's best number: the **within-set dispersion of csPMI predicts whether the arithmetic solution works, at about r = -0.70 and significant at 1%**, while the *mean* csPMI orders the analogy types almost monotonically from geography through verb tense to opposites and mean PMI does not order them at all. For us the instrument is therefore two scalars, not a clustering score: the set's agreement on the statistic (does it cluster) *and* where on the statistic's scale the set sits (what relation it is), and the second one is what lets two different analogies be distinguished even when both are tight. It also gives the right shape for a probe-direction claim in an activation space — gather the pair set, compute the internal statistic the code is said to hold constant, report its dispersion beside the direction — with csPMI replaced by whatever quantity the model's own training objective licenses, since csPMI's authority here comes entirely from the Levy-Goldberg factorisation, which the authors name as the sole reason GloVe and SGNS are in scope. Coreference `arxiv-2310.17611` (a conditioning set that decides whether a direction is clean — the same insistence that the claim is relative to a gathered set) and `arxiv-2411.13117` (a reported gap that is meaningless without naming which of two objects — dictionary or inference — the number describes).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 462): **A single word pair can never confirm or refute a linear relation, because the theorem is an iff over a set: the displacement must be the same for every pair in the set and the cross-pair quantity matched between any two pairs, so the unit of evidence is the set and the condition is that its statistic has a single value.** The coplanarity clause makes this literal and checkable — the four words of two pairs must lie in a plane, which the paper writes as a rank-at-most-two condition on three differenced rows of the factorised matrix — so "the relation is linear" reduces to a small rank statement about data, the same species of check as the rank obstruction in `arxiv-2411.13117` and the zero-data Gram diagnostics the dictionary entries rely on. The fragility this exposes is exactly the one a probing account inherits: the noise section shows accuracy collapsing to **0.092 on the currency analogy whose pairs have a median co-occurrence frequency of 19, against 0.954 on capitals at 3,436.5**, and the paper reads that as estimation variance rather than as evidence that the relation is absent — so a direction that looks real on a well-attested pair set and absent on a thin one is one claim about sampling, not two claims about meaning, and the two should never be reported as a contrast. Coreference `arxiv-2206.05829` (claims hold over a region of contexts, not over a point) and `arxiv-1902.11260` (local consistency does not imply global membership — the same per-set versus per-point asymmetry in a third vocabulary).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 462): **Either direction of the noise argument here should stop us assuming that a better-reconstructing representation is a cleaner one: the authors argue that *some* reconstruction error is beneficial, because it suppresses relations that satisfy the theorem by coincidence, and they use that to explain the known result that shrinking embedding width up to a point improves analogy accuracy — too little noise admits spurious exact linearities, too much destroys the real ones.** That is a genuinely uncomfortable claim for a folder whose dictionary entries all report reconstruction as a headline column, and it has a concrete operational form worth copying: model the residual variance as a decreasing function of a pair's corpus frequency, then state that a relation is reportable only where the frequency supports the estimate. The corollaries that survive are the ones a white-box account can reuse without the theorem's assumptions — squared Euclidean distance being affine in the negative statistic gives distance-as-dissimilarity its first derivation, and addition favouring the rarer operand (the summed vector's statistic equals the log probability of the other word plus a constant) is a free explanation of why composition down-weights stopwords, with the honest caveat that **the authors cannot test either addition corollary**, since a summed vector is not in the vocabulary and has no co-occurrence statistics to compare against — the paper says so plainly. Coreference `arxiv-2209.10652` (a loss curve where more capacity buys superposition, not error reduction) and `arxiv-2411.13117` (reconstruction and feature legibility moving as separate dials).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 461): **The instrument a probing account should be built on is not a test but a strength, and this paper supplies the cheapest one with the right endpoints: zero if and only if conditionally independent, one if and only if determined, computable in n log n from ranks and two nearest-neighbour searches, with no bandwidth, kernel, density or tuning parameter anywhere.** The construction is worth remembering in one sentence because it explains why it beats the alternatives: threshold the target at every level, and for each level ask how much of the remaining variance of that indicator survives conditioning on both sets relative to conditioning on one — the average of that ratio is the coefficient, and a nearest-neighbour proxy for "the closest sample point in (X,Z)" versus "the closest in X" estimates it without ever modelling a conditional density. For us this is the correct replacement for the residual-cosine threshold used in `arxiv-2310.17611` and the generalised partial correlation that carries the finite-sample theory of `arxiv-2206.05829`: both are second-order statistics and blind to dependence that leaves residuals uncorrelated, which is exactly the regime a nonlinear network creates. Coreference `arxiv-2310.17611` (residual cosine and the 0.015 threshold) and `arxiv-2206.05829` (the same weakness diagnosed from the theory side).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 461): **The paper's own impossibility remark is the most useful sentence in it for us: there is no uniformly level-correct test of conditional independence over continuous variables without unverifiable assumptions, so a probing report that prints significance for "these directions are independent given that set" is printing something the mathematics does not license — whereas a coefficient estimate with its sample size and conditioning dimension is a claim that can be attacked and defended.** The two endpoints also give a reporting scale that is self-checking: a value near zero is an independence claim, a value near one is a determination claim, and the borderline is not a decision point but a place where the estimate is simply uninformative at that n. The rate compounds the discipline — n to the power minus one over the sum of the two conditioned dimensions, so the coefficient is cheap to compute and expensive to trust exactly where an account wants a large boundary, which is the same currency as `arxiv-2206.05829`'s effective-dimension bound read from the other side. Coreference `arxiv-1902.11260` (the axiom-side check: what shape a relation may take) and `arxiv-2406.01506` (a claim about determination rather than independence, i.e. the other endpoint of this scale).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 461): **A predictor can be useless alone and decisive in company, and the toy models here are the cheapest possible template for testing any selection instrument: a target that depends on two variables through a circular sum is marginally independent of one of them while conditionally a function of it, and the estimator reads near zero unconditionally and near 0.9 conditionally at n = 1,000.** That shape is the exact functional form a probe's conditioning set has to detect — an activation that looks irrelevant until the right partner is conditioned on — so the constructions are reusable as regression tests for our own boundary search before it touches real activations, and the reported spread across simulations rather than a single estimate is the reporting style to copy. The FOCI stopping rule carries a caveat that travels with it: it stops at the first non-positive coefficient, and the consistency proof assumes a fixed margin between sufficient and insufficient sets, so a search built this way silently assumes the smallest available gain is not vanishingly small — with 1,000 candidate predictors, 2,000 samples and a 0.01 prediction-error gap on real data, the accuracy is comparable to the baselines while the selected sets are a fraction of the size, which is the trade we would want but should print as a two-column result. Coreference `arxiv-2310.17611` (random-subspace projection search, the label-free cousin of this greedy ordering) and `arxiv-2411.13117` (a report that separates dictionary quality from inference quality — the same two-column rule applied to selection).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 460): **The whole axiomatic validity question about an independence relation reduces to a finite local check with a very small basis, and this paper supplies the exact list: an n-gaussoid is an n-gaussoid if and only if every 3-face restriction of it is one of the eleven 3-gaussoids, which fall into five symmetry types (empty, two kinds of singleton, belt, full) — so a probe's measured CI relation can be validated exhaustively by enumerating its 3-variable restrictions and matching them against eleven patterns, with no need to test axioms over large conditioning sets and no model.** This is the cheapest instrument the folder has been offered for the assumption shared by `arxiv-2206.05829` and `arxiv-2310.17611`: both assume compositional-graphoid structure, both are stated for arbitrary such structures, and neither says how to check one. The caveats travel with the theorem and are worth quoting in any account that cites it — the puzzle property needs the 3-local axioms to be genuinely local in the cube, and the paper's own Remark 3.11 says the trick then fails for realizable gaussoids (no puzzle property) and for graphical ones (basis lacks the singletons), so "local basis exists" is a property of the class, not of independence in general. Coreference `arxiv-2206.05829` (the interval labelling of conditioning sets — a global object computed per variable, where this is a purely local check) and `arxiv-2310.17611` (the empirical relation whose graphoid status was asserted, not tested).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 460): **The axioms are almost certainly not tight, and the gap is priced: the gaussoid axioms admit doubly exponentially many structures (log count between a constant times n·2^n and a constant times n²·2^n), while the realizable ones are only single exponential once a positive-definite covariance is turned into a vector matroid on 2n elements — so an account that checks its relation against axioms has checked something much weaker than realizability, and the difference is not a constant factor but an exponential.** For us the practical consequence is a phrasing rule: "our measurements are consistent with a gaussoid / a compositional graphoid" is a weak claim and should be said that way, whereas "our relation is graphical" is a strong structural claim, because the graphical classes collapse onto undirected graphs (2^{n choose 2}), triangle-free complements, forests of paths, partitions (Bell numbers) and involutions (2^{n-1}), all matched to OEIS sequences and therefore all independently checked. The trichotomy — doubly exponential, single exponential, or vanishing above a small dimension — is also a ready-made sanity check: several natural-looking classes simply die (the class LUB has counts 9, 111, then 0 for all n ≥ 5), so a small-class assumption can be refuted by looking at four or five variables. Coreference `arxiv-2605.09887` (a budget argument where the price is geometry) and `arxiv-2411.13117` (a rank argument where the price is encoder capacity — the same shape of "you cannot afford this" result in a different currency).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 460): **Building a global structure out of consistent local pieces is not the same as building it out of the pieces you can observe, and the paper's 4-cycle example is the cleanest demonstration in this folder: every 3-minor visible in the induced subgraphs of the graph is a singleton type, all consistent, yet the smallest class containing the gaussoid is a strictly larger one, because the constraint that decides membership lives in overlapping faces rather than in any single one.** The repair is the transitive graph Q(n,k,p,q) — edges join faces that both meet some p-face in at least q dimensions, so an independent set is a set of places that can be filled freely — and the degree formula is what makes the argument quantitative. This is directly the anatomy of our own problem: a per-layer or per-patch account whose pieces are each locally valid can still fail globally, and the diagnosis is not "the pieces were wrong" but "the pieces were chosen in a pattern with conflicts". Coreference `arxiv-2405.14860` (a local representation that is clean in a slice and wrong globally) and `arxiv-2602.14687` (a generator that builds correlated structure by construction — the instrument that would let us test the conflict pattern on our own fits).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 459): **The item a probing report should quote is not a boundary but an interval, and this paper proves the interval is the natural unit: for a fixed target, the sets that share one minimal separating set form a convex sublattice, and the distinct such intervals partition the entire power set of the other variables — so "what is the minimal context that makes this direction redundant" and "which other contexts are indistinguishable from it" are one object, computed once, and every CI query then reduces to a set-inclusion check.** Concretely on their 15-node example one node carries 62,592 distinct elementary relations out of 114,688 candidates, and all of them follow from 319 stored intervals obtained with 2,208 queries; the naive sparsity-only count of intervals is too conservative by about an order of magnitude. For us the consequence is a reporting rule with a number attached: our accounts should state the boundary size *and* the size of the interval it labels (equivalently M minus m), because an interval is what turns a single lucky context into a claim about a region of contexts, and it is the region — not the singleton — that a predictive white-box model needs to reproduce. It also gives the correct reading of entry `arxiv-2310.17611`'s observation that boundaries of size eight to ten drive residual cosine to 0.015: if several distinct large conditioning sets label the same interval there, a smaller boundary was available and the reported one was arbitrary. Coreference `arxiv-2310.17611` (partial orthogonality as an instance of this theory, with the boundary as the only object named) and `arxiv-2406.01506` (the conditional-versus-unconditional distinction written as direct-sum decomposition rather than as an interval partition).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 459): **The information an account carries is limited by its test, not by its axioms, and here the gap is visible in the design: the theory is stated for arbitrary compositional graphoids, but the finite-sample machinery is a thresholded generalised partial correlation — regress each variable on the conditioning set nonparametrically and normalise the inner product of the two residual streams — which is a second-order statistic, so a dependence that leaves residuals uncorrelated is invisible no matter how strong it is.** The authors are explicit that their concentration result is for this measure and that they only claim it extends to any measure with a similar inequality, which they do not supply. For us this is the sharpest version yet of a rule the folder keeps rediscovering: a CI structure read off residuals should be reported with the name of the test that produced it, because every nonlinearity a learned network exhibits is exactly the case that this instrument cannot see, and "conditionally independent in the graphoid sense" and "zero residual correlation" are different claims that the prose happily conflates. The recovery bound is otherwise the useful part and it is the same currency as entries 455 and 458: with an α-separation margin, the effective dimension is the boundary size t rather than the ambient d, so structure stays recoverable when d is far larger than n at a log d cost — and in the Gaussian case the estimation term collapses to the parametric log n / n, which is stated as evidence the general gap condition is tight. Coreference `arxiv-2310.17611` (the same instrument used on CLIP embeddings, where d << n and the intersection axiom fails) and `arxiv-2605.09887` (a budget argument where the price is geometry rather than sample size).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 459): **The lattice structure is not a notational convenience, it is inherited from geometry: in an L² space, partial orthogonality is the vanishing of a product of orthogonal projections, the sets of variables whose projection onto a fixed direction is unchanged form a convex sublattice because the projection operators themselves form one, and for Gaussian data the probabilistic lattice, the projection lattice and the "regression lattice" of equal-support partial regression coefficients all coincide — with the probabilistic one only a subset of the regression one outside the Gaussian case.** That last inequality is the part worth carrying: partial orthogonality is strictly weaker than conditional independence, so an account built on second-order structure is describing a coarsening, and every claim should say which of the three lattices it was computed in. It also fixes the level at which superposition questions are answerable — the regression lattice is defined for rank-deficient covariance, and the projection-lattice proof holds for infinite-dimensional spaces and dependent variables as long as one stays at the level of projections rather than mapping them back onto variable sets, which is exactly the degenerate dictionary regime the sparse-autoencoder entries here live in. Coreference `arxiv-2406.01506` (whitening the unembedding to make an inner product meaningful — the same insistence that orthogonality is a statement about a chosen metric) and `arxiv-2508.16560` (a strict-descent construction that fixes the conditioning set while moving the penalty).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 458): **The explanation of a vector is a subspace, not a direction, and the paper gives the conditioning set that decides which is right — condition on the parent concept and the residuals of the children become mutually orthogonal, which is why "related to vegetable" and "is purple" are separable even though eggplant, tomato and amethyst all sit near each other before conditioning.** That is entry `arxiv-2406.01506`'s hierarchy theorem reached from the other end (there via whitened canonical inner products and direct sums, here via the independence-model axioms and projection residuals), and together they settle a reporting rule for our own accounts: any claim that direction *d* means concept *c* should name the set whose span was projected out, because a direction that is a clean vector for *c* in one conditioning context is a mixture in another. The axiom list is the checkable part — partial orthogonality is only a semi-graphoid plus composition unless the conditioning vectors are linearly independent, so a claim of "these two are independent given those" over a fixed training dictionary with n >> d is *structurally* allowed to fail composition, and saying which axioms the relation actually satisfies is a testable statement about our own dictionary that costs nothing. Coreference `arxiv-2406.01506` (hierarchical concepts as direct sums) and `arxiv-2310.11431` (a direction as the unit, with cluster centroids asserted to be features without any conditioning set named).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 458): **The exact notion of "explained away" is nearly vacuous in an overcomplete set, and this is a clean statement of why: if the target vector lies in the span of the others, an exact Markov boundary must reconstruct it *exactly*, which in a set of n vectors in d dimensions with n >> d is a linear-algebra triviality rather than a scientific finding — so the paper replaces "every residual is orthogonal" with "the average cosine of residuals is zero" and the strict version, once relaxed, yields boundaries of about eight to ten vectors with average residual cosine at 0.015 and below.** Two habits for us: report the size of the conditioning set beside any "these are independent" claim, because the statistic is defined by an average over the complement and shrinks mechanically as the set grows; and treat the filtering of synonyms (cosine 0.9, Wu-Palmer near 1) as part of the measurement rather than housekeeping, since without it the method is free to find the neighbours it is supposed to explain. The random-projection candidate search is the reusable trick: project out many random subspaces and keep what stays correlated, which lifted top-10 Wu-Palmer from 0.343 to 0.422 on common nouns where plain cosine had plateaued — a cheap, label-free way to ask what survives after marginalising over arbitrary context, and a decent first-pass ranking for probe directions before paying for an SAE. Coreference `arxiv-2411.13117` (a rank bound making exact recovery impossible rather than vacuous — the opposite escape from the same linear algebra) and `arxiv-2508.16560` (a fidelity-style criterion that cannot distinguish the right dictionary from the wrong one).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 458): **Whether an embedding *can* preserve a distribution's independence structure is answered constructively and then priced: invert a perturbed adjacency matrix of a minimal I-map, take U Σ^{1/2} of the inverse, and the resulting vectors reproduce the graph's separations exactly; compress them with a random projection and separations survive within epsilon at a dimension that scales with log(n) and exponentially in the largest boundary size r, so sparsity of the explanation is exactly what makes a small representation legal.** For a white-box model this is the first entry here that states a representability result with a *budget* attached in the currency we care about — if the true conditional-independence structure has large boundaries, no small-dimension representation can preserve it, which converts "this model cannot be described by k directions" from an empirical complaint into a theorem-shaped one. It also bounds the opposite claim: the worst case (all variables mutually independent) needs as many dimensions as variables, so low-dimensionality of a model's activations is itself evidence that its concept structure is not an independence structure of that shape. Coreference `arxiv-2411.13117` (a dimension-versus-sparsity floor on *inference*) and `arxiv-2605.09887` (a layer's geometry pricing how many features fit — the same budget argument read off curvature instead of graph structure).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 457): **"A latent for mammal and a latent for animal" is a representation the theory says cannot be clean, and this paper says so about dictionaries directly: the feature vectors of a parent and its child are collinear by construction, so a sparse set of separate per-concept features must contain strongly co-linear atoms, while the same information written as parent plus orthogonal residual is cleanly separated and equally interpretable.** That is the sharpest sentence in the folder for our own dictionary work, because it names a case where the atoms a dictionary is asked to find are the wrong objects rather than merely missing. The reporting rule it implies: for any concept family we claim to have recovered, print the cosine between the parent and child vectors, and if it is high, report the residual basis instead of the raw atoms — this is the same gauge question entry `arxiv-2505.11756` meets from the capacity side and `arxiv-2310.11431` from the K-Means-versus-neuron side. Coreference `arxiv-2209.10652` (superposition derived in a toy model) and `arxiv-1704.05796` (hierarchical concepts and embedding geometry, the parent statement of this framing).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 457): **Orthogonality is only a claim once the inner product is named, and here the entire hierarchy result evaporates under the naive metric: whitening the unembedding matrix gives near-zero cosine for child-minus-parent against parent, while centring alone does not — so "the model disentangles these" and "these are orthogonal" are statements about a coordinate choice, not facts about the network.** Two consequences for us. First, any disentanglement or uniqueness claim in our own accounts must print the metric it was computed in, exactly as entries `arxiv-2411.13117` and `arxiv-2606.08365` do with the decoder Gram matrix. Second, the strongest evidence in the paper is not the near-zero cosine but the control that nearly disqualifies it: with shuffled unembeddings the orthogonality persists because the estimator sees set inclusion in the token sets, and only re-estimating from an independently chosen 70% of each synset separates the real effect from the artefact. That is the pattern in this folder's methodology line — declare the null the estimator could satisfy for free, then break it. Coreference `arxiv-2305.01610` (a basis rotation as the same style of control) and `arxiv-2406.08365` (a pre-registered screen).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 457): **The theory is predictive in the sense we want — the effect of an intervention is computed rather than measured — and the reason it works is also its limit: because the readout is a linear map followed by softmax, steering along a concept vector changes the logit difference between any two token pairs by a quantity that does not depend on the context at all, so parent pairs move 5 to 14 logits while child pairs stay within their ±1.2 standard deviation.** The authors say plainly that they do not address the internal structure of the network and that the whitening trick is available only at the final layer. For a white-box model this is a boundary marker rather than an obstacle: at the readout, prediction under intervention is exactly linear algebra, and every non-linear claim we make should be understood as a claim about how much of that final-layer simplicity fails to hold one layer down. Coreference `arxiv-2606.08365` (a paper that predicts intervention behaviour from frozen statistics without the linear guarantee) and `arxiv-2610.21261` (intervention effects decomposed into orders rather than assumed linear).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 456): **The cheapest available explanation for "our learned dictionary beats the neuron basis" is that any overcomplete set of directions beats the axes, and here the cheapest method wins: plain K-Means on averaged activations scored higher on the authors' own interpretability index (mean -0.0159) than every baseline including a single-layer L1 sparse autoencoder (best mean -0.0188), at the same width as the layer.** Two reporting consequences for this folder. First, any entry claiming a dictionary is more interpretable than units should carry a K-Means or PCA row at matched width, because the width comparison alone is confounded with the method. Second, the width sweep is null where it was run — K in {128, 256, 512} in a 256-unit layer produced no II difference, so neither narrowness nor overcompleteness explains the gain, which is the opposite of what the dictionary entries here report on language models and is worth watching: if the vision result does not transfer, the likely culprit is the space-averaged convolutional activation rather than the dictionary. Coreference `arxiv-1610.01644` (the untrained-network baseline — same argument applied to training) and `arxiv-2305.01610` (the random-basis rotation control — same argument applied to the coordinate system).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 456): **The metric's validity is layer-local and the authors say so, which makes this the folder's cleanest example of a measurement carrying its own domain with it: human agreement reached AUC 0.71 on the early ResNet50 layers, weakened deeper, and every subsequent claim was confined to layer 1 of the CIFAR-10 model — the layer where the metric had been checked, not the layer where superposition is supposed to be most consequential.** That is a discipline our own accounts should copy literally: print the validation domain beside the metric, and treat a metric validated on one layer (or one model, or one distribution) as unlicensed elsewhere. It also means the paper's headline result is untested where it matters most — mixed selectivity is a late-layer phenomenon and the interpretability index was never validated against humans there — and the honest reading is that the tie between superposition and mixed selectivity is demonstrated in the one regime where the instrument works. Coreference `arxiv-2411.13117` (automated-interpretability F1 as a borrowed yardstick with its own failure modes) and `arxiv-2606.24026` (an explanation score whose ranking does not survive a change of judge).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 456): **The unit-versus-direction gap survives the removal of training, so what training buys is alignment of directions with a semantic level rather than the existence of the directions: at initialisation the clusters already beat the axes, predictable by colour, and after training the same gap is better predicted by label information.** For a white-box model the consequence is sharp — a probe or dictionary that recovers interpretable directions from a randomly initialised network has found a property of the input distribution and of the readout geometry, not of what the network learned, and the diagnostic that separates the two is whether the recovered directions' predicted content shifts with training. It also re-prices the privileged-basis argument the paper makes in Appendix E, where ReLU quadrant counting is used to explain why any neuron should be interpretable at all: the argument is about the readout, so it cannot be evidence about learning. Coreference `arxiv-1610.01644` and `arxiv-2410.10811`. The synergy triad travels with it as a composition warning: a pair's interpretability cannot be predicted from its members' correlation (correlated pairs are more synergistic but the relationship is loose), neurons that already score well score worse in their best pairing, and the whole pattern replicates on macaque IT and AM data — so any account that composes a behaviour from separately-measured units needs a measured pairwise term, exactly the interaction-order residual that `arxiv-2610.21261` fits on coalitions.

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 455): **The folder now has the bound rather than only the curve: because the toy autoencoder can be dressed as a compressed-sensing algorithm — threshold the reconstruction to its top sparsity-count entries, then solve the convex problem of finding the nearest sparse vector with that support consistent with the projection — it inherits the deterministic recovery floor, so inner width must grow with the sparsity count times the log ratio of features to count.** This is the first statement here about how much compression is *impossible*, and it is the correct yardstick for every overcomplete-basis account in this folder: entries 440-454 all report how many more latents than dimensions a dictionary managed, and none printed the floor that says how many could never have been recoverable at that sparsity. The honest part is that the authors flag their own bound as probably loose (it lets superposition grow dramatically as features get sparser) and note their matrix is learned and importance-aware rather than incoherent — so the theorem prices the *recovery* question, not the dictionary the model actually learned. Coreference `arxiv-2411.13117` (the opposite result — a rank obstruction no amount of dictionary quality repairs, a floor on inference rather than on width).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 455): **A per-feature scalar computed purely from the weight matrix separates "no dimension", "half a dimension" and "a whole dimension", and its values cluster at the exact fractions of specific uniform polytopes — so a dictionary's packing can be read off its geometry with no data and no ground truth.** The quantity is squared embedding norm over summed squared projections of all other embeddings onto that direction; it sums to the width when packing is efficient, a commenter in the same document identifies it as the matrix leverage score under a near-isotropic assumption, and it resolves the three outcomes the paper cares about in one number. Two reporting rules follow: print dimensionality beside every latent-level claim about how much of the model a direction "is", and treat a fractional value as *information* rather than as noise, since the neighbouring entries spent ten runs discovering pathologies that all surface as latents holding a fraction of a dimension. Coreference `arxiv-2411.13117` (a decoder Gram matrix as the zero-data interference diagnostic — the same instinct one level down) and `arxiv-2505.11756` (hedging degree, a hand-built per-latent redundancy score that dimensionality could replace).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 455): **Correlation does not merely perturb the arrangement, it competes with the mechanism, and the competition has a measured direction: correlated features prefer to be orthogonal and, in a larger model, settle into a local almost-orthogonal basis inside an otherwise superimposed representation, while insufficient capacity collapses a correlated pair into its principal component — so PCA and superposition are two strategies on one axis, selected by correlation strength one way and sparsity the other.** For us this is a trap with a precise shape: a dictionary fitted on a correlated sub-distribution will report a clean, small, non-superimposed feature set for that slice while the model as a whole is superimposed, which is exactly the failure a probe trained on a narrow slice of inputs would exhibit and misreport as a global account. The paper's own reading is that this makes local bases insufficient for the safety-grade claim it wants, because a mechanistic account has to hold across the full distribution and off it. Coreference `arxiv-2602.14687` (a synthetic generator that builds correlation and hierarchy by construction — the instrument for testing this on our own fits) and `arxiv-2606.08365` (a predictor whose per-setting ranking changes with regime — the same lesson about local validity).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 454): **The dictionary and the coefficient vector are two objects, and the second one is bounded by a rank argument that no amount of dictionary quality repairs: because the encoder is a linear map followed by a pointwise nonlinearity, its pre-activations pass through M dimensions and their rank cannot exceed M, so on the diagonal code set — where the required output has rank N — the map cannot invert every admissible sparse source once M < N, which is exactly the regime where compressed sensing says unique recovery is possible (K·log(N/K) ≤ M). Reported empirically as a gap that persists at matched compute and widens with dimension.** For this folder the consequence is a reporting rule: an interpretability claim names whether it is about the *dictionary* (a set of directions, checkable against truth by matching) or about the *inference* (a code vector, checkable only against a ground truth or an optimality residual), and a reconstruction number silently spanning both is a number that cannot be attacked. Coreference `arxiv-2602.14687` (a ground-truth ladder separating reconstruction from feature recovery) and `arxiv-2503.17547` (a training-time architectural constraint that changes what the dictionary can express — here the wall is on the other side of the decoder).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 454): **Encoder capacity and dictionary geometry are separable dials, and in this entry they move the same way on the real model while the dictionary-side interventions in entries 445-453 moved them apart: on GPT-2 Small layer 9 at the same L1 penalty, an MLP encoder improves both reconstruction (normalised MSE 0.055 versus 0.061) and feature legibility (median automated-interpretability F1 0.83 versus about 0.6, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn/Bonferroni post-hoc), whereas whitening, Matryoshka nesting and synthetic-benchmark architecture changes each bought legibility at a fidelity cost or the reverse.** That is not a contradiction but a level distinction worth carrying into our own evaluation: a change to *how the code is inferred* can raise both columns, so a one-column win should be reported with the axis it came from. Two side results make it checkable — the MLP pays in dead latents (22% versus 11%) and therefore trains fewer live features than the SAE at nominally higher L0, and SAE+ITO warm-started from SAE latents climbs in steps to the best score of the three, which is the same trajectory entries 443-445 reported for gradient-pursuit refinement. Coreference `arxiv-2511.13981` (a strictly worse reconstructor as a strictly better feature set) and `arxiv-2602.14111` (reconstruction improving while feature recovery stays flat).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 454): **Plot performance against total FLOPs, not steps, because the step axis manufactures wins: here every MLP converges faster per step, and yet all widths cross the SAE's plateau at roughly the same total compute — about 3×10^14 FLOPs in the large synthetic regime — which converts "the MLP is better" into "past a fixed compute budget the MLP is better, and below it the SAE is", and the width of the MLP stops mattering on that axis.** The second lesson is a diagnostic that needs no ground truth at all: the decoder Gram matrix, where sparse coding learns near-orthogonal columns while the SAE and MLP keep large off-diagonals even when there is enough capacity for none — superposition visible in the weights rather than inferred from activations, which is the cheapest instrument this folder has found for "is the dictionary spending its dimensions on interference". Coreference `arxiv-2610.18462` (a budget choosing the answer) and `arxiv-2610.25700` (still unread, weakest topical fit of those named).

- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 453): **A failure that is provably loss-preferred can be answered without touching the penalty, by removing the capacity to express it: requiring each nested prefix of the dictionary to reconstruct the input on its own means a later latent cannot be the one that carries a general concept, so absorption at L0 40 falls from 0.49 to 0.05 and the number of latents needed per first letter falls from three to one, with no extra regulariser — this is the constructive twin of entry `arxiv-2409.14507`, which showed the same degenerate solution is strictly preferred at exactly perfect reconstruction.** Read with entry `arxiv-2602.14687`, it also fixes which column of that trade-off to trust: the Matryoshka dictionary explains 70% of the variance where BatchTopK explains 72%, yet the downstream cross-entropy of feeding reconstructions back into Gemma-2-2B is comparable at larger L0 and the feature-quality column is decisively better — so a fidelity number printed alone would have ranked the better dictionary last, the third time in this folder that a reconstruction metric has inverted the ranking of a feature metric. Coreference `arxiv-2505.11756` (the mixture optimum derived from an expected loss — the same pathology attacked by changing the loss instead of the architecture, which is what this paper avoids) and `arxiv-2511.13981` (a strictly worse reconstructor being a strictly better feature set, here reproduced as an architectural choice).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 453): **How much the latents share can be measured without ground truth by fitting a small dictionary to the decoder matrix itself, and the number is a width-dependent prediction rather than a static quality score: a meta-SAE at a quarter of the width with about four active latents explains 55% of the variance in BatchTopK decoder directions against 42% in Matryoshka directions at the largest width, and the gap widens as width grows because the unfixed architecture accumulates shared structure while the nested one stays flat.** This is the instrument our own accounts have been missing — average maximum pairwise decoder cosine says a pair looks similar, whereas the meta-SAE says how much of the whole dictionary is redundant with the rest of it, and entry `arxiv-2505.11756`'s hedging degree is the hand-built version of the same quantity. Two habits travel: report the statistic per width, because a composed dictionary and a hierarchical one are indistinguishable at 4k and clearly different at 65k; and note where the repair does not reach — on the chess model at hidden size 512 Matryoshka matches the field below L0 150 and degrades above it, which is the paper's own bound on the claim and is stated in an appendix rather than the conclusion. Coreference `arxiv-2605.09887` (a dictionary property that must be reported against the layer's own geometry instead of as a constant) and `arxiv-2610.18462` (a budget choosing the answer at fixed condition number).
- Pattern 2026-11-20 (run 453): **The ablation table is where the mechanism is actually identified, and here it says the hierarchy does not come from the nested loss being present but from how it is weighted: weighting each prefix reconstruction by its share of the new latents recovers BatchTopK's cross-entropy at the 200M-token ablation budget while giving up absorption and erasure quality, so equal weighting is the operative ingredient; a stop-gradient arm — training each prefix independently — improves absorption at low L0 but loses loss recovered, probing and erasure; three groups interpolate back toward the flat baseline and ten groups over-shrink the small prefixes into bad automated-interpretability scores.** Three reporting lessons for our own intervention studies: the parameter that price performance (loss weighting) and the parameter that buys the property (equal weighting) are the same one, so the trade-off is a dial rather than a constraint and should be reported as a curve; a variant that improves the headline pathology while degrading everything else is evidence that the pathology metric alone is insufficient; and the reproduction budget is a confound — the ablations run at 200M tokens while the main result runs at 500M, and the authors explicitly note the cross-entropy gap closes with more training, more L0 and more width. Coreference `arxiv-2606.08365` (a screen called strong only when both axes move) and `arxiv-2602.14111` (a constraint sweep where the reconstruction column responds and the downstream columns do not).
