- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 452): **A failure of a dictionary can be proved to be the objective's optimum rather than the optimiser's mistake, and the cheapest such proof in this folder is a one-parameter weight construction: hold the parent's encoder at the parent direction minus a fraction of the child, put that same fraction of the parent into the child's decoder, and reconstruction stays exactly perfect for every value of the parameter while the sparsity term for the pair falls linearly in it — so with the child firing at all, full absorption is strictly loss-preferred.** That is the same move as entry `arxiv-2508.16560`'s strict-descent theorem and entry `arxiv-2505.11756`'s interpolation-minimum curve, made arithmetic rather than approximate: three input cases, no training, and the conclusion survives the objection that the optimiser got stuck. For us it is a template for any account that decomposes a network into parts plus a sparse combiner — write the construction that keeps reconstruction fixed and moves the penalty, and if the penalty moves monotonically, the degenerate account is not a local quirk of your fitting procedure. Coreference `arxiv-2505.11756` (the mixture optimum derived from an expected loss rather than a construction) and `arxiv-2508.16560` (the same inversion of "what the loss prefers" versus "what we want", on real-width dictionaries).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 452): **A latent's interpretation is only accessible through its false negatives, and the paper supplies a way to find them external to the dictionary: train a linear probe on the same activations, take the tokens the probe classifies and the latent misses, and then run an ablation over every latent on exactly those tokens — if a latent with near-zero alignment to the probe carries by far the largest causal effect there, the feature lives in that latent's direction, not in the one that advertises it.** The control is what makes it a measurement rather than a story: project the probe direction out of the stealing latent and re-ablate, and the effect vanishes, which separates "this latent knows about the concept" from "this latent happens to be large". Two operational habits transfer to any account of ours: report recall alongside every interpretability claim (the case study's advertised latent scores 0.81 F1 while silently missing an obvious positive), and accept a detector's conservatism explicitly — the metric here requires a single dominant absorber and fully silent parents, so its rates are floors and the authors say so rather than rounding up. Coreference `arxiv-2501.17727` (an aggregate score hiding what a per-latent statistic shows) and `arxiv-2606.08365` (a pre-registered screen that is only called strong when both axes move).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 452): **The standard knob does not fix this failure, it amplifies it, and the failure is architecture-independent: absorption rises with L0 and with width across the whole Gemma Scope grid, appears in dictionaries trained on two other model families under both L1 and TopK objectives, and is reproduced in a batch-TopK toy that has no L1 term at all — so the cause is the preference for firing fewer latents, not the specific penalty.** Read against the neighbouring entries this closes a loop: entries 448-451 established that the fidelity frontier and the sparsity budget choose what a dictionary can say, and this entry adds that the same budget makes the *content* of what it says dependent, in a direction the practitioner would not predict (wider and sparser look more principled and are worse). The stated fixes are all structural — decompose a latent into atoms, attribute contributions explicitly, impose the hierarchy on the penalty — which is the folder's recurring answer to capacity failures. Coreference `arxiv-2508.16560` (too-low L0 corrupting every latent) and `arxiv-2605.09887` (the width exponent priced by geometry, i.e. the budget's effect being a function of the layer rather than a constant).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 451): **A scaling law is a layer-local calibration, not a property of the architecture, and this folder now has the layer-resolved version: fitting the standard width–sparsity surface separately at every layer of two models and regressing the per-layer width exponent on four neighbourhood statistics of the layer's own activation cloud, multi-scale curvature predicts it with leave-one-layer-out explained variance 0.869 at 9B (0.738 for intrinsic dimension, 0.793 for tangent variation) and 0.976 at 2B, and the same coefficients — standardised with the TRAINING model's moments so no test statistic leaks — predict the other model's exponents to within 0.009 of that model's own in-sample ceiling in both directions.** Two reporting habits make it credible and both belong in our own accounts: the null is the intercept-only model, i.e. exactly the assumption a single-layer law makes when extrapolated, and its leave-one-out score is the analytically known finite-sample bias −1+(n/(n−1))² … reported as −0.049 at 42 layers and −0.082 at 26 — so the baseline is computed, not assumed; and every hypothesis is also checked against a layer-permutation null that is shown to sit entirely below zero, which is the rare case of a paper printing the null distribution's shape rather than just its p-value. The honest failure sits in the same table: the four-feature model scores *worse* out of sample than a two-feature pair at 9B (0.806 against 0.863) because the summaries covary, and the authors read that as collinearity rather than signal loss. For us the operational rule is that any claim of the form "the dictionary at layer L has property X" should be reported against that layer's geometric position, because the exponent that prices X is depth-dependent by nearly a factor of the model width. Coreference `arxiv-2508.16560` (a budget whose wrong setting makes every latent wrong — the same ceiling, read as curvature instead of L0) and `arxiv-2610.18462` (the coordinates of the fit, not the information, deciding what the features are).- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 451): **The residual of a sparse linear dictionary is not a resource ceiling but a geometric wall, and this is the folder's first quantitative version of that claim: at the six layers where the released width grid is rich enough to identify a floor, the fitted floor's vertical ordering follows the layers' intrinsic-dimension and curvature ordering in both models, and the mechanism is stated in a form we can test — a k-sparse combination spans a flat k-dimensional affine subspace, a curved manifold departs from that span by a term proportional to curvature times squared neighbourhood scale, and that term survives as n→∞.** The distinction from the published single-layer account is the part worth carrying: Gao et al. explain an irreducible floor by *unstructured* content (their synthetic Gaussian-noise experiment gives a much shallower exponent), and this paper splits the floor into a dimension channel that recovers that reading and a curvature channel that predicts a non-zero floor on a fully structured but curved low-dimensional manifold — so a floor is not automatically evidence of noise-like activations. The paper's honesty about identifiability is the model to copy: because the released family shares only two widths across all 68 layers, the six-parameter surface is fitted where the grid allows and the claim is restricted to those six layers, with a floor-attenuation identity explaining why the floor-free exponent must underestimate the true one and why the residual gap against the published number is largest exactly at the high-curvature layers. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (structured rather than noise-like residual, measured directly) and `arxiv-2605.09887`'s own §E (the two channels separated).- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 451): **Every distance this folder quotes is a measurement in a chosen metric, and here the choice is made explicit: because an activation's meaning is the next-token distribution it encodes, the natural distance is the Fisher–Rao metric pulled back through the model's Jacobian, not ambient Euclidean distance, so two atoms orthogonal in the ambient inner product can be near-collinear under the predictive metric and vice versa — which makes "the direction of feature f" a metric-dependent, layer- and input-local object rather than a fixed vector, and predicts that a steering intervention's effective size varies across inputs and that the additivity assumed by circuit discovery holds only under a metric that locally linearises the predictive map.** The reframing is a demand on our own reporting rather than a result to cite loosely: cosine similarities, decoder overlap, and linear probes are all ambient-geometry statistics, and the paper's own empirical work is careful to say the four neighbourhood estimators are ambient proxies for a metric it does not compute. Two small methodological transfers ride along and are worth stealing outright: the robustness battery over four reconstruction metrics including a norm-free cosine distance (which agrees with the trimmed NMSE in shape, so the depth profile is not an artefact of heavy norm tails), and the discipline of measuring geometry and error on disjoint document ranges so the predictor cannot overfit token-level artefacts. Coreference `arxiv-2511.13981` (whitening, i.e. a metric change, moving both the objective and the features) and `arxiv-2211.12312` (a direction's meaning valid only inside a bounded region — the local-validity half of the same claim).- Could not read: **nothing failed to fetch. - Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 450): **A mixture of two features inside one latent is not a failure of the optimiser but the global optimum of the objective, and this folder now has the smallest possible demonstration: in a two-feature, one-latent, tied toy SAE the expected MSE+L1 is minimised at an interpolation strictly between the two true features for every firing regime tested, and the sparsity penalty does not move that minimum.** The proof is one curve and it removes the escape route that the solution was merely a bad local basin — the authors initialise the latent at the correct direction and watch it drift, which is the same strengthen-the-null move entry `arxiv-2508.16560` makes with its strict-descent theorem on real-width dictionaries, reached here from the degenerate one-latent end. For us the operational consequence is a precondition test we can run before quoting any latent-level claim: if the dictionary is narrower than the feature count and the features co-fire at all, singling out one feature is *suboptimal*, so a mixed latent is evidence about the budget rather than about the model. Coreference `arxiv-2511.13981` (a strictly worse reconstructor being a strictly better feature set — the same inversion of "what the loss prefers" and "what we want") and `arxiv-2602.14687` (Matryoshka winning the quality column while Matching Pursuit wins reconstruction — two axes from one objective).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 450): **Two failure modes that are fixed by opposite interventions are indistinguishable from one side of the dictionary, and the paper's cure is the cleanest example in the folder of reading a latent pair as a signed sum: absorption pushes a negative component of the child into the parent encoder, hedging pushes a positive one, so a matryoshka level coefficient around 0.75 beats both the plain SAE and the stock matryoshka SAE on most SAEBench columns by letting them cancel.** It also supplies the discrimination rule for our own dictionaries — decoder change means hedging, encoder-only change means absorption — because an absorbing SAE can revise a parent's encoder without touching its decoder, while a narrow SAE forced to carry a second feature must move both. The honest failure is worth as much as the win: at heterogeneous child firing rates no single β balances all three children (their β = 0.17 toy leaves a little of both), the authors propose per-latent coefficients and leave it open, and SCR *worsens* at the balanced setting while being flagged as the noisiest metric — so a repair chosen on a majority of benchmarks is reported with its dissenting column intact. Coreference `arxiv-2602.14111` (a constraint sweep that moves the reconstruction column and barely touches the downstream ones) and `arxiv-2606.08365` (a screening rule that declares success only when both axes move).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 450): **Width is not a neutral hyperparameter, and this is the first entry where that is a measured prediction rather than a caveat: hedging degree falls monotonically from narrow to wide and still does not reach zero at 65,536 latents, so "the features this SAE has" is a statement whose content changes with the budget.** The paired-within-dictionary design is what makes it credible — the same SAE is trained further both with and without 64 appended latents, and the difference between the two continuations is projected onto the new latents with a random-direction projection subtracted, so the null is built into the statistic instead of assumed. Two things to carry: a width or capacity budget in our own accounts must be printed beside any latent-level claim, and the *direction* of a truncated account's error is predictable, not random — a narrow account reports mixtures where a wide one reports atoms, which is exactly the bias a model of the network would acquire if it were fitted at a small budget. Coreference `arxiv-2508.16560` (starting L0 too low leaves the run in a basin it cannot anneal out of — the same budget-chosen solution, read dynamically) and `arxiv-2610.18462` (moving where the factors are generated flipping the winner at fixed condition number — the budget deciding the answer).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 448): **The optimisation objective can actively prefer the wrong answer to the right one, and this folder's standard evaluation plot cannot tell which it got: at L0 = 5, below the toy model's true L0 of 11, a corrupted SAE whose latents mix correlated features reaches an MSE of 2.73 while the ground-truth SAE forced to fire at the same L0 reaches 4.88 — so a sparsity–reconstruction curve ranks the correct dictionary worse than the wrong one, and the authors state plainly that a method returning perfect features would be rejected by it.** The proof matters more than the number: the disentangled dictionary is shown to be not merely non-optimal but *not a local minimum* of expected MSE under the sparsity cap, with a strict descent direction toward mixed latents that acts on nearly every latent at once, and the proof needs only *co-occurrence*, not statistical correlation — correlation only sets the magnitude and sign. For us this is the folder's clearest statement that a fidelity number prices a dictionary against the objective it was trained on rather than against the truth, and it converts the recurring reconstruction-is-not-recovery warning into a constructive theorem. Coreference `arxiv-2602.14111` (random baselines matching trained piles on every downstream column while reconstruction separates them) and `arxiv-2511.13981` (a strictly worse reconstructor being a strictly better feature set — the same inversion measured on real activations).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 448): **The direction of a design error decides whether it is recoverable, and here the asymmetry is measured in training dynamics rather than argued: starting L0 too high and annealing to the correct value ends with the true features, while starting too low and annealing to the same value does not fully recover, because the low-L0 latents sit in a basin that gradient descent prefers under the cap.** The companion asymmetry in the static result sharpens it — at L0 = 18 the damage is partial and many latents stay correct, at L0 = 5 every latent is affected — and the paper's own account of the difference is exactly the loss-surface story: the mixed solution is a *better* optimum at low L0 and merely an accessible one at high L0. Two operational consequences for our own accounts: any sweep over a budget-like hyperparameter should be run from the *generous* end downward, since the failures we risk are the ones that do not anneal away; and a single fitted point from an under-budgeted run cannot be described as "the features this model has", because the run may be sitting in a basin chosen by the budget. Coreference `arxiv-2610.18462` (a training budget changing which coordinate the winner is measured in, with the gap shrinking from 0.0198 to 0.0016 as the budget grows) and `arxiv-2412.06410` (a sparsity budget that moves the trade-off curve without changing what the dictionary is — the same knob, read statically rather than dynamically).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 448): **A scalar summary of the dictionary's own geometry can locate the correct hyperparameter with no labels and no forward pass over the model, and the metric is one line of code: mean absolute cosine across all distinct decoder column pairs, minimised at the true L0 in five-seed toy runs, still roughly minimised under superposition noise, correctly shifted down in a deliberately narrow SAE, and coinciding with peak sparse-probing F1 at roughly L0 200 in Gemma-2-2b layer 5, Llama-3.2-1b layer 7 and Gemma-2-2b layer 12.** The honest part is as reusable as the metric: its curves have broad shallow minima, so it is strong at *ruling out* wrong settings (especially too sparse) and weak at pinpointing an optimum, and it agrees imperfectly with probing at high L0 — the authors lead their discussion with those limitations and recommend it as one signal among several, which is the strength at which we should quote it. It also earns a claim we can test on our own dictionaries: a JumpReLU dictionary that stays near the same L0 across a wide range of its sparsity coefficient is self-correcting because its thresholds receive gradients per latent, whereas a global TopK cap cannot adjust and the histogram at L0 = 750 shows a narrow core plus a heavy tail — some latents over-firing while others under-fire at the same setting. Coreference `arxiv-2606.08365` (decoder crowding as a *predictor* of steering collateral, the same statistic with a different job) and `arxiv-2605.09887` (geometry deciding what a dictionary can represent, arrived at from the manifold side).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 447): **A behaviour can be predicted from statistics frozen before the intervention, and the prediction is strongest exactly where the folder keeps warning it should not be trusted: the no-magnitude predictor set beats frequency-only and activation-magnitude-only baselines in all four settings (mean CV Spearman +0.390/+0.421/+0.193/+0.451 over frequency for GPT-2/Pythia/Gemma/Llama) and survives residualisation of the label against effect magnitude, intervention strength and natural activation in three of four — yet every dominant predictor is different (decoder crowding in GPT-2 at ρ = 0.466, direct-logit L2 in Pythia at 0.391 and Llama at 0.464, encoder norm in Gemma at 0.350), and the one setting where residualisation fails (Gemma) is also the one whose absolute-stability target no predictor can reach (0.028).** For us the reusable form is the same discipline this folder has been applying to dictionaries, now applied to a predictor: the claim that transfers is the *procedure*, and the paper names it method-level transfer while explicitly rejecting mechanism-level transfer — so an account of model behaviour should print its per-setting ranking of predictors and not promote the winner in one model into the account of the phenomenon. The confound control is cheap and should be copied verbatim: refit the label on the nuisance variables, then re-run the identical regression on the residual. Coreference `arxiv-2610.18462` (a predictor that got every synthetic sign right and every reserved-direction sign wrong — transport failing the same way) and `arxiv-2610.15850` (an observational statistic that cannot license an intervention; here the intervention is the label, not the input).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 447): **Screening that works on one axis and fails on the other is the normal outcome rather than a weak result, and the paper's pre-specified grading rule is what makes that legible: stability and collateral per effect are separate targets, four settings produce four different verdicts (both axes in GPT-2, stability only in Pythia at p = 1e-8, collateral only in Llama at p = 1.3e-4 with effect L2 balanced, collateral only and magnitude-tainted in Gemma), and a 4× dictionary-width change moves Llama from "collateral" to "stability via a different selector" while the predictive gain barely moves (+0.451 to +0.420).** Two design moves are worth stealing outright. First, the ranker is matched on predicted effect size before the contrast is measured, and the realised effect size is then checked for balance — so a group that steers more cleanly cannot be winning merely by steering harder, which is exactly the confound that would make an ablation-based claim in our own work meaningless. Second, a screening result is called strong only when both axes move; the paper refuses to let the axis that happened to move stand for "the screen works". Coreference `arxiv-2602.14111` (a metric and a budget each deciding the winner of the same comparison) and `arxiv-2511.13981` (a strictly worse reconstructor being a strictly better feature set — the same two-axes-do-not-align shape on the fidelity side).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 447): **Where a component sits in the dictionary's own geometry is the cheapest available predictor of collateral damage, and the paper supplies the mechanism sketch that makes it checkable: because the downstream change of a feature under a small edit is approximated by the gradient dotted with the decoder direction, a direction that overlaps many neighbours should drag more neighbours along — so decoder crowding predicts downstream collateral count in the ReLU settings (ρ = 0.466 in GPT-2, cross-validated 0.512 from geometry alone) while predicting it poorly in the one setting with much lower crowding and much larger coactivation counts (Pythia geometry-only collateral 0.087).** The diagnostic table that accompanies this is more useful than the predictor: the four settings occupy different regimes (GPT-2 and Pythia highest crowding, Gemma low crowding but large coactivation count, Llama the widest decoder-norm variation), which turns "the predictor signature is model-dependent" from an excuse into a measurement, though the author flags four settings as too few for a causal reading. For our white-box account the takeaway is that dictionary geometry is a *state variable* worth reporting per layer, not a constant — and that a failure of a geometry predictor is informative about the regime, not about the predictor. - Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 446): **A more expressive encoder can improve reconstruction by fitting the interference rather than the signal, and this is the first entry where the failure is isolated to a single variable: as the hidden dimension shrinks and feature overlap rises, explained variance falls for every architecture except Matching Pursuit, which rises while its matching and F1 fall — its serial residual projection can absorb the noise that superposition creates.** That is a checkable adversarial test for any account we fit, and the paper's framing makes it a precondition rather than a curiosity: it is run in a world where the linear hypothesis holds exactly, so the failure cannot be blamed on the representation assumption. Two supporting ablations make the mechanism legible rather than suggestive — increasing the spread of firing magnitudes improves matching but lowers F1 for every architecture, and in that high-spread regime the plain L1 dictionary has the best matching of all, which the authors report as unexplained. For our own predictive white-box work the discipline is the same ladder — synthetic ground truth, then a reproduction of known real-model phenomena in it, then the real-model rung — and no claim should jump the middle rung; the authors also list the honest limit, that the synthetic world's *hyperparameters* (how many features, how much correlation, how deep the hierarchy) are guesses because real models' ground truth is unavailable. Concretely: whitening changes the latent scale the sparsity penalty acts on, so whitened-vs-standard is a basis *plus* an effective-penalty change, and the paper reports no penalty sweep that holds sparsity constant across the pair. When we quote any paired comparison from this folder, the arm difference must be exactly one thing.

That is the same instrument our own predictive-white-box work needs — score the whole surrogate family against behaviour, not the single fitted point — and it recurs in the geometric-wall framing already on the free list (`2605.09887`).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 444): **An instrument that cannot separate a trained model from a norm-matched randomly initialised one is not measuring learning, and here three of the four standard axes fail that test across 70M-6.9B: fuzzing auto-interpretability AUROC for SAEs on the randomised variants overlaps the trained curve while the deliberately broken control sits at chance, and the reconstruction axes, explained variance and L1 follow the same pattern.** The control arm is the design lesson and it is not the obvious one — the floor is not random weights, it is inconsistent token vectors, i.e. per-occurrence Gaussian embeddings on the *trained* model, so the instrument is first shown working on the arm that should defeat it and only then fails on the arm that matters. Two consequences for us: a chance-floor arm has to be one the instrument *can* separate, otherwise a null result is indistinguishable from an instrument that reports nothing; and a dictionary claim that says only better than chance must print which chance. Coreference `arxiv-2602.14111` (three frozen-random dictionary baselines matching trained SAEs on interpretability, probing and editing — the same failure reached by randomising the dictionary instead of the network) and `arxiv-1610.01644` (the untrained network absorbing most of a probe's reading — the probe-side version of the same null).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 444): **Aggregates hide exactly the difference the paper is looking for, and a per-latent statistic recovers it for nearly nothing: token-distribution entropy — the entropy of a latent's total activation over token IDs across its top examples — rises with layer for the trained model and stays low and flat for every randomised variant, and the per-latent scatter shows why the aggregate score could not see this, because randomised SAEs have an inverse relation between entropy and AUROC (their well-scored features are single-token ones) while trained SAEs contain a branch of latents that are simultaneously high-entropy and well explained.** This is the folder's cheapest reusable measure so far: no training, no grader, computed from the same maximum-activating examples every auto-interpretability pipeline already collects. The qualitative appendix confirms what the number means — randomised variants get descriptions about parts of proper nouns and function words, trained ones about size adjectives and economic-development nouns — and the authors call the statistic a proof of concept rather than a measure of abstractness. For us: every dictionary report carries a per-latent shape column, and a feature that fires on one token ID is labelled a token detector before it is labelled a concept. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (aggregate reconstruction error concealing structured residue — the same aggregation error in the fidelity column) and `arxiv-2305.01610` (a mean over units hiding which units carry the effect).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 444): **A null result about an instrument can itself have a mechanism, and this paper supplies a toy model rather than leaving the failure a mystery: an affine map provably carries superposed data to superposed data, changing only the noise covariance and the feature-to-activation map, and a randomly initialised two-layer ReLU MLP not merely preserves but improves the sparsity attainable at fixed explained variance — the Pareto frontiers for superposed toy data, for GloVe vectors and for Pythia embedding matrices all move in the favourable direction after the random MLP.** That is a specific, checkable reason a dictionary fitted on a random network can look good: it is interpreting a computation that really happens, a sparsification of an already-sparse input distribution. Two reporting habits travel. First, the toy models are presented as evidence for plausibility with the authors explicitly declining to say which of two mechanisms dominates, which is the right strength for a mechanism sketch. Second, the ordering anomaly is explained rather than smoothed — the re-randomised variants sit closer to the trained model than the genuine initialisation checkpoint because the randomisation preserves each weight matrix's norm and the true initialisation does not — which is the confound to expect whenever an arm is compared against a checkpoint rather than a matched construction. Coreference `arxiv-2408.05451` (a randomly initialised layer already linearly representing the target circuit — a random network computing something real) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (unlearned readers matching learned ones at matched size).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 444): **One column of the standard suite is structurally unavailable in the null arm, and the authors say so instead of dropping it: loss recovered — the fraction of the cross-entropy damage of zeroing activations that the reconstruction avoids — makes sense only for the trained model, because the randomised variants' own language-modelling loss is poor whether the original or the reconstructed activations are used.** This is a category the folder should keep separate from the others: some measures are relative to a baseline state of the model and cannot be computed at all when that baseline is destroyed by construction, whereas AUROC, explained variance and L1 are computable in any arm and can therefore be shown to fail. The practical rule: when a suite is run across randomised arms, print the measures that are undefined in an arm as undefined with the reason rather than deleting the column, and know that only the surviving columns can carry a null comparison. Coreference `arxiv-2412.06410` (an object trained as a batch rule and deployed as a threshold — the same this-metric-only-exists-for-one-of-the-two-objects defect) and `arxiv-2610.15850` (an observational statistic with no licence for an intervention — the missing-column problem one step further upstream).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 443): **The folder finally has a null hypothesis to test its dictionaries against, and the null wins on every downstream column: three baselines that never learn a direction — random frozen decoder, random frozen encoder, and a decoder pinned within cosine 0.8 of random — reproduce interpretability 0.87 vs 0.90, single-latent probing 0.69 vs 0.72 and causal editing 0.73 vs 0.72, while the authors' own significance table shows the trained model ahead on all 30 reconstruction comparisons but only 21/30 probing and 20/30 editing.** The mechanism is not mysterious and is worth stating in our own terms: with tens of thousands of latents, a hard sparsity cap, and a linear-plus-sparsity objective, an encoder can do amortised sparse selection over an expressive random dictionary, and the reported decoder drift in Appendix C (cosine similarities still near 0.8 after the loss has plateaued at 5% of training) is consistent with that. For us the rule is now mechanical and cheap: every claim of the form "this account beats chance" ships with a same-shaped random-direction arm, and the margin is quoted per metric rather than as a verdict. Coreference `arxiv-1610.01644` (the untrained network absorbing most of a probe's reading) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (unlearned readers matching learned ones at matched size) — the same control arriving from the dictionary side, the probe side and the reader side respectively.
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 443): **Reconstruction and recovery are formally different quantities and here the gap is measured in a generator where both are computable: at matched expansion factor and matched L0, three of four architectures reach 0.67–0.73 explained variance while recovering 7–9% of the long-tailed true features (3 of 3,200 above 0.8 cosine for BatchTopK in the constant setting), and TopK — the one architecture with a hard per-sample cap — recovers 99.9% there and 43% in the long tail.** The pattern of the failure is the important part: recovery is concentrated almost entirely on the highest-frequency features, so the reconstruction objective buys the head of the distribution and abandons the tail, which is exactly the regime our feature-level claims live in. Two controls make the result trustworthy and both should be copied: the expansion factor is set to 32 rather than the ≈2 of earlier toy studies, and the same four architectures are re-run on an external correlated generator in an appendix, where TopK's MMCS rises from 0.644 to 0.825 when the cap is loosened from 20 to 100 while BatchTopK goes 0.322 to 0.489 — a width-versus-recovery curve that is a checkable prediction rather than a claim. Coreference `arxiv-2610.18462` (reconstruction improving while feature quality does not, driven by coordinate weights) and `arxiv-2412.06410` (the sparsity budget moving the trade-off curve without changing what the dictionary is).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 443): **A constraint sweep can separate a metric that measures the object from a metric that measures the setup, and this paper's τ ablation is the cleanest instance in the folder: tightening the decoder's cosine cap to its random initialisation from 0.8 to 0.9 to 0.95 drops explained variance 0.785 → 0.734 → 0.691 while probing stays 0.659 → 0.639 → 0.637 and editing 0.728 → 0.712 → 0.681, so the reconstruction column responds monotonically to a change that the downstream columns barely register.** Read with the paper's rejected-baseline cells (a covariance-initialised frozen encoder at Llama layer 16 scoring exactly 0.000 explained variance and exactly 0.500 probing, the guessing floor), the conclusion for our instrumentation is that a degenerate baseline is a statement about the baseline's geometry and has to be reported as such, not averaged into a headline. The generalisable rule: when an account's hyperparameter is a boundary (a cap, a threshold, a budget), sweep it and publish which of your metrics move — the ones that do not move are the ones that cannot certify anything. Coreference `arxiv-2407.14435` (a density-at-the-boundary reading of a hard threshold, and a fidelity frontier that failed to move the legibility column) and `arxiv-2412.06410` (a budget parameter whose sweep exposed the baseline's inability to hold L0 fixed).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 442): **Two dictionaries trained on provably identical information can disagree about which features exist, and the disagreement is caused by which coordinates the squared error weighed: because the readout scales one direction by 100 and another by 1, equal errors before scaling contribute in the ratio 10,000:1, so logit-trained features spend their capacity on the amplified directions while gain-free features spend it evenly — and moving where the factors were generated, at a fixed condition number, flips the winner (+0.4095 F1 to −0.4460 F1 at κ=100, K=2).** The rule for us is mechanical: an account of "which features the model has" is incomplete without the statement of the coordinate system in which the dictionary was fitted, and a disagreement between two dictionaries over the same activations is evidence about neither until the training geometry is matched. Coreference `arxiv-2610.21261` (a dictionary claim read out behaviourally, where the residual rather than the coordinate system was the question) and `arxiv-2412.06410` (a sparsity budget that also moves the curve without changing what the dictionary is).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 442): **The exact wrapper is the cleanest control the folder has seen for "is this a fact about the model or a fact about the optimiser": transforming encoder input, decoder output and error metric together reproduces RC-DS training to 1.33e-15 in nine numerical checks, so any residual difference is geometry and only geometry — whereas reweighting the loss alone, which still feeds scaled inputs to the encoder, recovers 0.6284 of the 0.8176 that the full transform reaches.** That three-way split (wrapper 0.8176 / loss-only 0.6284 / ordinary 0.4841) is the template: to attribute an effect to training rather than information, build the transformation that should make the two arms literally the same computation, run it, and show it converges — then any gap you keep is the thing you claim to have found. Coreference `arxiv-2407.14435` (a straight-through estimator that is exactly a kernel-density estimate of the true gradient — the same move, an exactness check that converts a heuristic into a known quantity) and `arxiv-2610.17898` (a closed-form identity reported as an implementation check rather than as an empirical result).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 442): **A reconstruction improvement is not a feature-quality improvement, and this paper supplies all three ways the inference fails in one grid: the metric decides the winner (gain-free EV favours RC-DS in 18/18 settings, logit EV favours the baseline in 17/18), the budget decides it (the gap falls from 0.0198 to 0.0016 between 60 and 1,000 epochs and both fresh-prompt intervals include zero), and a zero-cost baseline beats both (raw singular coordinate probes score higher than every trained RC-DS label detector in all 18 settings, differences 0.0002 to 0.1838 AUROC, because multiplying a coordinate by a positive gain cannot change its ranking).** The frozen predictor is the closing lesson: it got the sign right in all 36 synthetic pairs and then got all four out-of-band reserved-model directions wrong and scored worse than predicting zero, a gap the authors attribute to having only three development task groups — so a directional forecast validated inside a synthetic family does not transfer to a new model population, and the paper reports the failure at the same prominence as the success. Coreference `arxiv-2410.10811` (an unlearned arm matching a learned one, revealed as nothing) and `arxiv-2610.15850` (an observational statistic that cannot license an intervention — the transport failure here is the same shape one level out).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 441): **"These methods agree with each other" is now a measured dead end rather than a caution, and the measurement is the useful part: in the nonlinear arm IG, GA and SHAP form a correlated cluster (ρ 0.42 to 0.80, all p < 0.0001) while none of them tracks the intervention, and the zero-cost probe-weight baseline is uncorrelated with all three (ρ ≤ 0.037).** The linear arm makes the trap explicit rather than rhetorical — there IG, GA and interventional SHAP are *analytically identical* (max absolute difference 6.32e-7), so the perfect rank agreement is a closed form the authors report as an implementation check and explicitly refuse to present as evidence that the methods agree in general. For us the rule is mechanical: inter-method agreement is a consistency statistic, never a validity statistic, and any account whose evidence is "several methods converge" needs a fourth column holding the measured intervention. Coreference `arxiv-2610.15850` (a discovery score and a probe coefficient can both be right about the data and wrong about the edit) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (unlearned readers matching learned ones — agreement at matched size, revealed as nothing).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 441): **Importance and directional faithfulness are separable and the best method for one is the worst for the other, which is the sharpest report format the folder has found for a predictor-versus-intervention gap: the zero-cost probe weights were the only linear-arm method with real directional faithfulness (ρ = 0.410, q < 0.0001) while every gradient and SHAP method sat near zero, and those same methods were the ones with moderate importance faithfulness (ρ 0.256-0.279, q 0.0088-0.0111).** Read together with the local-versus-global result — local attribution wins on direction in both arms under both the active-only and the continuous-activity control, while its advantage on magnitude is fully explained by knowing which features are switched on (and reverses in the MLP arm once inactive features are excluded, global +0.371 versus local +0.077) — the conclusion is that averaging is not uniformly good or bad, it depends on which of the two properties you need, and the choice must be stated rather than assumed. For our accounts: every predicted influence carries separate magnitude and sign scoring, and every averaged/aggregated explanation states which property it was validated on. Coreference `arxiv-2610.15850` (the three-term decomposition — its omitted-variable term is the same "you are looking at a different coordinate than the one you edit" defect) and `arxiv-2408.05451` (localisation and causation coming apart under ablation).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 441): **The asymmetry between insertion and deletion is the operational warning the folder needs before it ever cites a null ablation: with a known ground truth the same methods recover inserted sentiment well above chance (local SHAP AUROC 0.792, causal recovery ρ = 0.536) and sit exactly at chance for deletions (0.520 local, 0.509 global, ρ 0.254 and 0.163) even though the readout registered the deletion correctly in 77% of pairs — so the effect is there in behaviour and smeared across the representation, with each feature moving too little to outrank the noise.** The authors' stated implication is the one to carry: a null ablation result should not be read as evidence that no feature carries the effect. Two design elements make the claim trustworthy and both are worth copying: the distractor set is sampled at random rather than by top global attribution magnitude (which would have forced SHAP's AUROC toward zero) and the SHAP background is the canonical training background rather than the pair's own activations (which would have tautologically inflated AUROC), and the near-zero-on-natural-text result is read against a harness-sensitivity arm instead of being asserted as method failure. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (a residue the instrument cannot see, so absence needs a blind-spot statement) and `arxiv-2505.05410` (a number stated as a ceiling with its direction of error named).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 440): **The separation the folder keeps asserting is now a theorem with a boundary condition attached, and the boundary is what makes it actionable: for any response function class closed under adding affine functions, every observational statistic — correlation, class-mean difference, rank test, probe coefficient, any discovery score — takes the same value under two responses that differ in their gradient along directions the observed activations never vary in, so an intervention that pushes along such a direction has an attribution the data cannot pin down at all.** The identified set is the whole real line exactly when the mean edit is not a combination of observed activation differences, and the paper measures that condition in its own evaluation design: the median share of the mean steering edit lying outside the observed span is nearly one. For our account this converts "presence is not use" from a slogan into a computable precondition — report the share of the edit outside the span, and where it is high, no observational evidence of any kind can substitute for a gradient. Coreference `arxiv-2211.12312` (a direction is valid only inside a bounded region — the geometric form of the same statement) and `arxiv-2408.05451` (a randomly initialised layer already linearly represents the target circuit, so presence is cheap independently of training).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 440): **When an instrument and its target disagree, the productive move is not to pick a winner but to write the disagreement exactly as a sum of interpretable parts, and here the error of a probe-based prediction splits into three terms each of which vanishes under a nameable condition: a Stein residual (probe slope across prompts versus mean local sensitivity — zero when the response is affine everywhere or the activations are Gaussian), an omitted-variable term (the activation pattern the probe reads versus the coordinates the intervention edits — zero when the edit lies along the read direction, and equal to the whole gap when a final-position probe is asked about an edit at positions it never reads), and an edit-gradient covariance (zero for steering, whose edit is fixed, and potentially dominant for ablations, whose edit varies with the prompt).** Each term is one backward pass per prompt to estimate. This is the decomposition template the folder should reuse for every predictor-versus-intervention gap we report: the residual says the response is curved across the data, the omitted-variable term says the readout is looking somewhere the edit is not, and the covariance term says rare firings are doing the work. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (the unexplained residue as a first-class object) and `arxiv-2311.07568` (a rival solution fitting the same observations — association underdetermining mechanism).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 439): **The folder's entire direction-based apparatus carries an unstated validity condition, and this paper supplies both the condition and a cheap way to measure its edge: a direction does not mean the same thing at every magnitude, so a claim of the form "this direction is feature X" is licensed only inside a bounded region, and the boundary of that region can be estimated from forward passes alone by dividing the Hamming distance between binarised activation codes by the Euclidean distance between the points.** That density statistic costs one forward pass per point, has no trained parameters, and turns "is this input off-distribution" from a judgement into a number with a confidence interval — which is exactly the object our predictive account needs if it is to say where its predictions hold. Two further structural points travel. First, binarising the activation code keeps most of the magnitude information, because a code implicitly defines the linear constraints that bound a small region, so a reader that throws away magnitudes is not throwing away as much as it appears to — a useful fact for any hash-based or code-based index we build. Second, the authors' own scaling experiment shows the instrument pointing the wrong way: density peaks in a shell between the origin and the activation, so boundaries mark the *inner* edge of validity rather than the places where the answer changes. A cheap instrument that is right about the existence of a boundary and wrong about its location is the normal case, and reporting which of the two you got is what makes it usable. Coreference `arxiv-1610.01644` (probe curves measure linear usability along a chain of maps, not information — the same "the instrument's shape is not the network's shape" clause) and `arxiv-2405.14860` (geometry present, behaviour absent).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 439): **The strongest argument in the folder against expecting a perfect dictionary to yield prediction comes from a paper about geometry, and it is an argument rather than a measurement: even a complete sparse overcomplete basis leaves the problem intact, because every *combination* of active features meets the nonlinearities differently, so which units are above threshold cannot be known without computing the interference terms and running the forward pass.** The authors state the consequence as a limit on their own alternative too — that is why they are pushed to local rather than global bases in the first place. For our goal this fixes what a dictionary-based account can and cannot claim: it can license statements about what is represented at a point and about reconstruction, and it cannot license a prediction of which units fire downstream unless the account adds either the region structure or an explicit assumption that interference is negligible. Any claim of the second kind we print should name which of those two it is standing on. Coreference `arxiv-2408.05451` (a randomly initialised layer already linearly represents the conjunction circuit — presence without use, from the theory side) and `arxiv-2412.06410` (a budget trained as one mechanism and deployed as another — the same gap between the object we fit and the object we run).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 439): **The one statistical result in this paper is small, significant and reported honestly, and the reporting is the reusable part: the y-axis of the density figure begins at 80%, the effect is described in the text as small but significant, the test statistic and p-value are printed, 99% bootstrap intervals are attached, and the *untrained* network is the control that makes the trained difference mean anything — in the untrained condition the intra-class density is not lower.** That is the fourth entry in recent runs where the untrained or randomly initialised arm is what prices an apparent effect, and it is now the folder's default expectation rather than a refinement. The authors also decline to over-claim where the check was qualitative: predictions 1 and 2 are said to be supported, prediction 3 only partially, and the untrained network's odd behaviour (all inputs collapsing to one answer) is openly attributed to batch normalisation in their model variant and left uninvestigated. Printing the rung a result reached, next to the result, is the same discipline the field survey names and the same one our own entries should follow. Coreference `arxiv-2305.01610` (the random-basis rotation arm paying for the true-basis result) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (unlearned readers matching learned ones at matched size).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 438): **Move the sparsity budget from per-item to per-batch and the trade-off curve moves without any change to what the dictionary is: keeping the n*k largest latents across a batch of n samples lets a low-information sample spend one feature while a dense sample spends more than eighty, at the same average cost — and the histogram showing that spread is the entire evidence that the constraint is worth relaxing.** The sharper lesson for our own instrumentation is what happened at deploy: the trained object is a sorted batch rule, but a single activation at test time cannot be sorted, so it is replaced by one global threshold estimated as the expected smallest positive activation, and the adaptive allocation is trained but no longer applied. Any account of ours that trains with one mechanism and predicts with another must say which of the two its claims are about. Coreference `arxiv-2407.14435` (the threshold-in-the-loss construction this paper is measured against, and whose L0 has to be swept rather than set) and `arxiv-2502.04878` (dictionary width deciding which units exist — the same argument one dimension over, where the budget parameter is the width rather than the count).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 438): **Fidelity and downstream usefulness inverted with scale in the authors' own results, and they report it as a split rather than picking a winner: BatchTopK reconstructed better than JumpReLU on both models at every setting, yet on the larger model it carried the lower cross-entropy degradation only at the loosest budget (k = 16) and lost on both fixed and swept settings.** That is the third instance in the folder of a reconstruction-column win failing to survive the behavioural column, and the first where the deciding variable is model size rather than architecture. Two practices keep the comparison honest and cost nothing: the two axes (dictionary size, target sparsity) were run as separate fixed-one-axis experiments instead of being blended, and the baseline's inability to hold a fixed L0 during a sweep was stated rather than papered over, so the reader knows the baseline points are approximately matched. - Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 436): **The paper's own numbers are the argument against reading a fidelity curve as a legibility curve: JumpReLU is at or past the frontier everywhere, yet the automated simulation correlation moves only "a small but notable" amount from Gated to JumpReLU with the within-group spread clearly wider than the between-group gap, and the human ratings are statistically indistinguishable across all three architectures.** The authors state the consequence rather than burying it — the science of SAE evaluation is "in its infancy" and they do not know that these ratings correlate with the downstream usefulness of a dictionary — and they print a control that makes the automated score interpretable: a randomly initialised SAE, whose clipped random projections score markedly worse but with a clearly non-zero mean, which is the number that prices the whole pipeline. For us this is the reporting rule the folder has been converging on, now with a concrete instance: a dictionary claim ships reconstruction and legibility as separable columns, and when an instrument is a language model grading a language model, the random-weights baseline and the per-item spread ship with the mean. Coreference `arxiv-1610.01644` (the untrained-network arm that absorbs most of a probe's reading) and `arxiv-2305.01610` (max-activating examples as a biased sample — the legibility side of the same "the score is not the object" problem).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 436): **A discontinuous parameter inside a loss is not untrainable — it is untrainable per example and perfectly trainable in expectation, and this paper's cleanest result is that the straight-through estimator so trained is *exactly* a kernel-density estimate of the true expected-loss gradient, with the kernel bandwidth playing the bandwidth role and the pseudo-derivative applied only where a pre-activation lands within that band of the threshold.** The derivation is worth keeping as a template because it separates the two forces explicitly: raising a feature's threshold costs reconstruction in proportion to how much that feature was contributing at the margin, and saves sparsity at the price of the L0 coefficient, and both are weighted by the density of activations near the threshold — so a feature whose activations never approach its threshold is simply not tuned, which is a price the training hyperparameters (threshold 0.001 and bandwidth 0.001, swept and reused across models, sites and layers) are tuned around. The general lesson for our own instruments: whenever an account's parameter is a boundary (a cut, a gate, a firing threshold), the measurement of "does this matter" is a density at the boundary, and a flat gradient reading is the signature of an empty band rather than of an irrelevant parameter. Coreference `arxiv-2504.02922` (a regulariser that manufactures the finding it was meant to reveal — the same "the training pressure chose the answer" hazard in loss form) and `arxiv-2502.04878` (dictionary width deciding which units exist).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 436): **Decoupling "is it on" from "how much of it" is the single move that fixes both failure modes at once, and the paper's Figure 1 makes the dilemma mechanical: with a ReLU encoder, false positives can only be suppressed by lowering the encoder bias, and lowering the bias systematically underestimates the magnitude of the features that stay on — so the two errors are traded one for one until a separate threshold interrupts the trade.** The same structure appears in their loss design: an L1 penalty drags magnitudes down as well as counting features and is not even invariant to reparameterising encoder against decoder, which is why they train L0 directly and why the field's reparameterisation-invariant variant rescales each coefficient by its direction's norm. Two smaller things travel and are cheap to copy: sparsity is *selected*, not merely penalised, so the reported curve is a sweep over the coefficient rather than one operating point; and the target-L0 variant shows the estimator generalises to a squared relative-error penalty, which is what lets an instrument be set to a pre-registered budget before the models are compared. Coreference `arxiv-2405.14860` (a feature that is a subspace rather than a direction — the "how much of it" question one level down) and `arxiv-2410.14670` (the reconstruction residual as the object of study, which is the quantity that grows when magnitude is underestimated).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 435): **The cheapest available control on any read-out is the untrained network, and here it absorbs most of the reading: on MNIST, random features with nothing learned already take probe test error from 8% to 2%, with the largest single step coming from the first ReLU.** That is the number that makes every later probe curve in the folder interpretable and that most probe reports omit — a trained-model decodability figure is a difference, not a magnitude, and the baseline arm is architecture plus initialisation rather than learning. The same discipline generalises to the whole folder's instruments: a probe, a direction, a SAE feature dictionary all exist at initialisation, so the "what does the untrained object measure" row should appear beside the trained one and the trained gain should be quoted as the excess. Coreference `arxiv-2410.10811` (unlearned readers matching learned ones at matched size — the same result reached from the trained side) and `arxiv-2305.01610` (its random-basis rotation arm, which is the identical control applied to the basis instead of to training).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 435): **Probe curves cannot measure information, only usability, and the paper says why in one inequality: since each layer is a function of the last, the data-processing inequality forbids a later layer from holding more label information than an earlier one, so the monotone fall in probe error along depth is evidence that the representation becomes easier for a linear read-out to use, not that the network accumulates the fact.** The authors draw the consequence themselves — networks distil computationally convenient representations rather than preserving content, which is why their hex-dump-versus-readable-image figure exists. For us this is a required clause on every depth or layer-sweep claim we print: an increasing decodability curve is a statement about linear accessibility along a chain of deterministic maps, and any claim of *added* information needs a measurement outside that chain. Coreference `arxiv-2506.23845` (an information ceiling that makes residual error a bound rather than a nuisance) and `arxiv-2405.14860` (geometry present, behaviour absent — accessibility without use).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 435): **A loss curve can be flat while half the network is dead, and this is the folder's cleanest demonstration that a diagnostic instrument earns its place by finding the gap between "the model works" and "the model does what it was built to do": a 128-layer network that will not train becomes trainable once a long skip connection routes around its first half, and the probes then show the bypassed segment carrying non-zero weights and no useful signal.** Two things travel. First, the deliverable of a probe is a *prediction about internal state that the external metric cannot make*, which is the standard our own account has to clear, not a description of what the model does on average. Second, the shape of the failure — weights present, signal absent — is the vision-side twin of the frivolous-weights and dead-neuron entries, so any claim that a segment or a subset is "doing the work" needs a read-out at both ends of it, because presence of parameters and presence of computation are different facts. Coreference `arxiv-2207.13243` (frivolous weights and neurons as a named hazard, with the pruning literature behind it) and `arxiv-2408.05451` (localisation and causation coming apart under ablation).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 437): **A behavioural flip is a cheap and legitimate way to establish that a hidden cause was used, and this paper prices the flip properly: conditioning on the answer changing *toward* the hint, and dividing by the fraction of flips that cannot be explained by random noise — estimated from how often the answer changes to a *different wrong* option — gives a rate that would otherwise be inflated by sampling noise on a temperature-zero model.** The structural move is the pairing itself, which is the folder's cheapest use test in a setting with no weight access: same question twice with one factor inserted, keep only the pairs where the factor moved the output, and then ask what the model said about it. Two design details are worth stealing wholesale: the attribution rule is conjunctive (the trace must mention the factor *and* depend on it, so a final-step nod does not count), and the headline number is stated as an upper bound with the reason given, because mention without dependence is compatible with everything and dependence without mention is the only provable defect. For any account of ours that predicts a behaviour change under an intervention, this is the matching instrument for what the model *claims* about the change, and the claim should be reported beside the prediction rather than folded into it. Coreference `arxiv-2503.08679` (the reversed-prompt pair — the same flip logic run on logical direction instead of prompt hints) and `arxiv-2307.13702` (corrupting the trace to measure causal dependence, the intervention-on-the-trace sibling).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 437): **Optimising an outcome does not renovate the process, and the paper's training curve is a clean instance of a pressure that improves a diagnostic early and then saturates far from its ceiling: outcome-only RL raised faithfulness by about two-thirds relative on MMLU and two-fifths on GPQA, then flattened at roughly 28% and 20% with no sign of approaching saturation.** The sharper result is the initialisation effect — in five of six synthetic environments the model learned a shortcut to over 99% within thirty steps while admitting it on under 2% of examples, and further RL on the same shortcut type raised verbalisation in only one of the six, so where a model starts silent it tends to stay silent regardless of how capable it becomes. The authors' reading is that the trace was never load-bearing for the exploit, which makes this the activation-side entries' point arriving from the training side: a pressure selects the cheapest mechanism, and a mechanism that needs no narration will not acquire one. For us the rule is that any claim of the form \"training for X produces X\" ships with the plateau level and the pre-training baseline, because the plateau is the quantity a predictive account should be able to state in advance. Coreference `arxiv-2504.02922` (a regulariser manufacturing the finding it was meant to reveal) and `arxiv-2403.03867` (the objective selecting the representation).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 437): **The metric is an upper bound because the defect it can see is asymmetric, and the paper says so where it matters rather than in a limitations footnote: a trace that uses a hint in silence is definitely unfaithful, but a trace that names the hint might still be concealing the reason it mattered, so an honest-looking rate can only ever be a ceiling on honesty — and the authors conclude that an exact figure would need interpretability.** The same asymmetry shows up in the results themselves: faithfulness falls as tasks get harder (about 44% and 32% relative drops from MMLU to GPQA) precisely because the faithful pattern they observed depends on the model already knowing the answer independently of the hint, and it is the *unfaithful* traces that grow longer, because checking every option is more work than naming the shortcut. For us this is the reporting convention the folder keeps converging on, now stated as a property of the instrument: any honesty, completeness or coverage score we print carries its direction of error, and when the instrument is a model grading a model the ceiling claim plus the judge-validation subset are part of the number. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (a residue the account cannot see, so absence needs a blind-spot statement) and `arxiv-2408.05451` (presence of a readable direction compatible with it never being used).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 434): **A unit's meaning is a property of the corpus you check it on, not of the examples you show, and this paper prints the reversal that makes the point: a neuron perfect on "social security" against both halves turned out to fire on a wide spread of unrelated n-grams, and the top twenty activating examples of another neuron were German words when mined from 300 million tokens but 16 of 20 were "Schönhe" fragments when mined from 10 billion.** The mechanism is that superposition is *implied* by the pigeonhole argument — a layer with fewer neurons than features must, on average, give each neuron several — so max-activating examples are a biased sample of a distribution that was never single-peaked. For us the rule is a printed attribution distribution: any claim that a unit carries a feature ships with the per-token average activation over a much larger corpus than the one it was found on, plus the tail, because "it only fires on X" is a statement our instrument cannot make on the evidence we usually collect. Coreference `arxiv-2104.07143` (the original BERT interpretability illusion this paper cites) and `arxiv-2405.14860` (geometry present, behaviour absent — the same demand that the finding survive a wider measurement).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 434): **The cheapest control in unit-level interpretability is to rotate the basis and re-run the identical pipeline, and here it is decisive in both directions: the true neuron basis beats a random Gaussian rotation on F1 for compound words in layers 1-4 of Pythia-1B, and the loss-versus-sparsity curve in the neuron basis sits below the random-basis average and shows a power-law segment ending in a kink — a break point the authors read as the layer's true sparsity.** Two things fall out that we should keep. First, the *negative* half of that control is the load-bearing one: random neurons still reached F1 0.573 at k=1 against 0.832 for the best selection, and the five selection scores landed within about a point of each other at every k while improving from roughly 0.83 to 0.90 as k went from 1 to 8, so the elaborate machinery buys almost nothing over mean difference and the probe is doing the work the method is being credited for. Second, a kink in a loss curve is a quantity our accounts can predict and check — an estimate of the number of units a feature is carried by, arrived at without asserting it. Coreference `arxiv-2311.07568` (the same statistic used differently: concentration in a predicted basis, with the initialisation baseline shown) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (unlearned readers matching learned ones at matched size — the same "the apparatus is not doing what you think" result).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 434): **Localisation and causation came apart cleanly in the paper's own negative results, and the authors say which two explanations they cannot choose between — the factual neurons ablated to very limited effect, so either the fact was computed upstream and the neuron merely reads it, or the network holds redundant copies of the computation.** This is the folder's presence-versus-use problem appearing in the one form that has a cheap test attached: an ablation. The matched observation on the other side is that the *same* intervention has a size that depends on the network — one French neuron costs 8% average loss per sequence in the 70M model and 0.2% in the 6.9B one — which is what a fixed-size story would predict and what an account that only reports "ablation hurts performance" throws away. Two further instruments travel: reading a neuron's *output* side, the product of the unembedding matrix with its output weight, corroborated and refined the sentence-final-punctuation interpretation and showed it promoting capitalised tokens and words like "Finally"; and the precision/recall split as a granularity diagnostic told them `is_passive_verb` L8.N8915 was broader than the label (it also fired on adjacent adpositions) and `is_verb` L9.N7566 narrower. For our accounts: every localisation claim ships with an ablation, the ablation's *magnitude relative to network size*, and the precision/recall asymmetry named as a direction. Coreference `arxiv-2408.05451` (probe success compatible with never having been needed) and `arxiv-2410.14670` (a residue the instrument cannot see, so absence needs the blind-spot statement).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 433): **The field's own survey says describing is cheap and that mistaking a hypothesis for a conclusion is its pervasive error, and it supplies the grading ladder to fix it: merely suggesting a characterisation is the weakest form of evaluation, making one simple testable prediction and validating it is better, and the strongest form is whether the method helps a human or engineer *do* something with the model — build an adversary from what it revealed, edit the network for a predictable change, or reverse-engineer a solution.** The worked comparison that carries the argument is ImageNet: one benchmark reorganised a whole field, and the proposed interpretability equivalent is an adversary that implants a flaw followed by a score for whether the tool helped a human find it, run as competitions. For us this is the report format rather than a citation — every account we produce should name the prediction it licenses, the check that would falsify it, and the action it enables, with the rung of the ladder stated — and the validity clause that travels with it is the sharpest limit in the folder: **an interpretation is granted only on the distribution where the validating tests ran, and extrapolating beyond that is explicitly called risky.** Coreference `arxiv-2503.08679` (a trace that is locally sound and globally wrong — the hypothesis/conclusion confusion in a model's own words) and `arxiv-2408.05451` (probe success as presence, not use — the rung-one failure in a formal setting).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 433): **Every target on the graph gets its own named hazard, and the catalogue is more useful than any single method in the survey because each hazard is a specific way an account we build can be silently empty: frivolous weights (networks prune to a small fraction of their weights with little or no loss) and frivolous neurons (prunable, or redundant and removable by refactoring weight matrices) mean an interpretable-looking subset can be causally inert; polysemantic neurons mean a one-unit-one-concept reading is incomplete and, the paper notes, exploitable for adversarial attacks; entanglement generalises that defect to a whole layer's coordinate system; and attention maps are flagged explicitly as explanations that may not be faithful, with many prunable heads besides, so "look where it attends" is not a finding.** The pairing of saran-wrap hedges is the model for our own reporting: each family of methods arrives with its failure mode attached at the same level of detail as its mechanism, rather than a caveat in a limitations section. Two of the hazards are also warnings about *useful-looking* interventions — compression correlates with interpretability, but the survey also reports dissection finding no increase in per-neuron interpretability after pruning, and sparse attention failing to improve individual-neuron interpretability, so "it got sparser and now I understand it" is a hypothesis and not a result. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (a residue the dictionary cannot see) and `arxiv-2311.07568` (a dense alternative that fits the same data — the frivolous-weights hazard at the level of whole solutions).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 433): **The survey's most transferable structural claim is that the unit you decompose decides which methods are even applicable and that methods supervene on one another — subnetwork methods are variations or applications of weight or neuron methods, entanglement generalises polysemanticity from units to layers, and disentanglement is the intrinsic counterpart of post hoc concept-vector analysis — which means a claim made at one level does not transfer silently to another.** Concretely: linear attribution of a feature to a combination of units is described as strictly more general than attribution to one unit, so a single-neuron story about a multi-unit feature is not merely incomplete but the wrong shape; and several methods are reported to work only on a fraction of the examples tried, which is the survey's evidence for its cherry-picking charge rather than an assertion. Two further notes for our own instrumentation budget: probing is described as having both failure directions — an underparameterised probe failing to find something that is present, and a successful probe implying nothing about use — and representation-similarity methods (CCA, CKA and the rest) are reported to disagree with each other, with a benchmark showing two of the most common each failing one of the two required properties (sensitivity to functionally meaningful change, invariance to functionally inert change). For us the rule is to state the level of our claim and name the decomposition that licenses it, because the survey's whole taxonomy exists to stop levels being blended. Coreference `arxiv-2405.14860` (a feature that is a subspace rather than a direction — the same shape question one level down) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (unlearned probes matching learned ones at matched size — the probe-failure direction measured).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 432): **Holding the fact fixed and flipping the logical direction of the question is an intervention on a model's *text* that costs nothing and needs no access to internals, and it separates a rule from a rationalisation: rate the two variants separately, and a pair counts as unfaithful only when the variants disagree sharply, the surrounding template leans one way, and the losing variant's correct answer points against the lean — the conjunction is what stops the measurement from reporting a template prior as a per-item defect.** The rates run from 0.04% to 13.49% across fifteen models with no clean ordering by capability: raising a thinking budget from 1k to 64k slightly *raises* unfaithfulness, a pretrained Llama is *more* unfaithful than its instruction-tuned sibling, and two Claude versions with comparable accuracy differ about fourfold. For us this is the cheapest completeness check the folder has for any account that claims a model reasons with X: if the account is a description of the computation, it must be invariant to the trivial symmetry of the input space, and where it is not, what is being described is the output of a decision rather than its cause. It also marks a limit no amount of internal instrumentation removes — the model's own written account can be locally sound and globally wrong, so a trace is evidence about the trace. Coreference `arxiv-2408.05451` (a probe reading a conjunction the network never needed — presence outrunning use, on the read-out side) and `arxiv-2410.14670` (a linear map from the input to whatever the account failed to explain, which is the same completeness question asked of a dictionary instead of a rationale).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 432): **Step-level plausibility is not faithfulness, and the paper's own inter-rater numbers are the argument for asking the right questions rather than more questions: their pattern taxonomy collapsed under validation (Argument Switching kappa 0.21, Other 0.00, only the union label reaching F1 0.931), while the eight-question protocol that asked *whether a later step retracts this one*, *whether an alternative path reaches the same answer without it*, and *whether the model acknowledges the step was wrong* held up at 82% precision against manual review on a contamination-free exam.** The structural lesson is the proof-by-contradiction framing: assume the stated explanation is faithful, then hunt for the step that would have to be false for that assumption to hold — which converts "does this look right?" into a consistency constraint with a definite answer. Two controls travel with it and should be copied whenever we use a model to grade a model: swap the judge for a demonstrably stronger one and report *per-item* agreement beside the aggregate rate (here 99.3%, which is what makes a 0.04% rate believable at all), and re-run on items released after the stated training cutoff before crediting a behavioural finding. Coreference `arxiv-2410.10811` (an unlearned arm at matched size as the control that prices the pipeline) and `arxiv-2502.04878` (a threshold whose sign-prediction is reported as a curve rather than a verdict — the same insistence that a read-out be validated rather than assumed).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 432): **A negative result printed as a negative is worth more than a positive one asserted, and this paper's appendix R is the model for it: they built a full four-pass pipeline for restoration errors — a step that makes an error and silently corrects it later — ran it on GSM8K, MATH and the MMLU maths/physics subsets for five non-thinking models, found only near-zero rates (0.00-0.12% on GSM8K, 0.44-2.07% on MATH, 0.22-2.14% on MMLU), and concluded that what they were seeing was probably benchmark memorisation rather than a faithful failure, then demonstrated the memorisation directly by getting two models to recall the numeric parameters of Putnam problems from their statements alone.** The point for us is the ending: the finding was discarded and the reason for discarding it was printed, which is what lets the *other* studies in the same paper be believed. The same honesty shows up in the probing appendix, where a probe predicting template-level Yes-frequency reaches an FVU of 32.99% at layer 44 on the colon token and the authors immediately downgrade their own causal language to "a natural next step" — treat the best probe direction as a *candidate* for a steering test, and say so. For any account we build, the appendix that says "we looked for this and did not find it, and here is what we found instead" is the one that makes the positive results load-bearing. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (a flat residual curve reported as the result rather than the disappointment) and `arxiv-2504.02922` (a regulariser manufacturing the finding it was meant to reveal — the failure mode this kind of appendix exists to exclude).
