- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 431): **A negative that a whole subfield relies on has a formal counterexample here: because a randomly initialised layer already epsilon-linearly represents the pairwise-AND circuit, a linear probe — and by the same argument an SAE feature — can pick out a conjunction the network never needed, so \"we found a direction for X\" is compatible with X being an artefact of the geometry rather than part of the computation.** The authors say this themselves in their practical-takeaways appendix, citing work where arbitrary XORs of concepts were probeable in language models and warning that 80% of variance explained is not evidence of use. For us the operational rule follows directly: every feature claim ships with a *use* test (an intervention whose effect is measured) and not only a *presence* test (a probe, a dictionary or a variance fraction), because presence is now known to be cheap in a way that has nothing to do with training. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (a residue the dictionary cannot see that is nevertheless linearly readable from the input — presence again outrunning the account) and `arxiv-2311.07568` (a dense alternative that fits the same data — presence outrunning fit).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 431): **Whether a representation is usable is a property of the *definition* you choose, and this paper shows two plausible definitions coming apart: two features can each be perfectly linearly separable while no MLP layer separates their AND, because separability constrains nothing about the margin, so \"the model represents f\" as usually stated does not imply the model can compute with f.** The fix is to quantify the margin as a per-input error bound and require it uniformly, which is what makes composition provable — and it is a definition our own accounts could adopt verbatim, since an epsilon read-off is exactly the object a probe or a dictionary decoder already produces. The lesson for any account that claims a layer hands something to the next layer: state the error at which the *downstream* consumer can read it, not the accuracy with which we can, because our instrument is usually much more patient than the network's next layer. Coreference `arxiv-2408.10920` (a storage format invisible to linear readers — the same \"usable\"-versus-\"present\" gap with the reader as the variable) and `arxiv-2405.14860` (a reducibility property that had to be relaxed into a degree before it could be measured at all).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 431): **Two predictions in this paper are cheap enough to test on a real checkpoint and are the sort of thing we should be running: first, that the number of features a network can store *and compute with* is quadratic in the activation dimension, which argues for dictionaries far larger than the square-of-dimension sizes the early SAE line used and for features spread across many neurons rather than localised on one; second, that error correction predicts plateaus — regions around an activation vector where small perturbations barely change the output — which is the opposite signature from the sensitivity that perturbation studies usually look for, and which the authors point to as already reported in GPT-2-small.** Both are framed as predictions from a model rather than as measurements, which is the shape we want for our own claims: a model of the network that says what *must* be observable, stated before the check, with the check named. Coreference `arxiv-2502.04878` (dictionary width decides what units appear — the prediction that width matters for a theoretical reason) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (a FLOP-versus-accuracy cost argument for behavioural over static reading at small scale).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 430): **The object you decompose decides what an absence can mean, and this paper moves the object from activations to the per-sample parameter gradient so that "this direction matters for these inputs" becomes a mechanical test rather than an interpretation — the impact score is one inner product, the sample's gradient component along the direction averaged over reference outputs, and the check is to perturb along it and see whether the same samples move.** The construction detail worth stealing is the reference: instead of a fixed target or the mean output, each sample is graded against the output of a *randomly drawn other sample* from the same distribution, which preserves the correlations a mean would average away and lets convexity noise wash out over draws. For us this is the parameter-side twin of the folder's activation-side controls — a claim about a direction ships with the ranked sample list it predicts, and the intervention is graded on the same list, so "meaning" is defined operationally before any reading of the direction happens. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (the residual as the object — decomposition of what a dictionary fails to explain) and `arxiv-2408.10920` (the same problem on the representation side: a variable can be present in a format your instrument cannot see).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 430): **Fit score and interpretability came out inverted across the two deployed models, and the authors print it as a mild shrug: the CNN block reconstructed at 23% error against the transformer's 40%, yet the transformer's circuits read as phrase detectors and subject-trackers while the CNN's needed a pixel-attribution pass to even guess at, and 40% of its 100 subnetwork slots were dead.** The suspicion offered is that reconstruction error is being bought by components whose job is a shape or form that only localised attribution would reveal — which is precisely the warning the folder keeps re-deriving, that a lower reconstruction loss is a statement about the instrument's coverage and not about the account's legibility. Two further details keep the error numbers honest and should be copied: the k budget was held fixed across all models (k = 0.1) even where the true circuit count implies it should rise, and the squaring model's 32% error is attributed to exactly that, so a fixed hyperparameter across models of different true sparsity is itself a confound on the error column. First, an arbitrary learned direction has no preferred sign, so the recovered subnetwork is as likely to point opposite the original (stated explicitly, and visible in the reported table). Second, rank-1 parameter tensors represented the rank-5 model of correlated feature blocks nearly as well as rank-5 tensors did, so the "true rank" of a circuit is not identifiable from reconstruction alone — an argument for reporting the rank sweep beside the chosen rank, as they do in Figures S2 and S3. For our accounts: whenever we score a method against a model we designed, pair the qualitative direction plot with one scalar re-derived from the method's own output and compared against the generator's truth. - Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 429): **Turn a hypothesis about format into an intervention algebra and competing formats can be ranked instead of argued about: define the variables, learn a near-bijective map from the hidden state into them together with its inverse, intervene in feature space, invert and decode — each candidate format costs one small trained analyser and returns an exact-match number, so here three formats are ordered across six widths (unigram 0.00→1.00, bigram 0.01→1.00, onion 0.83-0.95) and the crossover from non-linear to linear is a visible gradient rather than a single cell.** Two design details travel: the inverse maps back into activation space, which is what makes an intervention-grounded claim rather than a probe-accuracy claim; and the featuriser can be non-linear while the variables remain stated and modular, so "the model is non-linear" does not force us to give up named variables. - Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 428): **A linear account of a residual stream is a *derived* claim and not an observation to be re-found each time, and this paper supplies the derivation while also printing its conditions: linearity follows from exact log-odds matching (the concept's learned log-odds must match its marginal in every context that does not pin it), or failing that from the max-margin bias of training on the per-concept exponential-loss subproblem — so a direction claim is legitimate exactly when one of those two applies and is unfounded when neither does.** The condition is testable on a checkpoint and almost never tested: take contexts that do and do not pin the concept, and check whether the learned log-odds differ across them. For us the operational rule is that every direction claim carries a stamped reason — matched log-odds (with the conditioning set named), or implicit bias plus a stated subproblem — and where the data never conditions on a concept at all, the account is silent rather than confident, because the paper explicitly notes the log-odds route breaks there and hands the gap to the second route only. Coreference `arxiv-2311.07568` (the other named selection principle — margin maximisation in a homogeneous one-layer net, with a dense alternative that also fits), `arxiv-2405.14860` (linearity found but not one-dimensional, i.e. the derivation grants a line and the measurement finds a plane).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 428): **Match the two halves of a claim separately or the average will hide a real asymmetry, and this paper's ablation ladder is the cleanest example in the folder: dropping concept support leaves unembedding linearity nearly intact (0.951 at 10 concepts, 0.896 at 12) while the embedding-to-unembedding alignment collapses from about 0.98 to 0.777 and then 0.551, so the same intervention that a single combined score would report as a modest loss is a near-total failure of one component.** The authors give two explanations and refuse to choose — undertraining on an exponentially larger problem, and the zero probabilities themselves violating the positivity the theory needs — which is honest and is itself instructive: an ablation that removes an assumption *and* shrinks the training signal cannot attribute the effect to either without a matched control. The transferable instrument is the four-rung ladder applied to one statistic (complete conditionals, a random 50-100 mask subset, missing concept support, narrower width) plus an optimiser swap as a fifth rung, because the paper shows the result survives all but one and that the one that breaks it breaks only half. For us: whenever we report that our account survives missing coverage, publish the components separately and add the matched-size control that separates "less data" from "the assumption is gone". Coreference `arxiv-2504.02922` (a sparsity regulariser manufacturing the very finding it was meant to reveal — the same "which change caused it" problem in the training-time setting) and `arxiv-2502.04878` (an add-one-latent test whose sign, not whose existence, is the evidence).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 428): **A low cosine similarity is not a refutation, and the authors say so in the honest form we should copy: their LLaMA-2 Winograd numbers are 0.042 mean for matching pairs against 0.011 for non-matching (maxima 0.161 and 0.081) — a three- to four-fold relative gap on absolute values roughly an order of magnitude below the simulated 0.97 — and they offer two explanations without adjudicating, natural-language noise and the possibility that the concept is not one-dimensional so that cosine is simply the wrong instrument.** That is exactly the diagnostics we need for our own negative results and for the folder's positive ones: a statistic can fail because the account is wrong, because the object is not one-dimensional, or because the measurement instrument assumed a shape the object does not have. The paper reports the matching/non-matching split rather than the matching score alone, which converts a weak absolute number into a defensible comparative claim — and it prints the maxima beside the means so a reader can see the tail rather than being told a mean. - Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 427): **A description of a trained network and an explanation of why that network exists are different objects, and this paper supplies the sharpest demonstration in the folder that describing is cheap: it exhibits a construction that fits the modular-addition dataset perfectly while being dense in exactly the Fourier basis in which real trained networks are one-sparse (two neurons per input pair, built from one-hot vectors, so every frequency carries mass).** Correct classification is therefore massively overdetermined, and the sparse solution is selected not by fit but by having a larger margin — which converts "our account reproduces the model's behaviour" from a success criterion into a non-criterion. For us the operational rule is a printed pair: any account of ours that claims a feature is the thing the model computes with must state what else fits the same data, and must say which selection principle (margin, regularisation strength, homogeneity, an architectural constraint) is the one that excludes the alternatives. Where we cannot name the principle we should say the account is descriptive and make no necessity claim, because a dense alternative always exists and this paper writes one down.
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 427): **A witness is cheaper than a taxonomy, and the certificate-pair argument is the reusable device: instead of characterising the set of maximisers directly, exhibit one network and one distribution over training points that are mutually best responses, and max-min duality does two jobs at once — it certifies that one network is optimal, and it forces every other optimal network to be supported on the same atoms with support-tightness on the same points.** In the multi-class case the trick has a second, more interesting half: the max over wrong labels blocks the per-neuron decomposition, so they maximise a relaxed class-weighted margin instead and then check that the weighting only ever places mass on labels that are already the argmax, at which point the relaxation is exact. For our accounts the transferable template is to find whichever quantity *does* decompose over the units we care about, prove the statement there, and then print the condition under which the relaxed quantity equals the quantity that matters — because a per-unit argument about a relaxed objective is exactly the kind of claim that reads as a result about the model while being a result about the relaxation.
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 427): **Two diagnostics make a prediction about weights auditable on a real checkpoint without any intervention, and both are unsupervised, and their pairing is the point: per-neuron concentration in the predicted basis (maximum normalised power, measured at initialisation and again after training so the *shift* from scattered to concentrated is the evidence rather than the end state alone) plus population spread across the predicted atoms (compared against the proportions the construction itself dictates).** Here the quadratic network's concentration reaches essentially 1 while the ReLU network's sits near 0.9 — i.e. the prediction is exact only where the homogeneity and regulariser assumptions hold, and the architecture that breaks the assumption lands close but not on it, which is exactly the residual degree of freedom an honest report should show rather than round to agreement. For us: whenever we claim a basis is the right one for a layer, plot the concentration statistic at initialisation and at the checkpoint, and plot the population histogram against the predicted proportions, because a concentration claim without the initialisation baseline cannot distinguish "training produced this" from "this statistic is high for any weights".

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 426): **A crisp property that has to be turned into a score to be measurable is the point where a claim quietly changes kind, and this paper says so on the page: Definition 2 states irreducibility exactly (no rotation and translation makes the parts independent or non-co-occurring), Definition 3 replaces it with two continuous indices, and the Limitations section then admits the result is a possibly subjective degree of reducibility.** The indices are still worth taking, because they are distribution statistics on a point cloud that cost one gradient-descent run and one 1000-angle sweep, and because they separate the two ways a decomposition is fake — independence (latitude/longitude) and non-co-occurrence (a one-hot on a simplex) — a distinction most decomposition papers never draw. The reusable discipline is the sentence we should attach to every score we invent: which exact property it relaxes, in which direction it can be wrong, and what a high value licenses. Coreference `arxiv-2410.14670` (a linear-error floor fitted across scales and extrapolated with dotted lines — the same honesty problem in a different instrument) and `arxiv-2502.04878` (a cosine threshold whose sign-prediction is reported as an ROC curve rather than as a classification).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 426): **Representation present and behaviour absent is printed as the paper's own control, and it is the sharpest negative in the folder: GPT-2 has the weekday and month circles yet scores 8/49 and 10/144, while Llama 3 8B scores 29/49 and 143/144 and Mistral 7B 31/49 and 125/144 — so finding the geometry is not evidence that the model computes with it, and the causal section exists precisely because the correlational one cannot answer that question.** It sharpens in the inverse direction too: both large models are near chance on plain modular notation for the same arithmetic, so the circle is bound to the natural-language framing and not to the operation, which means a geometry claim has to name the prompt distribution it was found on. For us the operational rule is a two-by-two table for any account we build — geometry present/absent by behaviour present/absent — with the geometry-present-behaviour-absent cell filled by a real run rather than left empty, because that is the cell where an over-eager account would otherwise have been believed. Coreference `arxiv-2410.10811` (learned probes beaten by random ones at matched size: the same demand that the apparatus, not the pipeline, be shown to matter) and `arxiv-2405.08366` (a labelled-attribute dictionary beating a learned one — basis choice as the variable under test).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 426): **Sample the whole interior of the claimed variable instead of patching in one known-correct state, and the account becomes a functional prediction rather than an existence proof: sweeping radius and angle inside the circle shows the answer token tracking the angle and only weakly the radius, which is what "the angle encodes the day" actually means and would have been invisible to a single patch.** Two more instruments travel. First, a robustness comparison nobody usually runs: fit the probe in the plane the unsupervised method found and evaluate it at neighbouring layers — it costs a little on its own layer (−2.01 against −2.58 average logit difference) and survives a two-layer shift where the per-layer fitted probe collapses (0.029), direct evidence that the clustered subspace is more invariant than a supervised probe over the same activations. Second, the cheapest instrument in the paper is EVR: linearly regress the activations on one-hot encodings of the operands you already understand and look at the residual, since the answer representation was invisible in raw PCA and became a clean circle once the two operand directions were removed. For our predictions, every claim of the form "coordinate z carries x" should come with a sweep of z showing the read-out monotone in z, a transfer test of the same read-out at another layer, and the residual after regressing out the confounds we already understand. Coreference `arxiv-2403.19647` (sparse feature circuits, the causal-graph form this line builds on) and `arxiv-2410.02472` (a reader that scored well without a control that could refute it).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 425): **A residual that is linearly predictable from the input is not an absence of knowledge — it is knowledge the account has not admitted — and the price of finding out is one linear regression: R² of a probe from activation to squared error norm runs about 0.70-0.95 across widths, sparsities, layers and models, and the same probe on the error *vector* only reaches about 0.15-0.72, so what resists a sparse dictionary splits into a part any linear map can recover and a part nothing simple does.** This is the completeness instrument the folder has been missing: `2504.02922` printed residual-error arms and `2502.04878` demanded a reinstatement test, but neither asks whether the leftover is *structured from the outside*, which is a question about the input rather than about the dictionary and therefore costs no training. The operational rule for our own accounts is to fit a single linear map from the network's input to whatever our account leaves unexplained and report its holdout R² beside the reconstruction score, because a high R² there says the account is missing a linearly representable thing (recoverable) rather than an irreducible one, and a low R² with a large error says the failure is of the second kind and deserves a different response. The baselines make the instrument credible: token identity, sparsity, activation norm and model loss all do significantly worse than the full activation at the layers that matter, and token identity beats the activation only in the first few layers where per-token processing dominates — so the probe is not merely re-reading token frequency. Coreference `arxiv-2504.02922` (the residual-error arm that beats the dictionary over full responses) and `arxiv-2502.04878` (the add-one-latent test that separates "coarser" from "missing").
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 425): **"More capacity helps" and "more capacity helps on a residue that is flat in the same variable" are different claims, and this paper is the clearest case in the folder of a flat curve being the result rather than the disappointment: at a fixed sparsity in middle layers the nonlinearly predictable fraction of the error is roughly constant across orders of magnitude of width while the total error falls on a power law with a constant, so the observed curve is consistent with a floor that no wider dictionary removes — and the paper draws that floor as a horizon line from a fitted hypothesis, with dotted extrapolations.** The mechanism proposed is that the residue consists of dense structure plus error the dictionary introduces by approximating features badly, both roughly constant in width, with the unlearned-feature tail being the only part that shrinks. Two things transfer. First, the test itself: any claim of the form "our account will get better if it gets bigger" should be printed as a curve in the size variable with the residual component shown separately, because an average that improves can hide a component that does not — and here the per-token appendix confirms the two halves genuinely diverge, linear error shrinking while nonlinear error stays put, so the flatness is not an averaging artifact. Second, the honesty of the form: the flatness is a hypothesis fitted across observed scales and extrapolated, the grids are sparse and interpolated between trained dictionaries, and peripheral layers disagree with the middle ones — a shape we should copy, since a floor claim asserted from three points with no stated extrapolation assumption is what this paper deliberately avoids. Coreference `arxiv-2502.04878` (a sweep with no knee, where extra units could be refining, duplicating or composing) and `arxiv-2402.12560` (an aggregation choice that changes the ranking — the same warning that a component's trend must be read separately from the total's).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 425): **The cheapest way to test whether two accounts are measuring the same thing is to predict the bigger account's per-item failures from the smaller account's, one scalar and no new training: a single-coefficient regression from a small SAE's per-token error norm to a large one's keeps high R² and degrades smoothly as the two dictionaries move apart in scale, which means larger dictionaries mostly struggle on the same contexts — and adding the nonlinear component's norm to that predictor buys a small but measurable improvement in forecasting the larger error, up to about a five percent cut in unexplained variance.** That is a reusable scaling forecast: a new architecture's behaviour at size can be estimated from a small run's error *and its decomposition* rather than from the size run itself, which is the practical version of the paper's "make SAEs better, not just bigger". For us the two instruments are (a) the cross-account correlation table, one row per pair, which converts "our account is finer" into a measured claim about which items the finer account fixes, and (b) the discipline of decomposing the predictor rather than only the target — because the improvement here comes from knowing which half of the small account's error forecasts the large account's, not from the total. The counter-case in the same paper is worth carrying: inference-time gradient pursuit on a frozen decoder lowers total unexplained variance by a few percent while leaving the nonlinear fraction almost untouched, which is exactly what a fix aimed at the wrong component looks like — and the authors only know that because they reported the decomposition beside the total. Coreference `arxiv-2502.04878` (width, not seed, decides what the units are) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (an unlearned arm at matched size as the control that prices the pipeline).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 424): **A regulariser can manufacture the finding it is supposed to reveal, and here the mechanism fits in one line of algebra: charging a sparse dictionary's penalty as the sum of two model-specific norms rather than the norm of their concatenation makes a concept present in both models cost the same whether it is carried by one shared latent or split across two, while under a top-k budget the split version is the *less* competitive one — so the dictionary splits, and each split-half looks like a concept that emerged during fine-tuning in exactly one model.** The empirical size of the artifact is the point: 3,176 candidates collapse to 134 under a loss swap that changes no data, no layer and no latent budget, and the failure rate runs 49.5% to 98.3% across five model pairs, worst on the two narrow tunes (95.5% and 98.3%) where the dictionary has the least room to represent a difference honestly. For us the operational rule is that any comparison instrument charged per-side (crosscoders today, and by extension any paired dictionary, any delta-SAE, any two-model probe) must be validated against a substituted sparsity mechanism before its absent-side counts are believed, and the substitute should be the one whose inductive bias we can state out loud — here top-k competition, which prefers the three-latent solution because it is sparser in L0. Coreference `arxiv-2502.04878` (width, not seed, decides what the units are — the same "the instrument's budget decides the result" shape) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (learned probes beaten by random ones: the learning was not doing the work, and here it is the penalty that was).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 424): **A read-out's validity is a property of the pair (quantity, training procedure), not of the quantity, and this paper prices it in both directions: the same relative decoder norm that is uninformative or inverted under the L1 dictionary becomes a usable ranking under top-k, where it correlates with the expensive diagnostic at Pearson 0.73 (reconstruction side) and 0.87 (error side) and its top half removes about 50% of the behavioural gap against about 6% for the bottom half.** So a metric validated elsewhere does not travel with a citation — it must be re-validated on the artefact it is applied to, which costs one correlation and one top-half/bottom-half split. The second half of the lesson is the diagnostic itself: Latent Scaling is a single closed-form least-squares coefficient, the best scale at which a candidate direction reconstructs the *other* model's activations, and its ratio is a cheaper and more direct test of "this concept is present in both" than any training-time quantity, because it asks the question on activations rather than on the artefact's own parameters. For our own claims the rule is: for every direction we say is absent from a checkpoint, print the best-fit scale on that checkpoint's activations, and for every statistic we import from the literature, print a control measured on our own mismatched setup. Coreference `arxiv-1811.00636` (a sufficient condition on a direction that says nothing about a threshold's error rate) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (the matched-size unlearned arm as the control that prices the pipeline rather than the method).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 424): **A dictionary can account for how a response opens while accounting for almost nothing about what it says, and the paper's own baselines make the inversion visible: replacing all latents cuts KL by about 78% over the first nine response tokens but only about 59% over full responses, while the residual-error arm — the part of the activation the dictionary does not represent — beats the dictionary over full responses and is more than twice as bad on the early tokens.** Two instruments follow. First, the full-replacement bracket must be printed beside the "best features" row, because a set of features can look strong only because the whole dictionary is weak. Second, the residual-error arm must be run at all, since within-dictionary reconstruction is not completeness. And the third result in the same section is the sharpest caution about unit choice: 40% of the chat-only latents fire predominantly on template tokens, and patching nothing but those positions reaches a KL as good as the best half of the ranked latents — so a dictionary fitted to understand content will present a change that lives in a handful of positional anchors as a diffuse property of many features. For us: report every reconstruction-style score over early and late output positions separately, and check whether a small set of structural positions explains a result before crediting a semantic feature set. Coreference `arxiv-2403.19647` (faithfulness and completeness printed together so a one-sided result cannot pass) and `arxiv-2501.19271` (a score that ranks well while estimating something else).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 423): **A read-out can get worse as you give it more supervised behaviour, and the paper's own grid is the demonstration: sentiment alone reaches about 0.75 on held-out deception, sentiment plus emotion plus language identification collapses to 0.5, and the model trained on all four behaviours ranks only fourth — while the untrained reader sits near 0.20, so every trained arm is a gain and some gains are most of what the best arm has.** The authors attribute the non-monotonicity to interference between training behaviours and explicitly leave it unexplained, and one dataset's effect flips sign between the two meta-model families (language identification hurts with phi-2 and helps with InternLM), which is what an interaction term looks like rather than a main effect. For us the operational consequence is that the dataset-combination grid — not the best cell — is the deliverable when a reader is trained on one payload and evaluated on another, that the untrained-reader row is printed beside every trained row, and that a dataset's contribution is reported as a paired difference across combinations rather than as its own accuracy, because "more data helped" and "more data helped here" are different claims and this paper contains both signs of the second one. Coreference `arxiv-2501.19271` (a score that ranks well while estimating something else) and `arxiv-2410.10811` (learned probes beaten by unlearned ones at matched size — the same demand that the learning, not the pipeline, be shown to do the work).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 423): **An artefact can be useful and still not be an instrument, and the tell is that the paper's central comparative claim is never run: the conclusion states that meta-models generalize to out-of-distribution tasks better than traditional probing methods, and no probe is fitted, trained or scored anywhere in the paper — the only baselines are an untrained meta-model and the chance rate of a balanced binary task.** The reader is itself a language model answering a yes/no question about a behaviour, so the accuracy mixes the injected activation channel with the prompt's own ability to guess: there is no arm where the placeholders are filled with permuted or mean activations, no arm that asks the question with the activations withheld, and no test of whether the reader answers the same way when the behaviour is defined only by the question text. The transferable lesson is a three-row control template for any reader we build — real activations, permuted or mean activations, question-only — because a reader that scores well on all three is a language prior and the delta back to the first row is the only part attributable to the internal state. Coreference `arxiv-2602.18458` (a judge that grades the story rather than the science) and `arxiv-1811.00636` (a bound on a direction mistaken for a detector's operating characteristic: the same gap between a claim and the measurement that could refute it).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 421): **A learned representation can be no better than an untrained one, and the test costs nothing: here the optimized probes are matched or beaten by random synthetic images and by random real images at the same budget (128 probes — learned 0.955 / 0.808 / 0.936 / 0.889 against synthetic 0.959 / 0.856 / 0.917 / 0.893 and in-distribution 0.959 / 0.856 / 0.941 / 0.930), on three of four benchmarks outright.** So the probes were never the informative part on those tasks; the classifier and the network's response were. The transferable instrument is the *unlearned arm with a matched size and the same classifier*: for any probe set, dictionary, or read-out we report, an equally sized random or in-distribution substitute should be scored on the identical pipeline, and where the learned version does not clear it the claim must be about the pipeline, not the learning. This is the probing-side twin of the folder's other null controls — against-random-initialisation (`arxiv-2402.12560`-adjacent) and the control task — and it is the one that can be run in a single training job. Coreference `arxiv-2501.19271` (the read-out that scores well while estimating something else) and `arxiv-2410.02472` (the activation analogue of weight oracles, still free).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 421): **A rich-looking representation may be a scalar summary in disguise, and the price is on the page: a classifier built from nothing but the entropy of each probe's output distribution reaches 0.877 Kendall tau on CIFAR10 Wild Park, against ProbeGen's 0.933 on the same task and 0.889 for vanilla probing — so roughly the whole of a 128-dimensional probe fingerprint is reproduced by one number per probe.** The authors report this as a pleasant interpretability finding (ProbeGen's logits sharpen as accuracy rises), and it is, but it is also the floor any content claim has to clear: if a per-probe confidence scalar already explains the effect, the probe's *spatial* or *semantic* content is doing little. Operational rule for us: before attributing a read-out to the specific structure we designed, print the cheapest sufficient statistic of the same vector — a norm, an entropy, a mean — as its own predictor row. Coreference `arxiv-2501.19271` (concept scores vs the weighted term that actually enters the logit) and `arxiv-2404.16014` (a scalar summary hiding a clumpy field).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 421): **Capacity is not the same as structure, and the ablation that shows it is the one where removing expressivity improves the result: the generator loses its nonlinearities and every task improves at every depth (1 through 5 layers), while adding L2 weight decay on the nonlinear generator needs non-standard strengths (1e-7 to 1e-8) and per-task retuning to reach 0.982 / 0.870 / 0.947 / 0.928 against the linear generator's 0.984 / 0.877 / 0.957 / 0.932, and still loses.** The authors' reading is that the right regularizer is architectural — a shared, low-expressivity generator imposes structure on its outputs — and that a stronger model fitted to the same targets overfits them, which is why the learned probes look like adversarial texture. It recurs as the folder's base-choice lesson from the other end (`arxiv-2405.08366`: a labelled-attribute dictionary beating a learned one), and the transferable rule is that when two accounts differ in expressivity, the more expressive one must beat the constrained one on held-out models before its extra freedom is credited, with the constrained account tried first because it is cheaper and often better. Coreference `arxiv-2402.12560` (the control task that separates a method's expressivity from its finding) and `arxiv-2502.04878` (granularity, not capability, is usually the real axis).

Read from: **full text** — v1 HTML, 58,549 chars after whitespace normalisation, read end to end in four slices: abstract and byline, §1 Introduction (the three properties of a canonical unit, feature splitting, the colour-shape composition example), §2 Sparse Autoencoders (the encoder/decoder/loss definitions), §3 Related Work, §4 SAE Stitching (§4.1 the stitching equation with the bias mixing, §4.2 novel versus reconstruction latents, the cosine threshold and the bipartite graph), §5 Meta-SAEs (§5.1 the GPT-4o-mini explanations and the five-way choice, §5.2 the comparison to smaller SAE latents), §6 Conclusion, references, **Appendix A** (A.1 glossary, A.2 SAE variants, A.3 example latents with the active/inactive MSE table, A.4 latent families, A.5 training details and Table 2, A.6 stitching figures and the same-size agreement result, A.6.1 Gemma Scope replication, A.7 meta-SAE figures, A.8 sparse probing and targeted probe perturbation with Figures 21-23). **Substance:** two models (GPT-2 small, Gemma 2 2B), ten SAEs (eight trained here, two released), two proposed instruments, one second-level dictionary, two downstream probe evaluations, and five named negative or cautionary results (incompleteness of small dictionaries, composition rather than atomicity in large ones, non-monotone probe accuracy across width, hand-set thresholds, and no method for choosing width).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 420): **A gain that keeps arriving as you enlarge the object is not evidence that the object is the right one, and this paper's sweep is the cleanest instance in the folder: reconstruction error and cross-entropy recovery improve monotonically from width 768 to 98,304 (2.72 → 1.14 MSE; 0.876 → 0.970 recovery under mean ablation) while the number of active units stops rising after the middle of the sweep (35.2 → 42.4-43.9) — so the curve has no knee, and a reader given only one width has no way to know whether the extra units are refining, duplicating or composing.** The consequence for us is that every claim of the form "our account of size k captures the behaviour" needs at least two sizes of account printed, and a second seed at one of them, because the paper also shows that two runs of the same width agree at 94% of latents while a factor of two in width changes what the latents *are* — non-uniqueness here is a function of granularity, not of training noise. Coreference `arxiv-2503.19859` (structure at every iteration versus at convergence: the same demand that a reported quantity be shown to be a property of the phenomenon and not of the chosen budget) and `arxiv-2602.15195` (a layer × rank grid printed rather than one chosen cell).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 420): **"The smaller thing is merely coarser" and "the smaller thing is missing information" are different claims and only an addition test separates them: adding into the 768 SAE every latent of the 1,536 SAE with maximum cosine similarity below 0.7 lowers its MSE by nearly ten percent, and on the inputs of a single such latent the small SAE's error rises 0.589 against the larger one's 0.293, which is the answer a pure feature-splitting story cannot give.** The transferable instrument is the *add-one-latent* test with its sign reported — if a unit from the larger account improves the smaller account it is carrying information the smaller one lacks; if it hurts, it is duplicating something already there — and the paper's own ROC curve over thresholds (Figure 13, appendix) is the honest form, since the classification is a threshold rather than a fact. For our accounts the rule is that an omitted-part claim must be demonstrated by reinstating the part and measuring the improvement, not by noting that the part exists in a bigger dictionary, because capacity alone predicts no missing information. Coreference `arxiv-1811.00636` (a threshold whose precision is unrelated to its sufficient condition) and `arxiv-2403.19647` (faithfulness and completeness printed together so a one-sided result cannot pass).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 420): **A unit is only a unit relative to a finer dictionary that can take it apart, and the meta-SAE gives the test: a second sparse dictionary fitted to the *directions* of the first recovers about four components per latent, explains 55.47% of the decoder matrix's variance, and its components score 73% in a five-way identification against a 20% chance rate — so a large dictionary's units are mostly compounds of a smaller dictionary's vocabulary, not atoms.** Two methodological lessons travel. First, the object we fit a dictionary to can be a set of weight vectors rather than activations, which is exactly the move our weight-side accounts need when a direction we found turns out to be a blend. Second, the semantic evidence is a five-option multiple choice against random distractors, which is a weak instrument: 73% is far above chance and far from confirmation, and the meta-latents could be scoring on style rather than content — so a compositional account of ours should be scored against distractors drawn from the *neighbourhood* of the latent, not uniformly at random, which is the harder bar the paper does not run. Coreference `arxiv-2501.19271` (score the read-out that actually enters the decision; a number above chance is not a number about the mechanism) and `arxiv-2405.08366` (a labelled-attribute dictionary beating a learned one — the basis question arriving from the other side).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 419): **Parity on the clean side and dominance on the triggered side are two numbers on the same checkpoint, and reporting them together is what makes the claim airtight rather than merely suggestive: here clean error sits at most 0.17 points above the baseline (and up to 0.05 below, on the all-to-all variant, where clean error is 0.48 against the baseline's 0.50) while triggered error is at most 0.09 for the same weights.** The construction is worth copying literally into our own effect tables because it forecloses the two explanations a single number leaves open — a degradation that is just a worse model, and a preservation that is just a model that ignores the input property. The transfer arm sharpens it further, since the adapted network is *more* accurate than an honestly transferred one on clean data (74.9 against 72.7) and still falls to 61.6 when the trigger is present, so the behaviour is not decaying along with the weights but riding on them. For us the operational rule is that any claim of the form "the model does X because of Y" prints the X-preserved column beside the Y-conditional column for the same checkpoint, and where the clean side is better than baseline (as it is in three of the arms here) that is reported rather than smoothed away, because it is the strongest form of the claim. Coreference `arxiv-2004.06660` (the same clean-parity two-number structure carried into the text setting, where the flip rate is quoted beside clean accuracy and macro F1) and `arxiv-2602.15195` (a detector whose accuracy column is meaningless without the clean-accuracy collateral printed beside it).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 419): **An installed behaviour survives operations that change the classifier and not the features: retraining every fully connected layer on clean Swedish signs, with the last layer widened from three classes to five, leaves the trigger response intact — triggered accuracy 61.6 against the honest transfer's 70.2 — and the units in the last convolutional layer that fired only on the trigger in the U.S. network still fire on it afterwards.** The mechanism the authors give is that the trigger detector lives in the frozen convolutional stack and the newly trained head merely reads it out, which is the folder's cleanest evidence that a read-out taken from an adapted or retrained model is not licensed by a result obtained from the base model — the same asymmetry that bites LoRA-side claims, where the adapter is the part that is trained and the frozen part is the part that carries. Two transfers: a before/after table over an adaptation step should include the *adaptation alone* arm (here, the honest transfer's triggered accuracy, 70.2) so the reader can see the trigger was already partly damaging the honest pipeline before the backdoor is credited; and the unit-level localisation is what lets the authors predict *where* the effect will survive, which is the difference between showing persistence and explaining it. Coreference `arxiv-2601.06305` (the frozen-weights-versus-adapter split, reached from the opposite direction: the adapter is inert without a term that makes it carry the task) and `arxiv-2503.19859` (structure that is a property of the training trajectory, hence not removable by retraining a head).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 419): **A cause-preserving amplifier is the cheapest instrument in the folder, and its value is the cost curve it prints rather than the strength it adds: multiplying the incoming weights of the identified trigger-only units by a factor k drives triggered accuracy from 61.6 at k = 1 down through 45.1 at k = 20 and 30.8 at k = 100, while clean accuracy falls far more slowly, 74.9 → 68.3 at k = 20 and 59.4 at k = 100 — so the effect is graded and attributable, and the arm at k = 20 is the one the authors name as the useful operating point, paying three clean points for more than twenty-five on the triggered side.** This is the sufficiency check our own accounts need: if a component really carries the behaviour, scaling it should move the behaviour in the predicted direction, and the amplifier must be applied in the direction the account implies (here, input weights of specific neurons) rather than as a global knob. The second lesson is the disclosure discipline — the k sweep reports both sides at every step instead of quoting the best trade, which is what makes the claim auditable rather than a tuned result. Coreference `arxiv-1811.00636` (a spectral removal with a survivor count printed beside it, the deletion-side twin of this amplification) and `arxiv-2402.12560` (the control task that separates a method's expressivity from its finding — the same demand that an intervention be graded rather than asserted).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 418): **The same structure can be the *subject* of a claim or the *premise* of one, and the two need different evidence — this paper separates them explicitly as structure at every iteration (a theorem about the optimisation trajectory, tested by principal angles between the current and initial singular subspaces) versus structure at convergence (an equivalence between the objective you ran and an explicitly regularised one, tested by whether the recovered spectrum matches the predicted shrinkage).** The distinction is operational, not bookkeeping: a dynamics claim is falsified by a trajectory leaving its subspace, a convergence claim by a solution off the predicted spectrum, and a paper that reports only final singular values cannot distinguish "these directions were always the ones moving" from "these directions ended up large". The same distinction bites our white-box programme, where most of our weight-side claims are convergence claims presented as if they were dynamics claims. The reusable artefact is the angle-to-initialisation plot — one panel per intervention, printed beside the magnitudes — because it is the cheapest read-out that turns "the weights changed here" into "the weights moved within this subspace", and it costs an SVD you are already computing. Coreference `arxiv-1811.00636` (a leading singular direction whose meaning depends on a chosen layer and statistic) and `arxiv-2602.15195` (a layer × rank grid reported as the result rather than one cell).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 418): **A quantity you thought was a hyperparameter turns out to be an output of training, and the clearest case in this survey is rank: against a requested budget of 8 on STS-B, Deep LoRA's adapters converge well below it and are numerically zero in the majority of layers, so the layer's effective rank was decided by the optimiser and the budget was only an upper bound.** The survey's own explanation is an implicit per-layer rank selection with the outer factors trained more slowly than the inner one, and it credits this for better test loss in the sample-starved regime. The general shape recurs all over the folder from different directions — a real-data gap where the attack's effect size is not the nominal one (`2004.06660`), a threshold whose precision is unrelated to its sufficient condition (`1811.00636`), an extreme-value correction that changes the ranking (`2402.12560`) — and the transferable rule is that any intervention whose headline is "we set X to k" should report the value X actually took in the trained artefact, because the difference between requested and effective is where these claims usually fail. Coreference `arxiv-2601.06305` (a strength parameter whose ordering interacted with adaptation to produce a survivor population) and `arxiv-2502.20914` (identification questions that only mean something relative to a chosen granularity).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 418): **Depth is not a free architectural knob when the training is regularised, and this survey prices it: because Frobenius regularisation on factorised weights is equivalent to a Schatten-2/L quasi-norm on the product, adding layers tightens the rank penalty on the same weight-decay coefficient, so an L-layer run and a 2-layer run at equal lambda are not comparing architectures, they are comparing two different regularisation strengths.** This is the kind of confound that is invisible in a results table and decisive in a causal conclusion, and it has a direct analogue in our own comparisons: if we read structure out of a deep adapter versus a shallow one, or compare a deep model's weights to a shallow control at matched hyperparameters, the honest control is one where the *induced* penalty on the prediction — not the coefficient in the config — is held fixed. The general lesson is to write down, for each comparison across depth or width, which quantity is being held constant and whether the transformation that relates the two settings preserves it. Coreference `arxiv-2601.06305` (an adaptation variable that has to be perturbed rather than assumed) and `arxiv-2403.19647` (faithfulness and completeness printed together so a one-sided result cannot pass).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 417): **A directional edit is inert without a second term that carries the information, and this paper's ablation prices it on the same table: Embedding Surgery — writing a target-class mean embedding into five rare trigger rows — reaches only 30.1-38.6% flip alone, applying it *after* the gradient-restriction step is worse still at 25.7-38.0, and only the ordering in which surgery initialises and the restriction then steers gets to 50-100%.** That is the same shape run 413 found in a defence paper from the opposite side (`arxiv-2601.06305`: an orthogonality edit doing nothing until a dropout term forced the adapter to carry the task), and the coincidence is the point — the edit and the compensation are separate objects, and a table that reports only their sum cannot say which did the work. For us the operational rule is a three-row ablation for any weight-side or direction-side claim: the edit, the compensating term, and both, with the order of application printed; and where an intervention is reported on a checkpoint that will later be adapted, the *adaptation* is itself a variable that has to be perturbed. Coreference `arxiv-2601.06305` (the same ablation from the defence side) and `arxiv-1811.00636` (a spectral direction whose value is only meaningful given a chosen layer and statistic).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 417): **The axis that decides whether a manipulation survives is not the size of the manipulation but the strength of the optimisation that undoes it, and the sweep shows a defence nobody intended: raising the victim's learning rate to 5e-5 drops the flip rate from 100 to 65 while clean accuracy falls only to 90.1, a smaller batch barely dents it at 99.7, and weight decay and SGD leave it untouched at 100 — so the perturbation grid is ranked by the property it moves, not by an intuition about regularisation.** The authors' own reading is that a rate close to divergence is the mechanism, and they cannot separate magnitude from the mismatch between poisoning-time and fine-tuning-time rates. The transferable artefact is the four-row perturbation table itself: for any claim about a persistent structure in weights, the report should carry a small grid over *the operation that will act on those weights* (rate, batch, optimiser, epoch count) with the structure's score in every cell, because the interesting cases are the ones where the score is stable on one axis and vanishes on another. Coreference `arxiv-2402.12560` (max-over-regions-then-mean-over-layers as an aggregation choice that changes the ranking) and `arxiv-2602.15195` (a layer × rank grid reported as the result rather than one chosen cell).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 417): **A detector that reads a signature is only as good as the signature's simplicity, and the same defence behaves completely differently on two tasks in the same paper: plotting every vocabulary word's flip rate against its corpus frequency separates the planted triggers cleanly on SST-2 and OffensEval, and produces no separable cluster on Enron — because the attack there flipped only about 58% of instances, putting the triggers inside the ordinary cloud of rare words.** The honest shape of this result is that the defence inherits the attack's effect size, so a detection claim and a strength claim computed on the same run are not independent evidence. For our own read-outs the rule is that any "we can see X in the weights" claim ships with the effect size it is distinguishing and a second regime where X is weaker, because a detector that works only where the phenomenon is glaring is measuring the phenomenon's magnitude rather than its presence. Coreference `arxiv-2501.19271` (existence versus localisation scored separately, same dissociation) and `arxiv-2102.12452` (a read-out compared to a control computed the same way).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 416): **A spectral signature exists in the representation and not in the input, and the paper's first figure is the demonstration: on raw pixels the clean and poisoned populations overlap so badly that the same robust-statistics machinery cannot separate them even with augmentation switched off, while on a later layer's representation the poisoned examples sit on one side of the top singular direction and the separation is visible by eye — and even there, weaker scalars fail, with L2 norms overlapping substantially and correlation with a random vector overlapping almost completely.** The consequence for us is that "this direction separates the two groups" is a joint claim about a chosen representation, a chosen statistic and a chosen layer, none of which is neutral: the authors picked the second-to-last residual unit because it removed the most poison, which is a selection made with the outcome in hand. Any spectral claim we publish should name the layer, name the statistic, and print the weaker-statistic arms beside it — because a signature that only appears under the best of several candidates is a property of the search rather than of the phenomenon. Coreference `arxiv-2602.15195` (per-backbone feature tables where the strongest statistic changes with architecture) and `arxiv-2102.12452` (the probe-versus-baseline discipline: a read-out compared to a control computed the same way).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 416): **A population-level bound is not a detector's operating characteristic, and the gap between them is visible in this paper's own numbers: the theory says the top eigenvector correlates with the mean-difference direction once squared separation exceeds six variances over epsilon, and the measured shift is 6.2-7.3 against a mean norm of 79-90 while the leading singular value roughly doubles, yet the empirical outcome is a range of survivors from zero to 57 poison examples across rows — so the theorem's sufficient condition is comfortably met in bulk while the per-run experience varies from complete removal to more than half the estimated budget left behind.** The lesson is not that the theory is wrong but that a bound on the *direction* does not bound the *threshold's* error rate, which is why the paper has to choose a removal budget of 1.5x epsilon and report what survives rather than claim a guarantee. For our own intervention tables the analogue is exact: a sufficient-condition proof about a subspace does not license a claim about precision or recall, and the honest artefact is the survivor count (or the false-positive count) printed beside the bound. Coreference `arxiv-2601.06305` (a threshold asserted by a proposition, then replaced by a measured sweep) and `arxiv-2403.19647` (faithfulness and completeness printed together so a one-sided result cannot pass).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 416): **Reporting a raw, unit-bearing spectral quantity beats reporting a decision, and this paper gets it right almost by accident: its Table 1 prints the leading three singular values of the class covariance for clean and poisoned sets side by side (1,194 / 1,116 / 968 before, 1,613 / 1,207 / 1,130 after; and 1,017 / 892 / 878 against 1,884 / 1,031 / 914), so a reader can see that the poison lifts the first direction by about a third to a half while leaving the second and third almost untouched — a claim about *one* direction, which no accuracy table could have conveyed.** That is the format the folder's weight-side entries want and mostly lack: the spectrum itself, before and after the manipulation, with the change visible in the numbers rather than asserted in prose. The inverse is worth naming too: the accuracy grid (Tables 2-5) is dense but unreadable as evidence of mechanism, since every cell mixes detection quality with whether the backdoor installed at all. For us the rule is one spectral-value row per intervention, unpivoted, and the downstream score kept as a separate column. Coreference `arxiv-2602.15195` (the same demand, met there with univariate feature tables) and `arxiv-2501.19271` (a ranking score whose relation to the quantity of interest is uncalibrated).

Read from: **full text** — v3 HTML, 85,948 raw / 81,945 whitespace-normalised chars, read end to end: abstract, §1 Introduction (the three contributions and Figure 1's two marked-up examples), §2 Related Works (reasoning; utility of explanations; failure cases of explanations; jailbreaking), §3 Experiment setup (ECQA 500 problems at "second-best", SNLI 300 + 300 labelled E and C explained as N, four API explainers, three open-weight evaluators, Figure 2's two prompt templates), §4 Human evaluation (the four-score MTurk protocol and Table 1), §5 Automatic evaluation (the argmax-over-scale-token scoring rule and the degeneracy note), §6 Strategies (ten-strategy taxonomy, GPT-4-Turbo detection, Table 2), §7 Structural analysis (graph construction with B and L, the node-name randomisation control, the results), §8 Discussion (AH versus unfaithfulness / plausibility / hallucination / sycophancy / over-trust, the "cannot be guardrailed at the LLM level" claim and the three recommendations), §9 Conclusion, §10 Limitations, references, Appendices A (Figure 5), B (annotation UI), C (the detection prompt with all ten strategy definitions), D (Table 3, the Zeng et al. taxonomy replication), and the NeurIPS checklist. **Substance:** two benchmark datasets, four explainers, three proxy evaluators, one human study, one strategy detector, one synthetic graph task; no intervention on any model, no internal access.
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 415): **A score can rise because the explanation is persuasive rather than because the answer is right, and the cleanest demonstration is a reader who is shown only one explanation and cannot tell which of the two properties moved them — the same texts here are rated fluent at 4.46-4.85 and largely factually correct at 3.86-4.68 while pushing the wrong answer's convincingness up by 0.57, 0.06 and 0.10 points, so the two favourable ratings and the harmful effect come from the same paragraph.** For us the consequence is that any human or LLM rating of an explanation we publish must be split into a *truth-facing* column (does the explanation survive an execution or annotation check) and a *reader-facing* column (does it read well), because the paper shows the second rises on exactly the texts the first fails, and a single blended rating cannot be reported without collapsing the distinction that matters. This is the natural-language restatement of the folder's oldest split — decodable versus used — applied to prose instead of to features: fluency is the readable intermediate, and the readable intermediate is what persuades. Coreference `arxiv-2506.23845` (naming a concept and dropping the activations: the falsifiability clause this supplies for text) and `arxiv-2602.18458` (a judge that grades the story rather than the science, which is the same failure on reviewer prose).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 415): **Significance without agreement is the trap this paper documents against itself, and the numbers are worth memorising as a template for how an LLM-as-judge table can be entirely true and entirely uninformative: the proxy evaluators move significantly in two of three cases, and in the same paper no item-level human-versus-proxy correlation is significant on any score and every pair of proxies agrees at Cohen's kappa below 0.1, with mean scores that differ by more than a scale point on several cells (Mixtral 1.13-1.64 where humans average 3.0).** The lesson is not that the LLM judges are wrong — the authors' honest reading is that each carries its own baseline marking rubric — but that a judge with its own calibration is measuring something other than the human scale, so a p-value across the two is a comparison of two instruments rather than of two conditions. Operational rule for our own tables: any LLM-judge column ships with an agreement statistic against the reference rater beside it and with its own mean printed, and a judge whose kappa is near zero is reported as a separate measurement rather than as corroboration. Coreference `arxiv-2305.09863` (a self-consistency scorer that is informative only conditional on its own corpus) and `arxiv-2606.24026` (the kappa of 0.46 that refused one metric official status).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 415): **A persuasive text can be produced without the structure its surface implies, and the test is cheap: rerun the same task with the systematic names randomised — when node labels that encoded branch-and-depth were replaced by arbitrary characters, every model except GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo fell to zero success, and GPT-4 still failed nearly half the trees at depth 6 — so the appearance of tracing a six-step argument survives only as long as the labels leak the answer.** The transferable instrument is this *label-randomisation control*: any evaluation of a model's grip on a structure should have an arm where the structure is real and the surface cues are destroyed, because a name that correlates with connectivity lets a model score without reading the edges at all. Our own read-outs have the same vulnerability at one remove — a probe on a component whose name, layer index or position encodes the label will score without the feature; the randomisation arm is how that gets caught. Coreference `arxiv-2402.12560` (the control task that prices how much of an effect is earned, constructed as a benchmark row) and `arxiv-2403.19647` (faithfulness and completeness printed as a pair so a one-sided reading cannot pass as confirmation).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 414): **Score the read-out that actually enters the decision, and the paper's own table prices the difference: ranking concepts by the projected bottleneck value alone gives 84.3% existence at top-1, while ranking by that value times the classifier weight — the term that really determines the logit — gives 49.3%, on the same images, same model, same annotation.** The gap is not noise; it is two different questions being scored with the same name. The authors are unusually direct that the attractive number is the misleading one, and their reason is the folder's oldest lesson in a new costume: a legible intermediate is legible because it is small and unweighted, and an unweighted intermediate is not the mechanism. For us the operational rule is that any score we compute on a bottleneck-like object (a probe output, a concept projection, a low-rank subspace coordinate) must be computed with the downstream linear map folded in before it is compared to task behaviour, and the folded and unfolded versions printed side by side so a reader can see which one the claim rests on. Coreference `arxiv-2305.09863` (a score that ranks well and estimates something else) and `arxiv-2404.16014` (aggregating a field into a scalar that hides the units that carry the effect).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 414): **An alignment claim needs two separate scores — does the thing exist, and is it in the right place — because the two dissociate by a factor of four at equal effort: at the tightest region (a twelfth of the image) the annotated centre pixel lands inside the concept's activated region 13.3% of the time, while existence for the same ranking is 49.3%, and the localisation score only approaches the existence score once the "region" is half the image.** That shape — a low score that a loose threshold rescues — says the heatmap is not localised but diffuse, which is exactly what a whole-object activation mask would produce; the middle row (33.4% at a quarter of the image) exists only because the authors swept the threshold rather than choosing one, and the paper's discussion shows the failure qualitatively (a "blue crown" map lighting up the leg). The transferable instrument is the three-point threshold sweep for any locality, region, patch or feature-attribution claim we make, since a single threshold lets either the optimistic or the pessimistic number be the one that gets reported. Coreference `arxiv-2602.15195` (a scalar summary of a clumpy field) and `arxiv-2403.19647` (two criteria printed together so a one-sided result cannot read as confirmation).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 414): **Concepts are correlated with each other in the data, so a model can score well on a concept task while naming the wrong member of a co-occurring pair, and the paper's failure examples are all of this kind — "grey leg" for grey bill, "white throat" for a black-throated bird, a blue-crown map on the leg — which is a different failure from the model not knowing the concept at all.** The consequence is that a global alignment score computed against annotation is a joint test of the concept and of its co-occurring neighbours: the annotated matrix has structure the model can absorb without representing any single row, so a negative cosine on one row (black eye colour at −0.63) is consistent both with the model ignoring that concept and with it folding it into the colour block. For our accounts the rule is that a concept or feature we name must be shown to be separable from its nearest co-occurring neighbours before it is reported as a unit — an ablation that removes the neighbour and leaves ours, or a control task where the neighbour is present and ours is not — because otherwise the unit is a slice of a correlated block. Coreference `arxiv-2402.12560` (the arbitrary-label control that separates a method's expressivity from its finding) and `arxiv-2405.08366` (a dictionary built from labelled attributes beating learned ones, the same point about bases).

Read from: **full text** — v1 HTML, 58,064 chars after whitespace normalisation, read end to end in five slices: abstract, §1 Introduction (the three contributions), §2 Related works (backdoor attacks, defence families), §3 Preliminaries (weight-poisoning threat model, the proxy-dataset assumption), §4 Backdoor Forgetting in LoRA (§4.1 LoRA versus FFT with the direct-cancellation versus task-dominance split, §4.2 the spectral analysis with Assumption 4.1 and Proposition 4.2, §4.3 the two structural limitations), §5 RoRA (§5.1 clean-strengthened dropout, §5.2 the soft orthogonality penalty and the combined objective, §5.3 the layerwise post-training rescale, §5.4 the empirical validation of the rescale sweep), §6 Experiments (§6.1 main results with Tables 2 and 3 and the case study, §6.2 the component ablation and the coefficient/dropout sweeps), §7 Conclusion and Limitations, the full reference list, and **Appendix A** (A.1 implementation details including the provenance of the copied baseline columns, A.2 the proof of Proposition 4.2, A.3 the rank and scaling sweeps and the RoRA-on-variants table). **Substance:** three backbones (BERT-large, RoBERTa-large, LLaMA), three downstream datasets, two clean-label weight-poisoning attacks, one proposed defence, three LoRA variants re-measured, no competing spectral defence, and no random-subspace control.
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 413): **A directional weight edit is close to inert on its own, and the cleanest demonstration in the folder is an ablation that was run only for the purpose of showing it: the orthogonality penalty that pushes the adapter off the pretrained subspaces leaves attack success at 93.84 (RoBERTa, InSent) and 98.35 (LLaMA, InSent), while the completely different term — dropout on the frozen weights, which forces the adapter to carry task information itself — gets those same cells to 65.68 and 12.76, and only the two together reach 17.05 and 11.88, with the rescale added as a third.** The interpretation the paper gives is that subtracting a direction does not install anything: the poisoned model's behaviour survives an edit that removes projected mass because the remaining weights still implement it, so a directional claim is only as strong as the compensating term that fills the gap, and the ablation makes that visible where a single-cell result would not. For our own write-ups the operational form is a three-row ablation per directional claim: edit alone, whatever supplies the task alone, and both — because a report with only the third row cannot distinguish an intervention that worked by removing the named thing from one that worked by adding something else. Coreference `arxiv-2402.12560` (the arbitrary-label control that separates a method's expressivity from its finding) and `arxiv-2502.20914` (overdetermination, the reason an edit that removes one pathway leaves behaviour intact).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 413): **A threshold measured on an axis beats a threshold asserted by a bound, and this paper is unusually honest about which one it has: the proposition gives a scale beyond which the clean label wins, and Figure 3 then shows plain LoRA staying at maximum attack success through *small and moderate* scales and falling sharply after, exactly the flat-then-cliff shape a margin argument predicts — while the same sweep shows the far end costing clean accuracy, so the strength axis has a usable window rather than a direction.** That pair (a threshold curve with a working range) is a better reporting artefact than either the bound or a single tuned operating point, because it displays the two failure modes at once: too little scaling and nothing happens, too much and the decision boundary is distorted. The second half, which matters more for us, is the alignment gap's role: the same firewall that makes a threshold real makes it *movable*, since raising clean alignment and lowering trigger alignment lowers the scale needed, and the defence's own improvement is reported at much smaller scales than plain LoRA requires. Any intervention report of ours that argues "component X matters" by scaling X up should print the sweep, the clean-side cost, and the scale at which the effect first appears, because a claim that only holds at a large scale the practitioner would not choose is a claim about a regime rather than about the model. Coreference `arxiv-2404.16014` (a scalar summary hiding a clumpy field — the same demand for the axis rather than the cell) and `arxiv-2102.12452` (the sweep-versus-single-setting discipline on the probe side).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 413): **A fine-tuning result is partly a statement about how little the frozen weights left to change, and the number that makes this visible is an accuracy measured before any adaptation: the poisoned pretrained models here already reach 75.84 (BERT), 81.27 (RoBERTa) and 51.13 (LLaMA) on SST-2 and 86.19 / 83.87 / 75.10 on CR, so most of the clean behaviour is inherited and the adapter is making small adjustments on top.** The authors turn this into an argument — inherited accuracy means the adapter contributes little to the clean margin, which is why its spectral strength is small — but the transferable part is the confound it exposes in every before/after table: an improvement measured against the fine-tuned baseline attributes to the intervention whatever the frozen model already did, and a small clean-accuracy change means something different when the floor is 76 than when it is 51. The methodological rule is to print the no-adaptation score as a third column beside baseline and treatment, in any experiment where a trainable module is layered on a model that already works. Coreference `arxiv-1909.03368` (the control condition that reveals a score was not earned) and `arxiv-2006.00995` (behaviour measured against a baseline that already performs the task).

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 412): **A weight-space signature is real but not architecture-invariant, and the demonstration is the paper's own feature table: the same five spectral statistics rank different statistics strongest in each backbone (energy concentration 0.832 for Qwen, kurtosis 0.979 for Llama, entropy 0.823 for Gemma) while the two scale-like statistics are the weakest in all three (top singular value 0.619-0.651, Frobenius norm 0.570-0.606), and the fitted detector likewise leans on a different projection per family (value projection for Qwen, spread across q/o/k for Llama, q and v for Gemma).** The mechanism is the one we should expect from any weight read-out: magnitude carries the least information because a fine-tune naturally varies in magnitude, whereas *shape* statistics — how concentrated the spectrum is, how heavy the tails — carry the signal, and shape is conditioned on the architecture's own spectral furniture. The transferable rule for our white-box model is that a spectral claim needs three columns printed together: the statistic, the architecture it was strongest on, and the same statistic on a second architecture, because a number that is the best discriminator in one family and mid-pack in another is a per-family observation rather than a property of the phenomenon. Coreference `arxiv-2405.08366` (a random-direction dictionary arm making the same point about a basis) and `arxiv-2102.12452` (the probe-versus-baseline discipline that insists a read-out be compared to a control computed the same way).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 412): **Where an update is applied matters more than how large it is, and the sweep prices it: at rank 16 the composite separability score runs 0.27 at layer 3, 0.07 at layer 9, 0.79 at layer 21 and 0.74 at layer 27, while at layer 21 varying rank from 8 to 32 moves the same score only from 0.61 to 0.75 — so a factor of four in rank buys less than moving the update a dozen layers deeper.** That is the folder's cleanest quantitative instance of the (layer × rank × projection) reporting rule that `arxiv-2402.12560` reached from the intervention side, and it comes from the weight side, which is worth having: the same grid, the same conclusion that a scalar is a summary of a clumpy field, and a concrete default operating point the authors standardise on. For us the operational habit is to print the grid rather than the chosen cell, and to say in the caption which axis was swept and which was fixed — the paper is honest enough to call its composite a summary and to show the four constituent metrics separately in the appendix, which is the format our own intervention and spectral tables should copy. Coreference `arxiv-2402.12560` (max-over-regions-then-mean-over-layers as an aggregation choice that changes the ranking) and `arxiv-2404.16014` (aggregate nulls hiding a strongly positive partition).
