- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 392): **A dictionary's residual deserves to be a node, not a caveat — by rewriting the forward pass so each activation is its sparse reconstruction plus an explicit error term, the part the dictionary misses becomes an element of the computation graph with its own measured effect, and the authors report that circuits built on better dictionaries attribute a smaller share of the total effect to error terms (their SAE errors account for roughly 1-15% of activation variance here).** That makes the error share a *dictionary-quality read-out computed on the same run as the explanation*, and it is the cheapest answer this folder has to the "coverage" problem: the account states what it does not cover and prices it in the same units as what it does. Two consequences for us. (1) Any white-box account of ours prints an unexplained-but-located row beside every accounted row, in effect units, so a reader can see whether the account carries 95% of the behaviour or 60%. (2) Removing residual-stream error nodes here badly damages the model while removing MLP and attention error nodes is much less disruptive, so the error share is not uniform across components and should be reported per component type rather than pooled. Coreference `arxiv-2405.08366` (the occlusion failure mode: a live attribute silently absent from the dictionary), `arxiv-2608.30980` (a score against a dummy predictor, the same honesty in a single number).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 392): **Faithfulness and completeness of the complement are one instrument read in two directions, and printing both is what separates a circuit that carries a behaviour from one that merely overlaps it: mean-ablating everything outside the circuit nearly restores the task (under 100 feature nodes here), and mean-ablating the few circuit nodes destroys it, where a neuron circuit needs on the order of 1,500 nodes for the first and hundreds for the second.** The mechanism-level dividend is real: the across-relative-clause circuit splits into two pathways — subject-number detection plus boundary detectors that carry the number forward, and generic verb-form promoters — and the across-prepositional-phrase circuit shares >85% of its features with it, which is a *prediction about which other behaviours should use the same parts* that no single-behaviour account makes. For our own account tables the rule is: one row for what the named parts explain, one row for what their removal destroys, and, where a second task exists, the feature-overlap number as the prediction. Coreference `arxiv-2104.07143` (a direction re-labelled by a new corpus — the same overlap test refused), `arxiv-2606.16939`, `arxiv-2405.08366` (sufficiency vs necessity as the fraction-of-reconstruction form).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 392): **The human-judgement arm and the oracle-metric arm tie exactly, and the result is still informative: 55 features picked by a person asking "is this task-relevant?" and 55 picked by their measured effect on the spurious label produce identical debiasing columns (88.5 / 54.0 / worst-group 76.0), while the neuron version of the same procedure had to be abandoned because almost no implicated neuron could be interpreted and even the neuron skyline, handed the balanced data as an unfair advantage, reached only 75.5 / 73.2 / 41.5 against an oracle at 93.0 / 49.4 / 91.9.** Read correctly this is not a null: the metric-driven arm needed labels for the spurious attribute on a balanced set, which is precisely the data the method exists to avoid, so what the dictionary buys is a nameable unit that a human can screen *without* privileged labels — not a better selection rule. That distinction is the one our write-ups should make when we claim "humans can audit these features": the honest claim is about what a reader can judge with the information available to them, and the matched metric arm is the control that says the judgement added no ranking power.

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 391): **A dictionary read-out should be priced against a stronger reference, not a weaker one — hand-build the trivial dictionary from labelled attributes (conditional-mean directions per attribute value) and report every learned dictionary as a fraction of its sufficiency, edit success and F1, because that converts "our features decode X" into "our features recover N% of what a dictionary built directly from X would".** The five-way outcome is also the useful part: on the same task, supervised edits are single one-feature swaps that agree with the ground-truth counterfactual >80% of the time, task-trained SAEs need 2-6 features, internet-trained SAEs need 32+ and sometimes fail outright, and, critically, **a task SAE with decoder directions frozen at random initialisation performs on par with the internet-trained one** — so the learned dictionary buys nothing over random directions on the editing metric that this paper treats as the causal test. This is the constructive twin of `arxiv-2104.07143`'s random-direction parity for probe labels, and of `arxiv-2608.30980`'s dummy-predictor denominator: three different papers, three different metrics, same verdict that the control ties the method. For us: any read-out table we publish gets a skyline row (the trivial dictionary), a random-direction row, and the sanity row of the no-account method; and the skyline's existence is what makes the middle row interpretable at all. Coreference `arxiv-1810.03292` (the randomisation arm — random directions destroy the account there, fail to score here), `arxiv-2402.04614`, `arxiv-2301.13379`.
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 391): **Two named failure modes show that a dictionary's *coverage* is not a neutral measurement: a causally live attribute can be silently missing because a higher-norm neighbour absorbs the capacity (occlusion), and a binary attribute can be split into ten or more uninterpretable features because the split solution has strictly lower loss than the ideal sparse one (over-splitting) — so "we found N features for concept C" measures the training objective plus the magnitude ordering, not the concepts present.** Both have cheap tests in the folder now: occlusion is separated from a hyperparameter artefact by the monotonic response of the missing attribute's feature count when the dominant one is surgically subtracted (here α from 0 to 1 restores subject features one-for-one), and over-splitting is separated from overfitting by seed and dataset stability (present here) plus a constructed case where the split solution wins in the infinite-data limit for any L1 coefficient. For us: every coverage claim about a feature set gets a stated denominator (the skyline count for that attribute), a magnitude note, and — where we can afford it — the subtraction sweep that says whether the missing concept is absent or merely out-voted. Coreference `arxiv-2607.22925` and `arxiv-2611.20897` (other mechanism-level accounts of what a dictionary can and cannot hold).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 391): **The predictive objects in this paper are built out of dictionary entries, and they are worth copying: once query and key are decomposed, the attention score is a sum of pairwise dot products between query features and key features, and once head outputs are decomposed, the composition of one head into another's queries is a sum of per-feature direct effects — so a circuit stops being a graph of heads and becomes an attribution graph over feature pairs, with sparsity as the falsifiable claim ("most interactions are near zero") and the few non-zero cells as the prediction.** The empirical dividend is real and small: this decomposition surfaced one unremarked asymmetry (a name-mover head whose query inhibits the indirect object as well as the subject, so the head apparently discriminates on position alone) that the head-level circuit description does not state. For us this is the template for a white-box model's prediction step — predict the interaction, not just the component — and the reason to keep the reconstruction linear and additive in building the reference dictionary. Coreference `arxiv-2608.30980` (score relative to a dummy predictor), `arxiv-2403.19647` (sparse feature circuits, cited here), `arxiv-2505.23556`.

- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 390): **A read-out's label is a function of the probe set as much as of the model, and the same unchanged direction gets a different, equally convincing name on each corpus — so an interpretation reported without its corpus has no scope and no falsifier.** This completes the rejection set's fourth axis: `arxiv-1810.03292` destroys the weights and the account must move, `arxiv-1806.10758` retrains on ablated labels and accuracy must fall, `arxiv-1711.00867` shifts an input the model cannot see and the account must not move, and this paper changes *only the examples* and requires the account to stay put. For us the test is one line of work with a stated cost: refit the read-out's evaluation on a corpus from a different source (conversational vs encyclopaedic vs narrative, or our own held-out set drawn from a different distribution than the fit set) and print both labels with a scope qualifier. A label that changes was always a statement about the corpus. Coreference `arxiv-1810.03292` (the weight-side arm), `arxiv-2410.13032` (which comparison a verdict is relative to), `arxiv-2410.13787`.
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 390): **Random directions are the cheapest control in the folder and here they tie the thing being explained — 6.89 mean patterns per direction against 6.80 for neurons, and 82% of random-direction sets annotated as pattern-bearing against 80% for neurons — so "top activations show a coherent pattern" carries no information about learned units until the same pipeline is run on vectors with nothing learned in them.** The reusable accounting is not the existence of one good example but the *rate* of convincing names per condition, printed with the base rate: 48% of random ten-sentence sets already show a pattern because the corpora have topic bias, and only 12% of neuron sets were judged pattern-free against 38% of random sets. For us: every feature description is priced beside a random-direction row and a random-example row on the same metric, and the corpus's own base rate is the floor. This is the read-out-side twin of the two-row floor in `arxiv-1806.10758` and the dummy-predictor denominator in `arxiv-2608.30980`. Coreference `arxiv-2205.14140` (the random-effect explainer as a floor), `arxiv-2405.08366`.
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 390): **Whether a concept lives in a direction or in a neighbourhood is decidable with one distance histogram, and the answer changes what the account can claim — the locality score separates annotated-meaningful from annotated-meaningless directions (0.026 vs 0.010, p 0.0004) by asking whether top-activated items are close to each other in the original space relative to random items, which is the test that distinguishes a global direction from a local cluster.** Consequences for us. (1) A dictionary entry whose activating examples form one semantic neighbourhood is describing where those examples sit, not what the model computes with them, and the paper's own taxonomy (global / dataset-level / local) is the vocabulary to say which. (2) Cross-corpus monotonic token frequency is the falsifier that sorts claims: 25-33% of neuron/token pairs move monotonically inside one corpus but only 3-11% across three, and what survives is mostly function words — so "this direction encodes X" should be stated as surviving N corpora or not surviving them. (3) Report the per-corpus cells: two of the four locality cells here miss significance at 0.05, and an aggregate-only table would have hidden that. Coreference `arxiv-1711.00867` (the reference point as a first-class variable), `arxiv-2607.22925`.

Read from: **full text** — v1 HTML, 34,360 chars after whitespace normalisation, read end to end in three slices; abstract, §§1-5 (Introduction with the four contributions, §2 the invariance-of-the-model construction with the bias-folding algebra, §2.1 setup, §3.1 the three method families, §3.2 gradient and signal methods, §3.3 attribution methods with §3.3.1 gradient-times-input and §3.3.2 reference-point methods, §3.4 SmoothGrad, §4 reference-point importance with the cat attack, §5 Conclusion), acknowledgements, references. **No tables in the paper** — every result lives in Figures 1-6. **Substance:** network 1 is a 3×1024 ReLU MLP on MNIST in [0,1], 10 epochs mini-batch SGD, **98.3%** test accuracy (the paper says "3 layer" and then "1024 ReLu-activated neurons each", recorded as written); network 2 is the same model with the [−1,0] encoding, obtained by subtracting the shift from the first-layer bias (b₂ = b₁ − wᵀm), so activations, predictions and input gradients are identical; shifts tried: the constant −1, a checkered-box image, and a hand-drawn cat, the last clipped into [−0.3, 0.3] so the digit stays visible; methods evaluated: raw gradient, Guided Backprop, PatternNet, gradient-times-input, Integrated Gradients (zero-vector, black-image, and a constructed adversary), Deep Taylor Decomposition (LRP root and PatternAttribution root), SmoothGrad over each. Findings, all from body prose and figure captions: gradients, Guided Backprop and PatternNet are input invariant; gradient-times-input is not; IG is invariant only with the min-pixel black baseline and fails with the zero vector; DTD is invariant with the PA root and fails with the LRP root; the checkered-box shift defeats every IG baseline tried; SG inherits the base method's verdict exactly; the cat appears as the explanation for every method except the PA-rooted ones. **No number in this entry is digitised from an axis**; the only numeric results in the paper are the 98.3% accuracy, the [0,1]/[−1,0] encodings, the 1024 width and the [−0.3,0.3] clip, all stated in prose.
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 389): **The strongest invariance test in the folder needs no training and no statistics — fold the transformation into the first-layer bias and the two models are the same function, so a map that differs between them is reporting the input's offset rather than the network's sensitivity, and this holds exactly rather than within noise.** That is the third member of the rejection set: `arxiv-1810.03292` destroys the weights and requires the account to move, `arxiv-1806.10758` retrains on ablated features and requires accuracy to fall, and this paper *preserves* the function and requires the account to stay still. For our own read-outs the analogue is one line of work: recompute the account on a re-parameterised but functionally identical model (biases compensated, layers permuted, weights rescaled with inverse rescaling downstream) and report the disagreement. An account that moves under a symmetry the network has is not describing the network. Coreference `arxiv-1810.03292` (the destruction arm) and `arxiv-2410.13032` (which comparison a verdict is relative to).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 389): **A method that takes a reference point is a family, not a method, and the invariance verdict flips with the choice: Integrated Gradients passes with a data-relative baseline (the per-dataset minimum pixel) and fails with a zero vector, Deep Taylor Decomposition passes with a covariance-derived PatternAttribution root and fails with the LRP zero-root, and a checkered-box shift breaks every IG baseline tried.** The reason is worth keeping: the passing baselines are defined *after* the transformation, so the difference input-minus-reference is preserved, while a fixed zero is not. For us, every read-out that subtracts something — a mean activation, a zero-ablation baseline, a "neutral" prompt, a comparison class — carries the same index, and "our direction is invariant" means nothing until the reference is named. The report rule: name the reference, state whether it is fixed or data-relative, and print the verdict per reference rather than one aggregate. Coreference `arxiv-2205.14140` (the intervention direction as the thing a method must be coupled to) and `arxiv-2606.25092` (which null the score is against).
- Pattern 2026-11-19 (run 389): **The headline demonstration inverts the explanation rather than criticising it — pick a target attribution, solve for the constant vector that produces it, add it to every input, and the network's stated reason becomes a hand-drawn cat with the prediction untouched, for every method except the covariance-rooted one.** That is the folder's first *planted* explanation: not an explanation that is vague or unhelpful, but one an outside party can aim. Two consequences. (1) Any account we publish should be assumed adversarially constructible unless a symmetry or invariance argument says otherwise — the construction needs only the gradient, which is public for any released model. (2) The paper's own closing warning is the reason this matters beyond vision: a human catches the cat instantly in an MNIST heatmap, and in audio or language there is no equivalent look, so plausibility-checking is available exactly where it is least needed and absent exactly where attribution is claimed to be necessary. Coreference `arxiv-2312.06681` / `arxiv-2403.10949` (readable strands that turned out decorative) and `arxiv-2301.13379` (human plausibility ratings with a measured error rate).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 388): **A deletion curve measured at inference time is mostly a distribution-shift measurement, and the paper prices the error: the same 90%-removed ImageNet data scores 0.5% on the un-retrained model and trains a fresh model to 63.53%, and the toy inverted ranking — the worst possible explanation by construction — *looks* informative under the naive test and correctly shows no damage under the retrained one.** That is the sharpest available statement of the instrument our own surrogate claims need: the ablation must be applied to train *and* test identically and the model refitted, otherwise the account is being scored against off-distribution artefacts rather than against what the network uses. The mirror (KAR, keep instead of remove) is the cheap sanity arm — it separates almost nothing, which is evidence that *removal with retrain* is the discriminative direction and keeping is not. Coreference `arxiv-1810.03292` (the parameter-randomisation rejection test — the same "is the account about the trained model" question without an intervention) and `arxiv-2410.13032` (which comparison the verdict is relative to).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 388): **Three attribution methods with axiomatic guarantees — gradients, Integrated Gradients, Guided Backprop — fail to beat a random pixel ranking by any decisive margin, and a model-blind Sobel edge filter sits between them and random on all three datasets, so the honest verdict is "no better than the controls" rather than "worse than random".** The reusable discipline is the *two-row floor*: a random assignment (uses neither model nor image) and a fixed input-side heuristic (uses the image, not the model), because the paper's own abstract and its Table 2 lean different ways and only printing both rows lets a reader see that the base estimators are above the floor and below the heuristic. For us: any account of ours is priced against both rows, and "our method beats random" is reported as a null unless it also clears the model-blind heuristic. Coreference `arxiv-2205.14140` (the concept-side floor-and-baseline rule) and `arxiv-1810.03292` (the invariance verdict that explains *why* an input-side method tracks an edge detector).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 388): **The strongest account in the paper is the one nobody can explain — squaring each noisy estimate before averaging, or taking the variance of the noisy set, converts a floor-level attribution into one that removes entire objects and destroys accuracy (ImageNet 90% removed: SG-SQ-IG 29.41, VAR-IG 25.25 against random 63.53), while classic SmoothGrad averaging buys nothing — and the authors' own label for the behaviour is "emergent", with why-it-works left as future work.** Squaring alone recovers only 8.43 ± 0.97 of the gap, so the gain needs both steps, which is the part a white-box account would have to predict and which this paper cannot. For us the rule is direct: an explanation whose power lives in an unexplained aggregation is not yet a model we can predict from, and citing its success as evidence for the underlying method is the conflation this paper manages to avoid by naming the aggregation separately. Coreference `arxiv-2608.30980` (score relative to a dummy predictor) and `arxiv-2307.13702` (the mechanical filler-token control, the other way to show a signal is real rather than stylistic).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 387): **An account can be a function of its input and of nothing learned, and both tests say so for the same method: Guided Backprop and Guided GradCAM keep producing near-identical maps until the blocks nearest the input are re-initialised, so they are invariant to the higher-layer weights that carry what the network learned, while raw gradient, gradient-times-input, integrated gradients, SmoothGrad and GradCAM all change substantially.** The reusable form is one sentence per account — *what transformations leave it unchanged* — and the rejection rule that follows: if a transformation that destroys the thing the account claims to describe leaves the account intact, the account is not about that thing. For our surrogate read-outs the deliberate analogue is a decoder recomputed on a re-initialised model; if the decoded story is unchanged, it was never about the trained weights. Coreference `arxiv-2608.30980` (the dummy-predictor denominator, i.e. the same question priced as a score) and `arxiv-2205.14140` (a ground-truth-corrected score rather than an invariance test — the other way to establish that an account depends on the model).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 387): **Visual and perceptual similarity endorse accounts that the sign-sensitive metric rejects: after several blocks of cascading randomisation the bird is still recognisable, SSIM and unsigned rank correlation stay high, and only the signed Spearman correlation collapses to near zero as soon as the top blocks are randomised — so the two views a human reader would use are the two that cannot tell a trained network from a randomly initialised one.** That is the strongest warning in the folder for any evaluation of ours that leans on rendered figures, and it prescribes a reporting triple printed together: signed correlation, unsigned or perceptual similarity, and the metric's own value on a random object. Coreference `arxiv-2301.13379` (human plausibility ratings with a measured error rate — the same failure with people instead of pictures) and `arxiv-2410.13032` (which comparison the verdict is relative to).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 387): **The mechanism is analytic and it generalises off the picture domain: multiplying a fixed input by two independent random gradient fields yields maps that resemble each other and the input, and for a one-layer 3x3 convolution the local ReLU pattern alone determines each pixel's gradient, so edges are drawn no matter what the filter learned — which is why these methods behave like edge detectors.** For us the translation is a check to run before believing any decomposition of the form "coefficient times activation": if the coefficient is close to noise, the product is close to the activation, and the account has described an input-side quantity rather than the network's use of it. The paper's own hedge is worth keeping too: an explanation insensitive to parameters may still be informative about the architectural prior, so the honest verdict is "inadequate for tasks sensitive to data or model" rather than "meaningless". Coreference `arxiv-2611.20897` (a saliency-adjacent account whose guarantee is certified rather than statistical — the constructive counterpart to this rejection test).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 386): **Five of six published concept explainers fail to beat a naive sampling baseline, and one is worse than the floor: with a random-effect explainer at 0.67 and the sampled-counterfactual baseline at 0.44 on the magnitude metric, TCAV lands at 0.78 and ConceptSHAP at 0.56, while INLP ties the lead only on direction at 0.59 and is near-floor on magnitude at 0.73.** The paper's own diagnosis is the reusable part — the methods that win are the ones that know *which* intervention is being asked about and stay tightly coupled to the original model, whereas the methods that lose never see the intervention direction at all. For us this is a floor-and-baseline rule for every table we publish: an account's score appears beside (a) a naive substitution baseline that uses the same information, and (b) a random-effect floor, because a method that cannot beat "swap in a random other example with the right label" has not been shown to do anything. Coreference `arxiv-2608.30980` (the dummy-predictor denominator, same argument from the benchmark side) and `arxiv-2405.08366` (a ground-truth-anchored SAE evaluation, the activation-side twin of this test).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 386): **The ground truth is the model's own output difference on a human-edited pair, which makes this the folder's first template for scoring an account as a *prediction about an intervention* rather than a description: take two inputs differing in exactly one named concept, compute the model's measured effect, and score the explanation by distance from it — under three distances that separate direction (cosine), direction plus size (L2) and size alone (normdiff), which do not rank the methods the same way.** That triple is the design our own surrogate-model claim needs, because a read-out can get the sign of an effect right at no cost and the magnitude completely wrong, and only the separated columns show it. The dataset construction is the second half of the instrument: edit-group-split train sets (so no test item's near-duplicate is in train) and an exclusive one-text-per-group variant exist specifically to stop the model learning the effect trivially, which is the control any counterfactual benchmark of ours would need. Coreference `arxiv-2606.25092` (matched versus unmatched nulls — the same "which comparison is this score against" question) and `arxiv-2410.13032` (reference distribution decides the verdict).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 386): **A synthetic-looking negative result can be reported honestly only if the data's own noise is measured, and this benchmark prints that noise: 99% of edits achieve the intended aspect label, 88% of texts get a five-star majority, 176 double-edits made from the same original with the same goal mostly differ by at most one star, and a worker-identity probe bounds style leakage at slightly-above-chance for the five most prolific annotators (0.27 against 0.16).** That is the reporting checklist for any human-generated counterfactual set we build — intended-label hit rate, downstream-label agreement, repeat-edit divergence, and an author-identity baseline — and it is what lets the authors call their ground truth truth rather than preference. Note also that the labelled "ground truth" is human judgement of sentiment, not a mechanism, so this scores an explanation against what the data says the effect is, never against what the network computes; the two coincide here only because the classifier was shown to reproduce the human ordering. Coreference `arxiv-2402.04614` (faithfulness to a computation versus plausibility to a person) and `arxiv-2301.13379` Appendix D (inter-annotator agreement as the noise floor of a human rating).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 385): **"It is hidden elsewhere" is a rejectable claim, but only if the decomposition is checked against an accounting column and not just against accuracy — 480-to-10 squeeze, retrain, then an SAE on the squeezed layer: no curve-like unit returns (best shape correlation 0.52-0.72, photo match 0.09-0.14, and every one of the 91 most curve-responsive features still fires at the angle where the originals are silent), while the same SAE recipe on the original layer matches at 0.96-1.00.** That paired comparison, same recipe on two layers, is the cleanest positive control in the folder for a read-out's coverage claim, and it is exactly what our own write-ups lack: we report what a dictionary recovers and never what it should have recovered.
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 385): **Capacity pressure changed the units' breadth but not the learning principle — squeezed neurons stop being ten drivers and become one "curves & loops" unit, and the accuracy cost is real (58.35% top-1 at full width, and splicing the SAE in drops it 58.8% to 43.0%), so "broad" and "packed" are separable and only the first is observed.** For us this converts a sweep across model sizes into a confound check: the same fraction of illegible units at three sizes may be one phenomenon measured three times.
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 385): **A memorised fact never got its own unit — teaching a 7M model that an umbrella is a bee moved the answer from 44.2% to 0.03% umbrella and 0.07% to 52.8% bee in nine steps by fading umbrella-associated neurons and strengthening bee-associated ones in the last three blocks, and swapping those blocks into the untrained model reproduces the answer.** This is the folder's first memorisation result read at circuit granularity, and it sharpens the failure mode our read-outs must survive: a decoder that explains the answer can still be describing a route between existing parts rather than a fact stored anywhere.

Teaching budget **two examples** in every task; S pre-trained on 10 (rectangles) or 5 (elsewhere) prior examples; BR = one best response (extra rounds and joint fine-tuning after S pre-training reported as no better); boolean task used a 3→2→1 property curriculum. **Numbers, all from body prose or figure captions that state them:** strategy match 87% / 36% / 0% (boolean), 100% vs ≤20% (hierarchies); human arms — 60 Turkers, 30/arm, 10 concepts, 18% vs 8% mean accuracy with SD 19% vs 6% and max 70% vs 20%; 80 Turkers, 40/arm, 10 concepts, 4 test images, 76% vs 71%. **Relevance 2.**
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 384): **Legibility came from the order of optimisation, not from any constraint on the model: pre-train the student on the ordinary example distribution, freeze it, then fit the teacher to that fixed student, and the emitted artefact snaps to the strategy a human would have picked — 87% of boolean examples share only the concept-relevant properties against 36% for random and 0% for a jointly-trained teacher, and hierarchies go to 100% against a joint ceiling under 20%.** The mechanism the authors give is that a jointly-optimised pair is free to be an encoder/decoder, so the examples become tokens; a student shaped by the natural distribution forces the teacher onto the natural mapping. Two habits follow. (1) **Try decoupling the producer of an account from the consumer before adding a regulariser** — it is one comparison, it is domain-agnostic, and here it moved the score by the whole range of the metric. (2) **Report the joint arm as the matched-but-illegible control**, because it proves the ability is present and only the legibility changed; without it, "our account matches the intuitive rule" is compatible with "the model cannot do the task any other way". Coreference `arxiv-1810.08575` (the same two-party shape on the supervision side, where the scaffold is deliberately discarded) and `arxiv-2312.06681` / `arxiv-2403.10949` (where a readable strand turned out to be decorative).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 384): **A readable account can be scored without any human in the loop, and the cost is one hand-written rule per domain — but the human arm prices how much of the effect a reader actually gets, and here it collapses to 10 and 5 points (18% vs 8%, 76% vs 71%) from a strategy-match gap of 87 points.** The two criteria are printed as separate columns precisely because they disagree, and that disagreement is the reusable quantity: **strategy similarity is an upper bound on what a reader can be given, not the benefit itself.** For us, any "our decoder's account follows a recognisable rule" claim gets both numbers — the similarity score, which needs no subjects, and a reader-side count on a stated population with a matched no-account arm — because reporting only the first would overstate the second by an order of magnitude. Coreference `arxiv-2210.10860` (a fluent human-facing artefact worth roughly zero to readers, the null this paper's small positive sits against) and `arxiv-2211.03540` (the three-arm design with a stated ceiling, the fuller version of the reader experiment).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 384): **The paper reads the teacher's examples and never the student it teaches, so it was the model that drove the metric could have been doing anything: interpretation here is a property of the artefact, and the authors say plainly that they investigated one human limitation out of many rather than showing which make legible protocols emerge.** That is the sharpest statement in the folder of the boundary our own read-outs sit on — a decoder fitted so its output resembles a named strategy is in exactly this position, and the test that would close the gap (intervene on the named parts, check the behaviour moves) is absent here as it was in `arxiv-1810.08575`. Also a specific failure mode worth logging: **the human student's prior, not the examples, is what capped the human arms** — subjects assumed a unimodal concept space and over-weighted colour, exactly the "prior mismatch" problem a reader of our accounts will have. For us: when a reader misreads an accurate account, the entry's own remedy is to inspect the reader's prior, not to rewrite the account. Coreference `arxiv-1810.08575` (the scaffolding-versus-computation warning) and `arxiv-2211.03540` Appendix C (a reader who cannot check a claim accepts it anyway — the opposite prior failure).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 383): **The scaffold and the learned computation can be structurally unrelated by design, and this paper states it as a feature: the hierarchical decomposition is discarded at the end of training and "the actual procedure learned by the agent will generally not mirror the structure used in training", possibly ending as holistic heuristics that ignore the tree entirely.** That is the licence for a decomposition to be efficient rather than true, and it is simultaneously the warning every decomposition-shaped read-out in this folder needs — a tree of subquestions that produced the training signal is evidence about the signal, not about the network that consumed it. The test that closes the gap is missing here and cheap for us: intervene on the named parts after training (zero a subtree, swap a subanswer) and check whether the trained model's behaviour moves accordingly. For us: **any account whose parts come from a training scaffold gets an intervention row or it is described as a training artefact.** Coreference `arxiv-1805.00899` (one path as evidence about the tree — the same inference, licensed there by adversarial search rather than by construction) and `arxiv-2301.13379` (a faithfulness bought on one edge only, the constructive cousin of this point).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 383): **The supervisor can be the weaker party, and the useful target is the margin rather than the answer: at every point in training the composite is only modestly better than the agent alone, the agent imitates it, and the process is powered by that small gap — with efficiency explicitly not required, only that ten agents working together be any better than one.** Two consequences for us. (1) **Price a read-out by how many expensive consultations it needs, not only by its accuracy** — this paper's headline practical result is the ratio between tens of millions of supervised labels and 6,000-24,000 hand-coded decomposer calls, and the same accounting decides whether a human-in-the-loop explanation is defensible. (2) **Keep the target-network-style stabiliser** (here a Polyak average over the last 1000 batches used inside the composite instead of the live model): whenever the thing generating the account is the model being described, the account chases a moving target and the averaged copy is the version that gives a consistent signal. Coreference `arxiv-2211.03540` (human + model teams beating both parties by a margin, with a ceiling above them) and `arxiv-2210.10860` (where a fancier account bought a margin indistinguishable from zero).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 383): **The paper's motivating mechanism is the proxy argument, and it applies to explanations as much as to rewards: when the true signal is beyond human scale, practitioners substitute a correlated measurable — user satisfaction is their example — and optimising that proxy produces an agent that fakes the appearance instead of improving the thing.** For a white-box account the same substitution happens upstream: the account becomes the target (raters reward it, benchmarks score it) and an account optimised as a target stops being evidence about the network, which is the folder's plausibility-versus-faithfulness argument arriving from the supervision side. The reusable design rule is to keep the proxy and the thing it proxies separately measured and report both — here the tasks retain an algorithmic ground truth that training never touches, which is exactly the position a held-out test set holds. Coreference `arxiv-2402.04614` (plausibility and faithfulness as separately optimisable objectives) and `arxiv-2305.04388` (an account written after the answer, i.e. the proxy already gamed).

Human arm: no counts reported.
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 382): **The cheapest way to price an account is to build the adversary rather than find one: designate one player honest and one liar, then read the honest side's win rate against the judge's unaided accuracy — 59.4% to 88.9% on six pixels, 48.2% to 85.2% on four — so "the account is strong enough to be defended and attacked" becomes a number without a naturally deceptive model in the loop.** Precommit is the condition the paper leans on: the liar must stake the claim before any evidence is revealed, the honest player then wins 86.7-90.4% of games, and the authors' diagnosis is that a lie fixed in advance cannot be adapted branch by branch — but their table gives no honest-win figure for the no-precommit cell, so the "crucial" is prose rather than a like-for-like column, and this entry reports the cells it has rather than the adjective. Two rules follow for us. (1) **Any read-out we claim is checkable gets a designed adversary arm and a stated judge competence floor** — the comparison is against what the judge can do unaided on the same items, not against a rival method. (2) **Ask the predictor to commit before the explanation is generated**, because a claim fixed in advance is the only one that can be shown to have been refuted rather than revised. Coreference `arxiv-2211.03540` (the same honest-versus-liar idea run with a real model and human judges) and `arxiv-2307.13702` (the content-free arm, the other cheap control that needs no labels).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 382): **"One path through the argument tree is evidence about the whole tree" is the inference every circuit and feature account we write makes in one sentence, and this paper states both the licence and the price: the licence is that a strong enough pair of adversarial searchers picks the most contentious path, so a single line carries information about everything it skipped; the price is that the claim is about equilibrium play, and the authors list five ways approximate play breaks it — judges who accept what they already believe, debates longer than a judge can track, steps containing terms the judge cannot parse, capacity lost relative to direct training, and self-play that cycles through forgetting how to attack.** For us the practical consequence is that a shown path is a *sample* and the caveats are a reporting checklist: name the judge (here a fixed sparse-pixel classifier, i.e. one with strictly less information, not less competence), name the turn budget, and say whether the account is a claim about the search's best path or about a single beam. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13032` (reference distribution decides the verdict) and `arxiv-2606.25092` (which null the comparison is against).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 382): **The complexity-theory ladder is an analogy with a stated limit and it earns its place by naming which failure is structural: alternating claims move the judge's task up the polynomial hierarchy with each round, so the supervision signal rather than the model is the binding constraint — but the interval-branching protocol that produces the result requires deterministic transitions, and a liar who supplies plausible noise at every step defeats it while staying locally consistent.** That is the folder's cleanest statement of a shortcut that survives the removal of its supposed cause: the protocol is sound, the checker is sound, and the adversary wins by making each local check pass. For us it is a warning about any account that is verified step by step — local validity of every step does not bound the global error, and the check that closes it is a second, independent line of evidence rather than a harder local test. Coreference `arxiv-2208.14271` (where the value function ranks plausibility and its own appendix traces contain invalid steps) and `arxiv-2402.04614` (plausibility as the thing that is optimised).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 381): **A fluent, well-targeted, human-written set of arguments moved human accuracy by roughly nothing, and that is the price list for "this explanation helps a reader": the matched no-explanation arm is 74.8 against 72.8 correct with arguments, and the second round of counter-arguments — the thing debate theory says should be the mechanism — moved neither arm by more than 0.6 points.** The pair with `arxiv-2211.03540` is the folder's sharpest contrast because the two share a population, a task family and a citation lineage yet differ in design in three ways that are all now suspect: there, the helper was a model in conversation (not a written argument), the team could interrogate it over many turns, and the judgement was per-item with the answer revealed afterwards — here the arguments were fixed text, judged once, with one bonus note. Two habits follow. (1) **Any claim we make that a read-out *helps* a stated reader gets a no-read-out arm on the same items, same readers, same time budget**, because this paper shows a high-quality account can be worth zero and a reader study without that arm would have reported 72.8 as if it were a benefit of the design. (2) **Distinguish a written account from a conversational one before generalising** — the positive and null results in this pair are both true, and the variable that separates them is the interface, not the quality of the reasoning. Coreference `arxiv-2211.03540` (the positive side of this pair) and `arxiv-2402.04614` (usefulness versus plausibility, which this paper prices at zero).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 381): **Accuracy with abstentions removed is the wrong column — the harm here is entirely in the incorrect count while the headline moves the wrong way: adding arguments takes incorrect calls from 17.1 to 20.4 (first judgment) and 17.5 to 20.7 (second), so a design reporting only "correct, abstentions excluded" would have shown a 2-point dip indistinguishable from noise and missed a 19% relative rise in confident mistakes.** The paper prints three columns and the ratio beside them (3.6 against 4.4), which is what makes the direction legible, and the same three-column discipline is what run 377's transition-matrix rule asks for from the other side: report what the changed cases changed into. For us the rule is that **any read-out evaluation reports correct, incorrect and no-answer separately, plus the ratio between the first two**, never a single accuracy, because a well-calibrated abstention and a confident error are the two outcomes a surrogate model must keep distinct. Coreference `arxiv-2211.03540` (confidence-conditional accuracy as the deployability row) and `arxiv-2305.04388` (the transition breakdown that closes the noise objection).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 381): **Abstention incentive is a treatment and not a nuisance parameter: raising the penalty for skipping from "abstain below 60%" to "abstain below 75%" took abstention from 8.0 to 23.0 without arguments and from 6.8 to 26.1 with them, and it simultaneously removed the harmful direction of the argument effect — so the same account is neutral, harmful or helpful depending on what the reader is paid to risk, and any reader-facing evaluation of ours that omits this variable is a statement about one incentive level only.** The authors got there by modelling expected bonus under each response strategy against assumed accuracy rates (four strategies × six accuracy bins per incentive scheme) rather than by assuming the incentive worked, which is the reusable piece: **write the payoff matrix, check the strategy it makes optimal, then check the observed behaviour against it** — they found judges under-abstaining relative to the optimum, surveyed why (dislike of appearing indecisive, belief that the task was to pick), and changed both the payoffs and the framing. For us the translation is direct: a decoder whose stated confidence is used to gate an action has an implicit payoff matrix, and its calibration numbers are uninterpretable until that matrix is written down. Coreference `arxiv-2211.03540` (confidence-conditional accuracy, the same quantity in a model-only setting) and `arxiv-2410.13787` (calibration reported as a distribution over behaviours rather than a point).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 380): **A read-out that is meant to be used needs the same three arms as this paper's team experiment — the party alone, the model alone, and the two together, with an expert ceiling above them — because the pair can beat both parties while its stated confidence becomes systematically less trustworthy, and only the calibration column shows it.** The numbers here are the reason to run all four cells rather than two: individual teams gain 18.2 points on MMLU and 28.2 on QuALITY over unaided humans and 9.8/9.9 over the best model, yet calibration error goes the wrong way on MMLU for teams (12/18 against 6 for both parties alone) while improving on QuALITY (7 against 17/7), so "the team is better" and "the team knows when it is better" are separate claims that moved in opposite directions on one of two tasks. For our surrogate-model work the translation is direct: a decoder evaluated only on accuracy is a team evaluated only on accuracy, and the row that decides deployability is accuracy conditional on the confidence the system would express. Coreference `arxiv-2505.13763` (a full-access ceiling, the analogue of the expert row) and `arxiv-2608.30980` (the dummy-predictor denominator, the same argument about which comparison the score is relative to).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 380): **Confident-wrong accounts get accepted when the reviewer lacks the knowledge to check them, and this paper's Appendix C is a matched case rather than an anecdote: one participant, using the folder's own recommended strategy of interrogating each option as a true/false question, was told the 1939 leadership study showed authoritarian leadership was most productive, was told in the next conversation that laissez-faire was least productive and a participative style won, and then chose the wrong option anyway while being fully confident.** The model's own two statements are jointly inconsistent and neither names the correct answer, so the transcript prices the plausibility line from the human side: fluent, self-assured, wrong, and undetectable without the fact. Two habits follow. (1) **Never score a generated account on coherence to a reader who cannot check it** — the check has to be mechanical (does the answer move when the account is edited, does the quoted span exist) or it is a confidence measure wearing a faithfulness label. (2) **Prefer the account form that can be falsified cheaply** — on QuALITY participants converged on demanding verbatim quotes precisely because a quote can be searched in the passage, which is the same defence as citing an activation or a token span instead of a paraphrase. Coreference `arxiv-2402.04614` (the same failure stated as a definition) and `arxiv-2307.13702` (the filler-token arm, i.e. the mechanical version of "check that the cited span matters").

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 379): **There are two independent ways to install faithfulness and they cut different edges: `arxiv-2301.13379` makes the answer the deterministic execution of a program the model writes, while this paper denies information paths — the inference model cannot see the question and the answering model cannot see it either — so in both cases the answer-to-account edge is guaranteed and the *account-to-computation* edge (why this selection, why this inference) is left entirely unexplained.** The pair is now the folder's clearest statement of the boundary: construction buys the last edge of the chain and says nothing about the first, which is exactly where an activations-to-output decoder sits, and neither paper claims otherwise. For us the rule is to annotate every account as **faithful from X to Y, unexplained from W to X** with both pairs filled in, and to resist calling an architecture "faithful" without saying which edge it bought. Coreference `arxiv-2301.13379` (the program-execution route, with its own Limitations saying execution fidelity is not the reason the program was chosen) and `arxiv-2402.04614` (the same distinction as a definition without a construction).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 379): **The blocked-path control is the cheapest instrument that separates "the answer came from the account" from "the answer came from somewhere else", and it needs no labels: give the system a context in which the proof is impossible but a shortcut is still available — a random context from another problem, or rules without facts — and read how much accuracy survives.** Here the survival is 30.0% and 23.0% for the answering baselines against 9.4% for the structured model on EntailmentBank, and a 48.8-point drop against 4.3 and 0.1 on ProofWriter, and the *surviving* share is the shortcut's size rather than noise. This is the input-side twin of the mirror and null controls the folder already holds, and it is the measurement we should run on any surrogate whose claim is that its predictions are computed from the read-out: substitute an input in which the putative cause is absent but a known shortcut is present, and report the residual. Coreference `arxiv-2307.13702` (filler-token control — content removed, format retained) and `arxiv-2410.13032` (reference distribution, which is the same question on the ablation side).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 379): **An ablation table can credit the scaffolding with the score while the architecture earns only the trace, and this paper prints both in one table: on EntailmentBank, the proof-only baseline paired with *their* halter and search reaches 82.9 / 76.2 against the structured model's 83.2 / 72.9 — statistically indistinguishable, and worse on the distractor task — while the 0-1% fabrication rate and the 63-point context delta belong to the structure alone.** Two habits follow. (1) **Separate what a component is claimed to buy from what the pipeline buys**: every architectural claim should be accompanied by the same scaffolding applied to the strongest baseline, because otherwise the halter and the search get reported as evidence for the structure. (2) **Report the dataset-dependent collapse of a structural claim**: fabrication is 0-1% on the long-context EntailmentBank and indistinguishable from baselines on the short-context ProofWriter, so "the structure prevents hallucination" is only meaningful where copying is harder than inventing, and any structure we build gets its fabrication column on more than one context length. - Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 378): **Faithfulness can be installed by construction instead of measured, and the installation is a scoping move rather than a solution: make the answer the deterministic output of a program the model writes, and the chain becomes faithful to the answer by definition — but only to the answer, because nothing in the design explains why the model wrote that program.** The authors state this plainly in both their footnote and their Limitations, and it is the same boundary our surrogate-model work sits on: a decoder fitted from activations to predictions is exactly faithful along the one edge it is fitted on and says nothing about the map from input to activations. The reusable form is a sentence every one of our read-outs should carry — **faithful from X to Y, unexplained from W to X** — and this entry is the cleanest worked example of a system whose faithful edge is real, useful and insufficient. Coreference `arxiv-2402.04614` (the same distinction stated as a definition, plausibility versus faithfulness) and `arxiv-2410.13787` (a report that is faithful to nothing because the answer cannot be computed from the account at all).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 378): **A prompt component can be the one a human reads and still be the one that does no work, and the ablation table prices the split: removing every natural-language comment costs 0.5 points on GSM8K, 1.9 on Date and *gains* 1.0 on SayCan, while removing the solver costs 50.8 / 22.9 / 19.4 — so on three of four datasets the readable strand is decorative and the arithmetic strand does everything.** The CLUTRR column is the exception that proves the method: there the NL comments are worth 49.6 points, but 31.3 of that comes from a single formulaic line that only changes the shape of the generated code, which is format steering reported as a reasoning effect. Two habits follow. (1) **Ablate the interface, not only the content**: the solver arm is the intervention that reveals how much of the answer was ever computed from the account, and any generated rationale whose conclusion is supposed to follow from its premises should get the equivalent arm. (2) **Credit a prompt component only for what survives its removal** — a readable scaffold that changes accuracy by under two points may still be worth keeping for the human, but it must not be reported as the thing that produced the answer. Coreference `arxiv-2307.13702` (the filler-token control, which is the length-matched version of the same question) and `arxiv-2403.10949` (the per-token relevancy score, which prices the readable strand token by token instead of by ablation).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 378): **Human plausibility ratings are an instrument with a measured error rate and this is the folder's first entry to publish it: inter-annotator agreement per domain runs 0.455 to 0.947, and the authors' own audit finds annotators marking correct chains wrong at 41.7% on Date Understanding and 100% on the CLUTRR cases they inspected — which, together with a 66.7% correctness rate on StrategyQA where a True/False answer can be right by luck, means a crowd rating of an explanation is close to uninformative on the datasets where it matters and near-saturated on the ones where it is clean.** For us this makes two prior entries' casual use of human rating a liability rather than a support: `arxiv-2608.30980` decomposes its quality column for exactly this reason, and the safest form is to report agreement beside the score and to prefer a mechanical check (does the answer change when the account is edited) wherever one exists. Coreference `arxiv-2305.04388` (convincingness 4.0 -> 2.0 with 15% of rationalisations containing no detectable flaw, i.e. raters notice degradation but not deception) and `arxiv-2307.13702` (AOC as the mechanical substitute for asking a person).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 377): **A generated explanation can be coherent, correctly predict the answer, and still be a rationalisation, and the paper supplies the two counts that price the risk: 73% of sampled explanations are rewritten to argue for the answer the bias just pushed the model onto, 15% of those contain no error at all, and only 1 of 426 examined explanations names the biasing feature.** This is the folder's cheapest refutation of plausibility-as-validation and it is stronger than the framing entry because it is quantified against a manipulation rather than argued: convincingness falls 4.0 -> 2.0 with correct-answer explanations, so a human rater does notice degradation, but a well-formed minority survives with no detectable flaw. For us the rule is a required second column: **an explanation we generate is scored both for whether it supports the answer and for whether the input feature that demonstrably moved the answer appears in it**, and only the second distinguishes a report from a rationalisation. Coreference `arxiv-2402.04614` (the same distinction as a position paper, with no measurement) and `arxiv-2608.30980` (the same failure as a benchmark, split into parse-rate and quality).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 377): **The mirror analysis is the artefact filter this folder should have been running all along: rather than arguing that an accuracy drop is not noise, run the same manipulation on items where the bias points at the correct answer and check that accuracy rises by a comparable amount — here +31.9 and +24.1 points against drops of -36.3 and -30.6, which is what licenses the word "systematic" and makes the flips attributable to the feature rather than to variance.** Table 13 does the complementary accounting by transition type (correct-to-biased-wrong ~22-38%, correct-to-other-wrong ~1.2-4.5%), and the asymmetry is the finding: the *targeted* wrong answer absorbs nearly all of the change. Two habits follow. (1) **Any input edit we claim "causes" a behaviour change gets the sign-flipped arm** — a feature that hurts where it misleads must help where it coincides, and a one-directional effect is a warning about the design. (2) **Report the transition matrix, not the net delta**, because a net drop of the same size can hide a large bidirectional churn; the paper's own table is why its noise objection is closed. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13032` (reference distribution decides the verdict — the same argument from the ablation side) and `arxiv-2606.25092` (matched versus unmatched nulls).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 376): **Chain-dependence is a property of the task-model pair and not of the method, and the paper's own grid makes the point sharper than its abstract: answer-change rate ranges over more than an order of magnitude (AOC 0.02 on ARC Easy against 0.44 on AQuA, both with the same model and prompt), the ordering is stable across two independent instruments (early answering and adding mistakes agree on every task but one adjacent pair), and the ordering is uncorrelated with the accuracy the chain buys** — LogiQA is second-most chain-dependent with a 1.02-point gain, HellaSwag loses 4.69 points and is still less post-hoc than four tasks that gain. For us the consequence is a reporting rule: **a generated explanation's trustworthiness is quoted per task-model pair, never per model**, and the cheapest way to place an account on this axis is the zero-truncation proxy the paper itself adopts (does the answer change when the reasoning is removed), which costs two extra forward passes per item and needs no labels beyond the answer. Coreference `arxiv-2402.04614` (the same AOC construction described with no citation to its source) and `arxiv-2608.30980` (the trained-self-report twin: score per task, and quote the per-property column).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 376): **The cleanest control for "is this the content or just the tokens" is a length-and-position-matched uninformative filler, and it costs one substituted string: replacing the entire chain with ellipsis runs across zero to full length produces no accuracy gain on any of eight tasks (and a slight loss on two, where the token pattern is likely out of distribution), which rules out the test-time-compute hypothesis in a single arm and simultaneously rules out the lazy version of our own causal story.** The paraphrase arm is the matching control on the other axis — same meaning, different phrasing, prefix-only to stop the paraphraser from being handed the answer — and it shows essentially no accuracy change, so the information is in the content and not in the wording. For us these two are a template for any prompt or context intervention we report: **a content arm, a length-matched content-free arm, and a wording-only arm**, and a positive result is only the content arm beating both. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13032` (a reference distribution deciding the verdict before the metric does — the same lesson on the ablation side) and `arxiv-2606.25092` (a size-matched null rather than an unmatched one).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 376): **"Smaller models are more faithful" is a reliance measure and must not be read as honesty: the metric is how often the answer changes when the chain is removed, so a model that ignores its chain scores *unfaithful*, a model that cannot use its chain outscores both, and the paper's own appendix supplies the tell — below 13B the models gain little to no accuracy from the chain at all, which is why the 13B sits at the maximum of a curve whose low end is a floor rather than a peak.** The same inversion appears on the synthetic additions, where chain-dependence rises with size on *every* task and rises on *easier* tasks at fixed size, so the "inverse scaling" headline is a statement about how much capable models need their written steps, not about how accurately they describe themselves. For us the rule is that **every faithfulness score we report carries its reliance denominator and, beside it, the model's ability to do the task without the account** — otherwise a transparent-but-useless account and an opaque-but-effective one are indistinguishable, and the first will always win. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13787` (self-report failing exactly where the property needs a long rollout, i.e. ability and access confused) and `arxiv-2608.30980` (the dummy-predictor denominator as the formal version of this complaint).

- **Selection: `2402.04614` (*Faithfulness vs. Plausibility*), the id runs 373 and 374 both named as the criterion-side completion** — three consecutive entries had recorded "plausibility outrunning faithfulness" as the failure mode and the folder held no entry that defines the two terms. Collision-checked before any fetch: absent from `aether/` filenames, `core/` (195 files) and all four INDEX files, and absent from SEED_QUEUE.md. It earns a **2**, not a 3, because **there is no experiment, no metric, no benchmark and no number anywhere in it** — it is a position paper and every empirical claim it makes is borrowed from Turpin et al. and Lanham et al. Taken anyway for three measured reasons. (1) **It fixes the vocabulary the folder has been using loosely**: plausibility is defined as coherence with human reasoning, faithfulness as accuracy of the account to the model's own computation, and the argument is that these are *separately optimisable* because pretraining on human text and tuning against human raters both reward the first and neither rewards the second. (2) **It is the map of the black-box faithfulness instruments**, describing four in enough detail to reimplement: option-order swap, and perturbing the tokens the explanation flagged, both scored as the fraction of predictions that change; and truncating the chain or injecting mistakes into it, both scored as an area over the curve of consistency against the fraction shown or corrupted. (3) **It supplies two worked off-diagonal scenarios rather than data, and both are diagnostic for our side**: a chain citing medically sensible features while the real driver is something spurious like the day of the week, and a refusal explanation that names the offending concept while the same concept wrapped in a bereavement frame elicits compliance — the second is the folder's shallow-refusal-signal result stated as prose.

Read from: **full text** — v3 HTML, 50,481 raw chars, read end to end in four slices; abstract, §§1-7 (Introduction, Self-Explanations, Plausibility, Faithfulness, Plausibility or Faithfulness — Which one do we need? with 5.1-5.4, Call for Community, Conclusion), references, the two boxed definitions, and Figures 1-6 read as captions. **Substance:** no training, no models of their own, no data; three illustrative explanations produced with a mid-2023 chat model (a linear equation, a Rayleigh-scattering question, a sentiment sentence), one truthfulness-checking example with options swapped, one safety exchange with a jailbreak-by-framing pair; the analysis is of the self-explanation literature (Jacovi & Goldberg's faithfulness definition, Turpin et al. and Lanham et al. as the two measurement families, Ye & Durrett on few-shot explanation unreliability, Liao & Vaughan on transparency needs, Chen et al. on counterfactual simulatability). **Numbers: none** — the paper contains no measurement of its own, and this entry therefore makes no quantitative claim; the only quantities named are borrowed metric *definitions* (fraction of changed predictions, area over the consistency curve), quoted as definitions, not as values.
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 375): **Plausibility and faithfulness are separately optimisable and the training stack optimises the cheap one: a model is tuned to emit text that human raters call coherent, so a fluent account of its own computation is the default product and a true one is a coincidence — meaning a generated read-out's fluency is evidence about the training objective, not about the network, and must never be quoted as validation.** For us this converts a habit into a rule: **every natural-language explanation we produce ships with a line saying what was done to check it against the network, or it is labelled explanatory prose.** The folder now holds three working checks at three prices — a per-token treatment effect on a described vector (`arxiv-2403.10949`, one extra forward pass), an ideal-observer decoder on the same activations as a ceiling (`arxiv-2505.13763`, one regression fit), and the option-swap input edit (`arxiv-2402.04614` borrowing from Turpin et al., two lines of prompt code, no activations at all). Coreference `arxiv-2608.30980` (the same failure measured at corpus level, split into parse-rate and quality) and `arxiv-2410.13787` (where the answer must be simulated forward, read the report as a distribution and score it against a rival model).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 375): **The paper's sharpest example is a probe story told as a clinical anecdote and it names the artefact we are most exposed to: the model justifies a diagnosis with medically sensible features while the real driver is a spurious one like the day of the week, so the account is accurate about the concept space and wrong about the computation.** That is neither a lie nor a hallucination — it is a feature whose correlation with the label is real in the training data while its causal path runs through a shortcut — which makes high probe accuracy on that feature perfectly consistent with the behaviour being explained badly. Two rules. (1) **Before attributing a probe direction to a concept, check it against a shortcut baseline that shares the label but not the mechanism** (day-of-week under appointment data, format tokens, `arxiv-2606.10487`'s probe that read the output format, `arxiv-2610.30363`'s label-location pooling). (2) **A probe that predicts cannot substitute for a probe that intervenes** — the reviewer here is misled precisely because nobody ran the day-of-week counterfactual, which is one input edit. Coreference `arxiv-2406.09289` and `arxiv-2505.23556` for the refusal variant (the model names the concept and the concept is not the cause).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 375): **The folder's faithfulness vocabulary now has a stated boundary, and it needs stating because two entries have used the word in different senses: faithfulness here is a property of a *statement about the computation* ("this is why I answered"), while the intervention entries use it for a property of a *component* ("removing this changes the answer") — and the second implies the first only if the component is what the statement describes.** This changes how we report. A direction or circuit can be intervention-faithful while its generated description is unfaithful, and the two failures have different repairs (a better read-out versus a better description). The practical form: whenever an entry we write says "faithful" it must say **faithful to what** — the behaviour under ablation, or the account under inspection — and the second is the one this paper is about and the one the folder has never scored. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13032` (faithfulness as a score difference under ablation, the component sense) and `arxiv-2403.10949` (a generated description priced per token, the only entry that scores the account sense).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 374): **A generated description of a hidden vector is mostly the model talking to itself unless each of its tokens is priced against a no-injection run, and the price is one extra forward pass per token: the relevancy score this paper defines — the change in a description token's log-probability when the substitute embedding is present versus absent — is what separates "the vector caused this word" from "this word was the model's own plausible continuation", and the paper's own worked example (an embedding described as a popular tourist attraction when only the mountain is in it) shows the unstripped sentence is not a description of anything.** This is the folder's first *generated* explanation to carry a per-token causality control, and it retrofits onto the entries that produce text without one: `arxiv-2608.30980` measures the same failure at the corpus level (a strict score that splits into parse-rate and quality via Shapley) and `arxiv-2402.04614` names it as plausibility outrunning faithfulness. For us the rule is: any natural-language read-out we generate gets its tokens split into injected-versus-continued, and the score we report is the fraction of high-relevancy tokens, not the sentence's plausibility. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13787` (a behavioural report whose calibration is the analogue of relevance: is the sentence about the model, or about what a model would say).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 374): **The folder has now bracketed introspection at both ends and the boundary between them is where the asker stops supplying the answer: a model asked to *describe a vector* it computed recovers a hidden entity state as well as a 100-shot linear probe with no training at all (this paper), while a model asked to *state what it would do* on a hypothetical prompt needs 30,000 fine-tuning examples to beat a cross-trained rival by a few points and still fails on any property requiring a long rollout (`arxiv-2410.13787`).** The difference is not introspection ability but task form: here the answer is already in the activations at the position being read and the prompt supplies the option set, there the answer must be simulated forward and the prompt supplies nothing. Two consequences. (1) **Prefer the read-out whose answer is co-located with the query when we can construct one** — this is the design principle behind asking a model to choose between two named states rather than to predict its own continuation of a story. (2) **Do not cite a positive self-interpretation result as evidence that self-report works in general**; the two entries price the same word and land in different places, and `arxiv-2505.13763`'s ideal-observer ceiling is the instrument that tells which regime a given question is in.
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 374): **Editing one layer against a described target vector works and its measurable side effect is invisible, which makes the random-embedding control the load-bearing number: replacing a single layer's output on one embedding pair moves 100 held-out ethical scenarios from 100% to 96% on the intended preference, but the same procedure with a randomly chosen embedding and target moves them to 95% — so the edit is real and its specificity is 1 percentage point, on 100 items, with no significance test.** The fact-editing table has the same shape from the other side: fine-tuning wins efficacy (82.12) and loses the harmonic mean (26.98) because it destroys specificity (12.40), which is the folder's cleanest illustration that a control method must be scored on retention as well as on effect, and this paper does print both columns. For our intervention work the rule is that **a control's effect must beat its own matched-perturbation control by a margin the design can detect**, which is run 371's power requirement stated as an experimental template rather than as an annotation. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13032` (retained nulls published without power) and `arxiv-2410.13787` (a rival instrument rather than a rival perturbation).

- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 373): **A self-report score without a dummy-predictor denominator is uninterpretable, because the label distribution is the model's own and can be arbitrarily skewed: the paper's example is a model whose answers flip on 5% of examples scoring 0.95 by always saying "no flip", and its repair — skill = score minus the strongest constant predictor computed on the same evaluated model's label distribution — is one line of bookkeeping that makes two models' scores commensurable and makes a constant answer visible as zero.** This is the label-side twin of `arxiv-2410.13032`'s power statement for retained nulls: there the missing number was what the design could detect, here it is what a claim implies without knowing anything. For us the rule is that **every accuracy, AUROC-against-a-threshold or report score we publish sits beside the best constant answer for that model on that data**, and that a per-property score is quoted per property, because the paper's two main patterns are exactly that baselines differ widely across tasks and that raw-score rankings do not track general capability. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13787` (per-property mode baselines, and calibration as the discriminative column) and `arxiv-2505.13763` (a full-access decoder ceiling — the other denominator a read-out can be missing).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 373): **A trained self-report needs a rival fine-tune rather than another instrument, and the rival is cheap enough to run at scale: let a *different* model answer the self-modeling question for a target, and if training on the foreign target transfers as well as training on the target's own behaviour, the task rewards general patterns rather than self-access.** This paper runs it on nine formats and three families and finds the advantage is *not uniform* — a stronger Qwen explainer can beat Llama on Llama's own labels, while the Qwen3-8B/GPT-OSS-20B pair does show an own-model gain on Flip-Rate — which is a weaker and more honest shape of the claim than `arxiv-2410.13787`'s bidirectional per-property asymmetry, and the two together bound what a fine-tuned explainer can be said to prove: capability is a live hypothesis in both, and only a design where the rival is *matched on capability* isolates access. Beside this sits the Bloom-to-benchmark transfer, which is the same test with the training format as the variable: harder multi-turn data helps two models and hurts the third. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13787` (the designated rival, per property) and `arxiv-2605.28591` (meta-knowledge, where the read-out is about a fact rather than a policy).
- Pattern 2026-11-18 (run 373): **A strict score silently mixes two capabilities, and the split is model-dependent: writing the score as parse-rate times quality-on-parseable-outputs and attributing the change with a two-factor Shapley decomposition gives 38% quality for GPT-OSS-20B, 45% for Llama-3.1-8B and 88% for Qwen3-8B, so on two of three models most of the headline post-training improvement is better JSON rather than better self-knowledge.** The same accounting explains the paper's most counterintuitive training result, where all three SFT recipes finish *below* the untrained base on the aggregate suite while all RL recipes finish above it: SFT collapses onto one cached completion shape, the other formats produce unparseable output, and strict aggregation charges worst-case for it — which is a generation-distribution failure reported as a capability regression. Two rules follow. (1) **When any of our evaluation formats is structured, report parse-rate separately and never let a refusal or a malformed answer be scored as a wrong belief** (`arxiv-2410.13787` merges exactly these two in its compliance rules and says so). (2) **Prefer the training arm that keeps the output distribution diverse** — if we ever fine-tune a generator against our own scorer, the held-out-format matrix, not the held-out split, is the control. Coreference `arxiv-2410.13032` (scheme-dependent verdicts, from the ablation side) and `arxiv-2606.10487` (a probe score that turned out to read the format).

- **Selection: `2410.13787` (*Looking Inward*), one of the two ids run 371 named as preferred.** Collision-checked before any fetch across `aether/` file names, `core/` and both INDEX files: `2410.13787`, `2503.15299` and `2506.18167` are **all absent** (three measured, zero collisions), so run 371's verified pool is intact and two ids remain unread. It earns a **3** on three measured grounds. (1) **The rival is the method**: introspection is defined as a correct self-report of a fact that a stronger model given the same training data cannot report, so the control is another model trained on the same outputs rather than another instrument fitted to the same activations — and the bidirectional pairs (Llama self 48.5 vs GPT-4o cross 31.8; GPT-4o self 49.4 vs Llama cross 36.6) make capability and hyperparameters unavailable as explanations. (2) **The calibration result is the entry's reusable measurement**: trained only on temperature-0 modes, the self-trained model reproduces the temperature-1 behaviour distribution on held-out data (MAD 23.0 -> 8.7, where cross-training moves it to 21.3) and is calibrated on the second and third most likely behaviours too, which says a self-report should be read as a distribution rather than as an answer. (3) **The negatives are load-bearing and cheap**: no self-advantage on predicting its own "are you sure?" flip (74.5% self against 76.5% cross), failure on every property needing a long internal rollout, and no generalisation to SAD overall (0.48 self against 0.49 format-matched baseline) except the near-duplicate Predict Tokens task (0.41 against 0.26).
