- Done 2026-11-17 (entry 272): `arxiv-2611.18163` — On the Limits of Sufficient Explanations (Klaus Weinbauer, Thomas Gärtner, Sagar Malhotra — ML Research Unit TU Wien; Peter F. Stadler — Leipzig / MPIMIS / Santa Fe Institute; arXiv:2611.18163v1, cs.LG, 2026-11-13, CC BY 4.0). Full text via HTML (82,708 clean chars, §§1–6 + Table 1 + theorem statements; appendices skimmed). **Substance:** a general formalism (instance space, classifier, *select relation* = an acyclic order encoding which sub-instances an explanation formalism may pick, e.g. node-induced vs edge-induced subgraphs vs substrings) over which they define sufficiency, then the central result: **a sufficient explainer exists iff there is no co-bound**, a co-bound being an instance from which a sub-instance can be selected that is also contained in a differently labelled instance — a joint property of classifier and select relation, checkable on a dataset with no model and no perturbation. Extensions: class-wise sufficiency given monotone complementary classes (and for purely existential positive first-order graph classifiers), an unbounded selection order under which every explainer is sufficient, all constant-size instance spaces admit one, a probabilistic-sufficiency upper bound for any explainer built from the trivial explainer's coverage and same-label rate, and deletion sufficiency as always achievable but vacuous on monotone classes (empty or single-node explanations pass). Three dataset statistics — co-bound fraction, inter-class relation ratio, minimum relabelling accuracy loss over connected components of the relation graph — on ten molecular, protein, peptide and sentiment datasets. **Results:** 9 of 10 datasets contain co-bounds and 7 in every class; SST-2 21% co-bounds / 24% inter-class relations / 44% relabelling cost, MUTAG 14% / 46% / 23%, ENZYMES 2.2% co-bounds yet **82% relabelling cost** (co-bound count alone understates), Mutagenicity 0.3% / 0.35% and ToxinPred2 0% / 0%; minimum local probabilistic-sufficiency bounds 18% (ENZYMES), 58% (PROTEINS), 73% (MUTAG), 100% (ToxinPred2); runtimes 14 s (MUTAG) to 5 h (PROTEINS).
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 273): **Whether an explanation of the "this part alone determines the output" form can exist is a property of the data and the granularity of the part, not of the method — and the obstruction is a single pair of instances, in distribution, detectable before anything is trained: 9 of 10 datasets here contain a sub-instance selectable from one instance and contained in a differently labelled one, and one such pair rules out sufficient sub-instance explainers for the whole task.** For our battery the consequence is a column we have never carried: any claim of the shape "feature subset / state component / sub-trace X suffices for the prediction" is bounded above by the containment structure of the inputs, so report the ceiling beside the achieved score, or the achieved score is unreadable — and the second statistic is the one that matters, since ENZYMES has 2.2% co-bounds and an 82% relabelling cost while Mutagenicity has 0.3% and 0.35%, so the naive count of violating items is not the measure; the cost of *removing* them is. The same arithmetic applies to the identical-answer requirement in the folder's stratification entries: an input that appears inside another with the opposite label makes the pair unstratifiable by construction, which is the co-bound arriving from the behaviour side. (arxiv-2611.18163, arxiv-2609.35686, arxiv-2611.19889)
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 273): **A deletion test on its own measures nothing on a monotone class: if removing parts can never add the property, then a single node — or the empty explanation — is deletion-sufficient for acyclicity or planarity, and the widest possible interval is examined while the test passes unconditionally.** The paper makes the general point that deletion sufficiency is strictly weaker than sufficiency precisely because it quantifies only over deletions from the observed instance rather than over all containing instances, and that it is the weaker notion every perturbation-based fidelity script actually computes. We report ablated and masked variants constantly; the rule this suggests is to state, per behaviour, whether the property is monotone in the ablation direction, and to refuse a deletion or zero-fill result as evidence of dependence when it is — because there the intervention cannot move the outcome in the direction that would falsify. The companion result is the consistency-versus-sufficiency gap made concrete: a sentiment explainer that highlights a comma for positive and a full stop for negative is perfectly consistent and carries nothing, so consistency is a necessary hygiene check and never evidence. (arxiv-2611.18163, arxiv-2611.19684, arxiv-2611.15082)
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 273): **The ceiling can bite even when the violating items are rare and the item-level count looks reassuring: here 2.2% of ENZYMES instances are co-bounds but making the task co-bound-free requires relabelling 82% of it, and the minimum achievable probabilistic sufficiency is 18% on that dataset against 73% on MUTAG whose co-bound fraction is seven times larger.** The mechanism is graph connectivity in the relation closure — co-bounds sit in connected components, and one misplaced label propagates a relabelling through everyone related to it — which is the same shape as a contamination or leakage audit where a handful of shared items link most of the dataset. Two habits: compute the statistic on the relation graph and not on the item list, and when a per-instance sufficiency score comes out low, check whether the instance sits at the centre of such a component before attributing the failure to the explainer. For our monitoring tables the usable form is a per-instance upper bound (the paper's `1 − coverage·(1 − same-label rate)` against the trivial whole-input explanation), since it needs no trained explainer and gives each row its own admissible maximum instead of one pooled figure. (arxiv-2611.18163, arxiv-2611.19499, arxiv-2611.03439)

- Done 2026-11-17 (entry 271): `arxiv-2611.17620` — Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit (Sabrina Tang — UC Irvine; Nikolai Vo — Toledo; Carson Murillo — UCSD; Chira Sukumarnpiti — Berkeley City College; Sarah Wilson — Google; arXiv:2611.17620v1, cs.AI, 2026-11-13, BiAlign workshop "Dynamic Alignment in Human-AI Coupled Systems", arXiv perpetual non-exclusive licence). Full text via HTML (18,216 clean chars, §§1–5 + references). **Substance:** persona vectors for sycophancy and hallucination taken from the cited pipeline unmodified, applied in three conditions per trait per model — fine-tuned base with no steering, **preventative** steering (vector added to the residual stream by a forward hook during the same fine-tune, removed before evaluation) and **inference-time** steering (vector subtracted from the untouched Instruct model) — one residual layer per model and trait (Qwen-7B layers 20/16, Llama-8B layer 16 for both, Qwen-14B 34/27 scaled by relative depth because no published choice covered it), coefficient swept coarsely, scored at every point on HarmBench attack success with the official classifier, StrongREJECT rubric scores from GPT-4o-mini and XSTest unsafe-prompt compliance from GPT-4, beside trait expression and coherence from the cited scoring pipeline and MMLU. **Results:** hallucination steering cuts refusal far more than hallucination — HarmBench ASR 61.0% → 22.0% (Llama-8B), 72.3% → 4.4% (Qwen-7B), 91.2% → 6.3% (Qwen-14B) while trait expression stays ≥70% everywhere and most of the shift lands at a coefficient where trait expression is still >96%; coherence flat or rising and MMLU within 2.1 points in every sweep; non-monotonic on Llama (ASR minimum 14.5%), and XSTest plateaus at ~25–30% (7B) and 37–43% (14B) instead of following HarmBench and StrongREJECT to zero; sycophancy steering suppresses its own trait harder (88.9% → 27.9% on Llama) but moves safety only a little, with the sign flipping between benchmarks in all three models (Llama ASR 8.2% → 11.9% while XSTest falls 8.5% → ~6.5%; Qwen-14B HarmBench unchanged at 48% while XSTest compliance rises 42% → 59%); and the no-vector fine-tune baseline already carries most of the damage (ASR 8% vs 61% on Llama, 20% vs 72% on Qwen-7B, 48% vs 91% on Qwen-14B for sycophancy vs hallucination data). Limits as stated: one run per point, coarse sweep, no intervals, scaled 14B layers, benchmarks that probe different things.
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 272): **The behaviour an intervention was designed to move can be the smaller part of what it moves, and the metric the intervention was validated on can be completely flat while that happens: preventative hallucination steering shifts attack success by 39–85 points on three models while reducing hallucination expression by well under a third, with MMLU inside 2.1 points and coherence unchanged across every sweep.** The direction is one vector at one layer; the only difference between the recommended condition and an unsteered fine-tune is that the vector was present while the weights formed. For our battery this makes the **unclaimed-behaviour panel a required column**, not an optional robustness check: any steering result should name the behaviours that were not the target and report them at the same coefficients, because a target-only evaluation here would have reported a clean success — the trait does drop, capability is preserved — and stopped exactly where the deployment damage begins. The second habit is to report the panel even when it improves, which the authors do: they say plainly that in their runs the entanglement mostly helped safety, and that the one case where it did not (Llama sycophancy) is enough to refute the neutrality claim. A side effect measured only in the convenient direction is not a side effect measurement. (arxiv-2611.17620, arxiv-2611.20441, arxiv-2611.07913)
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 272): **Three safety benchmarks disagree in sign inside all three models, so a safety claim drawn from one benchmark is a claim about that benchmark's attack distribution and nothing wider: on Llama sycophancy steering raises HarmBench attack success 46% relative while XSTest compliance falls, on Qwen-7B both harm benchmarks fall while XSTest rises, and on Qwen-14B HarmBench ends where it started while XSTest compliance climbs 42% → 59%.** The instructive structure is in the divergence itself — the two harm benchmarks cover optimised attack strings and converge on "steering helped", while XSTest, which asks whether the model *over*-refuses benign lookalikes and whether it complies with plainly unsafe everyday requests, plateaus at 25–43% and in two models moves the other way. So the panel needs benchmarks that pull in opposite directions by construction, not three copies of the same probe, and a sign flip across them should be reported as the finding rather than averaged into a net effect. What we take for our own monitor tables: report each behavioural outcome **separately and with its own baseline**, and never a pooled "safety score", because a pooled number here would have hidden the one condition under which the intervention made things worse. (arxiv-2611.17620, arxiv-2611.19216, arxiv-2611.03439)
- Pattern 2026-11-17 (run 272): **Steering applied during training and steering applied at inference are not the same experiment, and the difference shows up in the control arm: the no-vector fine-tune trained on hallucination data already sits at attack success 48% / 72% / 91% on the three models, far above the 8% / 20% / 48% of the sycophancy-trained twin, so the recommended "preventative" condition works partly by undoing damage its own training data did.** That is a general hazard for any intervention applied inside a fine-tune: the arm everyone compares against is the steered one, and the more informative baseline is the unsteered fine-tune on the same data, which nobody reports. Two consequences. Any claim of the form "training with this intervention preserves X" needs the no-intervention fine-tune on identical data as its floor, and the interesting quantity is the gap between the two, not the absolute. And the two application routes cannot be compared at matched trait expression here — inference-time steering on the original Instruct model never reaches the fine-tuned model's trait range — which is the folder's recurring lesson in a new place: **if the two arms cannot be matched on the mediating quantity, the comparison is descriptive and must be labelled so**, rather than read as "training-time is better than inference-time". (arxiv-2611.17620, arxiv-2611.19499, arxiv-2611.15082)

Margolin, single author; arXiv:2611.17515v1, cs.AI, 2026-11-12, arXiv perpetual non-exclusive licence; working manuscript dated 2026-10-24, "evaluation in progress"). Full text via HTML (99,300 clean chars, §§1–8 + limitations + references); Tables 1–27 quoted as cells, Figures 1–9 via captions. **Substance:** Gemma 3 12B plays Deutsche Bank's silver trader in a simulation built from the London silver-fixing transcripts (46 dated chats 2007–2013, 12 trading days on one-minute prices, ~40k tokens/episode), with UBS issuing identical push requests in five wordings (neutral, loss, gain, blame, credit) and "going along" scored from the agent's own orders. 260 episodes + 30 controls over six levers (counterparty framing, management memos, inherited history, second-bank endorsement, combinations), episode-level permutation tests, Holm correction, request-level LPM and GEE logit; then Phase II replays the 1,740 saved moments at bfloat16 and reads (a) an order-direction probability after a fixed neutral line, (b) a direct "is this manipulation Yes/No" probability, (c) Gemma Scope 2 16k SAEs at layers 12/24/31/41, (d) frame, document, going-along and holding directions injected at swept layers and sustained at layer 22 through whole episodes with two blind graders. **Results:** loss 5% → 25% (p = 0.007), blame → 33% (p = 0.0003), credit → 18%, gain 10% (n.s.), harm $0.76M → $2.81M; management memos instead raised pre-chat volume 10–19× without raising participation; endorsement doubled only credit (18% → 40%, Holm p = 0.027); manipulation recognition halved (26.8% → 11.6–14.6%) and did not predict trades, while unprompted naming never co-occurred with going along (0/55 vs 52/245); history-framed beats request-framed 40.7% vs 18.3%; the registered frame-direction steering inverted (+6.4 / −9.2 points the wrong way) while a behaviour-built layer-24 direction worked (+14.0 / −6.0); whole-episode injections cross over against the words (loss/blame states refuse 60/60, gain state 33% going along); one shared direct request makes *every* state sell through the stop 9–10/10 vs 1/10 without; state monitor AUC 0.93 pooled, 0.83 within-date against 0.74; defence push 51% → 45% and 39% → 29%, with the readout going silent after the push while two states still complied.
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 271): **A state can be persistent, dose-responsive and cleanly readable along one direction and still have that direction be the wrong lever — here the loss-frame direction is measurable at layer 12 on every trading day for months after participation has stopped (gaps 0.35–1.47, p ≤ 0.01), yet adding it at the pre-registered layer lowered going along by 6.4 points and subtracting it raised it by 9.2, both the reverse of the registered prediction, while a direction built from the agents' own decisions at layer 24 moved the outcome the expected way (+14.0 / −6.0).** That is the folder's sharpest separation between *what carries a stimulus* and *what moves a decision*, and it puts a hard rule on our battery: separability, persistence and dose-response are properties of the stimulus contrast, and none of them is evidence that the direction is causal. The cheap fix is a change of contrast — build intervention directions from the behaviour split (who did the thing versus who did not) rather than from the input split (which words were said) — and the cheaper diagnostic is the angle: the two constructions land in different subspaces here, with management's and UBS's loss states aligned early (cosine 0.59 at layer 12 against 0.80 between UBS's own split halves) and pointing apart by the last layer (−0.52), which is visible before any behavioural run. (arxiv-2611.17515, arxiv-2611.20371, arxiv-2611.20441)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 271): **In a long-horizon agent the same internal state does opposite things at one moment and over an episode, and the two-condition replay shows why: at a single shared request every injected emotional state raised stop-triggering sales (9–10 of 10 replies, against 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random push), while sustained through whole episodes the loss and blame states produced cascades of refusals (all 60 requests) that then entered the agent's own context and did the work.** The factorial behind it needs no new sampling — swap only the current message with the history held fixed, then swap the history with the message neutral — and here it attributes nearly everything to the accumulated conversation (40.7% against 18.3%, with framing the latest request alone reaching only 24.6–29.7%). For us this is both a method and a warning: a state's behavioural effect is a function of what it says next and what has already been said, so "this direction raises behaviour X by N points" is only meaningful with the horizon and the context stated, and a single-turn steering result should never be carried into a long-horizon agent pipeline without the sustained arm. The companion measurement is that injecting a state and re-reading the same probe is not a check: after a defence push the readout went from flagging all four states to flagging none while two of them still sold through the stop, so the intervention arm's behaviour, not the post-intervention score, is the outcome. (arxiv-2611.17515, arxiv-2611.19216, arxiv-2611.15082)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 271): **The monitor that beats reading words is a state readout, and the size of the win depends entirely on the stratum you read it in: pooled AUC 0.93 collapses to 0.83 once you compare only requests from the same date (baseline 0.74), because framing, date and earlier compliance already score 0.90 on their own — and the words in this agent are nearly silent, with blind labels of its chat agreement present on only 7% of the decisions where it actually went along.** Two design consequences. First, a probe's headline AUC on a repeated-measures dataset is mostly a calendar: the confounds a monitor must be shown to beat are the request identity, the date and the agent's own earlier behaviour, and within-stratum scoring is the cheapest way to expose that. Second, the verbal signal that *does* track behaviour is unprompted naming of the misconduct (never present in the 55 replies where the agent went along, present in 21% of the 245 where it declined), which means a self-report monitor improves exactly where the agent is failing and a labelled canary of the thing the self-report is meant to catch is the cheapest guard. The complementary reading is that this paper's framing never touched the requested action at all — the same instruction was simply described in terms of loss, blame or a peer's endorsement — so any compliance filter that inspects only what is being asked is looking one level below the mechanism. (arxiv-2611.17515, arxiv-2611.19216, arxiv-2611.07913)

- Done 2026-11-16 (entry 269): `arxiv-2611.20441` — Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment (Koki Itai, Jun Hirako, Hiroaki Yamagiwa — SB Intuitions Corp.; arXiv:2611.20441v1, 2026-11-16, cs.CL, arXiv perpetual non-exclusive licence). Full text via HTML (111,398 clean chars, §§1–8 + Limitations + Appendices A–J); Table 1 quoted as cells, Figures 2–19 via captions. **Substance:** three abstention "perspectives" — query ambiguity (Q), model-knowledge limits (MK), human-values misalignment (HV) — each given its own mean-difference direction over the residual stream, with the dataset construction as the manipulated variable: **slot-flipped** counterfactual pairs (an LLM templates each query so the abstention-inducing element is one slot, then fills it with a same-type opposite-polarity phrase, so the two members differ nowhere else: qualifier or polysemous topic for Q, real vs fictional entity of matched type for MK, action+object from AdvBench vs Alpaca for HV) against the classical **source-independent** construction on independently sourced corpora; 1,199 / 767 / 377 pairs after rule filtering and LLM verification, **64 pairs per direction**, all layers 1–35 in Qwen3-4B (36 layers, width 2560, TransformerLens resid_pre at the final token) plus Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; additive steering x' = x + m·r̂ at every layer, |m| ∈ {2,4,8,16,32} for Qwen and {0.25,0.5,1,2,4,8} for Llama (chosen because unnormalised norms differ by ~10×), both signs, thinking and non-thinking modes; evaluated on 128 held-out pairs per perspective, three generations per query, gpt-oss-120b judge at temperature 0; controls: random unit directions (near-orthogonal at 0 ± 0.02), a >10% degeneration filter, cross-perspective steering, cosine geometry and Fisher discriminant ratio. **Results:** directions exist for all three and steer in the expected sign, effects concentrated in middle layers (~17–23); slot-flipped beats source-independent for every perspective, both signs and both modes, and acts at smaller |m|; at |m| = 32 over 10% of Qwen responses degenerate into repetition; thinking vs non-thinking layer trends correlate 0.94 (AR) and 0.93 (OAR); HV AR is 1.0 with no intervention so addition has no headroom; effective-layer cosines +0.163 (Q20–MK19), +0.190 (MK19–HV17), +0.092 (Q20–HV17); Fisher ratio peaks 2.65 (HV, layer 21) and 1.15 (MK, layer 23) but never rises for Q; cross-perspective effects asymmetric — steering Q moves MK's AR but not HV's, steering MK or HV moves both — and qualitatively harmful, with subtraction on a foreign perspective fabricating answers to fictional-entity questions; 510 GPU hours of generation plus 800 GPU hours of judging.
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 270): **The construction of the contrast set is a free parameter that nobody reports, and it is worth more than the direction itself here: the same model, layer sweep, injection budget and held-out pairs yield a direction that steers across all three perspectives from slot-flipped pairs and a visibly weaker one from the classical corpus-difference construction.** The mechanism is the one the folder keeps meeting from the other side — a mean difference vector is an average over everything that differs between the two sets, so independently sourced corpora donate topic, register, length and template to the vector alongside the property, and the dilution is invisible in any evaluation that measures the direction's own training distribution. Our own probes are built this way by default and the fix costs a templating pass: take a property we already probe for, rewrite each example so the property sits in one slot, fill that slot from a same-type pool of the opposite polarity, and compare the two constructions **on identical held-out items with the intervention metric as judge**. Two reporting habits come with it: state the pair count (64 here, against 128 for Arditi et al.'s refusal direction), and say whether the pairing is slot-matched or corpus-matched, since "our direction has AUROC 0.97" is compatible with both and the causal effect is not. (arxiv-2611.20441, arxiv-2611.19499, arxiv-2611.20371)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 270): **Class separability and causal efficacy dissociate inside a single paper and in the same model: for query ambiguity the Fisher discriminant ratio between the two polarities never rises above its baseline in any layer, yet steering along that direction still moves abstention there, while for knowledge limits and human values the separation peaks (1.15 at layer 23, 2.65 at layer 21) coincide with where steering works.** The authors' explanation is available and worth keeping — MK and HV slots carry a *semantic* property (a fictional entity, a harmful action) of the kind that becomes linearly decodable mid-stack, whereas the Q manipulation removes a qualifier, which is a property of completeness rather than of any content word. For us the two readings point in opposite directions and both are usable: a high Fisher ratio is neither necessary (Q steers with none) nor sufficient (the folder's decoding-versus-steering entries) for a direction to be causal, so neither should ever be reported as a stand-in for the intervention arm. The design lesson is that the quantity to match across conditions is the *effect at a fixed intervention budget*, not any pre-intervention statistic, and that a null on separability must not be written down as a null on the representation. (arxiv-2611.20441, arxiv-2611.20371, arxiv-2611.19176)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 270): **A one-concept intervention leaks into the behaviours it shares a component with, and the leak is asymmetric — steering query ambiguity moves the knowledge-limit rate but leaves the safety refusal untouched, while steering knowledge limits or human values moves both of the others — with the cosines small enough (+0.09 to +0.19) that nobody computing the vectors would have predicted which way the leak runs.** The cosine ordering does track it (the MK–HV pair is the most similar at 0.190 and the most mutually influential) but it does not give magnitudes, so geometry is a hint and not a forecast. The consequence for any dashboard built on a single steering vector is that the side effects are not symmetric noise around the target but a structured spill into adjacent behaviours, and here they are semantically harmful rather than merely off-target: subtracting the safety direction on a knowledge-limit question makes the model invent a nonexistent actress, and subtracting the ambiguity direction makes it invent a newspaper editor. Two habits for our battery. Sweep the direction of another concept as an arm whenever we steer, on the same items, because a control direction that shares a component is a different control from a random one and both are needed. And when a behaviour has several causes, compute a direction per cause rather than one pooled "the model declines" vector — the pooled vector is a linear combination whose largest component will dominate every intervention it is used for. (arxiv-2611.20441, arxiv-2611.17481, arxiv-2611.07913)

- Done 2026-11-16 (entry 268): `arxiv-2611.20371` — Pretty Linear Liars: Unregularized Probes Favor Intervention-Unfaithful Features (Karl Vilhelmsson Emneby, Julian Yocum, Cameron Allen — Center for Human-Compatible AI, UC Berkeley; arXiv:2611.20371v1, 2026-11-16, cs.LG, CC BY 4.0; workshop paper under the title "Interpretability as a Science"). Full text via HTML (41,402 clean chars, §§1–6 + Appendices A–D + references); Table 1 quoted as cells, Figures 1–9 via captions and the sentences that state their values. **Substance:** three ways of extracting a direction for one target on one set of activations — OLS, ridge swept over a logarithmic grid of penalties, and intervention-trained DAS as the causal reference — on the exhaustive Mess3 HMM (3-state, 4-layer width-64 transformer, 3-d belief on a 2-simplex, every sequence of length 1–8) and on Llama-2-7B birth-year probing (8,000 Wikidata prompts, 1900–1999, 4,096-d residual at layer 8, expected decade over ten digit tokens); closed-form per-principal-component weight (covariance over variance plus penalty over n) with a corollary that OLS weights on target-uncorrelated quiet directions scale as the target's spread over the direction's spread times root n and diverge as variance goes to zero; two interventions held to values the model exhibits (probe-mediated simplex steering over a 496-point target grid, and natural-magnitude base→source interchange along the candidate direction); mass-by-operativity read off the PC decomposition, plus a restricted-DAS search inside the OLS span and a split-half covariance estimate. **Results:** OLS decodes best and steers not at all — HMM probe loss 9.46e-5 against 3.99e-3 (ridge) and 3.21e-3 (DAS) with intervention loss 2.14e-1 against 1.95e-3 / 1.88e-3, at 89.8° from DAS; Llama probe loss 6.71e-2 against 2.51e-1 / 6.89e-1 with intervention loss 1.37e1 (equal to not intervening) against 7.07e0 / 6.42e0, at 84.7° against 26.3°; variance along the fitted direction 1.16e-8 → 5.10e0 and 2.10e-2 → 3.83e0; probe loss monotone in the penalty while intervention loss has an interior minimum; one HMM component at variance 1e-18 holds 0.915 of OLS mass, the heaviest Llama components covering 95% of ridge mass carry ~31% of OLS mass, restricted DAS finds nothing operative in the OLS span on either testbed, and 3,976 of 4,096 Llama layer-8 PCs sit within three standard errors of zero covariance; held-out decoding flags OLS on Llama (0.05 → 0.38, ridge 0.27 → 0.28) but not on the HMM (4.3e-4 held out, still inert).
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 269): **Probe accuracy and probe direction are chosen by the same fit, and the loss everyone reports is the one the failure mode is invisible in — here OLS achieves the lowest probe loss and the highest intervention loss on both testbeds (HMM 9.46e-5 against 2.14e-1, Llama 6.71e-2 against 1.37e1, equal to not intervening at all), while a ridge probe whose penalty was picked by the intervention test sits within 26–29° of the intervention-trained DAS direction against OLS's 85–90°.** The mechanism is one line and worth keeping in front of us: in the principal-component basis each direction's weight is its covariance with the target over its own variance, so a quiet direction with noise-scale covariance gets a weight that grows as its variance shrinks, and regularization simply puts a floor under the denominator. Two habits for our battery. Fit probes with a **penalty sweep selected on the intervention metric**, not on held-out decoding — the fit is closed-form and the sweep costs one solve per penalty, so the only new expense is the intervention arm we already run. And report **variance along the fitted direction** and the **share of probe mass on low-operativity components** beside accuracy, because here those two numbers, not the accuracy, separate a perfect decoder from a usable one. The sharpest warning is that held-out decoding caught the failure on Llama and completely missed it on the exhaustive HMM, so "our probe generalizes" is not evidence that the direction is the one the model uses. (arxiv-2611.20371, arxiv-2610.41445, arxiv-2611.19499)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 269): **The folder's standing null for a per-unit causal claim — "the effect is spread across many individually inert pieces" — now has a working control: confine an intervention-trained method to the span of the components a decodability-trained method selects, and ask whether any operative direction lives there; here DAS restricted to the 100 heaviest-weight OLS components on Llama-2-7B (34.8% of OLS mass) and the 7 heaviest on the HMM (over 99.9% of mass) finds nothing causally operative on either testbed.** That closes a loophole our own ablations are exposed to, since a mass-weighted heat map is a claim about individual units and a linear combination of inert units is not obliged to be inert. The companion read is the mass-by-operativity picture, which is cheap and diagnostic: a single HMM component with variance 1e-18 carries 0.915 of the OLS probe's mass, and on Llama the components that cover 95% of the ridge probe's mass carry only about 31% of the OLS probe's, the rest being a long tail of near-zero-operativity components — the signature of an unregularized fit is a heavy tail of weight on quiet directions, not a large weight on any one of them. Third reusable piece: the **split-half covariance estimate against its own sampling-error band** (one half of the prompts fixes the principal directions, the other supplies variance and covariance; 3,976 of 4,096 Llama PCs land inside three standard errors of zero) is the cheapest available sentence of the form "this direction carries noise rather than signal", and it needs no retraining. (arxiv-2611.20371, arxiv-2611.19176, arxiv-2611.16018)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 269): **A direction can be moved from dead to live by a change that touches nothing but the penalty — 55 to 60 degrees of rotation, an intervention loss two orders of magnitude on the HMM and roughly halved on Llama — and the resulting direction is *not* simply the loudest one: the intervention-optimal Llama direction has variance 3.83 and largely ignores the top principal component at variance 25,570, some 6,700 times larger, while a maximally regularized fit converges to the covariance direction and therefore carries no variance preference at all.** This is the anti-story to the usual "regularize so the probe generalizes" line, and it makes three columns standard for any ridge we fit: the penalty actually used, the variance along the recovered direction, and its angle to a causally fitted reference (DAS or a difference-of-means direction checked by interchange). The design notes worth importing are the conservative intervention protocols — belief shifts kept inside the simplex and interchanges that copy values the *source prompt actually exhibits* — which sidestep the standing objection that out-of-distribution patching activates pathways the model never uses, at the cost of making the published effects a lower bound; and the paper's own scope honesty, that its theory is a negative result (OLS is prone to spurious quiet directions) and its positive claim is two testbeds wide, one model, one layer, one continuous target, with the logistic version named as future work — which matters to us because most of our own probes are logistic and none of this transfers for free. (arxiv-2611.20371, arxiv-2611.17481, arxiv-2611.07913)

Full text via HTML (44,712 clean chars, §§I–VII + references); Tables I, III, IV quoted as cells, Table II in relative terms only, Tables V and VI prose-only, Figures 1–7 via captions. **Substance:** three frozen pretrained planners (Alpamayo 1.5 flow matching / 10 NFE / 36 expert layers / 73,728-d features; ReCogDrive-IL stochastic DDIM / 5 NFE / 4,096; HDP DPM-Solver++ / 11 NFE / 8,192), features taken from the *first denoiser evaluation's action tokens* with within-scene centring of features and target, ridge readers grouped by clip or driving log, swept over evaluation index and layer, compared against initial-noise and completed-trajectory readers, a ground-truth first-step preview and a final oracle, with MLP capacity checks, label shuffles within scene, random projection to 2,048 dims and 5%-training arms; deployed as early top-1 selection and validated in open loop, in NFE and measured DGX-Spark latency, and closed loop on NavSafe-3 (280 scenarios) and AlpaSim (100 scenes × 3 runs). **Results:** 17.8% / 13.4% ADE below random at 1cam/4cam, +1.03 / +0.50 PDM on the two NAVSIM planners, all four first-evaluation; initial-noise ridge near chance on ranking while state readers reach 64.7% / 59.2% pairwise; waiting for the final evaluation gives no detectable gain for the deterministic samplers and 0.36 PDM only for the stochastic one (0.06 with later noise disabled); selection coexists with 48.7% / 55.6% pairwise accuracy on NAVSIM and state readers beat the privileged first-step preview in 3 of 4 configurations; shuffled labels go below random, projection and 5% data survive; 17 NFE against 80, latency 4.09 → 2.30 s and 8.24 → 4.04 s, closed loop 49.90 → 50.35 driving score and +0.0516 / +0.0317 gated score with slightly higher collision rate.
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 268): **Ranking accuracy and selection gain are different quantities and can point in opposite directions: a reader that orders only 48.7% of eligible candidate pairs correctly — a coin flip with 945,782 pairs behind it — still beats random selection by a point of PDM, while a reader whose pairwise accuracy rises at an intermediate denoising step shows no matching improvement in the quality of the candidate it picks.** The reason is arithmetic and general: pairwise accuracy weights every eligible pair equally, so a swap between two near-identical candidates costs exactly what a swap between the best and the worst costs, and a reader that is confident only about large quality gaps can select well while ordering most pairs wrongly. Our own tables are exposed on the same flank, since AUROC is a pairwise statistic and we routinely read it as "the probe knows", then expect the knowledge to survive a decision. Two habits. Wherever a readout is used to *choose* rather than to *report*, print the chosen item's quality against a random-choice baseline and an oracle beside the ranking statistic, because the two are not monotone in each other. And when a ranking statistic improves without the decision improving, treat that as a property of the metric's weighting rather than as noise or a bug. (arxiv-2611.19684, arxiv-2611.15082, arxiv-2611.03439)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 268): **A within-context probe — subtract the candidate-set mean from both the features and the target, then predict relative, not absolute, quality — is the cheapest way to turn a global prediction into the local comparison an intervention actually needs, and it is the only reader here that works: absolute-metric readers of the same representations are beaten by ridge failing outright on completed trajectories (ADE 4.066 versus 3.224 for the MLP).** The construction costs nothing and buys three things at once: the reader cannot score a scene as hard or easy and so cannot explain a candidate by its scene, the labels are balanced by construction so a null is a coin, and the estimand matches what a selector or a steering decision asks. The capacity result is the one to carry with it — representation and reader have to be chosen together, since on internal state a linear reader is as good as an 18.9 M-parameter MLP, while on initial noise and on raw trajectory coordinates only the MLP recovers anything, so "our probe is nonlinear" and "our probe is linear" are claims about the pair, not about the state. The companion control is the initial-noise reader: it separates information that exists before the model has done any work from information the forward pass created, and here it is the control that makes the 64.7% figure mean something. (arxiv-2611.19684, arxiv-2611.10620, arxiv-2611.19216)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 268): **A privileged bound cheaper than the oracle is worth building, and here it fails in an instructive direction: a selector allowed to read the *ground-truth* quality of the first-step decoded trajectory is beaten by the state reader in three of four configurations, because candidate quality is not monotone as denoising proceeds and the preview is a bad proxy for the finished article.** So "the model already knows, it just has not finished computing" is not a safe assumption — the informative object is the internal state, not the current output, which is the same dissociation the folder has recorded between what a state carries and what the model's own head emits. Two further design notes. The early-select-then-complete form is an intervention that changes cost rather than behaviour, which makes it uniquely easy to validate: NFE 17 against 80 and latency 4.09 → 2.30 s are claims no counterfactual can argue with, while the closed-loop numbers were mixed in the honest way (gated score up, collision rate slightly up) and were left mixed in the entry. And a cheap readout still needs the 5%-data arm, which cost a few minutes here and moved the honest claim from "learnable" to "learnable from 120 scenes". (arxiv-2611.19684, arxiv-2611.18114, arxiv-2611.07913)

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 267): **A ranking can be plausible, faithful on a frozen model, and still point away from the best feature subset, and the folder now has the numbers on one scale: top-5 bands retrain to 0.8893 mIoU against bottom-5 at 0.9047 and random-5 at 0.9021, while deletion AUC in the same ranked order is 0.074 against 0.245 for a random order — so the ordering that a masking test calls excellent identifies the worst of 23 retrained subsets.** The structural reason is the one our own tables are exposed to: masking a frozen model measures that model's response to a counterfactual input, and in an input space with correlated units a substituted unit costs little while contributing nothing, so the ranking records which member of a redundant group this particular solution happened to lean on. Two habits for the battery. Any "these units carry the task" claim built on attribution, probing or masking should carry a **top-k versus bottom-k retrain** (or bottom-k versus random-k, which is the baseline that makes the reversal legible) and state plainly when it does not, because none of the cheaper checks can stand in for it. And when retraining is impossible, at minimum say that the claim is about the checkpoint explained and not about the task — this paper's own framing, "the ranking describes the solution this model happened to find", is the sentence to reuse. (arxiv-2611.19889, arxiv-2611.16018, arxiv-2611.03439)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 267): **Two training runs that share code, seed and configuration and agree to four decimal places in accuracy can produce opposite selection verdicts, and the difference here is one band: Run A's top-5 retrains 0.0155 *below* its bottom-5 (Holm p = 0.048) while Run B's, identical except that B05 replaces B12 in the top five, retrains 0.0106 *above* its bottom-5 (p = 0.010, higher on every seed).** Across four models only three bands survive in every Shapley top five, and the global order agrees loosely (ρ 0.92) precisely where practitioners do not look. This is the folder's sharpest instance of run-to-run underspecification at the level of an *explanation* rather than an output, and it makes one design demand on anything we publish: report the ranking from more than one training run and check the items that cross the decision boundary, since an aggregate correlation hides exactly the swap that carries the conclusion. Two cheap companions come with it — report the ranking under two aggregations (signed versus magnitude averaging here moves the top band from B07 to B08 and reverses the top-versus-bottom verdict too), and treat GPU nondeterminism as a legitimate second run rather than noise to be eliminated, because it is the cheapest available sampler of the set of equally accurate solutions. (arxiv-2611.19889, arxiv-2611.19216, arxiv-2611.15082)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 267): **Effective dimensionality of the unit axis is one line of arithmetic, needs no labels and no trained model, and it tells you before any experiment that fine-grained rankings will not be identifiable: across all 252 five-band subsets of a ten-band sensor the participation ratio stays between 1.35 and 2.62 against a ceiling of 5, three principal components carry 98.4% of the variance, and a PCA-10 model matches the raw-band model at 0.9144 versus 0.9131.** Two lessons make it usable rather than decorative. It is a warning light and not a selection criterion, since no redundancy measure here predicted which subset retrains best (|ρ| ≤ 0.30 over 23 retrained subsets) and the ones that looked informative to a *linear* classifier pointed at the opposite subset. And the redundancy estimate must be taken on the same units the claim is about, because the four nonlinear and task-probe variants all agreed that the bands are at least as redundant as the linear measures suggested, while the pixel classifier — a different learner — preferred precisely the subset the segmentation model disliked: band necessity is learner-relative, which is another way of saying our readouts are about one model. For our pipeline, print a participation ratio on the correlation matrix of whatever unit axis we rank (neurons, features, SAE latents) beside any top-k claim, and read a PR far below k as a statement that many subsets would do rather than that the top one is special. (arxiv-2611.19889, arxiv-2611.19477, arxiv-2611.10620)

Full text via HTML (177,840 clean chars, §§1–6 + Appendices A–H in part); Tables 1–3, 27, 28, 31 quoted as cells. **Substance:** modular addition mod 31 (two-hidden-layer width-256 ReLU MLP, 40% of pairs held out, full batch) with the Fourier algorithm verified independently for every rule that groks (input frequencies used, trigonometric fit of the logits, cross-seed and cross-rule agreement) so only implementation can vary; concentration measured as the **participation ratio of outgoing weight norms** (n·PR = effective neuron count) with activation-weighted and ablation participation as corroborating measures; **credit equalization** — per-neuron rescaling of the incoming-weight gradient magnitude toward the layer mean at strength β, direction preserved, before Adam — plus a group-size sweep, eight optimizers, DFC, a "ratio held" falsification arm, three non-gradient-term settings (coupled decay, Adam's ε, decayed per-neuron gain), reproductions on subtraction/multiplication/S₅/sparse parity/a wide-MLP transformer, and a 30M-parameter TinyStories GPT-2 as a scale test; consequences measured by random, norm-ranked and greedy deletion, magnitude and greedy pruning, and adaptation to subtraction, multiplication and readout-only targets. **Results:** β 0 → 1 moves participation 0.60 → 0.99 (154 → 254 of 256 effective neurons, ~84 nearly unused) at 0.998 → 0.976 test accuracy with loss, margin and parameter norm within a few percent; redistribution also works **after** grokking (>0.95 within 300 epochs, accuracy above 0.98, reference-rule control stays 0.60); groups of ≥8 sharing one factor stay at 0.60, fours reach 0.70, pairs 0.75, singles 0.99; only Nero (0.986) and DFC distribute among nine alternatives; rescaling only the non-gradient term reproduces it (0.993/0.981/0.997) while holding the ratio keeps concentration (0.574/0.818/0.343); distributed circuits tolerate deletion (random 0.770 vs 0.674, norm-ranked 0.581 vs 0.332, 61 vs 23 greedy removals) while concentrated circuits prune further (62% vs 20%) and adapt to subtraction in 640 vs 1540 epochs against 1410 from scratch, about two-thirds of that gap coming from the nearly unused neurons; at scale, per-unit decay balance cuts unused MLP units 23.9% → 1.3% with lower validation loss in every seed.
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 266): **A circuit-size number is a property of the training rule before it is a property of the task, and the folder now has this as a controlled dose-response: the same Fourier algorithm is implemented by 154 or by 254 of 256 neurons depending only on how per-neuron credit is scaled before the optimizer, at two points of test accuracy and with training loss, margin and parameter norm within a few percent.** The mechanism is one inequality — a neuron survives while its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update — and it is the sharpest reminder yet that every "N features/neurons/heads implement this" figure we publish is conditional on an optimizer setting nobody reports. Three habits for our battery. Name, for any structural claim about a checkpoint, the optimizer and *where* weight decay enters the update, since coupled L2, Adam's ε and a decayed per-unit gain are the same failure arriving by three routes. Report a spread-across-units statistic (participation ratio on outgoing norms is weight-only, monotone under a controlled intervention and cheap) beside whatever accuracy we credit to a component, because the two move independently. And never conclude "the task needs a sparse circuit" from one training recipe: here the concentrated circuit, the pruning-extracted circuit and the distributed one all compute the same function. (arxiv-2611.19477, arxiv-2611.15082, arxiv-2611.01493)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 266): **Interventions have to be applied at the granularity of the unit that carries the effect, and this paper's group-size sweep is the cleanest demonstration in the folder: normalizing credit per *neuron* distributes the circuit to 0.99, but one shared factor per group of eight leaves it at 0.60 — indistinguishable from doing nothing — with fours at 0.70 and pairs at 0.75.** The arithmetic is explicit: equalizing group means preserves every within-group ratio, so a neuron that received twice its neighbour's credit still does, and the differences that cause the concentration survive training. The consequence for us is that coarse averaging is not a weak version of a per-unit intervention, it is a different experiment, and any pooling step in our own pipeline — averaging gradients over a block, masking by head instead of by neuron, regularising at layer scale — should be checked against the per-unit version before a null is reported. The companion controls show how easy the confusion is: Lion and Adam-mini both give every neuron an update of the same norm and still leave the circuit concentrated at 0.586/0.594, because they rescale the decay along with the gradient and so hold fixed the ratio that matters — equalizing the wrong quantity looks like a correct intervention and buys nothing. (arxiv-2611.19477, arxiv-2611.19248, arxiv-2611.06001)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 266): **Spare capacity is a structural cost that shows up as a benefit: the ~84 nearly-unused neurons of the concentrated circuit cost nothing to delete (62% of the layer can go before test accuracy falls below 0.9, against 20% for the distributed circuit) and are exactly what makes it adapt about 2.4× faster to a related operation — 640 epochs to subtraction against 1540 distributed and 1410 from scratch, with removing those neurons from the source costing two-thirds of the gain.** Two things make this usable rather than anecdotal. The trade reverses cleanly under the deletion axis (random tolerance 0.674 vs 0.770, norm-ranked 0.332 vs 0.581, 23 vs 61 greedy removals), so concentration is a bet on compressibility and reuse against fault tolerance rather than simply better or worse. And the adaptation advantage **disappears for multiplication** (1800–2020 epochs, worse than 1200 from scratch) because that task does not share addition's Fourier frequencies, which is the control that keeps the claim about mechanism rather than about pretraining in general. For a predictive model this is a column worth predicting explicitly — how much of a layer is idle and whether a new task would recruit it — since an input-output model cannot make that prediction and a neuron-level one can. The structural read-out agrees across scales: in the 30M transformer most dead MLP units die in the first two blocks, outgoing column first. (arxiv-2611.19477, arxiv-2611.18114, arxiv-2611.10620)

(Afshin Sadeghi, Daniel Becker — AI Assurance and Assessments, Fraunhofer IAIS, Sankt-Augustin; arXiv:2611.19499v1, 2026-11-14, cs.CL, CC BY 4.0). Full text via HTML (149,234 clean chars, §§1–6 + Appendices A, B, E, F, G, H, M, N in part); Tables 1–4 quoted as cells, Figures 2–4 via captions only. **Substance:** a one-parameter family of directions w_λ ∝ (Σ_W + λI)⁻¹Δμ in units of τ = tr(Σ_W)/d, spanning the regularised discriminant (small λ) and the mean difference (large λ, up to scale the CAA/refusal direction); 13 grid points half a decade apart plus Δμ, computed in closed form on a 50% estimation split and evaluated on two held-out quarters; probing scored by held-out AUROC, additive steering (h + a‖h‖w from the last token) scored by answer-margin, word-log-odds or outcome change and **read at a common budget κ₀ of mean next-token KL on 200 neutral WikiText-2 sentences**, interpolated in √K between bracketing strengths; pre-registered plateau rule (every grid point within one standard error of the best), H1b on a *second* held-out split, H1c with ρ ≥ 0.8 / ρ < 0.5 fixed in advance; three instruction-tuned models (LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-3-12B) at one layer each, TruthfulQA + 2,000 Yelp reviews + 4,000 PopQA; six ordered cross-model pairs carried under the probe law (transpose of the reverse affine map) and the steering law (forward map), with an orthogonal-Procrustes control; matched-text, ten-depth layer-sweep and gated-rotation arms. **Results:** probe peak at λ = τ (AUROC 0.96–0.98) against 0.60–0.89 at Δμ, steering plateau at 10τ–316τ, separation in 6/6 main cases, 59/60 layer cells, 4/4 rotation cases and both matched-text arms; truthfulness best probe steers at only 0.21–0.64 of Δμ and no direction beats Δμ by the required 10% (largest 9.6%, Qwen) so H1b fails 3/3, sentiment 0.99–1.11 with a 27–56% gain on the second split so H1b holds 3/3 but the gain largely disappears under matched texts; probe-end cosine with Δμ 0.25–0.46 and only 1.3–1.5× the push at equal budget; carried probes keep 81–91% of above-chance AUROC in all 12 pairs (65–79% on d′), carried Δμ 44–93% of the steering effect and lower in 11/12, yet the pre-registered classification leaves 9 pairs inconclusive; two pairs into Gemma have mapped Δμ orthogonal to Gemma's own (cosine −0.17, −0.02) and no closer than a permuted-label null while still steering at 0.72/0.70; PopQA abstention +44/+30/+18 pp on uncertain versus +5/+4/+2 on confident errors, random direction at the same K +7/+9/+1, probe gate passes in Qwen only (entropy gate in LLaMA only), reachable-error correction 3–11% against 6–9% random.
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 265): **The folder's oldest default — read a concept with a linear probe, then steer with the same vector — is now measured rather than assumed, and the measurement is a scalar trajectory: along (Σ_W + λI)⁻¹Δμ, detection peaks where the regulariser equals the mean within-class variance (AUROC 0.96–0.98) while change peeks out at 10τ–316τ, and the mean difference that everyone steers with is the *worst* probe of the three (0.60–0.89).** The reason is available in closed form and worth internalising, because it tells us when to expect the gap: a linear probe's implied activation pattern is Σ_h w, which for the discriminant is proportional to Δμ, so the filter and the displacement are different objects whenever within-class spread is large along the discriminating axis — and the filter end steers weakly only because its cosine with Δμ is 0.25–0.46. Two habits for our battery. Compare any two directions **at equal side effect, not equal norm** (a neutral-text mean-KL budget, interpolated in √K between bracketing strengths, is the cheapest such normaliser we have seen and it is label-free), because otherwise "the probe direction steers less" is indistinguishable from "the probe direction needed a bigger push". And report the pair (AUROC, effect-at-equal-K) for both the filter end and the mean difference plus the cosine between them, which is a column our probe tables have never carried and costs one extra closed-form solve. (arxiv-2611.19499, arxiv-2611.17481, arxiv-2611.06001)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 265): **The asymmetry is stable while its size is not, and the paper is honest about which is which: the plateau ordering holds in 6/6 main cases, 59/60 layer cells, 4/4 rotation cases and under matched texts, but whether an intermediate direction beats the mean difference swings from "+27–56%, replicates across splits" to "no, and the gain was mostly the texts being different" between two concepts in the same model set.** That pattern — a robust inequality sitting on top of a fragile magnitude — is the one to expect from our own direction work, and the reporting shape that respects it is the pre-registered plateau rather than the argmax: a best-point claim here would have read as a 27–56% win in one concept and a 9.6% shortfall in another, both selected on the same split. Three controls did the work of making the fragile part visible and all three are reusable — matched texts for probe and steering, a second held-out split for any λ* chosen by maximisation, and a changed operator (gated rotation) to check that a result is about the direction rather than the arithmetic of addition. (arxiv-2611.19499, arxiv-2611.10720, arxiv-2611.09196)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 265): **A direction can transfer functionally while being geometrically orthogonal to the target's own, and the folder has no sharper instance: the mapped mean difference into Gemma has cosine −0.17 and −0.02 with Gemma's own — no closer to it than a permuted-label null — and still reaches 0.72 and 0.70 of its steering effect.** So "the vector works in the other model" is not evidence that the two models represent the concept the same way, and the two transfer ratios the paper compares (an above-chance AUROC share of 81–91% against an effect share of 44–93%) are explicitly not the same quantity, which is why their comparison is a tendency and not a test. The design notes worth importing are the two transfer laws — a probe is a linear functional and moves by the transpose of the reverse map, a steering vector is a displacement and moves forward through the forward map, and confusing them is a silent bug — plus the orthogonal-Procrustes control under which both laws give the same vector, and the honest bookkeeping that with three models every pair shares a model with four others, so 11 of 12 pairs is a pattern in three models and not twelve confirmations. (arxiv-2611.19499, arxiv-2611.07913, arxiv-2611.16018)

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 264): **A score that sums three things can be decomposed by deleting one of them, and the arithmetic here is the whole argument: two recipes in the same family differ by 0.340 top-1, of which +0.048 is the better encoder and +0.291 is the predictor — so a selection procedure that ranked on the headline score was in fact ranking on the term it never measured.** The design point costs one forward pass and no training: make an identical copy of the model with the trained module replaced by the identity, evaluate both on the same trials, subtract. Three properties make it a measurement rather than a robustness check — the copy shares the encoder, preprocessing and criterion, so the difference cannot be attributed to anything but the module; the difference is *paired per trial*, so it is a signed quantity with a meaningful negative; and the negative is reported, not clipped, which is how the paper can say a predictor was above chance and worse than copying. For our battery the missing column is a **floor arm**: every probe score we publish could be accompanied by the same pipeline with the trained part replaced by a trivial rule built from the input's most recent state, and no accuracy credited to the learned part before it has beaten that floor. (arxiv-2611.15082, arxiv-2611.03439, arxiv-2611.06001)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 264): **Cluster correction should be justified by showing where dependence saturates, not asserted at the level that happens to be convenient, and this paper prints the whole ladder: half-widths go from ±0.0053 at trial level to ±0.0112 at video level and then only ±0.0119 at actor level, with the headline contribution moving 1.00×, so video is where the clustering lives and coarser resampling buys nothing.** Two further checks make the interval machinery auditable rather than ceremonial. The bootstrap's own Monte-Carlo error is measured against the interval it is estimating (endpoint jitter ±0.00029 across eight seeds, 9.1% of the narrowest half-width, bias ≤ 0.00007), which is the difference between a nominal B and a sufficient one. And the pairing is preserved by construction — the per-trial indicator is formed first, then videos are resampled once per replicate — so a model and its control are never resampled independently, which is the error that would silently narrow a paired difference's interval. Our own probe tables cluster by item when we remember to; the habit to import is the grain study plus the printed Monte-Carlo error, both of which are computed from stored per-trial scores and need no re-inference. (arxiv-2611.15082, arxiv-2611.16018, arxiv-2611.07913)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 264): **Deleting the trained part can be a validity check rather than an ablation: with every predictor switched off, the bare encoders order themselves video-pretrained 0.444 > image-pretrained 0.315 > simulation-from-scratch 0.208 with all four intervals disjoint, an ordering the benchmark was not tuned for — which is evidence the probe tracks real signal without any predictor to credit.** The companion read is the horizon sweep, where persistence falls 0.554 → 0.308 over one to four seconds while the strong predictor falls in parallel 0.824 → 0.590 and holds a constant margin, and the weak family's curves stay flat and cross below their control at the shortest horizon: a predictive module should buy an approximately constant advantage as the future drifts from the present, and a flat curve that never leaves its control band is the shape of a module that is not doing the anticipating. Two habits. Report a *trivial-rule floor* per stratum rather than in aggregate, because the floor itself varies with the difficulty axis (here it drops by half across the horizon while the model drops by a third). And where a positional or input-budget bound exists, place the out-of-envelope rows in their own table with an explicit warning, since here the strong model's contribution turns negative past the 8 s bound purely because its address space was exceeded — an artefact that would read as a capability collapse if it were pooled with the rest. (arxiv-2611.15082, arxiv-2611.10620, arxiv-2611.01981)

- Done 2026-11-16 (entry 262): `arxiv-2611.19216` — Operating-Point Failure of Frozen Guardrail Probes Under Backbone Updates (Yusuf Khalid Shire, Sang-Chul Kim — School of Computer Science, Kookmin University, Seoul; arXiv:2611.19216v1, 2026-11-14, cs.CR, 137-entry pre-registered registry + code at github.com/ShirePyDev/frozen-probe-operating-point). Full text via HTML (98,630 clean chars, §§I–VII + acknowledgement/author blocks); Tables I–V quoted as cells, figures via captions only. **Substance:** freeze a probe, its standardisation, its layer and a 1%-false-positive threshold on a pre-update checkpoint and apply all of them unchanged to the post-update model; largest rise 1.01% → 15.12% with AUROC down 0.0058, no headline AUROC move above 0.0058, and a benchmark's criteria call **none** of the 18 stale while the AUC rule flags 0.019 of damaged layer cells at specificity 1.000; maximum per-layer paired ratio 3.27–53.92 across 1a–1g; minimum CKA ≥ 0.855 in 1a–1h yet 0.99302 on the pair with a ratio band [2.46, 4.71]; at 5% five of eleven damaged cells fall back inside; estimated-rate check 0.918 sensitivity / 0.898 specificity vs KS 0.966/0.543 and ATC 0.479 sensitivity (AUROC 0.965 vs 0.952); two-moment model within ×1.5 in 0.905 of 63 registered Phase 2 cells (0.773 of the 22 that moved, translation-only 0.409); threshold re-set on stored benign prompts gives FPR/target 0.98–1.02 at `L*` with true-positive rate 0.350–0.722, traffic-based repairs give 4.74–24.36 of target on 1% prevalence and 0.12–0.31 under 5% harmful prevalence, 1% reference poisoning leaves the re-set flagging 0.006–0.017 of harmful prompts, realignment keeps AUROC in 27/27 cells per arm but leaves the rate outside ×1.5 in 9/9 units with the ridge map; A2 blinds one category in 3/5 seeds under the KL bound and is caught only by the canary (8/8 blinded cells, 12/30 in all); registry 69 HELD / 24 FAILED / 5 NOT SUPPORTED / 3 REFUTED / 6 withdrawn or inconclusive / 30 outcome-only.
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 263): **A threshold is a separate object from the ranking behind it, and the folder now has the cleanest possible demonstration: one update moves a deployed guardrail's realised false-positive rate from 1.01% to 15.12% while AUROC falls 0.0058, so every official staleness criterion reads the probe as healthy and a deployer running a real system is flagging one prompt in seven.** The arithmetic reason is worth internalising, because it generalises to every monitor we ship: a 1% target on 1000 benign prompts is a threshold near the tenth-highest score, so it sits in the far tail of the benign distribution where a small mean shift buys a huge rate change — the tail mass is not linear in the shift, which is exactly why the operating point moves while the ranking does not. Two habits follow for our own probe tables. Report the **rate at the frozen cut, before and after, on the same items, as a ratio with a hard class boundary** (they use 2 and 0.5), and report the target rate it was set at, because five of eleven damaged cells here fall back inside the boundary when the target moves from 1% to 5% — a finding at one operating point does not transfer to another. And treat "the probe still has AUROC 0.97" as a statement about separability, not about the guardrail, since the same paper shows a refit on the updated activations recovers a median change within ±0.01 of AUROC while the frozen threshold is off target: the information survives, the calibration does not. (arxiv-2611.19216, arxiv-2611.10620, arxiv-2611.19216)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 263): **The cheapest useful monitor-health check needs no labels and no new data, and it beats the standard distribution-shift test on the axis that matters: computing Gaussian tail mass at the frozen threshold from the mean and standard deviation of stored benign scores flags 0.918 of damaged layer cells and clears 0.898 of undamaged ones, where a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test between pre- and post-update scores reaches 0.966 sensitivity at only 0.543 specificity and average-thresholded-confidence has the better AUROC (0.965 vs 0.952) but 0.479 sensitivity at the operating point.** The design notes that make it work are small and portable: the moments come from the *calibration* negatives only, disjoint from the evaluation negatives behind the realised rate, so the check is out of sample rather than a restatement; the flag threshold is the same 2 and 0.5 used to define damage, so nothing is tuned to the outcome; and the check is scored against a *class* of cells rather than a single number, which is why it can be compared to a KS test at all. A whole-distribution divergence is dominated by regions of the score distribution that never touch the threshold, which is precisely the failure of KS here, and it is the same denominators lesson the folder has recorded for AUROC — measure at the place where the decision is made. For our battery this is a free column: store the benign calibration scores at deployment, recompute their first two moments after any change, and print the estimated-versus-realised rate ratio beside the probe's accuracy. (arxiv-2611.19216, arxiv-2611.10620, arxiv-2610.41445)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 263): **A repair fitted on data the attacker can write to is not a repair, and the two-sided form of the failure is what makes it worth recording: poisoning 1% of a 1000-item reference with the harmful prompts the probe scores highest costs the threshold re-set 10 points of true-positive rate and leaves it flagging 0.006–0.017 of harmful prompts, while the attacker who supplies the *update* moved one target category past both label-free checks in 3 of 5 seeds at a KL bound tied to the clean seed-to-seed variation (0.08644 nats per token), refuting the authors' own registered hypothesis that no single attacker evades both.** The control that caught the second attack is the part to steal: a canary of held-out labelled harmful prompts that no split uses, thresholded to match the label-free check's clean false-alarm count, flagged every blinded cell with no false alarm in 603 clean draws — a detector for the label-free detector, cheap because it needs labels the deployer already had at deployment. Two consequences for anything we monitor. Re-centring or re-standardising on live traffic is a bet on prevalence and on who controls the stream: the same repair that returns the rate to target on 1% prevalence overshoots to 4.74–24.36 of target on mostly benign traffic and collapses to 0.12–0.31 when harmful traffic rises to 5%. And a green light on a label-free statistic is a statement about benign scores only, so where the consequence is asymmetric our dashboards should carry one labelled canary and print its false-alarm count beside the check it guards. (arxiv-2611.19216, arxiv-2611.07913, arxiv-2611.03439)

- Done 2026-11-16 (entry 261): `arxiv-2611.19176` — A Bag of Concepts? Testing Role-Filler Binding in the Verbalizable Workspace (Reya Dawlah — UT Dallas; Elizabeth McMillin — MiraCosta College; Michael Shihong Zhang — Waterloo; Badrish Ananth — UC Irvine; Rishi Adi Ruia — Washington; Ane Zuñiga — MIT; Thomas Jiralerspong — Mila/Université de Montréal; arXiv:2611.19176v1, 2026-11-14, cs.CL, CC BY 4.0; workshop paper under the title "Interpretability as a Science"). Full text via HTML (57,616 chars, §§1–7 + Appendices A–F); Tables 1–5 quoted as cells, Figure 1 via caption only, all mathematics legible. **Substance:** asks whether the verbalizable workspace — the small vocabulary-indexed subspace read by the J-lens (Gurnee et al.) and the relation-indexed R-lens (Blank et al.) — carries **role-filler binding** rather than a bag of concepts, since safety-relevant propositions share their concept set and differ only in argument assignment. Three dense models (Qwen3.6-27B 64L, Gemma-3-12B base 48L, Gemma-3-27B-IT 62L), two lens families plus a matched J-lens from the same release, two role-direction estimators (difference of means, LRE readout gradient); 600 minimal-pair families / 2,400 sentences per model across three concept pairs × four constructions × role × position, with a disjoint direction-fitting corpus; three tests — ridge probing of the full residual, the workspace slice (top-16 J-lens atoms by non-negative matching pursuit), the orthogonal remainder and a matched-rank random subspace; a calibrated ±sign push along the fitted direction scored by a two-sign **binding score** (difference of differences of the agent−patient log-odds gap, averaged over the two surface positions) against non-participant, random and shuffled-label controls with a pre-registered 0.5-log-odds strength floor; and a top-10 workspace ablation scoring a binding-specific deficit against a fresh matched-rank random-subspace ablation with a difficulty-matching precondition. Verdicts are pre-registered into four classes (positive binding / indistinguishable from controls / clean negative / uninterpretable strength failure) with family-level bootstrap and exact sign-flip permutation plus Holm-Bonferroni. **Results:** within-pair role decoding 0.989/0.975/0.978 from the full residual, 0.984/0.949/0.974 from the discarded remainder, 0.587/0.573/0.574 from the workspace — below the matched-rank random subspace's 0.643/0.589/0.590 — robust to quadratic and random-Fourier probes, a seven-order ridge sweep (workspace 0.645 ceiling vs 0.678–0.724 random) and layer/seed changes; LRE directions stable at 0.967–0.999 cosine and the readout moves +0.94 / −0.99 log-odds while the binding score never clears its null band (Gemma-3-27B-IT pooled −0.0134 → −0.1809 across c = 64 → 256 with the control growing in step, ratios 0.83/1.01/0.84); ablation damages binding specifically on Gemma-3-27B-IT at the entity token only (+0.275, CI 0.262–0.288; 0.284/0.334/0.297 across three lens variants) with nothing on the other two models at either site; entity-token cross-pair transfer above chance for residual, remainder and random (0.510–0.713) but at chance for the workspace, while the sentence-final position inverts below chance for **every** source (0.281–0.320), which the authors diagnose as a probing artefact rather than a workspace property.
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 262): **A verbalizable subspace can be reproducibly readable and still carry less of the property than a random projection of the same rank: the workspace slice decodes role at 0.587/0.573/0.574 against a matched-rank random subspace's 0.643/0.589/0.590, while the full residual reaches 0.989/0.975/0.978 and the part the lens throws away reaches 0.984/0.949/0.974 — so the information is in the stream twice over and in the readable slice not at all.** The design point our battery should steal is the *rank-matched* control, because the natural null (shuffled labels, mean ablation, an untrained probe) cannot distinguish "this subspace is uninformative" from "any 16-dimensional projection is uninformative", and every verbalizable or concept-basis readout in this folder so far has been reported without it. Two habits follow: when we report a score for a projected or dictionary-based representation, run the same probe on the full state, on the projection's complement and on a seeded random basis of identical rank, and print the four together; and treat the complement as its own readout, since the remainder here is functionally as good as the whole and the workspace contributes essentially nothing. The corollary for any monitor we build on a readable slice is that its near-ceiling accuracy on a clean contrast is a statement about the slice's convenience, not about the model's substrate. (arxiv-2611.19176, arxiv-2611.10620, arxiv-2611.03439)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 262): **A direction can be perfectly stable, demonstrably causal on the model's own report, and still do nothing to the computation you care about: LRE role directions sit at 0.967–0.999 bootstrap cosine and move the next-token role answer by +0.94 and −0.99 log-odds, yet the binding score never leaves the control band on any of the three models, and on Gemma-3-27B-IT the pooled effect grows more than tenfold across the dose sweep (−0.0134 → −0.1809) with the non-participant control growing in step (ratio 0.83/1.01/0.84).** This is the folder's strongest instance of steering a *report* rather than a *state*, and it means our own readout-versus-manipulation checks need a third arm the folder has never used: push the direction and score not only whether the behaviour moves but whether it moves *more than an entity-matched control push of the same norm* — because a push on a concept that has no role to bind also shifts the model's log-odds, and only the difference is binding. The verdict taxonomy is worth copying wholesale: four pre-registered outcomes where a failed strength check is reported as **uninterpretable** rather than as a null, and a "clean negative" additionally requires a tight CI on the effect size so that absence of evidence is separated from evidence of absence. Both of those are cheap formatting decisions that stop a dashboard of p-values from being read as a result. (arxiv-2611.19176, arxiv-2611.17481, arxiv-2611.06001)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 262): **One model of three is the shape of the causal result, and the confound is named rather than hidden: ablating the top-10 workspace vectors costs binding specifically at +0.275 (CI 0.262–0.288) on the instruction-tuned 27B, replicates across three lens variants (0.284/0.334/0.297), and shows nothing on a base 12B or on Qwen3.6-27B even where the workspace edit perturbs the residual about five times harder than the random control — leaving instruction tuning and scale entangled and a base Gemma-3-27B ablation as the named missing arm.** Three design lessons, each of which we would otherwise have to learn the hard way. A single positive result is what makes the other nulls interpretable at all, because it fires the design's own sensitivity check; a study with three nulls and no positive arm cannot distinguish "no effect" from "no instrument". Every ablation claim needs its edit-magnitude ratio printed beside it, since a null deficit from a 5×-stronger edit means something different from a null at 0.79×. And a task-normalised deficit (the binding margin drop as a share of its own baseline, minus the same share for a recall control) is the right form when the two tasks live on different log-odds scales, provided the difficulty-matching precondition is enforced — here it fails on two of the six cells, and those cells are marked rather than quietly included. (arxiv-2611.19176, arxiv-2611.10720, arxiv-2611.09196)
